ART.1.1.1.t: Describe ways people have used art to worship God and serve others.
Explain how making and offering art can be an act of worship rather than mere decoration.
Compare how different faith traditions have used visual art in worship spaces.
Evaluate a work of art you have made or studied by how well it directs attention toward God and serves its audience.

ART.1.1.2.t: Explain what it means that humans are made in the image of God (imago Dei) and how this relates to human creativity.
Describe biblical examples of God-given artistic skill, such as Bezalel and the craftsmen of the tabernacle.
Analyze how God's creative work in Genesis serves as a pattern for human making.
Interpret how being an image-bearer shapes an artist's purpose and responsibility.
Defend a biblical view of human creativity in response to a purely materialist account of art.

ART.1.1.3.t: Describe how a work of art can express approval or criticism of the culture that produced it.
Identify the values or assumptions an artwork promotes about its society.
Analyze how an artist uses imagery to critique injustice or cultural idols.
Evaluate a work's cultural critique against a biblical standard of truth and justice.

ART.1.1.4.t: Describe what makes a subject or image appropriate or inappropriate to portray in art.
Explain how the ideas of truth, goodness, and beauty help us judge a work of art.
Analyze how an artwork can be skillfully made yet promote a harmful message.
Evaluate an artwork using virtue and truth as criteria, distinguishing craft from moral content.
Defend a discerning response to a challenging work, explaining what to appreciate and what to reject.

ART.1.1.5.t: Describe qualities that make something beautiful and explain your reasons.
Distinguish between the claim that beauty is objective and the claim that it is only personal taste.
Explain how a Christian view grounds beauty in the character and creation of God.
Analyze how order, proportion, and harmony contribute to beauty in a work of art.
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of objective and subjective views of beauty.

ART.1.1.6.t: Explain how an artist can view creative talent as a gift to be stewarded rather than owned.
Describe practices of discipline, craft, and integrity that mark a faithful artistic calling.
Analyze how vocation and calling shape the goals an artist pursues in their work.
Evaluate your own gifts and articulate how you might steward them as a maker.

ART.1.1.7.t: Describe examples of art that depict ugliness, suffering, or brokenness.
Explain why an artist might portray something ugly in order to tell the truth about the world.
Compare how realism and modernism responded to beauty, ugliness, and the fallen world.
Analyze how depicting the ugly can point toward redemption, hope, or the need for it.
Evaluate whether a difficult or disturbing work is truthful and worthwhile, giving reasons.

BIB.10.1.1.t: Identify the Ten Commandments as the rules God gave his people for how to live
Identify everyday actions such as lying and stealing as breaking God's commandments
Explain what it means to honor parents and others in authority according to the fifth commandment
Retell the parable of the Good Samaritan and explain whom Jesus calls our neighbor
Explain that God sees and knows everything we do, so right and wrong are measured by God and not by who is watching
Summarize the two greatest commandments and show how they sum up duties to God and duties to neighbor in the Ten Commandments
Explain why Christians tell the truth by connecting honesty to the truthful character of God
Apply the Golden Rule to school situations such as bullying, teasing, and leaving others out
Compare what the surrounding culture says is right with what the Bible teaches on a given moral question
Explain that each commandment both forbids a sin and requires the opposite duty, using the sixth commandment as an example
Explain how Scripture describes conscience and the moral law written on every human heart
Analyze Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount that God's law reaches the heart as well as outward actions
Explain the Reformed teaching that obedience to God's law is a response of gratitude for grace and not a way to earn salvation
Apply the doctrine of the image of God to the value of human life in issues such as abortion and euthanasia
Explain the biblical view of work as a calling from God and the Scripture's warnings against laziness
Explain the biblical teaching on marriage and sexual purity as grounded in creation and the seventh commandment
Explain what Scripture teaches about justice and mercy toward the poor and vulnerable
Explain the Reformed doctrine of Christian liberty and the care owed to a weaker brother in matters Scripture does not command
Compare consequence-based, duty-based, and virtue-based ethical theories with biblical ethics' attention to God's law, right motive, and God's glory
Construct a biblical framework for moral decision making that weighs direct commands, scriptural principles, wisdom, and conscience
Distinguish the moral, ceremonial, and civil laws of the Old Testament and explain how the Reformed tradition applies each today
Evaluate complex ethical dilemmas such as war and bioethics using scriptural principles and the Reformed confessional tradition
Defend the existence of objective morality grounded in God's character against the claims of moral relativism
Distinguish the three uses of the law and explain the Reformed teaching on the law as a guide for the believer's life

BIB.10.1.2.t: Identify that God is holy, meaning he is perfectly good and set apart from all sin
Identify sin as any failure to obey God's law and as the opposite of God's holiness
Recite and summarize God's command to his people to be holy because he is holy
Describe how the Bible teaches that the Holy Spirit works in believers to make them more like Jesus
Explain the biblical meaning of holy as set apart for God using examples such as the Sabbath, the tabernacle, and God's people
Explain the difference between justification as a once for all act of God and sanctification as an ongoing work of God
Describe Isaiah's response to the vision of God's holiness and explain what the passage shows about sin and cleansing
Describe the two parts of sanctification, dying to sin and living to righteousness, as taught in Romans 6
Apply the put off and put on pattern of Ephesians 4 and Colossians 3 to sample situations from school and family life
Explain the biblical meaning of godliness as reverent devotion to God trained and shown in everyday life
Explain repentance unto life as a continual turning from sin to God using David's prayer in Psalm 51
Analyze sanctification as a progressive and lifelong work that remains imperfect in this life yet continues to grow
Explain from Scripture how the holy conduct of believers serves as a witness to the world
Interpret Paul's description of the struggle with sin in Romans 7 in its context and compare the main Reformed readings of the passage
Explain the Puritan teaching on the mortification of sin, drawing on John Owen and the biblical texts behind it
Explain how good works relate to sanctification as fruits of true faith rather than the ground of salvation
Construct a sample weekly pattern of spiritual disciplines drawing on Word, sacrament, and fellowship and explain from Scripture how each serves growth in holiness
Evaluate legalism and antinomianism as distortions of the pursuit of holiness in light of Scripture and the confessional teaching on the law
Defend the Reformed teaching that holiness is a necessary mark of those who are saved using Hebrews 12:14 and related texts
Analyze how the Reformed tradition presents union with Christ in his death and resurrection as the source of godliness
Compare the Reformed view of sanctification with perfectionist and passive views of the Christian life using key biblical texts

BIB.10.1.3.t: Identify prayer as speaking to God our Father in heaven
Recite the Lord's Prayer and name it as the prayer Jesus taught his disciples
Identify Bible passages that teach God hears the prayers of his people
Describe times in the Gospels when Jesus prayed and what he prayed about
Give an example of each part of prayer: adoration, confession, thanksgiving, and supplication
Explain why Christians pray in the name of Jesus
Explain the meaning of the preface and each of the six petitions of the Lord's Prayer
Compare private prayer with family and corporate prayer using examples from Scripture
Explain why the Reformed tradition names prayer, with the Word and sacraments, as an ordinary means of grace
Compose a prayer of intercession for others, including those who oppose or mistreat them, following Jesus' command
Analyze the requests Paul makes in his prayers for the churches and what they show about his priorities
Analyze psalms of lament and confession as models for bringing sorrow and sin to God in prayer
Interpret the role of the Holy Spirit and of Christ in interceding for believers
Explain how the Reformed tradition teaches that God ordains prayer as a means through which he accomplishes his purposes
Explain the biblical practice of fasting and its relationship to prayer
Explain how Scripture accounts for prayers that God answers differently than requested
Analyze the conditions Scripture gives for acceptable prayer, such as asking in faith, according to God's will, and with confession of sin
Construct an account of the believer's access to God in prayer grounded in Christ's high priesthood and the priesthood of believers
Compare the Reformed teaching that prayer is directed to God alone through Christ alone with the practice of praying to saints or angels
Evaluate the difference between mystical contemplation and biblical meditation on God's Word
Evaluate deistic and fatalistic objections to petitionary prayer using the Reformed doctrine of providence
Design a plan for regular personal and family prayer structured by the petitions of the Lord's Prayer and the parts of prayer

BIB.10.1.4.t: Identify the fruit of the Spirit as good qualities that God grows in his people by the Holy Spirit
Name the nine qualities listed as the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23
Retell Jesus' teaching that a good tree bears good fruit and a bad tree bears bad fruit
Give examples of actions at home and school that show qualities such as love, kindness, and patience
Describe how Jesus displayed qualities of the fruit of the Spirit in specific Gospel accounts
Summarize Galatians 5:22-23 in their own words, including Paul's statement that against such things there is no law
Explain from Scripture that the fruit of the Spirit is produced by the Spirit at work in believers rather than by human effort alone, as the Reformed tradition confesses
Explain the meaning of each of the nine qualities using cross-references from elsewhere in Scripture
Compare the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit as Paul contrasts them in Galatians 5
Apply self-control or another quality of the fruit to realistic scenarios involving anger, speech, or appetite, citing supporting Scripture
Explain what Paul means by walking by the Spirit, keeping in step with the Spirit, and crucifying the flesh in Galatians 5
Analyze why Paul uses the singular word fruit rather than the plural for the nine qualities
Analyze how biblical teaching on God's covenant faithfulness shapes the meaning of faithfulness as a fruit of the Spirit
Relate the fruit of the Spirit to the character of Christ and to the Spirit's work of conforming believers to his image
Explain how Scripture connects patience and joy with enduring suffering and trials
Explain the Reformed teaching that spiritual fruit and good works are the evidence of true faith and not the ground of justification
Analyze the Greek terms behind key qualities such as agape, chara, and praotes through a word study using lexical tools and cross-references
Distinguish the fruit of the Spirit from the gifts of the Spirit in purpose, distribution, and expectation
Defend from Scripture the claim that Christlike character matters more than spiritual gifts
Evaluate case studies and biographical accounts for evidence of the fruit of the Spirit, distinguishing genuine fruit from mere outward morality
Evaluate moralistic and perfectionist approaches to character growth in light of Paul's teaching on the Spirit and the flesh and the Reformed doctrine of sanctification
Compose an essay explaining how the Spirit produces fruit in believers through union with Christ and abiding in him

BIB.10.2.1.t: Identify the family as a gift God gives and name the members of a family
Recite the fifth commandment and name ways children honor their father and mother
Retell how God created the first man and woman and brought them together as husband and wife
Identify from Psalm 127 that children are a gift and blessing from the Lord
Give examples of how children obey and honor their parents at home
Explain what Genesis 2:24 means by leaving parents, holding fast to a spouse, and becoming one flesh
Describe how family members in Bible stories showed loyal love and forgiveness to one another
Explain the callings Ephesians 5 gives to husbands to love sacrificially and to wives to submit, as the Reformed tradition reads the passage
Explain the duties Scripture gives parents to instruct, nurture, and correct their children without provoking them
Explain how Jesus pointed back to creation when he taught about marriage
Explain how honoring parents extends to adult children caring for aging parents
Compare the household and the church as communities in which God gives order, care, and instruction
Explain the purposes of marriage named in the Westminster Confession and the Scriptures that support each
Interpret Deuteronomy 6 on parents teaching God's words to their children in the ordinary rhythms of daily life
Analyze how Ephesians 5 presents marriage as a picture of Christ and the church
Explain the Reformed teaching that covenant promises extend to the children of believers and how this shapes infant baptism and parental vows
Analyze the families of Isaac, Jacob, and David to show how favoritism and sin damaged the household
Explain the biblical purpose of parental discipline as loving correction aimed at wisdom and maturity
Explain how the seventh commandment guards marriage by requiring sexual faithfulness in thought and deed
Explain the biblical teaching that believers are to marry only in the Lord
Explain how Scripture honors singleness as a calling for serving the Lord
Construct a biblical definition of marriage as a covenant between one man and one woman
Explain what Scripture teaches about divorce and summarize the position of the Westminster Confession
Evaluate cultural redefinitions of marriage and family against Scripture and the church's confession
Defend the Reformed tradition's teaching that man and woman are equal as image bearers and distinct in their callings in marriage
Design a plan for family worship that includes Scripture reading, prayer, and singing, grounded in Scripture and Reformed practice

BIB.10.2.2.t: Identify that God made people to work and that work is a good gift from him
Name the things God made during the days of creation and recall that he rested from his work
Identify ways Adam was asked to care for the garden and name the animals
Recall that God made people in his image and gave them the job of ruling over and caring for the earth and its creatures
Describe how people in different jobs in a community serve and help their neighbors
Summarize the command in Genesis 1 to be fruitful, fill the earth, subdue it, and have dominion
Explain from Proverbs why diligence in work is wise and laziness is foolish and sinful
Explain the meaning of vocation as God's calling to serve him and others in every area of life
Describe how the curse in Genesis 3 brought toil and frustration into work without making work itself evil
Explain how the pattern of six days of work and one day of rest is grounded in God's own work in creation
Compare working to please people or only to earn pay with working heartily as for the Lord
Explain the biblical reasons Christians are called to work, including providing for themselves, serving neighbors, and sharing with those in need
Distinguish faithful dominion that tends and keeps creation from domination that exploits it
Analyze how human work has value as a reflection of the image of a working God apart from what it earns
Interpret 1 Corinthians 10:31 in its context and apply it to ordinary tasks of school, home, and work
Explain how God equipped Bezalel and Oholiab for skilled work and apply this example to how gifts relate to a calling
Explain how redemption in Christ renews the purpose of work so that labor done in the Lord is not in vain
Explain how Jeremiah's letter instructed exiled Israel to seek the welfare of the city through ordinary work and apply its principle to Christians today
Analyze Tolkien's concept of sub-creation as an account of human creativity flowing from bearing God's image
Construct a theology of work that traces its place in creation, fall, redemption, and consummation
Evaluate the sacred and secular divide in light of the Reformation teaching that every lawful calling can serve God
Defend the dignity of all honest labor using the examples of Jesus the carpenter and Paul the tentmaker
Compare the Reformed understanding of the cultural mandate with other historic Christian views of the relationship between Christ and culture
Evaluate how the cultural mandate and the Great Commission relate as Christians engage culture through their vocations
Create a reasoned account of how a chosen field of work can carry out the dominion mandate and serve neighbors

BIB.10.2.3.t: Identify that God made and owns everything, including the things people have
Demonstrate sharing materials and snacks with classmates and name a Bible verse that calls giving good
Recall that God gives his people their daily bread and provides what they need
Explain that money is a tool people use to get what they need and to help others
Identify stealing as breaking the eighth commandment and name ways to respect the belongings of others
Retell the story of the widow's offering and explain why Jesus praised her small gift
Describe how believers in Scripture brought tithes and offerings to support worship and ministry
Explain what Paul means when he says the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil
Explain stewardship as managing money and possessions that belong to God and giving account to him for their use
Explain what the parable of the rich fool teaches about trusting in possessions
Apply proverbs about honoring God, saving, and planning ahead to divide a sample allowance among giving, saving, and spending
Describe how the gleaning laws of Israel provided for the poor, the widow, and the stranger
Compare greed with contentment using the tenth commandment and Paul's example
Explain what Scripture teaches about borrowing, lending, and the burden of debt
Distinguish honest gain from dishonest gain using biblical laws and proverbs about just weights and fair dealing
Explain the principles of willing, proportional, and cheerful giving in Paul's collection for the Jerusalem saints
Analyze the sharing of the early church in Acts and distinguish voluntary generosity from compelled redistribution
Interpret Jesus' teaching about treasure in heaven and his warning that no one can serve both God and money
Explain how the Reformed tradition connects generosity with trust in God's fatherly providence over riches and poverty
Analyze the accounts of the rich young ruler and Zacchaeus to compare how each responded to Jesus regarding wealth
Explain how the eighth commandment protects private property and what duties toward the wealth of others the catechisms say it requires
Analyze the sabbath year and Jubilee laws for what they reveal about God's ownership of the land and his concern for the poor
Analyze the prophetic and apostolic condemnations of economic oppression, including withheld wages and exploitation of the poor
Construct a personal budget that applies biblical principles of giving, saving, avoiding unwise debt, and providing for one's household
Evaluate socialism and capitalism using biblical teaching on property, the poor, and human sinfulness
Defend from Scripture the obligation to care for the poor and distinguish the roles of the individual, the family, and the church's deacons
Evaluate the claims of the prosperity gospel against Scripture's teaching on godliness, contentment, and suffering
Create a written biblical theology of wealth that traces possessions through creation, fall, redemption, and consummation and applies the charge to the rich in 1 Timothy

BIB.10.2.4.t: Identify time, abilities, and our bodies as good gifts from God who made us
Recall from Psalm 139 that God formed each person's body and made it wonderfully
Describe everyday ways to care for the body God made, such as sleeping, eating well, washing, and playing actively
State the fourth commandment and describe the pattern of six days of work and one day of rest that God set at creation
Retell the parable of the talents and explain that God expects us to use what He gives us faithfully
Explain why the Reformed tradition keeps the first day of the week as the Lord's Day and describe activities that keep it holy
Explain what Paul means by making the best use of the time by reading Ephesians 5:15-16 in its context
Describe the difference between diligence and laziness using the wisdom of Proverbs
Explain from 1 Corinthians 6:19-20 why the Reformed tradition teaches that a believer's body belongs to God and is a temple of the Holy Spirit
Identify the spiritual gifts listed in the New Testament and explain that they are given to serve others in the church
Distinguish busyness from fruitfulness using the accounts of Martha and Mary and the vine and the branches
Explain how the sixth commandment requires lawful care of one's own life and forbids harming one's own body
Apply the principle of doing all to the glory of God to choices about eating, drinking, sleep, work, and recreation
Explain biblical teaching against gluttony and drunkenness as misuse of the body and identify self-control as fruit of the Spirit
Analyze Psalm 90 to explain how the brevity of life calls for wise use of time
Analyze Jesus' Sabbath controversies to explain the tradition's teaching that works of necessity and mercy are fitting on the Lord's Day
Interpret Romans 6 and Romans 12 to explain how the body is to be presented as an instrument of righteousness and an act of worship
Explain how Sabbath rest expresses dependence on God's provision and points to the rest fulfilled in Christ
Explain how Paul grounds sexual purity in the truth that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit
Identify personal abilities and propose specific ways to use them in service to the church and neighbor
Compare the biblical teaching that gifts are given for the common good with attitudes that treat gifts as marks of status or reasons for envy
Evaluate habits of technology and entertainment use as matters of time stewardship using biblical principles
Construct a weekly schedule that balances work, worship, rest, service, and care for the body and justify its choices from Scripture
Explain the historic Reformed position on the cessation of revelatory gifts and the continuing call to use ordinary gifts
Evaluate the idolatry of health and appearance against neglect of the body using Paul's teaching on bodily training and false asceticism
Defend the goodness of the physical body against Gnostic views using the doctrines of creation, incarnation, and resurrection
Analyze how the hope of bodily resurrection shapes the present stewardship of the body and of one's labor
Evaluate approaches to self-discipline in light of the Reformed teaching that holy living flows from grace rather than earning God's favor

BIB.10.3.1.t: Identify the Bible as the book where God tells his people how he wants to be worshiped
Retell the account of Nadab and Abihu and state what God said about the unauthorized fire they offered
Retell the account of the golden calf and explain why calling it a feast to the LORD did not make it acceptable worship
Explain how the second commandment teaches that God is to be worshiped only in the ways he has appointed in his Word
Summarize the regulative principle of worship as the Reformed teaching that public worship includes only what God commands in Scripture
Explain the normative principle of worship as the teaching that churches may include in worship whatever Scripture does not forbid
Compare the regulative and normative principles by showing how each one decides whether a new practice may be added to a worship service
Explain how Jesus rebuked worship shaped by human traditions in place of the commandments of God
Analyze Old Testament accounts of worship devised by human initiative to identify what made each one displeasing to God
Interpret Jesus' teaching on worship in spirit and truth within the context of his conversation with the Samaritan woman
Distinguish the elements of worship that Scripture commands from the circumstances of worship that the church orders by Christian prudence
Explain what Paul means by self-made religion and why the Reformed tradition applies it to human additions in worship
Explain how the Reformed confessions connect the regulative principle with the liberty of conscience from commandments of men in worship
Trace how Reformed, Lutheran, and Anglican churches of the Reformation era came to hold different principles of worship
Evaluate arguments within Reformed churches over applying the regulative principle to questions such as exclusive psalmody, musical instruments, and holy days
Evaluate a contemporary worship practice by applying both the regulative and normative principles and stating the conclusion each would reach
Construct an order of service that justifies each element from Scripture and identifies which features are circumstances rather than elements
Compose a written argument that states the regulative principle and responds to the strongest objections raised by proponents of the normative principle

BIB.10.3.2.t: Identify the main things God's people do when they gather for worship, such as hearing the Bible, praying, and singing
Name the sermon as the part of worship when the pastor explains God's Word to the congregation
Recall that Christians gather together on the Lord's Day to worship God as one church family
Recite the Aaronic blessing and identify it as words from Scripture used to bless God's people in worship
Describe what the congregation does during the public reading of Scripture in worship
Identify the kinds of prayer offered in corporate worship, including praise, confession, thanksgiving, and intercession
Explain the pattern of worship in which God speaks to His people through His Word and they respond with prayer and praise
Explain the purpose of the Call to Worship as God's summons that opens the gathered service
Explain how the Lord's Prayer serves as a pattern for the prayers of the congregation
Describe how baptism and the Lord's Supper take their place in corporate worship as visible signs of the promises proclaimed in the Word
Explain the purpose of congregational singing as praising God and teaching and admonishing one another
Explain the Benediction as God's blessing pronounced on His people at the close of worship
Explain how the offering functions as an act of worship in which God's people give thanks and support the ministry and the poor
Describe how the catechism directs a congregation to hear the preached Word with preparation, attention, and testing by Scripture
Analyze why the reading and preaching of the Word stand at the center of Reformed corporate worship
Analyze the function of the Confession of Sin and the Assurance of Pardon within the order of worship
Compare the elements of worship described in the early church with the elements of a present-day order of service
Explain the Westminster teaching that Word, sacraments, and prayer are the ordinary means of grace made effective by the Holy Spirit
Explain why the Westminster Confession directs that public prayer be made in the name of Christ, by the help of the Spirit, and in a known tongue
Analyze the Reformed teaching that the sacrament is joined to and depends on the preached Word of promise
Construct a scriptural explanation of why God gathers His people as an assembly to worship Him together
Compare Reformation changes to corporate worship, such as preaching and singing in the common language, with late medieval practice
Evaluate congregational songs by whether their words teach sound doctrine and serve the Word
Defend the necessity of preaching in corporate worship from Scripture and the Westminster standards
Analyze the order of a Reformed service as a pattern of covenant renewal moving from call and confession through Word and sacrament to blessing
Design an order of corporate worship and justify the purpose and placement of each element from Scripture

BIB.10.3.3.t: Identify water as the sign used in baptism and bread and the cup as the signs used in the Lord's Supper
Retell the account of Jesus sharing bread and the cup with his disciples on the night he was betrayed
Recall that Jesus commanded his church to baptize and to eat the Lord's Supper in remembrance of him
Retell New Testament accounts of people being baptized in the early church
Describe the words, actions, and signs used when a church administers baptism and the Lord's Supper, including baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
Explain that baptism signifies washing from sin and marks a person as belonging to God and his people
Explain that the Lord's Supper remembers and proclaims Christ's death until he comes again
State the Westminster Shorter Catechism definition of a sacrament and explain each of its parts in their own words
Explain why the Reformed tradition recognizes only two sacraments instituted by Christ in the New Testament
Distinguish between a sign and the thing it signifies using the water of baptism and the bread and cup of the Supper as examples
Explain how Scripture connects baptism to union with Christ in his death and resurrection
Describe whom the Reformed tradition teaches should come to the Lord's Supper and explain the biblical call to self-examination before coming
Explain the Reformed teaching that sacraments become effective means of grace through the blessing of Christ and the work of the Spirit rather than through power in the elements or the minister
Explain how the Lord's Supper expresses believers' communion with Christ and their unity with one another as one body
Compare the terms sacrament and ordinance and analyze what each emphasizes about baptism and the Lord's Supper
Analyze how Scripture connects circumcision as an Old Testament covenant sign to baptism
Interpret Jesus' words "This is my body" in their context by comparing them with other figurative statements in Scripture
Explain how the Passover meal anticipates and shapes the meaning of the Lord's Supper
Explain why the Reformed tradition administers baptism once while the Lord's Supper is repeated and how it relates baptism's efficacy to the time of administration
Explain what the Westminster Larger Catechism means by improving one's baptism and describe practices it recommends
Examine the biblical evidence used in debates over the mode of baptism and state the Westminster Confession's position on sprinkling, pouring, and immersion
Construct a biblical argument for infant baptism as the Reformed tradition holds it and summarize the credobaptist case accurately and fairly
Analyze Paul's warning against eating and drinking in an unworthy manner within the context of Corinthian divisions and explain its bearing on the church's practice of guarding the Table
Evaluate transubstantiation, the Lutheran view, the memorial view, and the Reformed view of Christ's spiritual presence in the Lord's Supper against Scripture
Evaluate the Reformed critique of the Mass as a sacrifice in light of the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ
Create a teaching presentation that explains how baptism and the Lord's Supper function as visible words that sign and seal the gospel promise

BIB.10.3.4.t: Identify ways a person can worship God alone and ways God's people worship Him together at church
Name the Lord's Day as the day the church gathers to worship God together
Recall Bible examples of worshipping God alone and with others, such as Daniel praying at his window and Jesus going to the synagogue on the Sabbath
Summarize Jesus' teaching on praying in secret and explain why He warns against praying to be seen by others
Describe the practice of family worship and explain its basis in God's command to teach His words at home
Explain the command not to neglect meeting together and the reasons Hebrews gives for gathering
Compare private devotion and public worship by identifying what each provides that the other does not
Carry out a simple pattern of private devotion in class that includes reading a passage, meditating on it, and praying in response
Analyze how the early church combined gathered worship with daily fellowship and prayer in homes
Interpret Paul's picture of the church as a body to explain why the tradition teaches that no believer is meant to grow in isolation
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that the preaching of the Word in the assembly is an especially effective means of grace alongside private reading of Scripture
Explain the Westminster teaching that God is to be worshipped in secret, in families daily, and more solemnly in public assemblies that are not to be neglected
Explain the Reformed teaching on the Lord's Day as a day set apart for public and private exercises of worship
Analyze the dangers of outward public worship without private devotion and of private spirituality that withdraws from the assembly
Construct a plan of daily and weekly rhythms that includes private, family, and public worship
Evaluate virtual church practices against biblical teaching on the physical gathering of believers
Compose an argument showing how private devotion and public assembly together serve both personal growth and the edification of the body

BIB.11.10.1.t: Identify God as the one true God who made all things
Recall that the things God made show that He is real and great
Name God as all-powerful and give an example of His power from a Bible story
Name God as all-knowing and give an example of something God knows that people cannot
Recall that God is present everywhere at the same time
Describe God as good, loving, and faithful using Bible verses that say so
Explain that God is spirit and does not have a body like ours
Explain that God is eternal, having no beginning and no end
Recite the Westminster Shorter Catechism definition of God and explain each attribute it names in their own words
Compare God's holiness with human sinfulness using Isaiah's vision of God
Explain how creation reveals God's existence and power and why Scripture says this leaves people without excuse
Classify God's attributes as incommunicable (belonging to God alone) or communicable (reflected in people made in His image) and justify each choice
Explain how God's justice and mercy are both fully true of Him using God's self-description to Moses
Describe how God's wisdom is displayed in creation and in redemption
Analyze the aseity of God by explaining what it means that God is self-existent and needs nothing from His creatures
Analyze what Scripture means by God's omnipotence, including why God cannot lie or deny Himself
Explain the doctrine of divine simplicity and connect it to the unity of God
Interpret the immutability of God, including passages that describe God as relenting
Distinguish the biblical teaching of God's infinity and omnipresence from pantheism
Explain the Reformed doctrine of divine impassibility and interpret biblical passages that describe God with human emotions
Explain the incomprehensibility of God and how Scripture's language about God is true though not exhaustive
Evaluate the cosmological, teleological, and moral arguments for God's existence in light of Scripture's teaching on general revelation and human suppression of the truth
Defend the Reformed position that God can be known truly though not fully
Evaluate Open Theism against classical theism using biblical teaching on God's knowledge and immutability
Synthesize the transcendence and immanence of God in a written account that draws on key biblical texts
Construct an integrated account of the divine perfections that shows how God's attributes cohere in His one simple being

BIB.11.10.2.t: Identify God as the King who rules over all things
Retell how Jesus says God feeds the birds and clothes the flowers to describe God's care for his creation
Recall from Scripture that nothing happens by chance apart from God, not even the fall of a sparrow
Define providence as God's most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing of all his creatures and all their actions
Retell the story of Joseph and explain how God used his brothers' evil actions for good
Explain from Scripture that God rules over both good times and hard times
Explain how Nebuchadnezzar's confession in Daniel shows God's rule over kings and nations
Compare the idea of luck or chance with the biblical teaching of providence
Explain how the Reformed confessions describe the comfort that the doctrine of providence offers believers in suffering
Define God's decree as his eternal purpose according to the counsel of his will by which he has foreordained whatever comes to pass
Explain how God carries out his decrees in the works of creation and providence
Distinguish God's secret decretive will from his revealed moral will using passages that teach each
Explain the Reformed teaching that God's decree establishes rather than removes the liberty of creatures and the working of second causes, and that God is not the author of sin
Analyze how the apostles' preaching about the cross holds together God's definite plan and the real guilt of those who crucified Jesus
Explain the doctrines of election and predestination as taught in Paul's letters and the Reformed confessions
Explain the Reformed teaching that election is unconditional and not based on foreseen faith or works
Explain how the Reformed confessions state the doctrine of reprobation and why they urge that it be handled with special prudence and care
Interpret Romans 9 within Paul's argument about God's faithfulness to Israel, including his use of Malachi on Jacob and Esau
Evaluate the Arminian and Reformed views of election by testing each against key biblical passages
Construct a structured summary of the doctrine of the decrees that traces God's eternal purpose through its execution in creation, providence, and redemption
Evaluate major responses to the problem of evil and defend the goodness of God as the Reformed tradition confesses it
Create a written argument showing how Scripture presents God's sovereignty as a basis for evangelism and prayer rather than a reason to neglect them

BIB.11.10.3.t: Identify the one true God as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit
State the church's confession that there is one God in three persons
Identify the names of the three persons in the baptism command and in the apostolic benediction
Retell the account of Jesus' baptism and identify what the Father, the Son, and the Spirit each do in it
Explain the Shield of the Trinity diagram to show that each person is God and that the persons are distinct from one another
Describe the biblical pattern of praying to the Father in the name of the Son by the help of the Spirit and use it to compose a short class prayer
Identify Bible passages that show the Son and the Holy Spirit are fully God
Explain from Scripture why the three persons are not three gods
Analyze common analogies for the Trinity such as water, an egg, or a shamrock and explain how each one misrepresents the doctrine
Explain how the eternal love among the Father, the Son, and the Spirit shows that God's love did not begin with or depend on creation
Distinguish the personal properties of the Father who begets, the Son who is begotten, and the Spirit who proceeds
Analyze how the persons are equal in power and glory while the Son humbly submits to the Father in his saving mission
Explain the historical setting of the Council of Nicaea and the meaning of the claim that the Son is of one substance with the Father
Trace the distinct work of the Father, the Son, and the Spirit in redemption through Ephesians 1
Interpret the Athanasian Creed's rule that the church neither confuses the persons nor divides the one divine substance
Compare modalism, Arianism, and tritheism with the orthodox doctrine and identify the Scripture each error contradicts
Analyze how Trinitarian doctrine shapes elements of Reformed worship such as baptism, the benediction, and the doxology
Construct an argument from Old Testament passages that anticipate plurality within the one God while explaining how progressive revelation shapes their reading
Evaluate the filioque controversy between Eastern and Western churches using the biblical texts on the sending of the Spirit
Evaluate Unitarian, Jehovah's Witness, and Latter-day Saint teachings about God against Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Explain the doctrine of inseparable operations that the three persons act together in every outward work while each acts in his own proper manner
Evaluate claims that the Trinity is a model for human relationships by weighing the texts offered against the tradition's teaching on divine simplicity and the Creator and creature distinction

BIB.11.1.1.t: Identify angels as spirits that God created
Explain that the word angel means messenger and name Gabriel as an angel God sent with a message
Recall from Scripture that angels are usually invisible to people and are mighty in strength
Describe the scenes in Isaiah and Revelation where angels worship God around His throne
Summarize what angels are as created, spiritual, and personal beings with mind and will
Explain that angels are a distinct kind of creature from humans and that people do not become angels when they die
Compare the power and knowledge of angels with that of humans and with the unlimited power and knowledge of God
Identify Michael and Gabriel as the only angels named in the canonical Scriptures and describe what the texts say about each
Categorize the kinds of angels Scripture names, including cherubim, seraphim, and the archangel
Explain how Paul's terms thrones, dominions, rulers, and authorities point to ordered ranks of spiritual beings created by and subject to Christ
Analyze the role of the cherubim as guardians of God's holy presence in Eden, the tabernacle, and Ezekiel's vision
Interpret Old Testament scenes of the divine council in which God presides over the assembly of spiritual beings
Connect the vast number of angels described in Scripture to the greatness and majesty of God
Explain the Reformed teaching that the holy angels are elect and confirmed in holiness
Explain from Hebrews 1 why the Son is superior to the angels in nature and rank
Explain from Scripture why angels, as fellow creatures, must not be worshiped
Analyze the angel of the LORD passages and evaluate the view held by many Reformed interpreters that some are appearances of the pre-incarnate Son
Evaluate popular cultural and sentimental ideas about angels against the teaching of Scripture
Defend the reality of an unseen created spiritual realm against naturalistic objections
Compare the restraint of Reformed angelology with speculative medieval hierarchies such as the nine choirs of angels
Construct a summary of the biblical doctrine of the nature, ranks, and moral state of the holy angels drawn from the whole of Scripture

BIB.11.1.2.t: Identify holy angels as servants God sends to help His people
Retell how the angels announced the birth of Jesus to the shepherds
Retell how the angel Gabriel brought Mary the news that she would bear Jesus
Recall that holy angels obey God's commands and praise His name
Explain from Jesus' words that angels rejoice in heaven when a sinner repents
Describe biblical accounts in which God sent angels to protect or rescue His people
Describe how angels worship God in the visions of Isaiah and Revelation
Explain how angels carried God's messages to people in Scripture using examples from both Testaments
Explain how the Lord's Prayer petition for God's will to be done on earth as in heaven points to the angels' willing obedience as a pattern for believers
Compare the worship angels offer God with the worship of the gathered church
Explain what Psalm 91 and Matthew 18 teach about God commanding angels to guard His people and how Jesus refused Satan's misuse of Psalm 91
Describe the work Scripture says angels will do at Christ's return
Trace the ministry of angels across redemptive history from the garden to the giving of the law to the early church
Interpret the angels' service to Christ at His birth, temptation, agony in Gethsemane, resurrection, and ascension
Explain from Scripture that God also uses angels as agents of His justice in judgment
Explain why the Reformed tradition forbids worshiping or praying to angels
Explain how the Westminster Larger Catechism presents angels as instruments God employs at His pleasure in the administration of His power, mercy, and justice
Analyze the argument of Hebrews 1 that the Son is superior to the angels, who are ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation
Evaluate popular beliefs about guardian angels, including praying to them and the idea that people become angels, in light of Scripture
Evaluate claims of new revelation received from angels using Paul's warning in Galatians and the sufficiency of Scripture
Construct a biblically grounded summary of the ministry of holy angels that keeps them subordinate to Christ and in service to His church

BIB.11.1.3.t: Identify from the story in Genesis 3 that the serpent tempted Adam and Eve to disobey God
Recall that God made all the angels good and that some of them chose to turn against Him
Name Satan as the leader of the fallen angels and the enemy of God and His people
Recall Jesus' teaching that Satan is a liar and the father of lies
Retell how the serpent twisted God's words in the garden by comparing God's command with the serpent's question
Describe how the angels who sinned left their proper place and are kept for God's judgment
Explain the Reformed teaching that the devil was created good and fell through pride
Explain from the opening chapters of Job that Satan can act only within the limits God sets
Compare Satan's limited power and knowledge as a creature with God's unlimited power and knowledge
Identify the names and titles Scripture gives to Satan and explain what each reveals about his character
Explain how Satan's temptation led humanity into sin while Adam and Eve remained responsible for their own disobedience
Analyze Satan's works as accuser, tempter, and deceiver in key passages of Scripture
Interpret Genesis 3:15 as God's first promise of a Redeemer who would crush the serpent
Explain the Reformed teaching that God's providence extends to the fall of the angels without making God the author of sin
Explain why Scripture offers no redemption to fallen angels in contrast to its offer of redemption to fallen humanity
Evaluate readings of Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 as descriptions of Satan's fall in light of their original setting as oracles against the kings of Babylon and Tyre
Construct a biblical account of the origin, fall, and final end of Satan from carefully chosen texts
Evaluate popular depictions of the devil as a cartoon villain, the ruler of hell, or God's equal opposite against the teaching of Scripture
Defend the reality of a personal and malevolent devil against claims that he is only a symbol of evil
Synthesize the biblical teaching that Satan's rebellion is real and serious yet wholly under God's rule and destined for defeat

BIB.11.1.4.t: Identify demons as angels who sinned against God and now work against Him and His people
Retell a Gospel account in which Jesus commands an evil spirit to leave a person
Recite the Lord's Prayer request to be delivered from evil and explain that it asks God for protection from the evil one
Recall from the Gospels that demons must obey Jesus because He is stronger than every evil spirit
Explain from Ephesians that the Christian's struggle is against spiritual forces of evil and not against other people
Describe each piece of the armor of God and the gospel truth it represents
Explain how Scripture joins resisting the devil to submitting to God and standing firm in faith
Demonstrate answering a temptation with a fitting passage of Scripture following Jesus' example in the wilderness
Compare biblical teaching on demons with popular superstitions, charms, and media portrayals of evil spirits
Explain why Scripture forbids occult practices such as divination, sorcery, and consulting the dead
Analyze the devil's tactics of temptation, deception, and accusation using the passages that describe each
Explain how the Word of God and prayer serve as the means by which believers stand against spiritual attack
Interpret Jesus' casting out of demons as a sign that the kingdom of God has arrived and the strong man is bound
Explain the limits Scripture places on demonic power, including God's sovereign permission and the believer's protection in Christ
Distinguish the devil, the world, and the sinful flesh as the sources of temptation that Scripture and the catechism name
Analyze how Scripture links false teaching to deceiving spirits and how believers are commanded to test the spirits
Interpret the encounters with evil spirits in Acts in their historical context, including the failed exorcism by the sons of Sceva
Evaluate both the denial of the demonic and an unhealthy fascination with it in light of Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Evaluate contemporary deliverance and spiritual warfare practices, such as naming territorial spirits or rebuking the devil by formula, against biblical teaching
Construct a sober biblical theology of spiritual warfare that integrates the reality of demons, their limits under God's sovereignty, and the ordinary means of grace

BIB.11.1.5.t: Identify from Bible stories and verses that Jesus is stronger than Satan
Name the cross and the empty tomb as the places where Jesus defeated Satan, sin, and death
Retell God's promise in Genesis 3:15 that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent's head
Recite Romans 8:38-39 and list the things Paul says cannot separate believers from God's love in Christ
Describe how Jesus overcame Satan's temptations in the wilderness by answering with the Word of God
Explain what 1 John 3:8 means by Jesus destroying the works of the devil using examples from His earthly ministry
Explain from Hebrews 2:14-15 why the Son took on flesh and how His death freed His people from slavery to the fear of death
Explain from Scripture that believers receive victory as a gift won by Christ rather than achieve it by their own strength
Trace the promise of the serpent crusher from Genesis 3:15 through its fulfillment in Christ and the promise of Romans 16:20
Explain how the resurrection of Christ defeats death and removes its sting according to 1 Corinthians 15
Explain from Luke 10:17-20 why Jesus directed His disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven rather than in power over spirits
Explain how Christ as King restrains and conquers all His and His people's enemies using Psalm 110 and its New Testament use
Analyze the already and not yet of Satan's defeat by comparing his overthrow at the cross with his final destruction
Interpret Colossians 2:13-15 in context to show how cancelling the record of debt at the cross disarmed the powers
Explain from Romans 8 and Revelation 12 why Satan's accusations cannot bring condemnation on those justified in Christ
Construct a summary of Christ's victory over Satan, sin, and death across His humiliation and exaltation with supporting texts
Compare the theme of Christ's conquest of the powers with penal substitution and explain how the Reformed tradition holds them together
Evaluate fear-driven and triumphalist views of the spiritual realm against the teaching of Scripture
Defend from Scripture and the confessions the finality of Christ's victory and the certainty of Satan's final judgment
Synthesize the biblical storyline into a theological essay presenting the gospel as Christ's conquest that secures His people forever

BIB.11.2.1.t: Identify people as a special creation that God made on purpose
Retell how God formed Adam from the dust, breathed life into him, and then made Eve
Recall that the Bible says God made people in his own image
Explain in simple words that being made in God's image means people were made to reflect what God is like
Describe how the account of the sixth day sets the creation of humans apart from the creation of the animals, including God's words Let us make man
Explain the Reformed teaching that God created humans in his image with knowledge, righteousness, and holiness
Compare humans and animals using Genesis and Psalm 8 to identify what Scripture says sets humans apart as image bearers
Explain from the Heidelberg Catechism why God made humans in his image so that they might truly know him and live with him
Interpret the words image and likeness in Genesis 1:26 and explain why Reformed interpreters generally read them as one idea
Analyze the substantive, relational, and functional views of the image of God by testing each against Genesis 1:26-28
Explain how the Fall defaced the image of God and use later passages to show that fallen humans are still called image bearers
Explain how the New Testament presents Jesus Christ as the perfect image of the invisible God
Explain how Scripture describes believers being renewed after the image of God through union with Christ
Distinguish the image of God in the broader sense from the image in the narrower sense and explain what Reformed theology says was lost and retained at the Fall
Trace the image of God across the storyline of Scripture from creation through fall and redemption to final glorification
Compare the Reformed view of the image of God with the Roman Catholic distinction between natural image and superadded gift and explain how each shapes its account of the Fall
Evaluate materialist and reductionist accounts of human nature against the biblical teaching that humans are created in the image of God
Construct a written theological account of the image of God as created, marred, renewed, and glorified, supported by Scripture and the Reformed confessions

BIB.11.2.2.t: Identify that God made each person with a body and a soul
Retell how God formed Adam's body from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life
Explain that the human body God made is good and not something bad or shameful
Describe from a Gospel account how Jesus cared for both a person's body and soul
Describe what Scripture teaches happens to the body and to the soul when a person dies
Summarize the Reformed teaching that a human being is one person made of a material body and an immaterial soul
Explain from the Gospels that Jesus took to himself a true human body and a reasonable soul
Compare the intermediate state, in which the believer's soul is with Christ, with the final resurrection of the body
Explain the Heidelberg Catechism's teaching that a believer belongs to Christ in body and soul, in life and in death
Apply Paul's call to glorify God in the body to everyday choices about work, rest, food, and care of the body
Analyze the dichotomist and trichotomist views of human nature using the biblical evidence each side cites
Explain why the Christian hope centers on the resurrection of the body and not on the soul's survival alone
Interpret 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Hebrews 4:12 in their literary context to determine whether they divide the person into separate parts
Explain how sin has corrupted the whole person in all the faculties of soul and body
Compare creationism and traducianism as Reformed accounts of the origin of each individual soul
Analyze biblical examples showing how the condition of the body and the life of the soul affect one another
Describe the faculties of the soul as the Reformed tradition has identified them, including mind, will, and affections
Construct a written account of the human person as a unity of body and soul supported by Scripture and the Westminster Standards
Evaluate materialism, the view that a person is only a physical body, in light of Scripture's teaching on the soul
Evaluate gnostic dualism and other body-denying spiritualities against Scripture's affirmation of the body
Synthesize how Christ's incarnation, bodily resurrection, and return together accomplish the redemption of the whole person, soul and body

BIB.11.2.3.t: Identify from Genesis 1:27 that God created people male and female
Retell the account of God forming Adam from the dust and making Eve from Adam's side
Explain that boys and girls, men and women, are both made in God's image and are equal in worth before Him
Identify that God called His whole creation, including man and woman, very good
Explain why God said it was not good for the man to be alone and how He provided the woman as a fitting helper
Describe marriage as God's design of one man and one woman joined together for life using Genesis 2:24
Compare the biblical pattern of man and woman as equal yet different with the idea that the sexes are simply the same
Explain how the Hebrew word ezer, translated helper, is also used of God and what this shows about the dignity of the woman's role
Identify the purposes of marriage taught in Scripture and summarized in the Westminster Confession, including mutual help, children, and purity
Describe how the fall distorted the relationship between man and woman according to Genesis 3
Explain how Scripture honors singleness as a calling using the teaching of Jesus and Paul
Interpret Jesus' appeal to what was so from the beginning in His teaching on marriage and divorce
Explain what the seventh commandment requires and forbids and how it guards God's design for man and woman
Explain Paul's teaching that marriage between husband and wife pictures the union of Christ and the church
Interpret Galatians 3:28 in its context, distinguishing equal standing in Christ from the removal of the distinction between male and female
Analyze how Paul in Romans 1 connects the exchange of God's created design to the exchange of the truth of God for idolatry
Evaluate contemporary claims about gender and marriage against the creation pattern of Genesis and the teaching of Jesus
Construct a written or spoken response to a question about sex and gender that presents the Reformed position with both truth and gentleness
Synthesize a biblical theology of manhood and womanhood that traces creation, fall, redemption, and consummation

BIB.11.2.4.t: Identify that God gave the first people the work of caring for the garden
Name the parts of God's command to Adam and Eve to fill the earth and rule over it
Give examples of everyday work at home and school that cares for the things God has made
Explain from Genesis that work was a good gift from God given before sin entered the world
Summarize the four parts of the Cultural Mandate as be fruitful, fill, subdue, and have dominion
Explain dominion as stewardship of creation that belongs to God rather than ownership that permits exploitation
Describe the pattern of six days of work and one day of rest that God set in creation and in the fourth commandment
Explain how Adam's naming of the animals shows people using God-given gifts to develop and order creation
Compare work before the Fall with work after the curse of thorns, sweat, and toil
Explain what Scripture teaches about diligence, laziness, and working in order to provide for oneself and give to others
Apply the command to do all work heartily as for the Lord and for his glory to ordinary classroom tasks
Analyze vocation as service to God and neighbor carried out in the callings of family, church, work, and community
Analyze the growth of herding, music, and metalwork in Genesis 4 as cultural development continuing in a fallen world
Explain how God renewed the command to be fruitful and fill the earth to Noah after the flood
Interpret Old Testament laws about land, trees, and animals as examples of how dominion includes care for creation
Explain the dignity of ordinary work using biblical examples such as Bezalel the craftsman and Jesus the carpenter
Compare the Cultural Mandate with the Great Commission in their scope, purpose, and relationship to each other
Explain how Reformers such as Luther and Calvin taught that every lawful calling, not only church office, is a place to serve God
Construct a theology of work that traces labor through creation, fall, redemption, and new creation
Evaluate views that treat secular work as less holy than sacred work in light of Scripture's teaching on vocation
Defend a biblical stewardship of creation against both exploitation of nature and worship of nature
Evaluate biblical principles for discerning a calling such as stewarding gifts, serving others, and seeking wise counsel
Evaluate contemporary attitudes that make work an idol or treat it as merely a means to money using the teaching of Ecclesiastes
Synthesize labor, rest, and dominion into an account of how the whole of human life can be offered as worship to the Creator

BIB.11.2.5.t: Identify that God made Adam and Eve good and without sin when he placed them in the garden
Name the one command God gave Adam about the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
Describe the good gifts God gave Adam in the garden, including food from every other tree, the tree of life, and work to do
Recall that God warned Adam that eating from the forbidden tree would bring death
Define a covenant as a relationship God establishes with promises, conditions, and consequences
Explain that God's command in the garden tested whether Adam would trust and obey him
Explain original righteousness as the uprightness Adam and Eve had at creation, with God's law written on their hearts and the power to obey it
Summarize the covenant of works as the Reformed tradition confesses it, in which life was promised to Adam and his descendants on condition of perfect and personal obedience
Identify the parties, condition, promise, and penalty of the covenant of works in Genesis 2
Explain why the tradition teaches that Adam was created able to keep God's law yet able to fall
Interpret the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil as signs of the covenant of works
Compare the covenant of works with the covenant of grace in their conditions, mediator, and promises
Explain the confessional teaching that the want of original righteousness belongs to the sinfulness of humanity after the Fall
Analyze Adam's role as covenant head who represented all humanity in the covenant of works
Explain how the broken covenant of works shows that fallen sinners cannot gain life by the law and so need Christ
Analyze the biblical evidence, including Hosea 6:7, that God's arrangement with Adam was a covenant even though Genesis 2 does not use the word
Explain how the moral law given to Adam as a covenant of works continues after the Fall as a perfect rule of righteousness
Explain how Christ as the last Adam fulfilled through his active and passive obedience what Adam failed to do
Explain why the Westminster Confession grounds the covenant of works in God's voluntary condescension rather than in any creature's strict merit
Trace the development of the doctrine of the covenant of works in Reformed theology from the sixteenth century through the Westminster Standards
Evaluate denials of a pre-Fall covenant using Scripture and the arguments of Reformed theologians
Defend the Reformed teaching that the imputation of Adam's guilt runs parallel to the imputation of Christ's righteousness
Compose a theological essay that traces the two covenant heads through Scripture, showing ruin in Adam and righteousness in Christ

BIB.11.2.6.t: Identify that God made every person and that every human life is precious to him
Recall the sixth commandment and state that God gave it to protect people's lives
Describe from Psalm 139 how God forms and knows each person before birth
Explain from Genesis 9:6 why taking innocent human life is a grave wrong because people bear God's image
Give examples of how God's law commands kindness and protection toward weak people such as the blind, the deaf, orphans, and widows
Explain the duties the sixth commandment requires for preserving one's own life and the lives of others
Explain why people of every nation and ethnicity have equal worth before God and why showing partiality is sin
Explain how Jesus taught that the sixth commandment forbids sinful anger, hatred, and cursing words as well as murder
Explain from Scripture why the Reformed tradition teaches that a person must care for his or her own body and life rather than harm it
Compare the biblical view of human life with practices in ancient and modern cultures that have devalued life, such as infant exposure
Analyze biblical passages that speak of unborn children as persons known and called by God
Distinguish murder from the taking of life in public justice, lawful war, and necessary defense as the Westminster Standards explain
Describe practical ways believers and the church can obey the biblical call to rescue and speak for those who cannot speak for themselves
Classify the duties and sins listed under the sixth commandment in the Westminster Larger Catechism as matters of heart, word, and deed
Analyze how the early and Reformation church applied the sanctity of life through care for abandoned infants, the sick, and the poor
Evaluate common arguments for abortion against Scripture's teaching on the personhood of the unborn and the sixth commandment
Evaluate arguments for euthanasia and assisted suicide in light of God's sovereignty over life and death
Defend the dignity of people with disabilities, the elderly, and the unborn against views that ground human worth in ability or usefulness
Evaluate contemporary bioethical practices such as embryo destruction and selective genetic screening using biblical principles of human dignity
Create a written Christian ethic of human life that traces human dignity through creation, fall, redemption, and resurrection

BIB.11.3.1.t: Name the two main parts of the Bible as the Old Testament and the New Testament
Identify that the Bible is made up of 66 books written by many human authors over a long period of time
Sort the books of the Bible into their main groups such as Law, History, Poetry, Prophets, Gospels, and Letters
Locate a passage in the Bible by book, chapter, and verse using the table of contents
Explain that the church recognized the books God gave as Scripture rather than creating or approving them
Describe why readers sometimes need help to understand hard passages of Scripture using the account of the Ethiopian official
Explain the Reformed teaching that what must be known for salvation is clearly set forth in Scripture so ordinary readers can understand it
Summarize the marks the early church looked for in recognizing New Testament books, including apostolic origin, agreement with the faith, and wide use in the churches
Apply the rule of context by reading the surrounding verses before stating what a single verse means
Explain how Jesus and the apostles affirmed the Hebrew Scriptures as the Old Testament canon
Identify the literary genre of a passage such as narrative, poetry, prophecy, parable, or letter and explain how genre shapes the way it is read
Compare the books of the Apocrypha with the canonical books and explain why Protestant churches do not receive them as Scripture
Explain how New Testament writers quoted and interpreted the Old Testament using examples such as Jesus's teaching on the road to Emmaus
Analyze the criteria the early church used to recognize canonical books and explain the Reformed position that the canon rests on God's self-attesting word rather than on church decree
Explain why the Reformed tradition holds that the canon is closed with the completion of the apostolic foundation
Interpret a passage by examining its words, grammar, historical setting, and original audience
Explain why the Reformation churches stressed the original languages of Scripture and faithful translation into the common language
Distinguish the illumination of the Holy Spirit in understanding Scripture from the giving of new revelation as the Reformed tradition teaches
Explain how biblical theology follows themes such as covenant and promise across the whole canon toward their fulfillment in Christ
Trace the historical recognition of the canon using sources such as the Muratorian Fragment, the 39th Festal Letter of Athanasius, and the councils of Hippo and Carthage
Apply the analogy of faith by using clearer passages of Scripture to interpret less clear ones
Evaluate the claims of Gnostic and other noncanonical gospels using the historical criteria of canonicity
Evaluate modern claims of ongoing revelation in light of the Reformed doctrine of a closed canon
Compare the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture with approaches that place final interpretive authority in church tradition
Create a written exegesis of a passage that applies context, genre, grammar, and the analogy of faith

BIB.11.3.2.t: Identify from Bible stories and verses that God always tells the truth and cannot lie
Recall that the Bible is God's word and so everything it says is true
Explain that because the Bible is God's word, God's people are called to believe what it teaches and obey what it commands
Define inerrancy as the teaching that Scripture in its original writings is without error in all that it affirms
Describe how Jesus treated the Old Testament as true and authoritative, using examples from his temptation and teaching
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that Scripture has authority over a person's feelings, opinions, and human traditions
Distinguish infallibility, meaning Scripture cannot fail or mislead, from inerrancy, meaning Scripture is without error
Explain the Westminster Confession's teaching that Scripture's authority depends on God its author and not on the testimony of any person or church
Explain the Reformed teaching that Scripture is sufficient, containing all that is needed for God's glory and for faith and life
Apply a clear command or principle of Scripture to a realistic moral decision, citing the passage that governs the choice
Summarize the main affirmations and denials of the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy
Explain how the Westminster Confession distinguishes the evidences of Scripture's divine authority from the inward work of the Holy Spirit that brings full persuasion of it
Interpret passages that use ordinary observational language, round numbers, or loose quotation and explain why these do not count as errors
Analyze how the authority of Scripture is connected to the lordship of Christ, who speaks through the apostolic and prophetic word
Distinguish an error in the original text from a textual variant in later copies and explain why inerrancy is affirmed of the original writings
Analyze an apparent discrepancy between parallel biblical accounts and propose a reasonable harmonization
Construct an argument for inerrancy from the truthful character of God and the self-testimony of Scripture
Evaluate common objections to the truthfulness of Scripture drawn from science, history, and alleged contradictions
Defend the Reformed doctrine of sola scriptura as Scripture being the supreme judge of all controversies, distinguishing it from a rejection of creeds and tradition
Evaluate views of limited inerrancy and views that Scripture merely contains or becomes the word of God against the Reformed confession of Scripture's full truthfulness
Compose an essay on the relationship between the ministerial authority of the church, its councils, and its creeds and the supreme authority of Scripture

BIB.11.3.3.t: Identify the Bible as the book in which God speaks to his people
Recall that the sky, the seasons, and living things show that God is great and powerful
Recall that Scripture is breathed out by God, using the words of 2 Timothy 3:16
Explain that people need the Bible to learn who Jesus is and how God saves sinners
Describe how God used human writers such as Moses, David, Luke, and Paul to write his words
Distinguish general revelation from special revelation using examples of each
Explain why general revelation leaves people without excuse but cannot teach them the way of salvation
Identify ways God revealed himself before Scripture was complete and explain why he had his word written down
Explain the four purposes for which inspired Scripture is profitable according to 2 Timothy 3:16-17
Use a passage of Scripture to show how it teaches, reproves, corrects, or trains in righteousness in a given situation
Analyze the meaning of verbal plenary inspiration and how Jesus and Paul treat the very words and letters of Scripture as significant
Contrast the doctrine of inspiration with a mechanical dictation view by showing how the writers' research, style, and personality remain in the text
Explain how sin's effect on the human mind makes Scripture necessary for knowing God savingly
Interpret 2 Peter 1:19-21 in its context to explain what it means that the prophets were carried along by the Holy Spirit
Explain the Westminster Confession's teaching that Scripture is most necessary because God's former ways of revealing his will have now ceased
Distinguish revelation, inspiration, and illumination and explain the Spirit's role in each
Analyze New Testament passages that treat what Scripture says as what God says
Analyze how the apostles understood their own teaching and writings as words given by the Spirit
Evaluate the neo-orthodox view that Scripture becomes the Word of God in encounter against the Reformed view that Scripture is the Word of God
Evaluate liberal and partial views of inspiration that limit it to human insight or to religious ideas alone
Construct an argument for the necessity of special revelation for salvation that answers the objection concerning those who never hear
Construct an explanation of the dual authorship of Scripture showing how God fully authored each word while human writers fully wrote as themselves
Write a defense of the divine origin of Scripture drawing on its self-witness and the marks the Westminster Confession identifies

BIB.11.4.1.t: Identify Jesus as God the Son
Name Jesus as the One through whom all things were made
Recall that Jesus lived with the Father before he was born in Bethlehem
Describe Gospel accounts in which people worshiped Jesus and he accepted their worship
Retell Jesus' words 'Before Abraham was, I am' and explain why his hearers tried to stone him
Explain the meaning of John 1:1 that the Word was with God and the Word was God
Contrast the eternal Son, who was not made, with everything that God created
Classify the titles of Christ that point to his deity, such as Lord, Son of God, Word, I AM, and God, using supporting verses
Explain how Scripture ascribes divine attributes and works to Christ, such as forgiving sins, knowing hearts, being unchanging, and judging the world
Analyze the 'I am' statements in the Gospel of John and explain how they echo God's name in Exodus
Analyze New Testament passages that apply Old Testament texts about the LORD directly to Jesus
Explain the Reformed teaching that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father and not made
Explain the Son's role as the agent through whom the Father created and now upholds all things
Analyze Old Testament appearances of the Angel of the LORD and evaluate the case that they reveal the preincarnate Son
Distinguish the Son's equality with the Father in essence from his distinction from the Father as a person
Explain how Philippians 2 and 2 Corinthians 8 assume the Son's existence in the form of God before his incarnation
Explain from the catechism why the Mediator must be true God
Construct a biblical case for the full deity of Christ using his names, attributes, works, and worship
Analyze passages often cited against Christ's deity, such as 'firstborn of all creation' and 'the Father is greater than I', and interpret them in context
Evaluate the Arian claim that 'there was when the Son was not' in light of Scripture
Defend the worship of Christ as worship that belongs to God alone
Explain how the Council of Nicaea's term homoousios, of one substance, answered Arianism and how the Westminster Confession restates it
Evaluate modern denials of Christ's deity, such as the rendering of John 1:1 as 'a god' and adoptionist views, using Scripture and the confessions

BIB.11.4.2.t: Identify from the Christmas account that God the Son was born as a real baby named Jesus to Mary
Name Jesus as both truly God and truly man
Retell the angel's announcements to Mary and to Joseph about the coming birth of Jesus
Describe from the Gospels ways Jesus showed a true human body and soul, such as growing, getting tired, being hungry, and weeping
Recite John 1:14 and explain in your own words what it means that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us
Explain the meaning of the name Immanuel and show how Matthew presents Jesus' birth as the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy
Explain the creed's confession that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary
Classify actions in a Gospel passage as showing Jesus' humanity or his deity, such as sleeping in the boat and calming the storm
Explain why Scripture teaches that the Son took a true body and a reasonable soul rather than only appearing to be human
Explain how Jesus shared fully in human nature yet was without sin
Analyze how the virgin conception by the Holy Spirit secures both Christ's true descent from Mary and the holiness of his human nature
Interpret the phrases form of God and form of a servant in Philippians 2 as describing the true deity and true humanity of the one Christ
Analyze the catechisms' reasons why the Mediator had to be true man, true God, and both in one person
Explain the hypostatic union as the Reformed tradition confesses it, two whole and distinct natures joined in the one person of the eternal Son
Explain the church's teaching that the Son remains God and man in one person forever and did not lay aside his human nature
Distinguish the theological terms person and nature as the church uses them to describe Christ
Trace the controversies over Christ's person raised by Apollinaris, Nestorius, and Eutyches that led to the Council of Chalcedon
Analyze the Chalcedonian Definition phrase by phrase, especially its confession of two natures without confusion, change, division, or separation
Analyze Gospel texts that show Jesus' human knowledge and human will, such as his not knowing the hour and his prayer in Gethsemane, in light of two natures in one person
Evaluate Apollinarianism, Nestorianism, and Eutychianism against Scripture and the Chalcedonian Definition
