Defend the sinlessness and impeccability of Christ from Scripture and the doctrine of the hypostatic union
Explain the terms anhypostasia and enhypostasia and how they describe Christ's human nature as subsisting in the person of the Son
Analyze how Scripture ascribes the properties of either nature to the one person in the communicatio idiomatum
Compare the Reformed and Lutheran accounts of the communication of properties, including the Reformed teaching that the Son is not confined to his human nature

BIB.11.4.3.t: Identify that Jesus, the Son of God, came down from heaven and became a baby to save His people
Retell how Jesus was born into a poor family and laid in a manger
Recall examples from the Gospels of Jesus obeying His earthly parents and His heavenly Father
List the steps of Christ's humiliation named in the Shorter Catechism, from His lowly birth to His burial
Describe events from the Gospels that show Jesus was hungry, tired, tempted, and rejected during His earthly life
List the steps of Christ's exaltation named in the Shorter Catechism
Explain from Philippians 2 what it means that the Son emptied Himself by taking the form of a servant
Explain what it means that Christ was made under the law and obeyed it perfectly on behalf of His people
Compare Christ's state of humiliation with His state of exaltation using Philippians 2:5-11
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that Christ's humiliation spanned His whole earthly life and not only His death
Describe practical ways to follow Christ's example of humble service as taught in Philippians 2 and John 13
Explain how the word therefore in Philippians 2:9 presents Christ's exaltation as the Father's reward for the Son's obedience
Analyze the phrase emptied himself as the Son veiling His glory by taking a human nature rather than surrendering His divine attributes
Interpret the catechism's teaching that Christ was buried and continued in the state of the dead and under the power of death until the third day
Compare the main interpretations of the creedal phrase he descended into hell with the Reformed readings given in the Heidelberg Catechism and the Larger Catechism
Analyze how Christ's willing obedience unto death fulfilled the covenant of redemption between the Father and the Son
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that Christ was exalted in His human nature, the same body in which He suffered
Trace the pattern of suffering followed by glory from Old Testament prophecy to its fulfillment in Christ
Evaluate kenotic theories which claim the Son gave up divine attributes in the incarnation against Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Construct a two-states framework that sets each step of Christ's humiliation beside the corresponding step of His exaltation
Analyze how the Reformed tradition applies the pattern of Christ's suffering and glory to believers through their union with Him
Write a synthesis explaining how Christ's humiliation accomplished redemption and His exaltation secures its application to His people

BIB.11.4.4.t: Identify Jesus as our Prophet, Priest, and King
Describe from John 10 how Jesus, the Good Shepherd, leads, protects, and cares for His sheep
Recall Gospel examples of Jesus teaching people the truth about God
Describe how Jesus prayed for His disciples and for those who would believe in Him
Explain that the title Christ means the Anointed One and that Jesus was anointed by the Holy Spirit for His work
Identify Old Testament examples of prophets, priests, and kings being anointed for their offices
Explain how Jesus fulfills the promise of a Prophet like Moses and is greater than Moses
Restate in their own words the catechism definitions of how Christ executes the offices of prophet, priest, and king
Compare the three offices by matching each to the human need it meets, such as ignorance, guilt, and bondage to sin
Describe the ways Christ exercises His kingly office in subduing, ruling, defending His people, and conquering His enemies
Categorize Christ's priestly work into His once-for-all sacrifice and His continuing intercession
Explain how Christ continues to exercise His prophetic office by His Word and Spirit, including through the Old Testament prophets and the apostles
Analyze how Hebrews presents Christ as High Priest after the order of Melchizedek
Explain how the Heidelberg Catechism describes believers as sharing in Christ's anointing as prophets, priests, and kings
Distinguish Christ's rule over all things from His special rule over His church
Analyze why the Old Testament kept the offices of priest and king separate and how Scripture foretells their union in the Messiah
Contrast Christ's priesthood with the Levitical priesthood in its permanence, holiness, and sacrifice
Trace episodes in the Gospels where Jesus acts in each of His three offices
Explain how Hebrews presents Christ as God's final word and why the Reformed tradition holds that earlier ways of revelation have ceased
Construct a biblical account of Christ's ongoing intercession for His people at the Father's right hand
Evaluate views that reduce Christ to only a moral teacher or only a political king
Defend the sufficiency and finality of Christ's priesthood against views that add further sacrifices or human mediators
Explain how Calvin's treatment of the threefold office in the Institutes shaped later Reformed confessions
Write a synthesis showing how the three offices together present Christ as the only Mediator and Redeemer

BIB.11.4.5.t: Identify that Jesus died on the cross to take away sin
Name Jesus as the Lamb of God and repeat John the Baptist's words about Him
Recall that Jesus took the punishment for sin that we deserved
Retell the Passover story and describe how the blood of the lamb points to Jesus
Summarize substitution as Christ dying in the place of sinners
Describe what the Bible teaches about the shedding of blood for the forgiveness of sins
Explain propitiation as Christ's sacrifice turning away God's righteous wrath against sin
Describe the Day of Atonement ritual and explain how Hebrews presents Christ as its fulfillment
Explain reconciliation as the restoration of peace between God and sinners through the cross
Compare the repeated Old Testament sacrifices with Christ's once-for-all sacrifice
Explain redemption as Christ paying a ransom to set His people free from sin and the curse of the law
Explain from Scripture how Christ's finished work is the ground of the believer's assurance of forgiveness
Explain why no sinner or mere creature could make satisfaction for sin and why the Mediator had to suffer as true man and true God
Analyze why, according to Scripture and the Reformed confessions, God could not simply overlook sin without satisfaction of His justice
Explain how the Reformed tradition connects Christ's active and passive obedience to the justification of sinners
Interpret Isaiah's Suffering Servant song in context as a prophecy of penal substitution
Distinguish expiation, the removal of sin's guilt, from propitiation, the turning away of God's wrath
Explain Christ's triumph over sin, death, and the devil as a biblical aspect of the cross grounded in His satisfaction for sin
Analyze the Gospel accounts of Gethsemane and the cry of dereliction to explain how Christ bore God's wrath in body and soul
Explain the Reformed doctrine of definite atonement from texts that describe Christ dying for His sheep, His church, and those the Father gave Him
Explain how the Reformed tradition holds together definite atonement and the free offer of the gospel to all people
Analyze universal-sounding atonement texts in their context and explain the Canons of Dort distinction between the sufficiency and efficiency of Christ's death
Trace the historical development of atonement doctrine from the early church through Anselm, Abelard, and the Reformers
Evaluate the ransom-to-Satan, moral influence, and governmental theories against the biblical case for penal substitution
Construct a reasoned defense of definite atonement that interacts fairly with Arminian and hypothetical universalist views
Evaluate modern objections that penal substitution portrays divine violence by examining the Trinitarian unity and willingness displayed at the cross
Compose a theological synthesis showing how the cross satisfies divine justice and displays divine love

BIB.11.4.6.t: Retell the Easter account of the women finding the tomb empty and hearing the angel say that Jesus is risen
Recall that the risen Jesus went up into heaven while his disciples watched and that he is alive there now
Name people who saw Jesus alive after he rose, such as Mary Magdalene, Thomas, and the disciples
Describe what the risen Jesus did to show his disciples that he had a real body, such as eating fish and showing his wounds
Summarize how Jesus rose on the third day just as he and the Scriptures had said beforehand
Explain why Christians gather for worship on the first day of the week by connecting it to the day of Christ's resurrection
Explain the ascension account in Acts 1 including the angels' promise that Jesus will return in the same way
Explain that being seated at the right hand of God is biblical language for Christ's place of honor and authority rather than a description of a physical chair
List the witnesses of the risen Christ in 1 Corinthians 15 and explain why Paul appeals to living eyewitnesses
Compare the Gospel account of the empty tomb with the report that the disciples stole the body
Explain the three benefits of Christ's resurrection as the Heidelberg Catechism states them
Distinguish Christ's resurrection to glorified life that never dies again from the restoring of Lazarus to ordinary mortal life
Explain how the Reformed tradition connects Christ's session at the right hand with his continual intercession for his people
Analyze the firstfruits imagery of 1 Corinthians 15 in light of the Old Testament harvest offering to show how the tradition sees Christ's resurrection as the pledge of believers' bodily resurrection
Interpret Psalm 110:1 and explain how the apostles apply it to Christ's ascension and session
Explain from Scripture why Christ's ascension was the occasion for his pouring out of the Holy Spirit
Explain how Ephesians presents the seated Christ as ruling over all things for the sake of the church
Analyze how Peter uses Psalm 16 to argue that the Old Testament anticipated the Messiah's resurrection
Trace Paul's argument about the consequences for preaching, faith, and forgiveness if Christ has not been raised
Explain the continuity and transformation of Christ's risen body as the tradition confesses it, the same body now glorified
Compare the Reformed teaching that Christ's human nature is now in heaven with the Lutheran teaching on the ubiquity of his body
Construct a historical case for the resurrection from the burial, the empty tomb, the appearances, and the rise of the early church's proclamation
Explain how Paul grounds the believer's union with the risen and ascended Christ and the call to seek the things above in Christ's session
Evaluate naturalistic theories such as the swoon, hallucination, and wrong tomb theories against the biblical and historical evidence

BIB.11.5.1.t: Identify the church as God's people rather than a building
Name believers together as the family of God who belong to one household
Recall from Jesus' words to Peter that Jesus builds His church and keeps it safe
Describe what the first Christians did together when they gathered as the church
Explain how Paul's picture of the body shows that every member of the church belongs and is needed
Identify Christ as the only head of the church using passages from Paul's letters
Explain the difference between the invisible church of all the elect and the visible church of all who profess the true faith
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that the visible church includes the children of believers
Compare a local congregation with the universal or catholic church spread through all times and places
Describe biblical ways members of a local church are called to serve and build one another up
Explain from Jesus' parables why the visible church on earth contains both true believers and those who only profess faith
Analyze what the biblical images of the church as body, bride, temple, and flock each teach about its nature
Explain how the unity of the church rests on the union of its members with Christ their head
Trace the continuity of the one people of God from Israel to the New Testament church
Explain the Reformed teaching on the communion of the saints including the shared gifts and mutual duties of believers
Explain the confessional teaching that outside the visible church there is no ordinary possibility of salvation and the duty to join it
Analyze how the visible and invisible distinction guards against both equating church membership with salvation and dismissing the visible church
Compare the Reformed doctrine of the nature of the church with Roman Catholic and broadly individualistic evangelical views
Evaluate the claim that a Christian can live faithfully apart from the church using Scripture and the confessions
Explain from Scripture and the Heidelberg Catechism how Christ gathers, defends, and preserves His church throughout history
Compose a structured essay presenting a biblical and confessional doctrine of the church as visible and invisible, local and catholic

BIB.11.5.2.t: Identify that a true church gathers to hear and learn God's Word
Name the Bible as the authority the church must follow in everything it teaches
Recite the four words the Nicene Creed uses to describe the church: one, holy, catholic, and apostolic
Identify preaching, baptism, and the Lord's Supper as practices Christ gave his church to carry out
List the three marks of a true church in the Reformed tradition: pure preaching of the gospel, pure administration of the sacraments, and church discipline
Explain why the faithful preaching of the gospel is the chief mark of a true church, using the Bereans' example of testing teaching by Scripture
Explain how administering the sacraments as Christ instituted them serves as a mark of a true church
Describe how church discipline protects the purity of the church and seeks the restoration of the one who sins
Explain that catholic in the creed means universal and distinguish this meaning from the name of the Roman Catholic denomination
Explain how the unity of the church rests on one Lord, one faith, and one baptism rather than on a single organization
Explain how the church is called holy because it is set apart by Christ even though its members still sin
Explain the Reformed view that the church is apostolic by continuing in the apostles' teaching rather than by an unbroken succession of bishops
Compare the marks of the true church with the marks of a false church as the Belgic Confession describes them
Explain from the parable of the wheat and the tares why even the purest churches contain mixture and error and how some churches decline until they are no longer churches of Christ
Distinguish the marks of the church, by which a true church is recognized, from the attributes of the church, which describe what the church is
Explain the Belgic Confession's teaching that believers are to join themselves to a true church and the role the marks play in recognizing one
Analyze Christ's letters to the churches in Revelation for signs of faithfulness and decline in relation to the marks
Compare Reformation statements that name two marks of the church with those that add discipline as a third and explain how discipline relates to the Word
Compare Reformed, Roman Catholic, and Eastern Orthodox accounts of what makes a church catholic and apostolic
Evaluate a described congregation's teaching and practice using the marks of a true church as criteria
Evaluate claims that one denomination alone is the true church in light of Scripture and the teaching that particular churches are more or less pure
Defend the necessity of the Word, the sacraments, and discipline together by explaining what a church loses when one is neglected
Construct a written account of the marks and attributes of the true church that integrates Scripture, the Nicene Creed, and the Reformed confessions

BIB.11.5.3.t: Identify Jesus Christ as the Head of the church who rules and cares for his people
Name the leaders Christ gives to his church, such as pastors, elders, and deacons
Describe how deacons in the early church cared for people in need
Explain from Scripture why church leaders are called to be godly examples to the people they serve
Summarize the two ongoing offices of elder for oversight and deacon for service
Practice praying in class for the pastors, elders, and deacons of a local church using what Scripture asks of members
Explain the character and ability qualifications Paul gives for elders and deacons
Describe how church officers are chosen, examined, and ordained according to the pattern in Acts and the Pastoral Epistles
Distinguish teaching elders who labor in preaching from ruling elders as the Reformed tradition reads 1 Timothy 5:17
Compare the responsibilities of elders in teaching and ruling with the responsibilities of deacons in mercy and service
Explain the biblical basis for members honoring and submitting to their elders along with the limit that obedience to God comes first
Explain how elders serve as under-shepherds who are accountable to Christ the Chief Shepherd
Analyze how Christ exercises his rule through the keys of the kingdom in preaching and church discipline
Distinguish the spiritual government of the church from the authority of the civil magistrate
Outline the steps of church discipline in Matthew 18 and the stages of admonition, suspension, and excommunication
Explain why the Reformed tradition holds that the public ministry of the Word requires gifted men who are lawfully called and approved
Explain the purposes of church discipline including restoration of the sinner, purity of the church, and the honor of Christ
Analyze the Jerusalem Council as a model for assemblies of elders deciding questions for the wider church
Analyze the New Testament use of the terms elder and overseer to explain the Reformed teaching of a plurality and parity of elders
Analyze how sessions, presbyteries, and assemblies relate and why their decisions bind only as far as they agree with Scripture
Evaluate episcopal, presbyterian, and congregational forms of church government against the teaching of Scripture
Evaluate the textual arguments for the Reformed tradition's position that the offices of pastor and elder are given to qualified men
Construct a reasoned case for a form of church government that answers objections from Scripture and church history
Compose a synthesis explaining how Christ rules his church as King through his Word, his officers, and his censures

BIB.11.5.4.t: Identify baptism and the Lord's Supper as the two sacraments Jesus gave to his church
Name water as the sign used in baptism and bread and wine as the signs used in the Lord's Supper
Recall that Jesus commanded his disciples to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit
Retell the account of Jesus giving the bread and the cup to his disciples on the night he was betrayed
Explain that the sacraments are signs that point to Christ and what he has done for his people
Define a sacrament, using the Westminster Shorter Catechism, as a holy ordinance instituted by Christ in which visible signs represent, seal, and apply Christ and his benefits to believers
Explain what baptism signifies, including washing from sin and union with Christ in his death and resurrection
Explain what the Lord's Supper shows forth, including the proclamation of Christ's death and the spiritual nourishment of believers
Explain how circumcision and the Passover served as Old Testament signs of the covenant that anticipate baptism and the Lord's Supper
Describe the self-examination Scripture calls for before coming to the Lord's Supper, including knowledge to discern the Lord's body, faith, repentance, love, and new obedience
Compare baptism and the Lord's Supper in how often each is received, what each signifies, and to whom each is given
Describe how the Westminster Larger Catechism calls Christians to improve their baptism throughout life and identify the Scripture it draws on
Explain how the Lord's Supper expresses believers' communion with Christ and with one another as one body
Explain the distinction between the sign and the thing signified and why Scripture can speak of the sign by the name of what it signifies
Explain the Reformed teaching that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the Lord's Supper and is received by faith
Explain the Reformed position that baptism is to be administered both to those who profess faith and to the infants of believing parents, tracing its basis in covenant continuity
Explain how the sacraments become effectual not by any power in themselves or in the one who administers them but by the blessing of Christ and the work of his Spirit
Distinguish worthy from unworthy receiving of the Lord's Supper and explain the consequences Scripture attaches to each

Explain the Reformed teaching that baptism is administered once, that its efficacy is not tied to the moment it is administered, and that grace and salvation are not so bound to it that no one can be saved without it
Analyze how the sacraments function as means of grace that confirm the faith the Holy Spirit works through the preaching of the Word
Analyze why the Reformed tradition recognizes only two sacraments by applying the criterion of direct institution by Christ
Evaluate transubstantiation, the Lutheran view, and bare memorialism against the Reformed teaching on the Lord's Supper using Scripture and the confessions
Evaluate credobaptist and paedobaptist arguments concerning the proper recipients of baptism in light of the biblical covenants
Evaluate arguments concerning the mode of baptism and explain why the Westminster Confession holds that immersion is not necessary
Compose a catechetical explanation that presents baptism and the Lord's Supper as visible words of the gospel sealing God's covenant promises

BIB.11.5.5.t: Identify the one true God as the only one people are to worship
Name the things God's people do when the church gathers to worship, such as praying, singing, hearing the Bible read and preached, and giving
Recite the second commandment and explain in simple words that God tells us how He is to be worshiped
Retell the account of the golden calf and explain why God was displeased even though the people called it a feast to the LORD
Describe ways Scripture shows God's people expressing reverence in worship, such as bowing, kneeling, standing for the reading of the Word, and singing together
Explain what Jesus meant when He said God seeks worshipers who worship in spirit and in truth
Explain from Isaiah and Jesus' teaching why God rejects worship offered with the lips while the heart is far from Him
Retell the account of Nadab and Abihu and explain what it teaches about offering God worship He has not commanded
Explain why Christians gather for public worship on the first day of the week, using New Testament evidence

Match each part of a Lord's Day service, such as the call to worship, confession of sin, Scripture reading, sermon, prayer, singing, offering, and benediction, to a passage of Scripture that supports it
Define the regulative principle of worship as the Reformed teaching that God may be worshiped only in the ways He has appointed in Scripture
Explain the Reformed teaching that worship is to be given to the triune God alone through the one Mediator Jesus Christ and not to angels, saints, or images
Explain the difference between offering all of life to God as worship and the gathered public worship of the church
Analyze Old Testament passages in which God rejects worship He did not command and identify the principle they share
Interpret the second commandment as the catechisms do, forbidding both images and any manner of worship not appointed in God's Word
Distinguish the elements of worship from its circumstances, such as time, place, and order of service, and explain how each is to be determined
Explain why Paul describes humanly devised religious rules as self-made religion and how this supports the regulative principle
Identify the ordinary and occasional elements of worship listed in the Westminster Confession and support each with New Testament texts
Explain how the regulative principle protects the conscience of worshipers from being bound by the commandments of men
Describe how Reformers such as Calvin and Knox reformed public worship and summarize the biblical reasons they gave for removing medieval practices
Compare the regulative principle with the normative principle of worship held in the Lutheran and Anglican traditions
Evaluate pragmatic and entertainment-driven worship practices by the standard of what God has commanded in Scripture
Construct a biblical and confessional defense of the regulative principle of worship that answers common objections
Evaluate the arguments made within the Reformed tradition about exclusive psalmody, hymns, and musical instruments in public worship
Design an order of worship for a Lord's Day service and justify each element and circumstance from Scripture and the Reformed confessions

BIB.11.5.6.t: Identify that Jesus told His followers to go and tell people everywhere about Him
Recall Jesus' promise to be with His disciples always as they carry out His command
State the good news the church shares, that Jesus died for our sins and rose again
Recognize from Scripture that God gathers people from every nation, tribe, and language to Himself
Describe praying for workers in God's harvest as one way the church takes part in its mission
Summarize the commands of the Great Commission to go, make disciples, baptize, and teach them to obey
Explain from Romans 10 why sending and preaching are needed for people to hear and believe the gospel
Trace the spread of the gospel in the book of Acts from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, and the wider world
Explain from the phrase to the end of the age why the Great Commission belongs to the church in every generation and not only to the apostles
Compare evangelism as proclaiming the gospel with discipleship as teaching believers to obey all that Christ commanded
Explain how the risen Christ's universal authority grounds and secures the church's mission to the nations
Describe the Holy Spirit's role in empowering the church's witness as shown in Acts
Describe concrete ways church members take part in mission through praying, giving, going, and sending, using biblical examples
Explain how the good works and holy conduct of believers serve the church's witness to unbelievers
Analyze the practices of the early church in Acts that marked it as a missionary community
Explain how the petition Your kingdom come in the Lord's Prayer expresses the church's mission as the Reformed catechisms teach it
Explain the Reformed teaching that Christ gave the ministry, Word, and ordinances to the church for gathering and perfecting the saints
Distinguish the church's central mission of gospel proclamation and disciple-making from the works of mercy that accompany and adorn it
Analyze how the Reformed doctrine of God's sovereignty in salvation supports rather than undermines the urgency of evangelism
Construct a biblical theology of mission that traces God's purpose for the nations from Genesis to Revelation
Evaluate the prosperity gospel and the social gospel against the apostolic gospel
Defend the exclusivity of salvation in Christ and the resulting necessity of missions from Scripture and the confessions
Evaluate approaches to communicating the gospel across cultures in light of Paul's practice
Compose a theological statement of the church's mission as making disciples of all nations for the glory of God

BIB.11.6.1.t: Identify from the Bible that every person will die one day
Name the Bible's teaching that believers go to be with Jesus when they die
Retell Jesus' words to Martha that whoever believes in him will live even though he dies
Explain from Genesis and Romans that death entered the world because of sin
Describe how Paul says Christians grieve at death differently from those who have no hope
Explain what Paul means when he says Jesus has taken away the sting of death
Summarize the Westminster Shorter Catechism's answer about what believers receive from Christ at death
Explain the Heidelberg Catechism's answer to why believers still die even though Christ died for them
Explain that Scripture describes death as the separation of the soul from the body
Explain how Psalm 90 teaches God's people to number their days in light of death
Explain why Paul considers departing to be with Christ far better than remaining in the body
Compare the state of the righteous and the wicked immediately after death as taught in Scripture and the Westminster Confession
Explain how the Reformed practice of Christian burial reflects the teaching that believers' bodies remain united to Christ as they rest in the grave
Interpret Jesus' promise to the thief on the cross in its context to show that believers are with Christ immediately at death
Explain from Scripture why a person's eternal destiny is fixed at death with no second chance afterward
Analyze New Testament passages that portray departed souls as conscious and active before the resurrection
Explain why the intermediate state is not the believer's final hope by connecting the disembodied soul to the future resurrection of the body
Explain from Scripture why God forbids attempts to contact or consult the dead
Analyze Old Testament language about Sheol and being gathered to one's people to trace how the hope beyond death unfolds across Scripture
Evaluate the doctrine of soul sleep against Scripture by interpreting the biblical metaphor of death as sleep
Evaluate the Roman Catholic doctrine of purgatory against Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Compose a theological essay on death and the intermediate state that integrates the key passages and confessional statements and distinguishes the intermediate state from the final state

BIB.11.6.2.t: Identify from the Bible that Jesus promised he will come back
Name Jesus as the King who will return in glory with his angels
Recite the line of the Apostles' Creed that confesses Christ will come to judge the living and the dead
Retell the account of Jesus' ascension and the angels' promise that he will come again in the same way
Retell the parable of the ten virgins and explain what it teaches about being ready for Christ's return
Describe what Jesus means by watching and being ready using the example of the faithful servant
Explain from Scripture that Christ will return personally, bodily, and visibly
Explain why no one but the Father knows the day or hour of Christ's return
Compare Christ's first coming in humility with his second coming in glory as part of his exaltation
Explain what New Testament images such as the thief in the night and the days of Noah teach about the suddenness of Christ's return
Explain how the apostles used the promise of Christ's return to call believers to holy living
Explain the parable of the talents as teaching faithful stewardship while awaiting the master's return
Analyze Jesus' teaching in the Olivet Discourse about the events that precede his coming
Explain how Paul used Christ's return to comfort the Thessalonians about fellow believers who had died
Explain why the New Testament calls the appearing of Christ the blessed hope of the church
Explain the comfort the Heidelberg Catechism draws from Christ's return for the suffering church
Explain how the prayer Maranatha and the Lord's Supper proclaimed until he comes express the church's expectation of Christ's return in worship
Analyze how Jesus applied Daniel's vision of the Son of Man coming with the clouds to his own return
Explain how the promise of Christ's return frames the church's mission of proclaiming the gospel to the nations
Analyze Paul's correction of the claim that the day of the Lord had already come
Analyze how the Westminster Confession explains God's purpose in keeping the day of Christ's return unknown
Evaluate historical attempts to set the date of Christ's return in light of Scripture's teaching
Defend the personal, bodily, and visible return of Christ against views that treat it as merely spiritual or as already fully past
Compose a theological account of Christ's return as judge and redeemer that draws on Scripture and the Reformed confessions

BIB.11.6.3.t: Identify from Scripture that God will raise the dead to life on the last day
Recall that Jesus will come to judge the living and the dead, as Scripture and the Apostles' Creed state
Retell the account of Jesus rising bodily from the dead and state that it shows God's power to raise his people
Identify from Scripture that every person, great and small, will stand before Christ to give an account
Explain that the same body that dies will be raised, changed in its qualities but not replaced by a different body
Describe the contrasts Paul draws between the present body and the resurrection body of believers
Explain what Scripture teaches will happen to believers who are still alive on the last day
Compare the resurrection of the just to honor with the resurrection of the unjust to dishonor
Explain from Scripture that the final judgment will bring every thought, word, and deed into account
Explain why the Father has appointed Christ as judge and how Paul presents Christ's resurrection as proof of the coming judgment
Explain how Paul uses the coming resurrection to instruct believers about grieving and about steadfast labor in the Lord
Analyze the final judgment in terms of its judge, its subjects, and its standard
Trace the hope of bodily resurrection through Old Testament passages and explain how the New Testament develops it
Interpret the separation of the sheep and the goats in its context, explaining how works serve as evidence rather than the ground of acceptance
Analyze Paul's firstfruits argument connecting Christ's resurrection, by the Spirit, to the resurrection of believers
Explain the purpose of the last judgment as the Reformed tradition confesses it, the display of God's mercy and justice
Explain the reasons the Westminster Confession gives for the certainty of the judgment and the hiddenness of its day
Explain how the Reformed tradition relates justification by faith to judgment according to works, including the open acquittal of believers
Analyze Paul's argument about the consequences for the gospel if there is no resurrection of the dead
Compare how the Westminster Standards, the Belgic Confession, and the Heidelberg Catechism state the doctrines of resurrection and judgment
Evaluate views that deny a bodily resurrection or a final judgment, from the Sadducees and early spiritualizing errors to modern universalism, using Scripture
Defend the justice of God in the final judgment against common objections using Scripture
Compose a theological essay that synthesizes resurrection and judgment as the vindication of God and his people, drawing on Scripture and the confessions

BIB.11.6.4.t: Identify heaven as God's promise that his people will live with him forever
Name the things God promises will be gone in the new creation, such as tears, death, sadness, and pain
Retell Jesus' promise that he is preparing a place for his people and will bring them to be with him
Describe the river of the water of life and the tree of life in Revelation 22 as pictures of the life God gives his people
Explain from Revelation 21 that God promises to make all things new, including a new heaven and a new earth
Describe ways the new creation restores the garden of Eden and ways it is even greater
Explain that worshiping and serving God will be at the center of life in the new creation
Explain from Romans 8 that creation itself groans under the curse and will be set free from its bondage to decay
Compare the present creation with the renewed creation by identifying effects of the curse that God will remove
Explain how Scripture connects the hope of the new creation to patterns of holy living in the present
Analyze what will continue and what will be transformed in the new creation, including the embodied life of God's people in a renewed physical world
Trace how the New Jerusalem fulfills the tabernacle and temple as the place where God dwells with his people
Explain the Reformed teaching that the full enjoyment of God, including seeing his face, is the chief blessedness of the redeemed
Explain the biblical teaching on the eternal rest and the gracious rewards God gives his people
Analyze how Revelation 21 and 22 take up the imagery of Isaiah's prophecy of new heavens and a new earth
Construct a biblical theology of the new creation that traces the theme from Genesis to Revelation
Analyze what Scripture means when it says the glory and honor of the nations will be brought into the New Jerusalem
Evaluate popular pictures of heaven, such as disembodied souls floating on clouds, against the biblical teaching of a renewed earth and embodied life
Evaluate the view that God will annihilate and replace the present creation against the Reformed view that he will renew it
Compose an account of the new creation as the goal of redemption in which God is all in all

BIB.11.6.5.t: Recall that the Bible teaches God is holy and good and will punish sin
Name hell as the place the Bible describes where the wicked are punished away from the presence of the Lord
Explain why sin against God is serious using verses that describe His holiness and the wages of sin
Identify passages where Jesus Himself warned about hell
Explain the tradition's teaching that hell is the just penalty for sin against a holy God
Compare the descriptions of eternal life and eternal punishment in Jesus' teaching about the sheep and the goats
Explain from Scripture how Christ delivers His people from the wrath to come by bearing God's judgment in their place
Explain how Paul and Jude connect the reality of coming judgment to urgent and compassionate persuasion of others with the gospel
Analyze the biblical images of hell such as fire, outer darkness, the undying worm, and the lake of fire
Interpret the phrases everlasting punishment and eternal destruction by comparing them with parallel phrases in their context
Distinguish the biblical terms Sheol, Hades, and Gehenna and how each is used in its context
Explain the biblical teaching that punishment in hell differs in degree according to knowledge and deeds
Analyze how the tradition connects the justice of eternal punishment to the holiness and majesty of the God who is sinned against
Construct a careful biblical case for the reality of hell from Old and New Testament texts read in context
Evaluate annihilationism against the biblical language of conscious and unending punishment
Evaluate universalism against biblical texts that teach two final destinies
Formulate a sober and respectful response to common objections to the justice of eternal punishment
Compose a theological essay synthesizing how divine justice and mercy are both displayed in the final separation of the righteous and the wicked

BIB.11.6.6.t: Identify Jesus as the King who reigns over all things now and forever
Recall that God's kingdom will never end
Identify a promise God made through a prophet and show from the Gospels how God kept it
Explain that the Old Testament prophets point forward to Jesus
Define the millennium as the thousand-year reign described in Revelation 20
Describe how the book of Revelation uses pictures such as the Lamb and the lampstands to show truths about Christ and his church
Explain the difference between reading a prophetic passage literally and reading it symbolically
Explain the Reformed principle that clearer passages of Scripture help interpret harder prophetic passages
Analyze how Revelation draws its images from Old Testament prophecy by comparing the beasts of Daniel 7 with the beast of Revelation 13
Compare premillennial, postmillennial, and amillennial views on the timing of Christ's return and the nature of the thousand-year reign
Explain from Romans 14 how the church distinguishes shared core doctrines of the last things from debated matters such as the millennium and treats those who differ with charity
Explain how each major millennial view affirms the certain final victory of Christ over his enemies
Interpret apocalyptic literature according to the features of its genre
Explain the already and not yet of the kingdom and how it shapes the millennial debate
Distinguish historic premillennialism from dispensational premillennialism including the teaching of a pretribulation rapture
Analyze the binding of Satan and the reign of the saints in Revelation 20 in light of Jesus' teaching on binding the strong man
Explain how differing views of the relationship between Israel and the church shape millennial positions
Trace the history of millennial views from early church chiliasm through Augustine and the Reformation to modern dispensationalism
Compare the preterist, historicist, futurist, and idealist approaches to interpreting Revelation
Explain what the Reformed confessions affirm about the last things and what they leave open regarding the millennium
Analyze whether Revelation 20 continues the events of Revelation 19 in sequence or returns to retell the church age
Evaluate date-setting and sensational end-times schemes that read current events into prophecy
Evaluate major interpretations of the seventy weeks prophecy in Daniel 9
Construct a reasoned position on the millennium from the whole of Scripture that engages the strongest arguments of other views

BIB.11.7.1.t: Identify that God made a very good world and made Adam and Eve good
Retell that Adam and Eve disobeyed God by eating the fruit He told them not to eat
Name the serpent as the one who tempted Eve to doubt what God had said
Recite the catechism answers about our first parents' fall and explain them in your own words
Describe the one command God gave Adam in the garden and the warning attached to it
Sequence the events of Genesis 3 from the serpent's question to the hiding and blaming that followed
Explain the covenant of works as the Reformed tradition describes it, including its promise of life and its threat of death
Explain that Adam and Eve were created upright yet able to sin, so the Fall came through their own free choice
Explain Genesis 3:15 as the first promise of a Redeemer who would crush the serpent
Compare how Adam and Eve related to God and to each other before and immediately after their first sin
Trace the steps of temptation in Genesis 3 and James 1 and apply them to a present-day example
Analyze the serpent's words to show how he questioned, distorted, and denied God's word
Analyze the first sin as rooted in unbelief toward God's word and a prideful desire to be like God
Explain what Scripture teaches about Satan as a fallen angel who sinned first and became the tempter of humanity
Explain why the New Testament says sin entered the world through one man even though Eve ate first
Explain how the Reformed tradition holds that God governs all things, including the Fall, yet is not the author of sin
Analyze the problem of how sin could arise in a good creature, evaluating the tradition's appeal to a changeable will and the limits of any explanation
Construct a theological summary of the Fall from a close reading of Genesis 3 in the context of Genesis 1 and 2
Evaluate interpretations that treat Genesis 3 as myth or allegory using the text's genre, genealogies, and later biblical references
Defend the historicity of Adam's fall by showing how Paul's parallel between Adam and Christ depends on it
Synthesize the Fall within Scripture's storyline from the first promise in Genesis to the removal of the curse in Revelation

BIB.11.7.2.t: Identify from David's words in Psalm 51 that people are sinful from the very start of their lives
Name Adam as the first man, whom God appointed to stand for all the people who would come from him
Retell in simple words how Romans 5:12 says sin and death came into the world through one man and spread to everyone
Recite and explain the three parts of original sin named in the catechism: the guilt of Adam's first sin, the lack of original righteousness, and the corruption of the whole nature
Explain the Reformed teaching of federal headship, that God made his covenant with Adam not for himself only but for all his descendants
Explain from Psalm 51:5, Psalm 58:3, Job 14:4, and Ephesians 2:3 why Scripture teaches that people are sinful from birth rather than becoming sinners only by copying bad examples
Distinguish original sin, the sinful condition people are born with, from actual sins, the wrong things people think, say, and do
Explain how Scripture presents Christ as the last Adam who represents his people just as the first Adam represented the human race
Analyze Paul's argument in Romans 5:12-14 that death reigned from Adam to Moses even before the law was given, showing that all were counted guilty in Adam
Interpret the confessional phrase by ordinary generation to explain how the corruption of Adam's nature is passed to all his natural descendants
Explain imputation as God's legal reckoning and compare its three uses in Scripture: Adam's sin to his descendants, the sins of believers to Christ, and Christ's righteousness to believers
Explain why Christ, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, did not inherit Adam's guilt or corruption
Distinguish imputed guilt, which is Adam's sin legally counted to his posterity, from inherited corruption, which is the sinful nature passed down to them
Explain how the Reformed confessions address infants who die in infancy in light of the doctrine of original sin
Compare the federal view of immediate imputation with the realist and mediate imputation views of how Adam's sin relates to his descendants
Construct a doctrine of original sin from a verse by verse study of Romans 5:12-21
Evaluate Pelagian and semi-Pelagian denials of original sin against Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Defend the justice of God in appointing Adam as representative of the race by showing that the same principle of representation grounds salvation in Christ
Write a synthesis of the two Adams that traces condemnation through the first Adam and righteousness and life through Christ across Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15

BIB.11.7.3.t: Identify from Scripture that sin affects every part of a person, including the heart, thoughts, words, and actions
Recall that the Bible describes people apart from God as dead in their sins
Recall from Scripture that no one can save himself by being good enough
Describe what Genesis 6:5 and Jeremiah 17:9 teach about the natural condition of the human heart
Explain the Reformed meaning of total depravity as the corruption of every human faculty rather than people being as wicked as they could possibly be
Explain from Romans 8:7-8 why the natural person cannot please God
Explain why the sinner's inability means that salvation must be entirely of God's grace
Compare the biblical picture of the sinner as spiritually dead with the idea that the sinner is merely sick or weak
Distinguish total depravity from utter depravity by explaining how unregenerate people can still perform outwardly good civil acts
Explain the bondage of the will as the slavery of the fallen person to sin using the words of Jesus and Paul
Interpret Jeremiah 17:9 within its surrounding passage to explain what it teaches about self-deception and the heart
Analyze John 6:44 and 6:65 to show how spiritual inability prevents anyone from coming to Christ unless drawn by the Father
Explain the noetic effects of sin by describing from Scripture how sin darkens the mind's understanding of God
Describe the fourfold state of the human will in innocence, in sin, in grace, and in glory
Distinguish the natural liberty of the will, which is not forced, from the moral inability of the fallen will to choose spiritual good
Trace the historical debates over the will between Augustine and Pelagius and between Luther and Erasmus
Construct a biblical argument for human inability that draws on texts from both Testaments
Evaluate Pelagian, Semi-Pelagian, and Arminian accounts of free will against the Reformed doctrine of total depravity
Defend the doctrine of depravity against the claim that people are basically good using Scripture and reasoned argument
Analyze how total depravity functions as the foundation for the other doctrines of grace, such as unconditional election and effectual calling

BIB.11.7.4.t: Identify sin as disobeying what God says in his Word
Give examples of sin in thoughts, words, and actions from everyday life
Recite the catechism definition of sin and explain in their own words what it means to fall short of God's law and to break it
Distinguish sins of commission from sins of omission using examples from Scripture and daily life
Compare outward sinful acts with the sinful desires and thoughts of the heart from which Jesus says they come
Explain how the tenth commandment shows that God's law forbids sinful desire as well as sinful deeds
Trace the progression from temptation to sinful desire to sinful act described in James
Analyze why breaking one commandment makes a person a lawbreaker of the whole law as given by one Lawgiver
Explain from the Mosaic law and the Psalms why unintentional sins and sins done in ignorance are still sins before God
Interpret Jesus' teaching on anger and lust in the Sermon on the Mount to show that God's law reaches the inner person
Explain from the examples of Joseph and David why all sin is ultimately committed against God himself
Distinguish actual sins from original sin as the Reformed confessions describe actual transgressions proceeding from a corrupt nature
Analyze the main Hebrew and Greek words for sin, such as missing the mark, rebellion, iniquity, transgression, and lawlessness, and what each reveals about its nature
Construct a biblical taxonomy of actual sin that organizes sins by thought, word, and deed and by commission and omission with supporting texts
Analyze how Scripture presents sin at root as a failure to love God and neighbor and as exchanging the worship of God for created things
Evaluate contemporary definitions of wrongdoing, such as harm to others or personal mistakes, against the biblical definition of sin as offense against God's law
Synthesize Paul's teaching that the law functions as a mirror that makes sin known and explain how the Reformed tradition describes this use of the law

BIB.11.7.5.t: Identify from the story of Adam and Eve hiding in the garden that sin separates people from God
Name death as the result and wages of sin
Retell how sin brought pain, hard work, and thorns into God's good world
Recall that sin makes every person guilty and accountable before God
Describe how sin broke relationships between people, using Adam blaming Eve and Eve blaming the serpent as an example
Summarize the misery of the fallen estate as loss of communion with God, being under His wrath and curse, the miseries of this life, death, and the pains of hell
Explain the difference between the guilt that makes a sinner liable to punishment and the pollution that defiles the sinner's nature
Describe how the whole created order has been placed under a curse and groans because of human sin
Compare physical, spiritual, and eternal death as Scripture describes them
Explain how Scripture describes fallen people as held captive under the power of Satan and the fear of death
Explain from biblical examples that sin brings real consequences in this life even when the sinner is forgiven
Analyze how Romans 1 presents the wrath of God as already revealed in the present through His giving people over to their sinful desires
Explain why Scripture presents physical death as an enemy and a penalty that entered through sin rather than a natural part of God's original creation
Distinguish the inward punishments of sin such as blindness of mind and hardness of heart from its outward punishments such as the curse on creation and death itself
Trace how Christ's redemptive work answers each consequence of sin, including guilt, curse, death, and wrath
Explain the Reformed teaching on hell as everlasting separation from God and conscious punishment, the just penalty for sin
Distinguish God's fatherly discipline of believers who sin from the penal condemnation that falls on the unrepentant
Construct a written synthesis organizing the consequences of sin under guilt, corruption, death, and wrath with supporting Scripture and confessional references
Evaluate universalism and annihilationism against the biblical teaching on final judgment
Defend the Reformed position that eternal punishment is just because sin is committed against the infinite majesty and holiness of God

BIB.11.7.6.t: Identify from the Bible that all people everywhere have sinned against God
Recall from David's prayer that every sin is first of all a sin against God
Recite Romans 3:23 and explain in their own words what it teaches about every person
Summarize Paul's teaching that Jew and Gentile alike are under sin and the whole world is accountable to God
Explain the catechism's teaching that every sin deserves God's wrath and curse
Explain why James teaches that breaking one command makes a person guilty of breaking the whole law
Compare biblical examples showing that some sins are more heinous in the sight of God than others
Explain why universal guilt means no one can be declared righteous before God by their own works of the law
Describe how encounters with God's holiness in Scripture reveal the seriousness of sin
Analyze how the person sinning, the party offended, the nature of the act, and its circumstances aggravate the heinousness of a sin
Explain the Reformed reasoning that the gravity of sin is measured by the holiness and majesty of the God against whom it is committed
Explain the confessional teaching that no sin is so great it brings damnation on those who truly repent, using Paul as an example
Interpret Jesus' warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit within its context in the Gospels
Evaluate claims of sinless perfection in this life using the teaching of First John
Distinguish the Reformed teaching that every sin deserves damnation while sins differ in degree from the Roman Catholic division of mortal and venial sins
Evaluate common cultural ways of minimizing sin against the biblical account of its extent and gravity
Construct an explanation of how universal guilt and the varied gravity of sin together show the need for the gospel offered to all

BIB.11.8.1.t: Identify the Holy Spirit as God along with the Father and the Son
Name actions the Holy Spirit does in the Bible, such as teaching and helping, that show He is a Person and not a force
Recall from Ephesians 4:30 that the Holy Spirit can be grieved, which shows He is a Person and not a thing
Describe how the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are each present at the baptism of Jesus
Explain that the Holy Spirit is the third Person of the Trinity, distinct from the Father and the Son yet one God with them
Explain from Acts 5:3-4 why Peter treats lying to the Holy Spirit as lying to God
Explain why the church speaks of the Holy Spirit as He rather than it, using the personal language Jesus uses for the Spirit in John
Compare the personal acts Scripture ascribes to the Spirit, such as teaching, willing, and interceding, with the behavior of an impersonal force
Classify the divine attributes Scripture ascribes to the Spirit, such as eternity, omnipresence, and omniscience, with a supporting passage for each
Analyze how Acts 5:3-4 and 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 each establish the deity of the Holy Spirit
Analyze how the New Testament applies Old Testament words of the LORD to the Holy Spirit as evidence of His deity
Analyze the single divine name in the baptismal formula and the threefold apostolic benediction as evidence that the Spirit shares the Godhead equally with the Father and the Son
Explain the Reformed confession that the Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son, using John 15:26 and the confessional statements
Explain why the Nicene Creed confesses the Spirit as the Lord and giver of life who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, in light of the fourth-century denial of His deity
Distinguish the eternal procession of the Spirit within the Godhead from His sending by the Father and the Son at Pentecost
Construct a scriptural defense of the deity of the Holy Spirit drawing on the names, attributes, works, and worship Scripture gives Him
Evaluate the claim that the Holy Spirit is an impersonal power, as taught by groups such as the Jehovah's Witnesses, using the biblical evidence for His personhood
Evaluate modalism and subordinationism as errors about the Holy Spirit by comparing them with Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Compose a written synthesis of the biblical and confessional teaching that the Holy Spirit is a distinct Person and true, coeternal God with the Father and the Son

BIB.11.8.2.t: Identify from Genesis 1:2 that the Spirit of God was present and at work when God made the world
Recall that the Holy Spirit moved the prophets and apostles to speak and write God's words in the Bible
Retell from Job and the Psalms how the Spirit gives breath and life to people and creatures
Recite Psalm 119:18 as a class prayer asking God for understanding before reading Scripture together
Explain in simple words what it means that all Scripture is breathed out by God
Identify Old Testament passages that show the Spirit speaking through prophets and leaders
Describe how the Spirit continues to sustain and renew creation as part of God's providence
Explain how the Spirit filled Bezalel with skill for crafting the tabernacle and what this shows about the Spirit's work in human abilities
Explain how Jesus' promise that the Spirit would remind the apostles of his words and guide them into truth relates to the writing of the New Testament
Distinguish general revelation from special revelation and describe the Spirit's role in giving special revelation
Compare inspiration, the Spirit's giving of the Word, with illumination, the Spirit's enabling of readers to understand it
Analyze how New Testament writers introduce Old Testament quotations as the speech of the Holy Spirit
Interpret 2 Peter 1:20-21 in its context to explain how human authors were carried along by the Spirit while their own personalities and styles remained
Explain how the Reformed tradition grounds the authority, infallibility, and inerrancy of Scripture in the Spirit's inspiration
Explain the inward testimony of the Spirit as the Westminster Confession describes it and distinguish it from the external evidences for Scripture
Compare verbal plenary inspiration with dictation and partial inspiration views and explain why the Reformed tradition holds the first
Evaluate the Reformed claim that the Holy Spirit speaking in Scripture is the supreme judge over church councils, traditions, and private claims to revelation
Construct a written account of the Spirit's work in creation, providence, and revelation that shows how it fits within the shared work of the Father, Son, and Spirit
Defend the Holy Spirit as the ultimate Author of Scripture against common objections such as human authorship and alleged errors
Evaluate the Reformed teaching that the Spirit's testimony, rather than church authority or rational proofs alone, is the final ground of certainty that Scripture is God's Word

BIB.11.8.3.t: Identify the Holy Spirit as the One who gives new life to God's people
Name the Holy Spirit as the Helper Jesus promised would live with and in his followers
Retell Jesus' conversation with Nicodemus about being born again of the Spirit
Explain how Jesus' picture of the wind shows that the Spirit's work of new birth is real even though it cannot be seen
Describe from Jesus' words how the Spirit bears witness to Jesus and glorifies him
Explain regeneration as the Spirit's work of giving a new heart, using God's promise in Ezekiel
Explain what Scripture means when it says the Holy Spirit dwells in every believer
Describe the spiritual deadness of a person before regeneration and explain from Scripture why no one can cause their own new birth
Compare the person who is in the flesh with the person who is in the Spirit as Paul describes them in Romans 8
Explain how the Spirit's indwelling makes the believer's body a temple and identify what Paul says this means for how the body is used
Explain from Scripture how the Spirit uses the Word of God as the means of regeneration
Trace the Old Testament promises of the Spirit's coming to their fulfillment at Pentecost
Analyze how the Reformed confessions describe the Spirit as the One who unites believers to Christ
Explain the Spirit's role in applying to believers the redemption purchased by Christ
Explain effectual calling and why the Reformed tradition teaches that regeneration precedes and produces faith
Explain the Spirit's baptism of all believers into the one body of Christ
Interpret Paul's description of the indwelling Spirit as a seal and a guarantee of the believer's future inheritance
Analyze how Romans 8 links the Spirit's present indwelling to the future resurrection of the body
Distinguish regeneration from conversion, justification, and sanctification as the Reformed confessions define them
Compare the Reformed monergistic view of regeneration with synergistic and baptismal regeneration views
Defend from Scripture and the confessions the Reformed teaching that the Spirit's regenerating work is necessary for salvation
Evaluate the second blessing view of Spirit baptism against the view that every believer receives Spirit baptism at conversion
Explain the Westminster Confession's teaching on the regeneration of elect infants and others incapable of being outwardly called by the Word
Compose a theological essay that synthesizes regeneration and indwelling within the Spirit's application of Christ's redemption

BIB.11.8.4.t: Identify the Holy Spirit as the helper God gives to make his people more like Jesus
Name the nine fruit of the Spirit listed in Galatians 5:22-23
Pray a short class prayer asking God for the help of the Holy Spirit, based on Jesus' promise in Luke 11:13
Recall from Romans 8:26 that the Holy Spirit helps God's people when they pray
Describe how each fruit of the Spirit can be shown in everyday actions at home and school
Summarize Paul's contrast between walking by the Spirit and gratifying the desires of the flesh
Explain why Scripture calls these qualities the fruit of the Spirit rather than the product of human effort alone
Define sanctification in the words of the Westminster Shorter Catechism and explain its key phrases
Compare grieving the Spirit and quenching the Spirit using the context of each command
Identify the Word, sacraments, and prayer as the ordinary means the Spirit uses to sanctify believers
Apply Paul's call to keep in step with the Spirit to concrete situations of temptation and choice
Distinguish justification from sanctification as the Reformed tradition confesses them
Analyze Romans 8:15-16 to explain the Spirit's witness with the believer's spirit that believers are children of God
Explain mortification and vivification as the Spirit's work in which believers actively put sin to death and live to righteousness
Explain how Scripture's language of the Spirit as seal and guarantee relates to the believer's security
Interpret the Spirit's intercession with groanings in Romans 8:26-27 within the context of Romans 8:18-30
Explain the three grounds of assurance named in the Westminster Confession and the Scripture behind each
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that assurance is attained through ordinary means without extraordinary revelation
Explain the command to be filled with the Spirit within its context of worship and household relationships
Explain the Reformed teaching that a believer's assurance may be shaken and later renewed by the Spirit
Analyze Romans 7:14-25 alongside the Westminster Confession to describe the ongoing conflict between the Spirit and remaining corruption
Evaluate perfectionist claims about the Spirit-filled life in light of Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Evaluate the relationship between the Spirit's witness and the Word as grounds of assurance against claims that rest assurance on private revelation or feeling alone
Construct a summary theology of the Spirit's role in progressive sanctification drawing on key texts and confessional statements
Compare the Reformed confession that believers may be assured of salvation with the Council of Trent's teaching on assurance
Write an essay synthesizing how the Spirit as seal, firstfruits, and guarantee links present sanctification to final redemption

BIB.11.8.5.t: Identify that the Holy Spirit gives gifts to God's people
Name examples of spiritual gifts listed in Scripture such as teaching, serving, giving, and encouraging
Explain, using Paul's picture of the body, how each member's gift helps the whole church
Explain that the Spirit decides which gifts each believer receives and gives them for the common good
Plan and carry out a way to use an ability to serve classmates or the church as Peter commands
Explain from 1 Corinthians 13 why love is greater than any spiritual gift
Explain how miraculous signs in the New Testament confirmed the message of Christ and his apostles
Compare the gift lists in Romans 12, 1 Corinthians 12, Ephesians 4, and 1 Peter 4 by sorting the gifts into speaking, serving, and sign gifts
Explain how Paul's teaching on gifts corrects both pride and envy among believers
Describe how the ministry gifts of Ephesians 4 equip the saints for service and build up the church to maturity
Analyze the foundational and unrepeatable role of the apostles and prophets in the church
Define cessationism and continuationism and state the main question that divides them
Explain how the Westminster Confession connects the completion of Scripture to the cessationist argument
Explain the continuationist case for the ongoing exercise of all spiritual gifts
Compare major interpretations of when the perfect comes in 1 Corinthians 13
Analyze Paul's regulations for tongues and prophecy in public worship including interpretation, order, and edification
Evaluate abuses of spiritual gifts such as Corinthian disorder and prosperity claims using biblical criteria
Evaluate claims of authoritative new revelation against the Reformed teaching on the sufficiency of Scripture and the biblical tests for prophecy
Construct a reasoned position on the cessationist and continuationist debate that engages the key texts and confessions and represents the other view fairly
Propose practical ways for believers who differ on the gifts to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the body of Christ

BIB.11.9.1.t: Identify from Ephesians 1:4 that the Bible says God chose His people in Christ before the world began
Recall that the Bible describes God's choosing of His people as a gift of His love and not something they earned
Recall Jesus' words that His disciples did not choose Him but He chose them
Describe how Jeremiah 1:5 and Psalm 139:16 show that God knew and planned for people before they were born
Summarize election as God's free and gracious choice of a people in Christ to be saved
Explain what Ephesians 1:5 means when it says God predestined His people for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ
Define the terms decree, foreknowledge, predestination, and election using Scripture and the Westminster Standards
Compare election by grace with being chosen on the basis of works using Paul's argument in Romans 11 and 2 Timothy 1
Explain how the Reformed tradition presents election as a ground for the believer's assurance and humility
Explain why the tradition teaches that God ordains the means of salvation as well as its end so that election does not make preaching, prayer, or faith unnecessary
Analyze Romans 9:11-16 to show why the Reformed tradition holds that election is unconditional and not grounded in foreseen faith or works
Distinguish the biblical sense of foreknowledge as God's prior set love from mere foresight of future choices
Interpret Romans 9:13 in light of its Old Testament sources in Genesis 25 and Malachi 1
Explain how election connects to the eternal covenant of redemption in which the Father gives a people to the Son
Explain the doctrine of reprobation as the tradition confesses it, distinguishing God's passing by of some from their condemnation for their own sin
Explain how the tradition holds together election with the free offer of the gospel to all and human responsibility to believe
Explain why the Westminster Confession and the Canons of Dort counsel that predestination be taught with special care and reverence
Summarize the Remonstrant controversy and the Synod of Dort's response on the doctrine of election
Construct a diagram of the golden chain in Romans 8:29-30 that explains each link from foreknowledge to glorification
Evaluate the Arminian view of conditional election against the Reformed view using the relevant biblical texts
Defend the justice and freedom of God in election by responding to the objections Paul answers in Romans 9
Compare the infralapsarian and supralapsarian views of the order of God's decrees and identify which view the Canons of Dort reflect
Compose a theological essay that synthesizes how Scripture and the confessions present election as a ground for humility, assurance, and gospel mission

BIB.11.9.2.t: Identify from Ezekiel that God promises to give His people a new heart in place of a heart of stone
Retell Jesus' conversation with Nicodemus and name being born again as something God does
Explain using Paul's picture of being dead in sin why people cannot make themselves spiritually alive
Describe how Jesus compares the Spirit's work in the new birth to the wind that blows where it wishes
Retell how the Lord opened Lydia's heart to pay attention to Paul's preaching
Recite the Shorter Catechism definition of effectual calling and identify its four parts
Define regeneration as the Spirit's work of giving new spiritual life and distinguish it from a person trying to become better
Compare the outward call of the gospel to all who hear with the inward effectual call of the Spirit
Explain how God uses the preached word as the ordinary means by which He effectually calls and gives new birth
Identify the marks John gives of those who have been born of God
Analyze the tradition's teaching that regeneration is monergistic, the work of God alone in which the sinner is passive
Interpret Paul's language of being made alive together with Christ while dead in trespasses
Analyze Paul's description of the natural person to explain why an inward work of the Spirit is needed for anyone to receive the gospel
Explain from Scripture why the Reformed tradition holds that regeneration precedes and produces faith
Explain why the Canons of Dort place the fault of rejecting the gospel call on the hearer rather than on the gospel or on God
Trace the Old Testament promises of heart renewal to Jesus' teaching on being born of water and the Spirit
Explain how the confessions describe the Spirit as renewing the human will rather than forcing it
Defend from John 3 the necessity of the new birth for seeing and entering the kingdom of God
Construct an account of effectual calling from Paul's teaching in Romans 8 and related texts
Explain the Westminster Confession's teaching on how the Spirit regenerates elect persons who are incapable of being outwardly called by the word
Evaluate the view that a person's decision causes the new birth against the Reformed teaching of sovereign regeneration
Evaluate the doctrine of baptismal regeneration in light of Scripture and the Westminster Confession's teaching on the sacrament and the Spirit
Analyze how Reformed theologians have related effectual calling and regeneration to each other and to the beginning of the order of salvation

BIB.11.9.3.t: Identify faith as trusting Jesus to save us, using a Bible account in which someone trusts Jesus
Name repentance as turning away from sin and turning toward God
Recall Jesus' first gospel preaching that people must repent and believe
Retell the account of Zacchaeus and describe how he turned from his sin to follow Jesus
Recite the Westminster Shorter Catechism answers that define faith in Jesus Christ and repentance unto life
Explain that faith and repentance always go together in the gospel call
Describe the three parts of saving faith as knowledge, assent, and trust
Explain the parts of repentance unto life as seeing sin, grieving over it, hating it, and turning to God with a purpose of new obedience
Distinguish godly sorrow from worldly sorrow by comparing the responses of Peter and Judas after their sins
Compare true saving faith with mere intellectual belief using biblical examples of false or shallow faith
Analyze Psalm 51 as a model of repentance by identifying its confession of sin, appeal to mercy, and resolve to obey
Examine how the apostolic sermons in Acts call hearers to repent and believe and describe how the hearers responded
Analyze faith and repentance as two inseparable sides of one conversion and explain why neither exists without the other
Explain that saving faith rests on Christ alone as its object rather than on the strength or quality of the believer's faith
Explain from Scripture that faith and repentance are gifts worked by the Holy Spirit rather than human achievements
Explain the Reformed teaching that repentance continues throughout the Christian life as the dying of the old self and the rising of the new
Explain why the Reformed confessions teach that repentance is no satisfaction for sin and yet is necessary for every sinner
Prepare a clear explanation of the gospel call to repent and believe that is faithful to Scripture and suited to a younger audience
Analyze how James 2 and Romans 4 together show that living faith is never alone but bears fruit in obedience
Defend the Reformed teaching that faith is the instrument that receives Christ and his righteousness rather than a meritorious work
Compare the Reformed account of repentance with the Roman Catholic sacrament of penance
Compare the Reformed view that faith and repentance flow from regeneration with the Arminian view of faith as preceding new birth
Evaluate easy-believism and works-righteousness as distortions of the biblical teaching on faith and repentance
Compose a biblical and confessional account of conversion as the sinner's Spirit-wrought response of faith and repentance to God's grace

BIB.11.9.4.t: Identify from the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector that God forgave the man who trusted in His mercy rather than in his own goodness
Name Jesus as the One who makes sinners right with God
Recall that God forgives sinners because of what Jesus did and not because of their good works
Retell how God removed Joshua's filthy garments and clothed him in clean ones and explain how this pictures God taking away sin and giving righteousness
Define justification in your own words as God pardoning all our sins and accepting us as righteous only for Christ's sake through faith
Explain how Abraham was counted righteous by believing God's promise and why Paul uses him as the pattern for all believers
Explain justification as a legal declaration by God the judge rather than a change worked inside the believer
Compare justification as a once-for-all declaration with sanctification as a lifelong work of renewal
Describe the benefits that Paul says flow from justification, including peace with God, access to grace, and freedom from condemnation
Explain from Romans 3 how God remains just while justifying sinners through the propitiation Christ made
Explain from Psalm 32 and Romans 4 how Old Testament believers such as David were justified in the same way as New Testament believers
Analyze the double imputation in which believers' sin is counted to Christ and His righteousness is counted to them
Interpret the phrase justified by faith apart from works of the law within the flow of Paul's argument in Romans and Galatians
Distinguish Christ's active and passive obedience and explain how both together form the ground of justification
Explain why faith is the instrument and not the ground of justification
Analyze how James 2 and Paul's letters use the words faith, works, and justify and show how the Reformed tradition reconciles them
Explain how the Reformed tradition teaches that justified believers still confess sin and seek forgiveness without losing their justified status
Evaluate the objection that justification by faith alone encourages careless living using Paul's response in Romans 6
Construct a written defense of justification by faith alone from Romans and Galatians
Evaluate the Council of Trent's view of infused righteousness and faith joined with works against the Reformed doctrine of imputed righteousness
Analyze the role of justification in the Protestant Reformation, including Luther's reading of Romans 1, and explain why it was called the article on which the church stands or falls
Evaluate recent reinterpretations of Paul's phrase works of the law, such as the New Perspective on Paul, in light of the texts and the Reformed confessions

BIB.11.9.5.t: Identify that God makes people who trust in Jesus His own children
Recite the opening words of the Lord's Prayer and name God as the Father in heaven whom Jesus taught His people to address
Describe ways Jesus says the heavenly Father feeds, protects, and gives good gifts to His children
Explain what the words Abba, Father mean and where Paul uses them to describe how God's children may speak to Him
Recite and explain in their own words the catechism definition of adoption as God's free grace receiving sinners into His family with all its privileges
Describe how adoption makes believers brothers and sisters in one household of God and give examples of how Scripture calls them to treat one another
Explain what Romans 8:15-16 teaches about the Spirit of adoption bearing witness with the believer's spirit that they are children of God
Explain how Scripture calls God's adopted children to resemble their Father in love, mercy, and conduct
Compare the standing of a slave with that of a son and heir as Paul and Jesus use these images to describe God's people
Compose a prayer that addresses God as Father following the pattern and boldness Scripture gives His children
Explain how first-century Greco-Roman adoption practice illuminates Paul's use of the term adoption
Interpret what it means that believers are heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, including Paul's link between sharing His sufferings and sharing His glory
Distinguish adoption from justification and regeneration by stating what each act of grace accomplishes for the sinner
Explain how Hebrews 12 interprets the Lord's discipline of believers as evidence of fatherly love rather than punishment
Identify the privileges of God's children listed in the Westminster Confession and match each to a supporting passage of Scripture
