Contrast Christ's eternal sonship by nature with believers' sonship by adoption and explain why the tradition insists on the difference
Trace the theme of God's sonship from Israel as God's firstborn son through the promises to David's heir to its fulfillment in Christ and the church
Construct a theology of adoption from Galatians 4:1-7 that accounts for the Father's timing, the Son's redemption, and the Spirit's witness
Analyze the already and not yet of adoption by comparing present sonship with the future adoption Paul links to the redemption of the body
Evaluate the claim of the universal fatherhood of God by distinguishing God as Creator of all people from God as Father of His adopted children
Explain the historical significance of the Westminster Confession devoting a separate chapter to adoption and assess what that choice contributes to Reformed teaching on salvation
Write a theological argument that defends adoption as a distinct grace of the gospel and shows its relationship to the other benefits of salvation

BIB.11.9.6.t: Identify that God makes His people holy and helps them grow to be more like Jesus
Name the Holy Spirit as the one who helps God's people grow in holiness
Explain that holy means set apart for God and that God calls His people to be holy because He is holy
List the fruit of the Spirit and give an everyday example of each one
Recite the Westminster Shorter Catechism definition of sanctification and explain its key phrases in your own words
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that growth in holiness continues throughout life and is not completed in this life
Explain what Scripture means by dying to sin and living to righteousness
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that believers do good works as the fruit of faith and gratitude rather than to earn salvation
Compare justification as a once-for-all act of God with sanctification as an ongoing work of God
Explain how God's working and the believer's working relate in sanctification using Philippians 2:12-13
Explain how the Reformed tradition understands God's moral law as a rule of life that guides believers in holy living
Apply the command to put off the old self and put on the new self to concrete situations in school and family life
Describe how sanctification extends to the whole person including mind, will, affections, and body
Distinguish definitive sanctification as a decisive break with sin's dominion from progressive sanctification as lifelong growth
Explain how Romans 6 grounds sanctification in the believer's sharing in Christ's death and resurrection
Analyze Romans 7 and Galatians 5 to describe the ongoing conflict between the Spirit and the flesh in the believer
Explain how the Word, prayer, sacraments, and fellowship serve as ordinary means God uses in sanctification
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that believers' good works remain imperfect yet are accepted by God through Christ
Construct a biblical account of the mortification of sin that identifies the Spirit's power and the practical means Scripture commands
Compare the Reformed distinction between justification and sanctification with the Roman Catholic view of justification as infused righteousness
Evaluate perfectionism and antinomianism as opposite errors in light of Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Defend from Scripture the necessity of holiness in the Christian life
Synthesize the biblical teaching on sanctification into an account of growth toward conformity to the image of Christ

BIB.11.9.7.t: Identify Jesus as the Good Shepherd who knows His sheep, keeps them safe, and never loses them
Recall from Romans 8 that nothing in all creation can separate God's people from His love in Christ Jesus
Retell Philippians 1:6 in your own words to show that God finishes the good work He begins in His people
Explain from Scripture that believers are kept by God's power and Christ's prayer rather than by their own strength
Recite Heidelberg Catechism Q1 and explain how belonging to Christ in life and in death gives comfort to His people
Define the perseverance of the saints as the Reformed teaching that those God has effectually called can neither totally nor finally fall away from grace
Describe from the account of Peter's denial and restoration how a believer may fall into serious sin and yet be restored by Christ
Distinguish true believers from those who make only an outward profession of faith using the teaching of Jesus and John
Analyze how the Reformed tradition grounds perseverance in election, Christ's intercession, the indwelling Spirit, and the covenant of grace
Explain how God uses ordinary means such as the Word, the sacraments, and prayer to preserve believers in grace
Identify the three grounds of assurance named by the Westminster Confession as God's promises, the inward evidences of grace, and the witness of the Spirit
Interpret the warning passages of Hebrews and 1 Corinthians in their context as means God uses to keep His people persevering
Explain the Reformed distinction between perseverance as God's keeping and assurance as the believer's knowledge of it which may grow, be shaken, and be renewed
Analyze the tests of genuine faith in 1 John and explain how John intends them to give assurance rather than doubt
Distinguish biblical assurance from presumption and careless security by explaining how the tradition holds that assurance moves believers toward holiness
Compare the Reformed teaching that ordinary believers may attain assurance with the Roman Catholic teaching that such certainty is not ordinarily possible
Evaluate the view that true believers can finally lose their salvation by weighing its arguments against Scripture and the Canons of Dort
Construct a pastoral counsel from Scripture and the confessions for a believer who doubts their salvation

BIB.11.9.8.t: Identify that people who belong to Jesus will one day live with him forever where there is no more sin, sadness, or death
Recall that Jesus rose from the dead with a real body and that God promises to raise the bodies of his people too
Retell Jesus's picture of the vine and the branches to describe what it means to be joined to him
Explain from Scripture that when Jesus returns God will make his people like Jesus in body and character
Describe glorification as the final step in which God completes his work of saving his people
Explain what the New Testament means when it says believers are in Christ using passages from Ephesians, Galatians, and 1 Corinthians
Identify the Holy Spirit and faith as the means by which, in Reformed teaching, believers are joined to Christ
Describe what the Westminster Shorter Catechism teaches that believers receive from Christ at death and at the resurrection
Compare the adoption believers have already received with the future glory Scripture says they still await
Explain how Paul relates present suffering to future glory in Romans 8 and 2 Corinthians 4
Identify the biblical images of union with Christ such as vine and branches, head and body, bridegroom and bride, and cornerstone and building, and explain what each teaches
Explain how union with Christ joins believers to his death, resurrection, and ascension using Romans 6 and Colossians 3
Analyze union with Christ as the source from which every saving benefit flows to the believer
Describe how the Reformed confessions present baptism and the Lord's Supper as signs and seals of union and communion with Christ
Analyze the golden chain of Romans 8:29-30 and explain why Paul speaks of glorification in the past tense
Explain the difference between the intermediate state of the soul after death and the final glory of the resurrection
Distinguish union with Christ from communion with Christ in grace and from the communion of saints as the Westminster Standards define them
Analyze Paul's description of the resurrection body in 1 Corinthians 15 to show both its continuity with and its difference from the present body
Explain the cosmic scope of glorification as Scripture describes creation set free and the new heavens and new earth
Evaluate the teachings of soul sleep and purgatory against Scripture and the Westminster Confession
Construct a written theology of glorification from an exposition of Romans 8:18-30
Explain the Reformed teaching that the glorified will see and fully enjoy God forever
Analyze Calvin's teaching that Christ's benefits avail nothing for us until he is united to us by the Spirit
Evaluate views that deny or spiritualize the bodily resurrection and glorification of believers
Evaluate mystical and merely moral accounts of union with Christ against the Reformed teaching that the union is real, spiritual, and inseparable without merging the believer into deity
Defend in an argued essay the Reformed claim that union with Christ holds justification and sanctification together without confusing them
Synthesize the order of salvation from election to glory as one unbreakable work of grace organized around union with Christ

BIB.1.1.1.t: Identify things in the world that show order and beauty and tell that the Bible says God made them
Explain in simple words that everything that is made has a maker and that God is the maker of all things
Compare a made object such as a house or a watch to the world to show how a made thing points to a maker
Describe cause and effect with everyday examples and explain why the universe, which had a beginning, needs a cause
Explain the argument from design using examples of complexity and purpose in living things
Identify the premises and conclusion in a simple argument for God's existence such as the argument from cause or design
Explain what Romans 1 teaches about God's eternal power and divine nature being clearly seen in creation and why this leaves people without excuse
Explain the moral argument that a shared human sense of right and wrong points to a moral Lawgiver
Analyze the premises of the Kalam cosmological argument and explain how its conclusion follows from them
Distinguish what arguments from nature can show about God from what is known only through Scripture, such as the Trinity and the way of salvation, as the Reformed confessions teach
Interpret the fine-tuning argument by explaining how the precise physical conditions needed for life point to an intelligent designer
Analyze the claim that objective moral values require a moral Lawgiver by comparing it with relativist and naturalist accounts of morality
Summarize Thomas Aquinas's Five Ways and identify which kind of argument each represents
Explain why an infinite regress of causes cannot account for the existence of things and why this points to an uncaused first cause
Analyze how Paul reasons from creation and providence to the true God in his addresses at Lystra and Athens
Explain Anselm's ontological argument and Plantinga's modal version and assess Gaunilo's objection to it
Formulate a response to the objection asking who made God using the doctrine of God's self-existence
Compare the classical use of theistic arguments with the presuppositional approach associated with Cornelius Van Til and explain the Reformed debate over their role
Evaluate Leibniz's argument from contingency as an answer to the question of why there is something rather than nothing
Evaluate the God of the gaps objection and explain why arguments grounded in what is known differ from appeals to ignorance
Construct a cumulative case for theism that combines cosmological, design, moral, and ontological arguments and anticipates major objections

BIB.1.1.2.t: Identify things God made, such as the sky, sun, animals, and trees, that show he is powerful and wise
Name general revelation as God making himself known to everyone through the things he has made
Retell how Psalm 19 describes the heavens speaking of God without words to every land
Describe how God's gifts of rain, seasons, and food show his goodness to all people
Explain that God also makes himself known through the conscience he has written on every human heart
Distinguish general revelation from special revelation by comparing the two halves of Psalm 19
Identify ways God points Job to creation to display wisdom and power far beyond human understanding
Explain that creation shows God's eternal power and divine nature but does not reveal how sinners are saved
Explain from Romans 1 how people suppress the truth about God they know from creation and are therefore without excuse
Analyze how Paul uses what his pagan hearers knew from creation and providence in his speeches at Lystra and Athens
Analyze the limits of general revelation by identifying truths it cannot reveal, such as the Trinity, the incarnation, and the atonement
Explain how the order and intelligibility of the universe reflect the eternal Word through whom all things were made and are sustained
Explain Calvin's teaching on the sense of the divine in every person and on Scripture as spectacles that bring creation's witness into focus
Explain the Reformed understanding of reason as a servant of revelation that works under the authority of Scripture
Explain how the Westminster Standards describe what the light of nature teaches about God, worship, and moral duty and why it leaves people accountable
Compare Thomas Aquinas's view of what reason can know about God apart from Scripture with the Reformed emphasis on the effects of sin on the mind
Compare how classical and presuppositional apologists within the Reformed tradition assess the use of natural theology
Evaluate the twentieth-century debate between Karl Barth and Emil Brunner over whether there is a natural knowledge of God
Write an essay arguing from Scripture and the Reformed confessions why special revelation is necessary to complete what general revelation shows

BIB.1.2.1.t: Identify that God made everything in the world and that the world did not happen by accident
Explain in simple words that some people live as if God is not there and that the Bible calls this foolish
Recall from the catechism that people were made to glorify God and enjoy him forever
Describe what an atheist believes about God and contrast it with what the Bible teaches about God
Explain how the Bible teaches that creation shows everyone that God exists
Explain how Scripture teaches that God's law is written on every human heart so that all people know right from wrong
Compare living for present pleasures with living in light of eternity using Jesus' parable of the rich fool
Explain the Christian hope of bodily resurrection and new creation as the Bible's answer to the secular claim that death is the end
Define secularism and identify secular assumptions in everyday messages such as advertising, media, and popular sayings
Analyze the materialist claim that only matter exists by contrasting it with Scripture's teaching that God is spirit and humans have souls
Interpret how Ecclesiastes portrays life under the sun as meaningless apart from God and connect this to the modern idea of nihilism
Analyze how purely naturalistic accounts of human origins shape views of human worth and contrast them with the doctrine of the image of God
Describe how secularism developed in Western thought from the Enlightenment to the present
Analyze the postmodern claim that there is no absolute truth and compare it with Scripture's claims about truth
Analyze Paul's address at the Areopagus as a model for engaging people who do not share a biblical worldview
Analyze the moral argument that objective moral obligations require a moral lawgiver
Explain how Reformed presuppositional apologetics argues that secular reasoning relies on assumptions about logic, order, and knowledge that only God supplies
Evaluate the core tenets of secular humanism, especially its confidence in human goodness, against Scripture's teaching on human sin
Evaluate how an atheist can account for the problem of evil without a standard of good and compare this with the Reformed doctrine of providence
Defend the claim that meaning, value, and purpose require God by evaluating secular attempts to ground them
Create a written or spoken dialogue that answers a secular objection to Christianity with gentleness and respect
Synthesize an argument showing how the Christian worldview, as the Reformed tradition holds, accounts for rationality, morality, and meaning better than secularism

BIB.1.2.2.t: Identify that some groups use the name of Jesus but teach things about him that the Bible does not say
Recall that the Bible is God's Word and the only rule for what we believe about God
State from John 1 and Colossians 1 that Jesus is truly God who made all things and is not a created being
Explain how Christians test what teachers say by comparing it with Scripture as the Bereans did
Summarize the main teachings of Jehovah's Witnesses about God, Jesus, the Holy Spirit, and salvation
Summarize the main teachings of the Latter-day Saints about God, Jesus, added scriptures, and salvation
Compare the doctrine of the Trinity as confessed by the church with Jehovah's Witness and Latter-day Saint teachings about God
Apply the Reformed teaching that Scripture is complete and sufficient to Latter-day Saint claims of added scripture and Jehovah's Witness reliance on the Watchtower organization
Use biblical texts showing that God is eternal and unchanging to answer the Latter-day Saint teaching that God was once a man
Describe the historical origins of the Latter-day Saints under Joseph Smith and the Jehovah's Witnesses under Charles Taze Russell and their claims to new revelation
Analyze the failed end-time predictions of the Watchtower Society using the biblical test of a true prophet
Analyze the New World Translation renderings of John 1:1 and Colossians 1:16-17 by comparing them with the grammar and context of the original text
Contrast the works-based salvation taught by Jehovah's Witnesses and Latter-day Saints with the Reformed doctrine of justification by grace through faith alone
Explain the biblical evidence for the personhood and deity of the Holy Spirit in response to the Jehovah's Witness teaching that the Spirit is an impersonal force
Demonstrate in a class role play how to present the gospel respectfully to a Jehovah's Witness or Latter-day Saint while defining shared terms carefully
Analyze the Jehovah's Witness claim that Jesus rose as a spirit in light of biblical teaching on his bodily resurrection
Refute Latter-day Saint teaching on many gods and eternal progression from passages affirming that there is only one God
Construct a biblical argument against the Arian Christology of the Jehovah's Witnesses drawing on the church's historic response to Arius
Analyze how the leadership structures of the Watchtower Society and the Latter-day Saint church control interpretation of Scripture and discourage members from testing teaching
Evaluate Jehovah's Witness and Latter-day Saint claims to be restorations of a lost true church against Christ's promise to preserve his church
Defend the doctrine of the hypostatic union against Jehovah's Witness and Latter-day Saint views of the person of Christ
Create a comparison chart of Reformed, Jehovah's Witness, and Latter-day Saint teaching on God, Jesus, the Holy Spirit, salvation, and Scripture with supporting texts

BIB.1.2.3.t: Identify God as a living Person who knows, speaks, and loves rather than a force or energy
Recall that God forbids fortune-telling, magic spells, and asking spirits for help
Explain why Christians pray to God alone instead of trusting lucky charms, crystals, or the stars
Explain that God made the sun, moon, and stars to serve as lights and signs so they cannot rule a person's life the way horoscopes claim
Describe what Jesus meant by calling himself the light of the world and why Christians look to him rather than to an inner light for truth
Explain why Christians avoid Ouija boards, séances, and other attempts to contact the dead using the account of Saul and the medium at Endor
Summarize pantheism and contrast it with the biblical teaching that God created all things and is distinct from his creation
Apply the first commandment to occult practices such as astrology, tarot, and spirit guides
Identify common New Age and occult practices in popular media and match each to the biblical warning that addresses it
Compare the New Age claim that humans are divine with the serpent's promise in Eden and God's refusal to share his glory
Analyze how monism, the belief that all is one, erases the distinctions between God and creation and between good and evil
Contrast the doctrine of reincarnation with the biblical teaching of one life followed by judgment and bodily resurrection
Distinguish the New Age idea of a Christ consciousness from the historical, incarnate Person of Jesus Christ
Connect the ancient Gnostic claim to secret saving knowledge with similar claims in New Age spirituality and Paul's response to them
Explain from Deuteronomy 18 why God forbids divination and how he instead provides guidance through his prophets and now his completed Word
Analyze how the apostles confronted sorcery and spirit possession in Acts and what these accounts show about Christ's authority
Contrast the New Age concept of karma with the biblical doctrine of salvation by grace through faith
Evaluate the moral relativism of New Age spirituality against the biblical teaching of objective truth and God's moral law
Evaluate the Eastern mystical roots of popular meditation and yoga practices by contrasting emptying the mind with biblical meditation on God's Word
Construct a defense of the personal, triune God against impersonal views of the divine by showing how eternal love and communication require Persons
Develop a biblical account of spiritual warfare regarding the occult that rests on Christ's victory and avoids both fear and fascination
Design a respectful gospel conversation with someone who holds New Age beliefs modeled on Paul's address at Athens

BIB.1.2.4.t: Identify from Scripture that God saves people by his grace through faith in Jesus and not by the good things they do
Name Jesus as the one mediator between God and people and the one through whom Christians pray to God
Recall that the Bible is God's Word and the highest authority for what Christians believe, above any church leader
Describe how to speak kindly and truthfully with Roman Catholic neighbors while naming that Protestants and Catholics disagree about how a person is saved
Identify beliefs that Protestants and Roman Catholics hold in common, such as the Trinity and the deity and resurrection of Christ, using the Apostles' Creed
Summarize the five solas of the Reformation and a Scripture passage that supports each one
Explain the difference between salvation by grace alone and salvation by grace plus works using Paul's argument in Romans
Compare the repeated sacrifices of the Old Testament priests with the once-for-all sacrifice of Jesus as High Priest
Describe the main events of the Protestant Reformation, including Martin Luther's protest against indulgences and his recovery of justification by faith
Apply the sufficiency of Scripture by testing a church teaching against what the Bible says
Analyze the difference between the Reformed view of Scripture as the supreme authority and the Roman Catholic view of Scripture, Tradition, and the Magisterium together
Compare the Roman Catholic view of justification as a lifelong process with the Reformed view of justification as God's once-for-all legal declaration
Compare Roman Catholic teaching on the Mass as a sacrifice and on transubstantiation with Reformed teaching on the Lord's Supper as a remembrance and sign of Christ's finished work
Explain why the Reformed tradition does not receive the Apocrypha as part of the canon of Scripture
Compare the seven sacraments of Roman Catholic teaching with the two sacraments confessed in the Reformed tradition
Evaluate the Roman Catholic doctrines of purgatory and indulgences in light of the sufficiency of Christ's atonement
Summarize the historical context and main decrees of the Council of Trent on Scripture, tradition, and justification
Analyze the Roman Catholic practice of praying to Mary and the saints, including the distinction between veneration and worship, in light of Christ's sole mediation
Evaluate the doctrines of papal primacy and papal infallibility, including the interpretation of Jesus' words to Peter
Defend the Reformed doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness against the Roman Catholic doctrine of infused righteousness
Evaluate the Marian dogmas of the Immaculate Conception and the Assumption against the teaching of Scripture
Evaluate whether modern ecumenical statements such as the 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification resolve the Reformation disagreement over the gospel
Create a gracious plan for a conversation with a Roman Catholic friend that explains justification by faith alone from Scripture

BIB.1.3.1.t: Retell that the women found the tomb of Jesus empty on the first day of the week
Name people who saw Jesus alive after He rose, such as Mary Magdalene, Peter, and the disciples
Identify ways the risen Jesus showed His followers that He had a real body, such as eating fish and inviting them to touch Him
Sequence the events of Easter morning using the Gospel accounts
Describe how the disciples changed from hiding in fear to preaching boldly in public after the resurrection
Explain why the willingness of the apostles to suffer for their testimony shows that they sincerely believed they had seen the risen Jesus
Explain why the Gospels naming women as the first witnesses of the empty tomb supports the honesty of the accounts
Compare the swoon theory with the Gospel details about the death and burial of Jesus
Explain why Paul teaches that the Christian faith depends on whether Jesus actually rose from the dead in history
Explain what the early creed in 1 Corinthians 15 records and why its early date matters as historical evidence
Analyze the minimal facts approach by identifying the facts about the death and resurrection of Jesus that most historians accept and how they point to the resurrection
Analyze how the conversions of the skeptic James and the persecutor Paul function as evidence for the resurrection
Analyze how the rapid rise of the church in Jerusalem and the shift to worship on the first day of the week point to the reality of the resurrection
Evaluate the stolen body theory using the account of the guarded tomb and the report of the guards
Apply historical criteria such as multiple attestation, early testimony, and enemy attestation to the resurrection accounts
Evaluate the hallucination theory in light of the group appearances and physical encounters reported in the New Testament
Defend the Reformed confession of a bodily resurrection against spiritualized interpretations using the biblical texts
Compare how evidential and presuppositional approaches within the Reformed tradition use historical evidence for the resurrection
Construct a written historical case for the resurrection that presents the evidence and answers major alternative theories

BIB.1.3.2.t: Identify a miracle as a wonderful work that only God can do, using the story of Jesus calming the storm
Retell a miracle in which Jesus showed his power over sickness, nature, or death
Explain from John's Gospel that the signs of Jesus were written down so that readers would believe he is the Christ, the Son of God
Distinguish a true miracle from a magic trick, using the account of Pharaoh's magicians admitting the finger of God
Explain two purposes of Jesus' miracles, showing compassion and proving his authority, using specific Gospel accounts
Classify the miracles of Jesus as nature, healing, exorcism, or raising the dead and explain what each kind reveals about his authority
Identify the main periods when miracles cluster in Scripture and explain how they accompanied and confirmed new revelation from God
Define a miracle using the biblical terms signs, wonders, and mighty works and distinguish it from God's ordinary providence as the Reformed tradition describes it
Explain how Jesus appealed to his own works as testimony to his identity and his unity with the Father
Analyze how Nicodemus and the man born blind reasoned from Jesus' signs to the conclusion that he came from God
Analyze the seven signs of John's Gospel and explain what each reveals about who Jesus is
Explain from Scripture why witnessing miracles does not by itself produce faith, connecting this to the Reformed teaching on the inward work of the Spirit
Compare the Reformed cessationist position on revelatory miracles with continuationist views and explain how each affects the use of miracles in apologetics
Evaluate claimed wonders in other religions and movements using the biblical tests for counterfeit signs
Explain how Scripture presents the Resurrection as the culminating sign on which the credibility of the other miracles depends
Evaluate the claim that science disproves miracles by distinguishing natural laws as descriptions of God's ordinary providence from philosophical naturalism
Analyze David Hume's argument against miracles and construct a reasoned response to its premises about uniform experience and testimony
Evaluate the role and limits of miracles as evidence by comparing evidentialist and presuppositional approaches in light of Scripture's teaching on faith and sight
Construct a written or oral argument from the biblical miracles that answers a common objection with gentleness and respect

BIB.1.3.3.t: Identify that God knows the future and tells his people what will happen
Name Bethlehem as the town where God promised long before that Jesus would be born
Retell God's first promise of a Savior in the garden and explain how Jesus kept that promise
Match the promise of a virgin-born child in Isaiah to its fulfillment in the birth of Jesus
Explain the biblical test of a true prophet, that his word from the Lord always comes to pass
Summarize the Old Testament prophecies of the crucifixion and match each detail to its Gospel account
Explain how Jesus fulfilled the Passover as the Lamb of God
Compare vague predictions such as horoscopes with specific biblical prophecies such as the naming of Cyrus
Explain how Jesus taught that the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms point to his suffering and resurrection
Explain from Scripture why God's past fulfillment of prophecy gives grounds for trusting his unfulfilled promises such as Christ's return
Explain how Jesus fulfilled Moses' promise of a coming prophet like him
Construct a chart of major Messianic prophecies with their New Testament fulfillment citations
Distinguish direct predictive prophecy from typological fulfillment using New Testament examples
Analyze the probability argument that one man fulfilling many specific Messianic prophecies is beyond chance, and identify its strengths and limits
Interpret Daniel's vision of the statue and the succession of empires in light of later history
Analyze Ezekiel's prophecy against Tyre in relation to the historical record of its destruction
Analyze the Suffering Servant passage and evaluate the claim that the Servant is the nation of Israel rather than the Messiah
Analyze Daniel's seventy weeks prophecy and compare the main interpretations of its timing for the Messiah
Evaluate the objection that Jesus deliberately arranged his life to fulfill prophecy by identifying prophecies outside human control
Evaluate the objection that biblical prophecies were written after the events they describe
Evaluate the objection that New Testament writers misused Old Testament texts by examining how they cite prophecy in context
Evaluate the role of the argument from prophecy within the Reformed teaching that full persuasion of Scripture's authority comes from the inward work of the Holy Spirit
Construct a reasoned argument for the divine origin of Scripture from predictive prophecy

BIB.1.3.4.t: Identify the Bible as one book made up of many smaller books that God gave through people who wrote down his words
Retell the account of King Jehoiakim burning Jeremiah's scroll and God having his words written down again
Describe how scribes copied God's Word by hand onto scrolls with great care
Distinguish a true account of real events from a made-up story using Luke's and Peter's descriptions of how they wrote
Recite Bible verses that promise God's Word will endure forever
Explain what an ancient manuscript is and that thousands of handwritten copies of the Bible still exist today
Identify the materials and forms ancient writers used, including papyrus, parchment, scrolls, and codices
Describe archaeological discoveries that confirm people and places named in the Bible, such as the Pool of Siloam, the Pilate Stone, and the Tel Dan inscription
Explain that the Bible was first written in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek and that the church translates it into the common language of every people
Compare the number of surviving manuscripts and the time gap to the earliest copies for the New Testament with other ancient works such as those of Homer, Caesar, and Tacitus
Describe the methods Jewish scribes and the Masoretes used, such as counting letters and words, to preserve the Hebrew text
Analyze the telephone game objection by explaining how many independent lines of copies allow scholars to compare manuscripts and recover the original wording
Explain the significance of the Dead Sea Scrolls by comparing the Great Isaiah Scroll with the Masoretic Text copied about a thousand years later
Explain why the New Testament writings being composed within the lifetime of eyewitnesses supports their historical accuracy
Describe the history of the English Bible from Wycliffe and Tyndale through the King James Version to modern translations
Classify textual variants by type, such as spelling, word order, and meaningful and viable readings, and explain how few affect meaning
Distinguish differences between English translations from variants that arose in the copying of manuscripts
Apply basic principles of textual criticism to bracketed passages noted in English Bibles such as the longer ending of Mark and the account of the adulterous woman
Construct a case for the reliability of the biblical text using bibliographical, internal, and external tests
Explain the Reformed teaching that Scripture's authority rests on God its author and how external evidences relate to the Spirit's witness
Distinguish the inspiration of the original writings from God's providential preservation of the text through copies as the Westminster Confession teaches
Evaluate Bart Ehrman's argument that textual variants undermine confidence in the New Testament
Evaluate conspiracy claims that the church altered the Bible at Nicaea using manuscripts that predate the council, such as P52, P66, and P75
Compare the Textus Receptus and modern critical texts by explaining the Byzantine and Alexandrian manuscript families behind them

BIB.1.4.1.t: Identify when a simple statement does not make sense because it says two opposite things, such as 'I never say anything'
Explain in their own words why a spring cannot pour out fresh and salty water at once and connect this to words that disagree with themselves
Retell Proverbs 26:4-5 in their own words as teaching that a wise answer neither copies foolish thinking nor leaves it unanswered
Explain from the parable of the wise and foolish builders how a way of thinking built on a weak foundation falls when it is tested
Practice asking 'How do you know that?' and 'Does that fit with what you said before?' in a classroom role-play
Explain from Romans that Scripture teaches all people know God and his moral law, so those who deny him still rely on truths that come from him
Identify examples of 'borrowed capital' in which a person who denies God still appeals to right and wrong, logic, or meaning
Explain the two steps of an internal critique drawn from Proverbs 26:4-5, standing on another view's assumptions for argument's sake and then showing where they lead
Analyze a self-refuting claim such as 'There is no absolute truth' or 'Only science gives knowledge' to show how it undermines itself
Distinguish among three kinds of internal failure in a worldview, logical contradiction, arbitrariness, and inconsistency between stated belief and actual practice
Explain Francis Schaeffer's method of 'taking the roof off' by pressing a person's presuppositions toward their logical conclusions
Analyze how a worldview that denies God struggles to account for calling anything truly evil when it raises the problem of evil as an objection
Explain why the Reformed tradition pairs an internal critique of unbelief with presenting the Christian position on its own terms
Apply questioning to expose an arbitrary claim by asking what basis the claim has within the speaker's own system of belief
Evaluate a common charge of contradiction against Christianity by testing whether the Christian worldview is consistent on its own terms
Construct an internal critique of materialism showing how it undermines confidence in reason and moral responsibility
Evaluate postmodern relativism for self-referential inconsistencies in its claims about truth and meaning
Critique a non-Christian worldview expressed in a film, novel, or essay by identifying where its author or characters live inconsistently with its stated assumptions
Compare the reductio ad absurdum approach of presuppositional apologetics with classical and evidential approaches and explain why Cornelius Van Til emphasized it
Create a written or spoken dialogue that carries out an internal critique with gentleness and respect and then presents the Christian answer

BIB.1.4.2.t: Identify that God made an orderly world where things like day and night and the seasons keep happening the same way
Recall that God never changes and always tells the truth
Explain that people are able to think, count, and learn because God made them in His image
Identify everyday examples showing that all people, including those who do not believe in God, rely on logic, right and wrong, and the regularity of nature
Describe how Scripture teaches that God holds all things together so that nature follows regular patterns
Explain that laws of logic, such as the rule that a statement cannot be both true and false at the same time and in the same way, are the same everywhere and do not change
Compare a universe produced by chance with a universe governed by God's providence in how each explains order and predictability
Explain the Reformed teaching from Romans 1 that all people know God through creation yet suppress that knowledge
Explain the idea of borrowed capital, the claim that unbelievers must use logic, morality, and the uniformity of nature that only the Christian worldview accounts for
Identify the preconditions of intelligibility, including the laws of logic, moral absolutes, the uniformity of nature, and the reliability of human reasoning
Distinguish a transcendental argument, which asks what must be true for any experience or reasoning to be possible, from evidential arguments that reason from particular facts
Explain the problem of induction and how the doctrine of providence accounts for the expectation that the future will resemble the past
Connect the universal, invariant, and abstract character of the laws of logic to God's nature as unchanging, everywhere present, and truthful
Explain why the Reformed tradition holds that binding moral absolutes require a personal and holy lawgiver whose law is written on the human heart
Analyze why a strictly materialist account of reality cannot ground the universal and immaterial laws of logic
Explain how Proverbs 1:7 and Colossians 2:3 support the presuppositional claim that all true knowledge depends on God and is found in Christ
Construct the transcendental argument in premise and conclusion form, showing that the Christian God is the necessary precondition of intelligibility
Evaluate the claim of the impossibility of the contrary, which holds that the denial of the Christian worldview undermines the very reasoning used to deny it
Evaluate common objections to the transcendental argument, such as the charge of vicious circularity and the claim that logic and nature need no further explanation
Defend in a written or oral argument the Reformed apologetic claim that the triune God of Scripture is the necessary foundation for rational thought, presented with gentleness and respect
Explain how Cornelius Van Til and Greg Bahnsen developed the transcendental argument, including the Creator and creature distinction and the idea that human knowledge is analogical to God's knowledge
Explain how Van Til used the doctrine of the Trinity to address the philosophical problem of the one and the many
Compose an essay that presents and assesses Van Til's transcendental method of apologetics

BIB.1.4.3.t: Identify the Bible as God's Word that tells us what is true
Explain that God decides what is true and right because He made everything and owns everything
Identify that people believe different things about who made the world and who is in charge of it
Describe a worldview as the set of beliefs a person uses to understand everything, using the picture of looking through glasses
Identify the big worldview questions of origin, meaning, morality, and destiny and state the Bible's answer to each
Explain from Scripture that every person trusts something as a final authority, either God or something in creation such as the self
Compare the biblical account of human origin and purpose with a naturalistic account that sees people as products of chance
Explain the Reformed teaching that Scripture is to be believed on the authority of God its author rather than on the testimony of any person or church
Use Scripture as the standard to test a claim heard in everyday life or media
Define a presupposition and identify the presuppositions underlying sample statements and arguments
Explain from Scripture why the Reformed tradition holds that no one reasons from a neutral standpoint
Explain how Proverbs 1:7 and Colossians 2:3 present the fear of the Lord as the starting point of true knowledge
Explain from Romans 1 why the Reformed tradition teaches that evidence alone does not persuade unbelievers who know God yet suppress the truth
Explain how the distinction between Creator and creature makes God's word the final authority over human reasoning
Explain why an ultimate authority cannot be proven by appeal to any higher authority, using God swearing by Himself as an example
Analyze a contemporary cultural work to identify its underlying worldview and the ultimate authority it assumes
Construct a diagram that traces a chain of justification for a belief back to the ultimate authority it rests on
Classify major philosophical positions such as rationalism, empiricism, and autonomous individualism by the ultimate authority each assumes
Compare the presuppositional approach to the authority of Scripture with classical and evidential apologetic approaches regarding where reasoning begins
Evaluate the charge of circular reasoning by distinguishing vicious circularity from the unavoidable circularity of any ultimate authority

BIB.2.1.1.t: Identify that God made the world and everything in it and called it very good
Retell how Adam and Eve disobeyed God in the garden and name what happened as a result
Recall that God sent Jesus to rescue sinners
Describe what Scripture says God will do when he makes all things new
Summarize the Bible's big story using the four parts of creation, fall, redemption, and restoration
Describe how God made people in his image and gave them work to do in his good creation
Explain from Genesis 3 and Romans 5 why all people need a Rescuer
Compare the Garden of Eden with the New Jerusalem to show how the end of the story answers its beginning
Explain how the Fall broke humanity's relationship with God, with one another, and with the rest of creation
Explain how Scripture uses the promise of final restoration to direct believers in how to respond to suffering
Analyze how individual Bible narratives fit within the larger arc of creation, fall, redemption, and restoration
Interpret Genesis 3:15 as the first promise of redemption and trace its fulfillment in Christ
Analyze examples of present-day brokenness in people, society, and nature as consequences of the Fall
Explain how God's single plan of redemption unfolds consistently from Genesis to Revelation
Explain why the person and work of Christ stand at the center of the redemption movement of the biblical story
Distinguish the biblical hope of a restored physical creation from views that picture salvation as escape from the material world
Construct an annotated timeline of the biblical metanarrative that places key events and supporting texts in each of the four movements
Evaluate the accounts other worldviews give of origin, problem, solution, and destiny against the biblical metanarrative
Defend the Reformed position that a historical Fall is necessary to the logic of the gospel
Analyze how the Westminster Confession and Heidelberg Catechism organize their teaching around the movements of the biblical story
Develop a written explanation of how the Reformed tradition understands the Christian's calling in the present age within the four-part story

BIB.2.1.2.t: Identify a covenant as a special promise God makes with his people and always keeps
Retell God's promise to Noah never again to flood the whole earth and name the rainbow as its sign
Recall that God promised Abraham a large family, a land, and that all nations would be blessed through him
Retell how God gave Israel the Ten Commandments at Mount Sinai after rescuing them from Egypt
Recall God's promise to David that a king from his family would rule forever
Name the six major biblical covenants in order and match each to the person through whom God made it
Give examples from the covenant stories that show God keeping his promises even when his people were unfaithful
Explain why God's rescue of Israel from Egypt came before the giving of the law at Sinai and what this shows about the relationship between God's promise and his commands
Describe the promise God spoke in the garden that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent and explain why the Reformed tradition sees it as the first announcement of the gospel
Identify the parties, promises, obligations, and sign in a given covenant passage
Describe the command and warning God gave Adam in the garden and explain why the Reformed tradition calls this arrangement the covenant of works
Explain what Jesus meant at the Last Supper when he called the cup the new covenant in his blood
Compare the old covenant written on tablets of stone with the new covenant promise of the law written on the heart
Identify the sign of each covenant and explain what each sign pointed to
Explain the Noahic covenant as God's commitment to preserve the created order and human life until the end of the age
Describe the covenant ceremony of Genesis 15 and explain what God passing alone between the pieces reveals about who guarantees the promise
Analyze the conditional and unconditional elements in the Abrahamic, Mosaic, and Davidic covenants
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that God relates to people by way of covenant as an act of voluntary condescension
Explain how Paul connects the promise to Abraham's offspring with Christ and with gentile believers
Trace how the blessings and curses of the Mosaic covenant explain Israel's exile and the promise of restoration
Explain the purposes of the Mosaic law according to Paul, including revealing sin and guarding God's people until Christ came
Trace the Davidic covenant promise through the Psalms and Prophets to its fulfillment in Jesus as the son of David
Explain the Reformed distinction between the covenant of works and the covenant of grace using Paul's comparison of Adam and Christ
Compare the structure of the Sinai covenant with ancient Near Eastern suzerain and vassal treaties
Construct a chart tracing the progressive revelation of God's promises from the Adamic to the new covenant
Explain how the Reformed tradition understands the sacraments as signs and seals of the covenant of grace, including the link it draws between circumcision and baptism
Analyze how Hebrews uses Jeremiah's new covenant prophecy to argue that the first covenant has become obsolete
Evaluate how covenant theology and dispensationalism differ in their account of continuity between Israel and the church
Defend from Scripture the Reformed teaching that one covenant of grace is administered differently under the law and under the gospel
Write a theological argument showing how Christ is the mediator and fulfillment of each biblical covenant

BIB.2.1.3.t: Identify that a shadow shows the shape of something real but is not the real thing, as a picture of how some Old Testament things point ahead to Jesus
Retell the story of the Passover and name Jesus as the Lamb of God whom the Passover lamb pointed to
Describe how God saved Noah's family through the ark and how the New Testament uses this to picture salvation in Christ
Connect the manna God gave Israel in the wilderness to Jesus' teaching that he is the true Bread of Life
Explain from Jesus' own words that the whole Old Testament speaks about him
Describe how the layout and furniture of the tabernacle teach God's holiness and the need for a God-given way to approach him
Define type, antitype, shadow, and substance using the language of Colossians and Hebrews
Compare the bronze serpent lifted up in the wilderness with Jesus lifted up on the cross
Compare the life of Joseph with the life of Christ, tracing the pattern of rejection, suffering, exaltation, and the saving of others
Classify biblical types as persons, events, or institutions and give an example of each
Explain how Paul presents Adam as a type of Christ, the head of a new humanity
Explain the Reformed teaching that Old Testament believers were saved through faith in the promised Christ whom the types and sacrifices foreshadowed
Analyze the criteria for a valid biblical type, including real history, genuine correspondence, escalation in the fulfillment, and warrant from Scripture
Compare the priesthood of Aaron with the priesthood of Christ, showing where Christ fulfills and surpasses it
Explain why Hebrews presents Melchizedek as a type of Christ's eternal priesthood
Explain how the temple finds its fulfillment in Christ's body and in the people of God joined to him
Explain why the ceremonial laws that served as types are no longer binding now that Christ has fulfilled them
Analyze how Hebrews argues that the repeated animal sacrifices revealed their own insufficiency and pointed to Christ's single sacrifice
Construct a study of the Day of Atonement that traces each element of the ritual to its fulfillment in Christ
Analyze how the Gospels present Jesus as the true Israel who relives and fulfills Israel's exodus and wilderness testing
Evaluate the difference between reading a passage typologically and allegorizing it, using examples from church history and Scripture
Defend the Reformed tradition's Christ-centered reading of the Old Testament against objections, using the New Testament's own interpretation
Synthesize the New Testament's greater than pattern to show how Jesus is the greater Moses, David, Solomon, and Jonah who fulfills the offices of prophet, priest, and king

BIB.2.1.4.t: Identify Jesus as the King whom the Bible says rules over all things
Retell the Bible story of Jesus announcing that the kingdom of God has come near
Recall that Jesus went up to heaven and now reigns at the right hand of God the Father
Describe what the Bible says the world will be like when Jesus returns and makes all things new
Explain from Scripture why sadness, sickness, and death still exist even though Jesus is King
Summarize the parables of the mustard seed, the leaven, the hidden treasure, and the pearl and state what each teaches about the kingdom
Explain that Christ defeated sin and Satan at the cross while believers still struggle against sin until he returns
Explain the meaning of the petition Your kingdom come in the Lord's Prayer using the catechism's answer
Compare the kingdom of God with earthly kingdoms in its king, its people, the way it grows, and how long it lasts
Identify Old Testament prophecies of an everlasting kingdom and explain how the Gospels present Jesus as their fulfillment
Explain what the New Testament teaches about how a person enters the kingdom of God through new birth, repentance, and faith
Define the already and not yet of the kingdom and classify New Testament kingdom statements as describing its present or future aspect
Explain how Paul presents Christ's resurrection as the firstfruits of the coming resurrection and the beginning of the new creation
Interpret Jesus' miracles and exorcisms as signs that the kingdom of God was breaking into the present age
Explain how the New Testament describes the Holy Spirit as the down payment and guarantee of the inheritance still to come
Analyze how the New Testament letters frame believers' present suffering in light of future glory
Analyze how the Reformed confessions relate the church to the kingdom, including the visible church as the kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ
Explain the Reformed teaching on Christ's kingly office in subduing, ruling, and defending his people and restraining his enemies
Explain the biblical and confessional teaching on the consummation of the kingdom at Christ's return, the final judgment, and the handing over of the kingdom to the Father
Evaluate the errors of an over-realized view that expects perfection now and an under-realized view that treats the kingdom as wholly future
Defend from the Gospels and Acts the spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom against expectations of a political or nationalistic kingdom
Construct a biblically grounded account of Christian engagement in culture shaped by the already and not yet of the kingdom
Compare the amillennial, postmillennial, and premillennial readings of Revelation 20 and how each relates the present and future kingdom
Synthesize the hope of the final consummation with the call to present faithfulness in a written argument drawn from Scripture and the confessions

BIB.2.2.1.t: Name Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John as the four Gospels that tell about the life of Jesus
Retell a story about Jesus that appears in more than one Gospel, such as the feeding of the five thousand
State that the Gospel writers wrote true accounts of Jesus as the Holy Spirit guided them
Identify key words that John repeats in his Gospel, such as light, life, love, and believe
Explain that Matthew, Mark, and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels because they see the life of Jesus together and share many of the same events
Explain the purpose John gives for writing his Gospel
Explain how John's Gospel emphasizes that Jesus is God the Son, equal with the Father
Compare parallel accounts of the same event in Mark and Luke, noting details each writer includes or leaves out
Identify the seven I AM statements in John and explain what each reveals about Jesus
Identify the signs recorded in John's Gospel and explain how John uses them to point to who Jesus is
Describe the Synoptic Problem as the question of how to explain the close agreements and differences in wording and order among Matthew, Mark, and Luke
Interpret the Prologue of John in light of Genesis 1, explaining its teaching that the eternal Word became flesh
Analyze how the audience and purpose of each Gospel shape its emphases, such as Matthew's fulfillment quotations and Mark's explanations of Jewish customs
Explain the main proposed solutions to the Synoptic Problem, including Markan priority, the two-source hypothesis, and the view that Matthew was written first
Use a Gospel synopsis to classify passages as triple tradition, double tradition, or material unique to one Gospel
Compare John's chronology and settings with those of the Synoptics, such as the timing of the temple cleansing and Jesus' visits to Jerusalem
Construct a harmony of a single event across all four Gospels and explain how apparent differences in detail can be reconciled
Evaluate source theories about the Gospels in light of the Reformed teaching that Scripture has both genuine human authors and a divine origin
Evaluate the unique theological contribution of John's Gospel, including its teaching on eternal life, the Spirit as Helper, and believing in the Son
Defend the reliability of the Gospel record by explaining the value of four distinct but harmonious witnesses
Synthesize the distinct portraits of Christ in the four Gospels into a unified account of his person as truly God and truly man

BIB.2.2.2.t: Retell that Jesus went up to heaven and promised to send the Holy Spirit to his followers
Identify the sound of wind and the tongues of fire as signs that the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost
Name Peter and Paul as leaders in the early church who told others about Jesus
Recall that the church began in Jerusalem and describe how the first believers learned, prayed, ate together, and shared what they had
Summarize how the gospel spread from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth as Jesus said it would
Describe how the church chose seven men to care for widows so the apostles could keep preaching and praying
Explain what happened at Pentecost, including Peter's sermon and how the crowd responded
Describe how the Bereans examined the Scriptures and practice checking a teaching against a Bible passage in class
Retell the witness and death of Stephen and the ministry of Philip in Samaria and to the Ethiopian official
Compare Peter's boldness before the council after Pentecost with his fear when he denied Jesus
Describe the conversion and calling of Saul and explain how it changed the direction of his life
Trace Paul's missionary journeys and his voyage to Rome on a map of the Roman world
Construct a timeline of the major events in Acts from the Ascension to Paul's imprisonment in Rome
Analyze the conflict over circumcision and how the Jerusalem Council resolved it
Explain how the apostles' preaching in Acts centers on their witness to the death and resurrection of Jesus
Interpret the significance of Peter's vision and the conversion of Cornelius for the inclusion of Gentiles in the church
Explain how persecution scattered believers and carried the gospel into new regions
Explain Acts as the second volume of Luke's work and identify its purpose from its prologue
Compare how Paul shaped his message for a synagogue audience and for Gentile philosophers in Athens
Explain how Peter reads Pentecost as the fulfillment of Joel's prophecy and how it contrasts with Babel
Describe the offices of apostle, elder, and deacon in Acts and explain how the Reformed tradition draws its church order from them
Analyze the accounts of baptism and the breaking of bread in Acts, including household baptisms, and explain how the Reformed confessions use them
Evaluate which events in Acts describe a unique apostolic era and which prescribe practice for the church today
Defend from the text the view that the risen Christ by his Spirit is the primary actor in the growth of the church in Acts
Synthesize how Acts traces the movement from a Jerusalem community of Jewish believers to a church of Jews and Gentiles across the empire

BIB.2.2.3.t: Identify that some books of the Bible are letters written to churches and to people
Name Paul, Peter, James, and John as people who wrote letters found in the New Testament
Recall that New Testament letters were sent both to whole churches and to individual people
Identify the sender, the recipients, and the greeting in the opening verses of a New Testament letter
Describe the usual parts of a New Testament letter, including the opening, thanksgiving, body, and closing
Explain from the letters themselves that the apostles wrote to teach, correct, and encourage churches
Distinguish the letters of Paul from the General Epistles by their authors and recipients
Locate the cities and regions that received New Testament letters on a map of the Roman world
Compare a personal letter such as Philemon with a letter written to a church such as Ephesians
Identify co-senders named in letter openings, such as Timothy and Silvanus, and explain their connection to the author
Outline the flow of thought of a short New Testament letter section by section
Explain how New Testament letters were carried, read aloud to congregations, and shared among churches
Analyze the occasional nature of the epistles by using clues in the text to reconstruct the situation a letter addresses
Compose a letter that follows the structure of a New Testament epistle to explain the teaching of a chosen passage
Connect the doctrinal teaching of a letter to the commands that follow from it, distinguishing indicative from imperative
Interpret the cultural background of a specific command and distinguish the abiding principle from its first-century expression
Explain the role of the amanuensis in the writing of New Testament letters using evidence from the text
Trace the argument of an epistle by analyzing connecting words such as therefore, for, and but
Analyze how the stated theme of a letter governs the development of its argument
Construct a historical and cultural background profile of a recipient city such as Corinth and explain how it illuminates the letter
Evaluate principles for applying letters written to first-century churches to the church today, including the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture
Defend the authority of the apostolic letters as Scripture using the testimony of the New Testament and the Reformed confessions
Compare the teaching of Paul and James on faith and works and explain how the Reformed tradition harmonizes them
Synthesize Paul's teaching on justification by faith across several of his epistles

BIB.2.2.4.t: Identify Revelation as the last book of the Bible, which tells that Jesus is coming again and that God will make all things new
Name John as the follower of Jesus who wrote down the vision while he was sent away to the island of Patmos for telling about Jesus
State that Revelation shows Jesus as the King of kings who defeats evil and wins in the end
Retell the promise that God will wipe away every tear and end death, crying, and pain in the new heaven and new earth
Recite one of the songs of praise sung around God's throne in Revelation and identify who is being praised
Describe how John saw the risen Jesus in glory in his first vision and what Jesus told him not to fear
Explain that Revelation uses picture language such as dragons, beasts, and a Lamb to show real truths about God, Christ, and evil
Explain that apocalypse means an unveiling and that Revelation uncovers the heavenly reality behind earthly events
Identify an encouragement, a warning, and a promise that Jesus gives to one of the seven churches
Compare the Lion of Judah and the slain Lamb in John's vision to explain how Christ conquers through his death
Identify the features of apocalyptic writing, including visions, angelic guides, symbolic numbers and creatures, cosmic conflict, and God's final triumph, in Daniel and Revelation
Explain how the first readers' situation of persecution and pressure to worship the emperor shapes Revelation's message of hope and endurance
Analyze the symbolic meaning of numbers such as 7, 12, and 666 in Revelation by tracing how these numbers are used elsewhere in Scripture
Connect images in Revelation to their Old Testament sources in Daniel, Ezekiel, and Zechariah to show how Scripture interprets Scripture
Explain the Reformed confession of Christ's visible return and the last judgment and relate it to John's vision of the great white throne
Explain the preterist, historicist, futurist, and idealist approaches to reading Revelation and the strengths and weaknesses of each
Analyze Jesus' teaching in the Olivet Discourse as apocalyptic instruction that calls disciples to watchfulness and endurance rather than speculation
Compare the garden of Genesis with the new Jerusalem of Revelation to show how the Bible's story ends in restored creation and God dwelling with his people
Compare the amillennial, postmillennial, and premillennial readings of the thousand years, noting which views have been common in the Reformed tradition
Analyze the structure of Revelation, including how the cycles of seals, trumpets, and bowls may retell the same period with increasing intensity
Construct a study of the throne room vision that explains how heavenly worship reframes the suffering of the church on earth
Evaluate the practice of setting dates for Christ's return in light of Jesus' teaching that no one knows the day or hour
Defend from Revelation the Reformed doctrine that God governs all of history, including the actions of persecutors, for his purposes
Evaluate how Revelation's call to faithful witness and patient endurance applies to Christians facing persecution today
Create a presentation tracing the theme of the Lamb from the Passover and the prophets to the worship of the Lamb as the climax of Revelation

BIB.2.3.1.t: Name the five books of the Pentateuch in order
Retell the creation account in the order of the six days and the seventh day of rest
Identify Moses as the leader God called to bring Israel out of Egypt and to give them his law
Retell the main events in the lives of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph
Recite the Ten Commandments in order
Retell the Exodus account including the plagues, the Passover, and the crossing of the Red Sea
Explain that the Hebrew word Torah means instruction or law and that it names the first five books of the Bible
Describe the fall of Adam and Eve and the first promise of a Savior given in Genesis
Summarize the main content and storyline of each book of the Pentateuch
Explain the purpose of the tabernacle as the place where God chose to dwell among his people
Explain how the preface to the Ten Commandments shows that God gave his law to a people he had already redeemed
Describe the wilderness wanderings and explain from the text why Israel spent forty years in the desert
Compare the narrative sections of Genesis with the law sections of Leviticus in form and purpose
Explain the meaning of the Shema and its command to love God and teach his words to the next generation
Explain the covenant identity God gave Israel at Sinai as his treasured possession and a kingdom of priests
Trace the promises of land, offspring, and blessing given to Abraham through their partial fulfillment in the nation of Israel
Analyze the structure of Deuteronomy in light of ancient suzerain vassal treaties
Explain the purpose of the main offerings in the Levitical sacrificial system
Interpret the holiness theme of Leviticus and explain how the New Testament applies it to God's people in Christ
Distinguish the moral, ceremonial, and judicial laws of the Pentateuch as the Reformed tradition classifies them
Explain the rituals of the Day of Atonement and how Hebrews presents them as fulfilled in Christ
Analyze the Passover as a type that the New Testament applies to Jesus as the Lamb of God
Explain how the Reformed tradition describes the continuing uses of the moral law summarized at Sinai
Analyze how the generations formula organizes the book of Genesis
Construct a timeline of the major events of the Pentateuch from creation to the death of Moses
Evaluate the Documentary Hypothesis and the case for Mosaic authorship using internal biblical evidence
Evaluate arguments concerning the historical reliability of the patriarchal and Exodus narratives
Analyze how New Testament writers interpret the Pentateuch as pointing to Christ, including the promise of a prophet like Moses
Synthesize the Pentateuch's foundational teaching about God, humanity, and covenant into a coherent written account

BIB.2.3.2.t: Name Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings as the books that tell the story of Israel living in the land God promised
Retell the story of the walls of Jericho falling when Israel obeyed the Lord's instructions
Retell the story of the Lord calling the boy Samuel in the night
Retell the story of David and Goliath and identify David's words that the battle belongs to the Lord
Identify Deborah and Gideon as judges the Lord raised up to rescue Israel
Explain why Israel's request for a king to be like the nations displeased the Lord and Samuel
Describe how Joshua led Israel into Canaan and how the text shows the Lord keeping every promise about the land
Summarize the repeated cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance in the book of Judges
Retell the contest between Elijah and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel and explain what it showed about the Lord
Explain the Lord's covenant promise to David of a house, a kingdom, and a throne established forever
Explain how Solomon's idolatry and Rehoboam's harsh answer led to the division of the kingdom into Israel and Judah
Sequence the major periods of the Former Prophets from conquest through the judges, the united monarchy, the divided monarchy, and the falls of Samaria and Jerusalem
Compare faithful kings such as Hezekiah and Josiah with unfaithful kings such as Ahab using the standard of covenant loyalty the books apply
Explain the reasons the narrator gives for the exile of the northern kingdom to Assyria and of Judah to Babylon
Explain why the Hebrew canon calls Joshua through Kings the Former Prophets and distinguish this grouping from the Historical Books of the English Bible
Analyze how the Former Prophets judge Israel's history by the covenant blessings and curses set out in Deuteronomy
Analyze the role of prophets such as Nathan and Elijah in confronting kings with the word of the Lord
Explain how the gift of the land and its later loss are tied to Israel's covenant relationship with the Lord
Apply attention to narrative features such as the regnal formula and the narrator's verdict that a king did right or evil in the sight of the Lord when interpreting a passage in Kings
Analyze Joshua's covenant renewal at Shechem and the people's pledge to serve the Lord alone
Trace the decline from conquest to exile by identifying patterns of idolatry and covenant breaking that recur across the Former Prophets
Compare the account of Sennacherib's invasion in Kings with Assyrian records of the same campaign
Analyze how the New Testament presents Jesus as the promised Son of David who fulfills the Davidic covenant as the tradition confesses Christ's kingly office
Construct a synchronized timeline of the kings of Israel and Judah and their prophets using the regnal formulas in Kings
Evaluate the character of David as a man after God's own heart in light of his sin with Bathsheba and his response to Nathan
Defend the justice of God in sending Israel and Judah into exile using the narrator's explanation and the repeated prophetic warnings
Evaluate interpretations of the conquest of Canaan in light of the texts on Canaanite sin, God's judgment, and the inclusion of Rahab
Compose a synthesis of the theme of God's faithfulness despite human failure across the Former Prophets including the hope signaled by Jehoiachin's release

BIB.2.3.3.t: Identify the Psalms as songs and prayers that God's people sang to worship him
Identify Solomon as the king who asked God for wisdom and wrote many proverbs
Recite Psalm 23:1-3 and describe how the Lord cares for his people like a shepherd cares for sheep
Identify David as the shepherd king who wrote many of the psalms
Name in order the poetic and wisdom books of the Old Testament: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs
Explain from Proverbs that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom
Describe how creation declares the glory of God using Psalm 19
Identify the different emotions the psalmists express, such as joy, sorrow, fear, and trust, and explain that the psalms show God's people bringing every situation to him in prayer
Retell the story of Job's testing, his response, and God's restoration of him
Explain the difference between a proverb as a general principle of wise living and a promise from God
Contrast the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked as presented in Psalm 1
Compare Job's questioning in suffering with the expressions of trust in God found in the Psalms
Describe the arrangement of the Psalter into five books, each closing with a doxology
Summarize the message of Ecclesiastes about life under the sun and its concluding call to fear God and keep his commandments
Explain the Reformed practice of singing psalms in worship and sing a metrical psalm in class
Analyze examples of Hebrew parallelism, distinguishing synonymous, antithetical, and synthetic lines
Analyze the figurative language and structures of Hebrew poetry, including metaphor and acrostic form
Identify the Writings as the third division of the Hebrew Bible alongside the Law and the Prophets, as Jesus referred to it
Explain how Jesus prayed and quoted the Psalms during his ministry and on the cross
Analyze God's speeches to Job and explain what they teach about God's sovereign providence and the limits of human understanding
Compose an original lament or praise psalm that follows the structure and parallelism of biblical examples
Explain how the Song of Songs celebrates covenant love in marriage and how the church has also read it in light of Christ and his church
Analyze the meaning of the Hebrew word hebel, often translated vanity or vapor, across Ecclesiastes and explain how it supports the book's conclusion
Explain how the New Testament applies royal and messianic psalms to Christ as prophet, priest, and king
Classify psalms by genre, including lament, hymn of praise, thanksgiving, royal, and wisdom psalms, and identify the typical structure of each
Analyze the personification of Wisdom in Proverbs 8 and how the New Testament presents Christ as the wisdom of God
Evaluate how Job, the Psalms, and Ecclesiastes challenge a simple view that suffering always results from personal sin
Evaluate the counsel of Proverbs on speech, work, money, and friendship and apply it to contemporary situations
Analyze the imprecatory psalms in their context and explain how they entrust judgment to God in light of New Testament teaching
Write a synthesis essay showing how the Wisdom books and Psalms point to Christ as the fulfillment of the pursuit of wisdom

BIB.2.3.4.t: Identify a prophet as a messenger whom God called to speak his words to his people
Retell the story of Jonah, including God's call, Jonah's flight, the great fish, and Nineveh's repentance
Recall that the prophets warned God's people to turn away from sin and return to the Lord
Retell the accounts of Daniel's friends in the furnace and Daniel in the lions' den and describe how God kept them faithful and safe
Identify promises in the prophets about a coming King and Savior and match them to their fulfillment in Jesus
List the books of the Major and Minor Prophets in their order in the English Bible
Summarize the prophets' twofold message as a warning of judgment for sin and a promise of comfort and restoration
Explain that the labels Major and Minor Prophets describe the length of the books rather than their importance
Describe the main sins the prophets condemned, including idolatry, injustice toward the poor, and empty religious ritual
Compare Isaiah's response to his call with Jonah's flight from his call
Classify the prophets as preexilic, exilic, or postexilic and describe the Assyrian, Babylonian, and Persian setting of each group
Explain how Jonah and Isaiah reveal God's purpose to show mercy to the nations beyond Israel
Explain how Malachi closes the Old Testament with the promise of a messenger that the New Testament fulfills in John the Baptist
Analyze the theme of the Day of the Lord as both judgment on the wicked and deliverance for God's people across several prophets
Explain how the prophets acted as messengers of the covenant who brought God's charges against his people based on the covenant's blessings and curses
Explain how the Suffering Servant passage describes substitutionary suffering and how the New Testament identifies the Servant as Jesus
Interpret the new covenant promises in Jeremiah and Ezekiel and explain how the book of Hebrews applies them to Christ
Analyze the literary forms of prophetic speech, including the messenger formula, judgment oracle, woe oracle, salvation oracle, and symbolic action
Construct a timeline that places each prophet alongside the kings and empires of his day using the superscriptions of the books
Apply the principle that the prophets testified beforehand to Christ when interpreting a prophetic passage
Analyze the symbolism of apocalyptic visions in Daniel and Zechariah and explain sound principles for interpreting them
Analyze Hosea's marriage imagery as a portrayal of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness and God's steadfast love
Evaluate how the prophets' call for justice and mercy informs Christian responsibility toward neighbors today
Defend the Reformed view that predictive prophecy displays God's sovereign knowledge and decree in response to critical claims about the dating of Isaiah and Daniel
Create a thematic synthesis tracing how judgment in the Latter Prophets serves God's purpose of preserving a remnant and leads to the hope of restoration and new creation

BIB.2.4.1.t: Identify the Bible as God's Word that families and classes read together every day
Follow a simple daily class Bible time by opening the Bible, listening quietly to a passage, and praying afterward
Name times and places in an ordinary day when a family or student can read the Bible, using the examples in Deuteronomy 6
Explain why Scripture compares God's Word to the daily food people need to live
Describe examples in Scripture of people who read or heard God's Word as a regular custom, such as Jesus in the synagogue and the Bereans
Use a simple chart to record daily Bible reading or listening across a full week
Compare forming a Bible reading habit with forming other daily habits and identify what helps a habit last, such as a set time, place, and reminder
Explain what the commands to the king and to Joshua teach about reading God's law regularly throughout life
Maintain a reading log that records the date, passage, and one key sentence for each daily reading over several weeks
Analyze a personal weekly schedule to identify obstacles to consistent Bible reading and propose specific adjustments
Explain the Reformed teaching that all people are bound to read Scripture both by themselves and with their families
Explain how Jesus' teaching about abiding in him and his words has been used to ground the practice of regular Scripture reading
Design a short routine for beginning and ending daily reading that applies the catechism's call to diligence, preparation, and prayer
Evaluate different times of day, settings, and formats such as print or audio for how well they support focused and consistent reading
Explain the historic Reformed practice of daily family worship and the place of Scripture reading within it
Distinguish between daily Scripture reading as an ordinary means of grace and reading as an attempt to earn God's favor
Analyze common causes of inconsistent reading and evaluate practical strategies for resuming the habit after missed days
Write an argument defending the priority of regular Scripture reading against the pressure of busyness using Scripture and the confessions
