Lead a younger class or peer group through a consistent daily reading routine over a set period
Create a sustainable personal rhythm for daily Scripture reading for life after graduation that plans for changing schedules and includes accountability

BIB.2.4.2.t: Describe the people, places, and actions shown in a picture of a Bible story before saying what the story means
Ask who, what, where, and when questions about a Bible passage read aloud and find the answers in the text
Identify words or phrases that are repeated in a short Bible passage
Name the three steps of inductive Bible study (observation, interpretation, application) and describe the question each step asks
Identify connecting words such as because, therefore, but, and so that in a passage and explain the relationship each one shows
Mark key words, names, places, and time references in a printed passage using a consistent system of symbols or colors
Explain why careful observation of what a text says must come before deciding what it means
Explain how the surrounding verses of a passage shape the meaning of a single verse within it
Identify the genre of a passage and describe how its genre shapes the questions a reader asks during observation
Use cross-references to compare a passage with related passages and explain the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture
Analyze a paragraph by listing its facts and noting contrasts, comparisons, and cause and effect relationships
Interpret the author's main point in a passage using only evidence drawn from observations of the text and its context
Distinguish exegesis, drawing meaning out of a text, from eisegesis, reading one's own ideas into it, using examples of commonly misused verses
Develop a specific, actionable application that follows from the interpreted meaning of a passage rather than from observation alone
Trace the structure of a passage by outlining its sections and the flow of its argument
Conduct a word study on a key term using a concordance or lexicon and analyze how its use in context determines its meaning
Construct a full inductive study of a New Testament epistle passage covering observation, interpretation, and application
Explain the Reformed teaching on the clarity of Scripture and the illumination of the Spirit and how these relate to diligent use of ordinary means of study
Research the historical and cultural background of a passage and use it to inform observation and interpretation
Evaluate commentaries and study tools against one's own inductive observations, explaining the Reformed teaching that Scripture is the supreme judge of all interpretation
Compare inductive Bible study with topical and deductive approaches and evaluate the strengths and limits of each
Produce a teaching outline based on an inductive study of a passage

BIB.2.4.3.t: Recite short key verses from memory such as Genesis 1:1 and John 3:16
Use repetition, motions, or song to learn a verse word for word until it can be said without help
Recite from memory a verse that tells of God's care in times of fear such as Psalm 56:3 or Isaiah 41:10
State the book, chapter, and verse reference together with each memorized verse
Recite longer passages from memory such as Psalm 23 or the Beatitudes
Recite catechism answers from memory along with a supporting proof text
Explain the meaning of a memorized verse in your own words
Explain from Psalm 119 and Deuteronomy 6 why God commands His people to store His Word in their hearts
Describe how Jesus answered each temptation in the wilderness by quoting Scripture
Select a memorized verse that addresses a specific temptation and explain how its truth answers that temptation
Distinguish between memorizing the words of Scripture and meditating on them using Psalm 1 and Joshua 1
Meditate on a memorized passage by working through it phrase by phrase and writing a question and observation for each phrase
Explain the Puritan picture of meditation as chewing on the Word using writers such as Thomas Watson or Richard Baxter
Connect a memorized verse to other passages that teach the same doctrine
Examine the context of a commonly memorized verse such as Jeremiah 29:11 or Philippians 4:13 to show how it is rightly and wrongly applied
Contrast biblical meditation, which fills the mind with God's Word, with forms of meditation that seek to empty the mind
Explain how the Reformed tradition relates reading, memorizing, and meditating on Scripture to the means of grace and to prayer
Construct a system for reviewing and retaining memorized Scripture over months and years
Evaluate from Scripture and Puritan writings the role meditation plays in resisting sin and cultivating delight in God
Compose a written meditation on a passage that moves from its meaning to its doctrine to its practical implications
Defend from Scripture the practice of hiding God's Word in the heart as part of the believer's spiritual armor, answering common objections to memorization

BIB.2.4.4.t: Identify one thing a Bible story shows about who God is, such as His love and care
Tell one thing God wants His people to do after hearing a Bible story
Explain that the Bible is God speaking to His people and why Christians pray before reading it
Apply a specific command from Scripture to a situation at school or home
Compose a short prayer of thanks or praise in class that uses words from a passage just read
Explain how a passage directs readers to love God and love their neighbor
Summarize what a passage reveals about God's character and describe a fitting response such as worship, trust, or obedience
Distinguish commands, promises, warnings, and examples in a passage as different ways the text calls for application
Explain from Jesus' own words why devotional reading looks for Christ as the center of Scripture's message
Pray through a Psalm in a guided class exercise by turning its praise, confession, and petition into prayer
Describe the practices the Westminster Larger Catechism gives for reading Scripture with profit, including reverence, attention, application, and prayer
Explain the Reformed teaching that the Holy Spirit illumines readers and uses the Word to sanctify God's people
Apply the truths and promises of a passage to common struggles such as fear, doubt, or temptation
Distinguish moralism from gospel-motivated obedience by comparing two applications of the same passage
Analyze whether a devotional application is faithful to a passage's context or reads a foreign meaning into it
Evaluate sample decisions and case studies in light of specific scriptural principles drawn from their original context
Construct a prayer shaped by the language and theology of a passage read
Produce a written devotional reflection that explains a passage in context and applies its theology to daily life
Defend from Scripture the Reformed view that reading the Bible aims at knowing God and obeying Him and not merely gaining information
Evaluate devotional books and resources for faithfulness to Scripture and sound doctrine

BIB.2.4.5.t: Retell the main events of a Bible story in the correct order
Identify the main characters and the setting of a Bible story
Ask questions about words or ideas in a Bible passage that are hard to understand
Answer who, what, when, and where questions about a passage using details from the text
Explain the plain meaning of a short passage in your own words without adding to it
Classify a passage as narrative, poetry, law, prophecy, gospel, or letter using clues in the text
Support each statement about what a passage means with specific words or details from the text
Use clues in the surrounding verses to determine the meaning of an unfamiliar word or phrase
Explain how the beginning, conflict, and resolution of a biblical narrative reveal its point
Compare two Bible stories to find similarities in how God acts toward his people
Explain how figurative language and parallelism in biblical poetry convey meaning
Determine the author's main point in a passage and identify the details that support it
Explain the tradition's teaching that the things necessary for salvation are so clearly set forth in Scripture that ordinary readers can understand them by due use of ordinary means
Explain how a passage fits within the flow of its chapter and book
Interpret the meaning of key words within their immediate context
Explain how Jesus taught that the Old Testament Scriptures speak of him
Apply the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture by using a clearer passage to clarify a harder one
Use historical and cultural background information to clarify the meaning of a passage
Explain the tradition's teaching on how the Spirit's illumination and diligent study work together in understanding Scripture
Trace the logical flow of an argument in an epistle by analyzing connecting words such as therefore, because, and so that
Perform an independent word study to clarify the meaning of a crucial term across its uses
Evaluate competing interpretations of a passage using textual evidence and context
Construct a detailed outline of a biblical book that shows its structure and major sections
Write a summary of a passage that accurately reflects the author's intent and argument

BIB.2.4.6.t: Listen to a short Bible passage read aloud slowly and retell one thing God said or did in it
Identify a word or phrase that is repeated or important in a short passage read aloud more than once
Explain why Christians pray for God's help to understand the Bible before they read it
Name the four steps of lectio divina as reading, meditation, prayer, and contemplation along with their Latin names
Compose a short prayer that uses words or ideas taken from a passage just read
Carry out the steps of lectio divina with a short psalm during a guided class reading
Explain what the Bible means by meditating on God's Word and connect it to the meditation step of lectio divina
Describe how slow, prayerful reading of Scripture developed in the early church and in monasteries that followed the Rule of Benedict
Explain how Guigo II's Ladder of Monks organized lectio divina into four ordered steps
Explain why the reading step must keep a passage in its context so that meditation stays tied to what the text actually means
Analyze how reading a passage slowly and repeatedly brings out details that a quick reading misses
Compare reading Scripture to gather information with the aim of lectio divina to respond in prayer to God speaking in His Word
Analyze the meaning of Psalm 46:10 in its context and contrast it with its common use as a call to wordless contemplative silence
Explain how meditation on a text leads into prayer whose content is shaped by that text
Explain how the Reformers critiqued the medieval fourfold sense of Scripture and how this shaped Protestant approaches to meditative reading
Compare the four steps of lectio divina with the Reformed and Puritan pattern of reading, hearing, meditating, and praying over Scripture
Evaluate the claim that God speaks through private impressions during contemplation using the Reformed teaching that the Spirit speaks in and through Scripture
Distinguish the contemplation step as taught in medieval mysticism from the Reformed teaching on communion with God through the Word and prayer
Evaluate modern practices such as centering prayer and mantra repetition against the biblical pattern of intelligible prayer
Evaluate the benefits and limits of slow meditative reading for students living in a distracted digital culture
Defend a position on whether and how lectio divina may be used within the Reformed tradition using historical sources, Scripture, and the confessions
Design a guided, Scripture-bound plan of slow reading and prayer that a small group could follow and justify each step from Scripture

BIB.2.4.7.t: Recall that the Bible has two main parts called the Old Testament and the New Testament
Identify Genesis as the first book and Revelation as the last book and explain that the Bible tells one story from beginning to end
Retell in order the major stories heard as an adult reads through a picture Bible from creation to the early church
Name the four Gospels and explain that they tell the story of Jesus so that people may believe in him
Sort the books of the Bible into their divisions such as Law, History, Poetry, Prophets, Gospels, Letters, and Prophecy
Summarize the storyline of the whole Bible from creation and fall through redemption in Christ to the new heavens and new earth
Locate any book of the Bible quickly using the table of contents and knowledge of its division
Use a reading plan to read one entire book of the Bible from start to finish while recording each completed reading
Explain from Scripture why the Reformed tradition teaches that God's people should read the whole counsel of God rather than only favorite verses
Describe how Israel publicly read the whole law to all the people using examples from Deuteronomy and Nehemiah
Compare the length, genre, and reading pace of different books such as Psalms and Mark to estimate the time a reading plan requires
Describe the Reformed practice of lectio continua as reading consecutively through whole books of Scripture in worship and at home
Analyze how canonical, chronological, and multi-stream reading plans are structured and what each emphasizes
Explain the directions the Westminster Standards give for how Scripture is to be read and apply them to keeping a long reading plan
Connect each book read in a plan to its place in the larger storyline of Scripture
Explain the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture and how reading the whole Bible equips a reader to apply it
Trace how the Old Testament prepares the way for Christ and the New Testament across a whole-Bible reading
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of historic and modern reading plans such as M'Cheyne, chronological, and canonical plans
Develop strategies for reading difficult portions such as genealogies, laws, and prophecies within a plan using the confessional teaching that not all Scripture is equally plain
Construct a personalized plan to read the entire Bible in one or two years with daily portions, pacing, and a catch-up strategy
Evaluate a completed reading record to identify neglected portions of the canon and revise a plan to cover them
Produce a written synthesis of a major biblical theme traced through a whole-Bible reading

BIB.3.1.10.t: Identify Saul, David, and Solomon as the first three kings of Israel
Retell the story of David and Goliath, naming David's trust in the Lord as the reason he faced the giant
Describe how David and Jonathan showed loyal friendship to each other
Name Solomon as the king who built the Temple as God's house in Jerusalem
Retell how Solomon asked God for wisdom instead of riches or long life
Recall that David wrote songs to God found in the book of Psalms and recite Psalm 23
Summarize how God chose David by looking at his heart rather than his outward appearance
Explain why Israel asked Samuel for a king and why the request displeased Samuel and the Lord
Describe how David refused to harm Saul because Saul was the Lord's anointed
Explain why Saul lost the kingdom by citing his disobedience to God's commands
Describe David's kindness to Mephibosheth as keeping his promise to Jonathan
Sequence the major events of the reigns of Saul, David, and Solomon on a timeline
Identify the wisdom writings the Bible associates with Solomon
Compare David's confession of sin after Nathan's rebuke with Saul's excuses after his disobedience
Analyze how Solomon's many wives, horses, and wealth broke the law for Israel's kings and led him away from the Lord
Explain the purpose of the Temple as the place of God's presence among his people and of prayer to him
Analyze the promises God made to David in the Davidic Covenant and their place in the covenant of grace
Interpret the political and spiritual significance of David making Jerusalem his capital and bringing the ark there
Connect Solomon's Temple dedication prayer to God's purpose of making his name known among the nations
Explain how God kept his covenant promise to David even while judging Solomon's unfaithfulness
Trace the consequences of David's sin with Bathsheba through the later troubles in his family
Analyze how the narrator of Samuel shows the Lord establishing David's rise despite Saul's opposition
Evaluate the role of the prophets Samuel, Nathan, and Gad in holding Israel's kings accountable to God's word
Construct a profile of the promised Messianic King from the Davidic promises and their New Testament fulfillment in Christ
Analyze the wealth and trade of Solomon's kingdom using the biblical record alongside historical and archaeological sources
Compare the portrayal of David and Solomon in Chronicles with their portrayal in Samuel and Kings and explain the purpose of each account
Evaluate the tension between God's kingship over Israel and the establishment of a human monarchy
Develop a written argument showing how the kingdom, Temple, and wisdom of the United Monarchy point forward to their fulfillment in Christ

BIB.3.1.1.t: Identify Joshua as the leader God chose to bring Israel into the promised land after Moses died
Recall God's command to Joshua to be strong and courageous because the Lord would be with him
Retell in order the story of Israel marching around Jericho and the walls falling down
State from Joshua that not one of the good promises the Lord made to Israel failed
Retell how Rahab hid the spies and how she and her family were saved by the scarlet cord
Summarize how Israel crossed the Jordan River on dry ground and why they set up twelve memorial stones
Explain why God told Joshua to meditate on the Book of the Law day and night and describe how that practice can be carried out
Explain how Achan's hidden sin led to Israel's defeat at Ai and what the account teaches about sin affecting the whole covenant community
Explain how the Gibeonites deceived Israel and what the account shows about the leaders' failure to ask counsel of the Lord
Locate on a map the Jordan crossing, Jericho, Ai, Gilgal, Shechem, the southern and northern campaigns, and the general tribal allotments
Compare Caleb's request for Hebron with his earlier report as a spy to show how he trusted God's promise over many years
Explain why Israel was circumcised and kept the Passover at Gilgal before the conquest and what the ceasing of the manna signaled
Explain the covenant renewals at Mount Ebal and Shechem, including Joshua's call for Israel to choose whom they would serve and the people's covenant response
Explain how the New Testament presents Rahab as an example of faith shown in action and as part of the line of Jesus
Analyze how the conquest narratives present the Lord as the commander who fights for Israel rather than Israel's strength or strategy
Interpret the conquest as the Reformed tradition reads it, as God's just judgment on long-standing Canaanite sin alongside His mercy to those like Rahab who turned to Him
Connect the allotment of the land to God's fulfillment of His promise of land to Abraham and his offspring
Explain the purpose of the cities of refuge and the Levitical cities and why the tribe of Levi received no territorial inheritance
Analyze the structure of the book of Joshua as entering, taking, dividing, and serving in the land
Explain how Joshua's name and his role in leading God's people into their inheritance point forward to Jesus

Evaluate the command to devote the Canaanite cities to destruction as a unique act of divine judgment tied to that moment in redemptive history rather than a pattern for later warfare or for the church
Evaluate the incompleteness of the conquest and trace how the tribes' failure to drive out the Canaanites set up the troubles that followed
Evaluate archaeological evidence and scholarly debates about Jericho, Ai, and the date of the conquest in light of the biblical text
Trace the theme of rest in Joshua and explain how Hebrews 4 presents the rest Joshua gave as pointing to a greater Sabbath rest for God's people

BIB.3.1.2.t: Identify God as the maker of everything in the creation account, including the first man and woman, Adam and Eve
Retell the story of Noah and the ark in order using pictures or toys
Name what God made on each of the six days of creation and that He rested on the seventh day
Identify the rainbow as the sign of God's promise never again to destroy the earth by a flood
Retell how Adam and Eve disobeyed God in the garden, naming the command God gave and what they chose to do
Describe what happened between the brothers Cain and Abel and how God responded to Cain
Explain how the consequences God announced after the Fall changed life for people and for the world
Describe how God formed the woman and joined her to the man as the first marriage
Sequence the major events of Genesis 1-11 from Creation through the Fall, Cain and Abel, the Flood, and Babel
Explain why God sent the Flood as judgment on human wickedness and why He spared Noah and his family
Describe the events at the Tower of Babel and explain why God confused the languages and scattered the people
Identify Shem, Ham, and Japheth as the sons of Noah from whom the nations of the earth descended
Explain what Genesis teaches about humans being made in the image of God, using both the creation account and the command after the Flood
Compare God's commands to Adam with His commands to Noah to show how the creation mandate is renewed after the Flood
Explain the covenant God made with Noah by identifying its parties, promises, and sign
Analyze the repeated pattern in the genealogy from Adam to Noah, including the refrain of death and the exception of Enoch
Analyze the spread of sin across the narratives of Genesis 3-11 from the garden to Babel
Contrast the line of Cain with the line of Seth as presented in Genesis 4-5
Interpret the Table of Nations as an account of the common descent of all peoples from Noah's family
Connect the scattering of languages at Babel with the gathering of the nations at Pentecost and in the Great Commission
Explain Genesis 3:15 as the first gospel promise and trace its fulfillment in Christ through the New Testament
Analyze how the repeated heading these are the generations organizes Genesis 1-11 and links Adam to Abraham
Explain how the Flood narrative presents an undoing and renewal of creation by tracing its parallels with Genesis 1
Compare the Genesis creation and flood accounts with ancient Near Eastern accounts such as Enuma Elish and Gilgamesh to identify how Genesis presents God and humanity differently
Evaluate the major interpretations of the sons of God and the daughters of man in Genesis 6 using the text and its context
Evaluate interpretations of the days of creation held within the Reformed tradition in light of the text and the confession's statement of creation in the space of six days
Construct an argument for the tradition's historical reading of Adam and the Flood using how later Scripture refers to these events
Synthesize the themes of creation, judgment, and grace in Genesis 1-11 into an account of how these chapters prepare for God's call of Abraham

BIB.3.1.3.t: Identify Elijah as the prophet God sent to call Israel back to Him and recall that God answered Elijah with fire on Mount Carmel
Retell how God cared for Elijah through the ravens and the widow's flour and oil
Retell the story of Jonah, including God's call to Nineveh, Jonah's running away, the great fish, and God's mercy to the city
Recall that after Solomon the kingdom split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
Identify a prophet as a messenger whom God sent to speak His words to His people
Retell how the foreign commander Naaman was healed of leprosy through the prophet Elisha
Summarize the contest on Mount Carmel and explain what it showed about the LORD and Baal
Describe, using examples of specific kings, how kings who did evil led the people to idols and kings who did right led them back to the LORD
Retell how young King Josiah responded when the Book of the Law was found in the temple
Explain why the kingdom divided, including Rehoboam's harsh answer and God's judgment on Solomon's idolatry
Describe how God met the discouraged Elijah at Horeb and told him of the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal
Locate Samaria, Jerusalem, Bethel, Dan, Mount Carmel, and Nineveh on a map of the divided kingdom period
Compare the Northern Kingdom of Israel and the Southern Kingdom of Judah by capital, ruling families, centers of worship, and length of existence
Explain what the ending of Jonah teaches about God's compassion toward the nations and about Jonah's resistance to it
Categorize the prophets of this period by whom they addressed, whether Israel, Judah, or other nations
Explain what Isaiah's vision in the temple reveals about the holiness of God and the calling of a prophet
Explain how Hosea's marriage pictures the LORD's faithful love toward unfaithful Israel
Analyze Jeroboam's golden calves as a political and religious choice that broke the second commandment and became the lasting sin of the Northern Kingdom
Explain the fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722 BC and the reasons Scripture gives for it
Analyze how the prophets brought the LORD's covenant lawsuit against His people by appealing to the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy
Analyze how the prophets joined the call to true worship with the demand for justice toward the poor and oppressed
Apply the biblical tests of a true prophet to the conflict between Jeremiah and Hananiah
Evaluate the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah against the requirements of Deuteronomy and explain why judgment on Judah still came
Trace the promises of a coming king from David's line in the prophets of this period and explain how the New Testament reads them as fulfilled in Christ
Construct a timeline of the kings of Israel and Judah and the prophets who ministered during their reigns
Evaluate the geopolitical situation involving Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt and the prophets' warnings against trusting foreign alliances instead of the LORD
Defend from Deuteronomy and the repeated prophetic warnings the tradition's teaching that the fall of Jerusalem was God's just judgment
Analyze the theme of the faithful remnant from Elijah and Isaiah to Paul's teaching of a remnant chosen by grace
Produce a study of the Day of the Lord theme in the prophets that traces its near judgments and its final fulfillment

BIB.3.1.4.t: Identify the Holy Spirit as the Helper whom Jesus promised and sent to his followers at Pentecost
Name Peter and Paul as apostles who preached the good news about Jesus to many people
Recall Jesus' command for his followers to be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the end of the earth
Describe how the first believers gathered for the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, prayer, and sharing with those in need
Retell the story of Philip explaining Isaiah to the Ethiopian official and baptizing him
Summarize the events of Pentecost, including the wind, the tongues of fire, the many languages, Peter's sermon, and the baptism of about three thousand people
Retell the healing of the lame man at the temple and explain why Peter and John kept speaking about Jesus when the council ordered them to stop
Explain how Saul changed from a persecutor of the church to an apostle sent by Christ to the Gentiles
Describe the choosing of the seven servants and the witness and death of Stephen
Explain how Peter's vision and the conversion of Cornelius showed the church that Gentiles receive the gospel without first becoming Jews
Outline the book of Acts using the pattern of Acts 1:8 to show the gospel moving from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and on toward Rome
Describe Paul's arrest, his trials before Roman officials, and his voyage to Rome as the way the gospel reached the empire's capital
Locate on a map the routes and major cities of Paul's missionary journeys
Describe the pattern of Paul's mission work, including preaching first in synagogues, turning to Gentiles, and appointing elders in new churches
Analyze the dispute at the Jerusalem Council by identifying the question raised, the arguments of Peter and James, and the decision sent to the Gentile churches
Explain how persecution in Jerusalem scattered believers and carried the gospel to new regions
Analyze how Roman roads, the common Greek language, Roman peace, and Jewish synagogues across the empire shaped the spread of the gospel
Place selected letters of Paul within the narrative of Acts by matching each letter to the founding of its church
Explain the foundational role of the apostles as eyewitnesses of the risen Christ commissioned by him to lay the church's foundation

Analyze the apostolic sermons in Acts to identify the common themes of their preaching, including fulfilled prophecy, Christ's death and resurrection, his exaltation, and the call to repent and believe
Interpret the significance of the destruction of the temple in AD 70 in light of Jesus' prophecy and the church's separation from the temple system
Evaluate how the early church moved from a movement within Judaism to a multiethnic body of Jews and Gentiles, using evidence from Acts and the epistles
Evaluate accounts of the apostles' deaths by distinguishing what Scripture records from later church tradition
Evaluate the Reformed approach to distinguishing what Acts describes from what it prescribes for church practice, using examples such as shared possessions, tongues, and the appointing of elders
Create an annotated timeline and map of the apostolic age from Pentecost to the close of the first century that integrates Acts, the epistles, and key Roman events

BIB.3.1.5.t: Retell how God kept Daniel safe in the lions' den when Daniel kept praying to God
Identify Queen Esther as the woman God placed in the palace to save her people
Recall that God's people came home from a faraway land to rebuild the temple and the walls of Jerusalem
Summarize the story of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and the fiery furnace
Describe how Daniel and his friends obeyed God while living in Babylon
Identify ways God cared for and protected his people while they were far from home in exile
Explain what exile means and why God sent Judah into exile in Babylon
Describe how God's people grieved in exile using Psalm 137 and Lamentations
Sequence the major events from the fall of Jerusalem to the rebuilding of the walls on a timeline
Compare the rebuilding of the temple under Zerubbabel and Ezra with the rebuilding of the wall under Nehemiah
Explain what Jeremiah instructed the exiles to do while living in Babylon
Describe the parts of Nehemiah's prayer and compose a prayer modeled on its pattern of praise, confession, and request
Explain the role of Ezra's public reading and teaching of the Law in renewing the returned community
Analyze how the book of Esther shows God's providence even though God is never named
Connect the decree of Cyrus to the prophecies of Jeremiah and Isaiah about the return
Interpret Ezekiel's vision of the valley of dry bones in its exilic context
Explain how Haggai and Zechariah called the returned community to finish rebuilding the temple
Explain why the return from exile did not change the people's hearts and how the prophets promised a new covenant
Analyze Daniel's prayer of confession as a response to the covenant curses and the promised seventy years
Construct a historical overview of how the Babylonian and Persian empires shaped Israel's history in this period
Evaluate the spiritual condition of the post-exilic community using the charges in Malachi
Defend the claim that God preserved the Davidic line through the exile using Old Testament promises and New Testament genealogy
Synthesize how the partial restoration after exile points forward to its fulfillment in Christ, using the already and not yet framework

BIB.3.1.6.t: Identify the pillar of cloud and fire as the way God led Israel and stayed with them
Retell how God protected baby Moses in a basket on the Nile and raised him up to lead His people
Retell how God parted the Red Sea to rescue Israel from Pharaoh's army
Describe how God provided manna, quail, and water for Israel in the wilderness

Retell God's call of Moses at the burning bush and explain what God revealed by the name I AM

Identify what the Song of Moses praises about God after the Red Sea crossing

Explain the parts of the Passover meal and why God commanded Israel to remember it every year
Explain how the preface to the Ten Commandments grounds Israel's obedience in God's act of rescue
Explain how Moses' intercession and God's description of Himself show both His mercy and His justice
Explain how Israel's grumbling in the wilderness revealed unbelief in God's promises and provision
Compare the Golden Calf incident with the worship God commanded, using the second commandment
Identify the main furnishings of the Tabernacle and explain the purpose of each
Explain the covenant God made with Israel at Sinai and their calling to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation
Explain how the New Testament presents Jesus as the true Passover lamb and the true bread from heaven
Explain why Moses was not permitted to enter Canaan after striking the rock at Meribah
Describe the main Levitical sacrifices and the Day of Atonement and explain what they taught Israel about sin and forgiveness
Analyze the passages that describe Pharaoh hardening his own heart and God hardening Pharaoh's heart
Explain how Jesus uses the bronze serpent in the wilderness to describe His own saving work
Connect the spies' report and Israel's rebellion at Kadesh Barnea to the forty years of wandering
Interpret the symbolism of the Tabernacle and the high priest's garments in light of the Book of Hebrews
Explain the theme of holiness in Leviticus as God dwelling among a people He has set apart
Summarize Deuteronomy as Moses' covenant renewal speeches to the new generation on the plains of Moab, including the Shema

Analyze how Hebrews uses the wilderness generation to warn and exhort the church

Write an essay tracing Exodus typology through Scripture as a pattern of redemption fulfilled in Christ

BIB.3.1.7.t: Identify Samson as a judge whose great strength was a gift from God
Retell how God gave Gideon's small army of 300 men victory over the Midianites
Name the judges as leaders God raised up to rescue his people from their enemies
Retell the story of Deborah, Barak, and Jael and how God defeated Sisera's army
Describe how a new generation of Israel forgot the Lord and served other gods
Describe how God called Gideon to lead Israel even though Gideon saw himself as weak
Retell how Ruth stayed loyal to Naomi and chose to follow Naomi's God during the time of the judges
Sequence the repeating cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance, and rest using the account of Othniel as a model
Explain from the text that God rescued Israel out of his own compassion and not because the people deserved it
Explain why God reduced Gideon's army to 300 men
Classify the nations that oppressed Israel by the judge God raised up against each one
Apply the cycle of Judges to the account of Ehud by labeling each stage in the story
Explain how Israel's failure to drive out the Canaanites led to intermarriage and idolatry
Explain how the genealogy at the end of Ruth links the period of the judges to King David and to Jesus
Compare Deborah and Samson as judges by examining their obedience to God and their effect on Israel
Explain the role of the kinsman-redeemer and how Boaz fulfilled it for Ruth and Naomi
Explain why Hebrews 11 names Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah as examples of faith despite their failings
Analyze the refrain that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes
Construct a chart that traces the downward spiral in the character of the judges from Othniel to Samson
Interpret Jephthah's vow in light of the Mosaic law and the influence of Canaanite religion
Analyze Abimelech's reign and Jotham's fable as a picture of false kingship in contrast to Gideon's confession that the Lord rules Israel
Analyze how the closing chapters of Judges show Israel's religious and moral collapse, including the parallel between Gibeah and Sodom
Connect the moral decline in Judges to Israel's need for a righteous king and explain how the Reformed tradition sees that need fulfilled in Christ
Explain how the worsening pattern of Judges illustrates the Reformed doctrine of the corruption of human nature
Analyze the literary structure of Judges with its double introduction, cycle accounts, and double conclusion
Distinguish genuine repentance from crying out merely for relief by examining God's response to Israel in Judges 10
Evaluate how the portrayal of women in Judges, from Deborah and Jael to the Levite's concubine, marks Israel's spiritual condition
Defend from Judges the Reformed teaching that God sovereignly works through flawed and sinful leaders without approving their sin
Produce a thematic study of apostasy that traces the pattern of Judges through later Scripture

BIB.3.1.8.t: Identify pictures of the manger, the cross, and the empty tomb and tell which part of Jesus' life each shows
Name the twelve disciples Jesus called and retell how he called the first fishermen to follow him
Retell the story of Jesus' birth in Bethlehem, naming Mary, Joseph, the angels, and the shepherds
Retell a miracle of Jesus, such as calming the storm or feeding the five thousand, in the correct order of events
Retell the visit of the wise men and the family's escape to Egypt
Retell the account of the boy Jesus in the temple and describe what it shows about his relationship to his Father
Retell the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son and explain what each teaches about God seeking sinners
State that Jesus is true God who became a true man, using John's words that the Word became flesh
Summarize the baptism and temptation of Jesus and describe the role of John the Baptist as the one who prepared his way
Explain the meaning of the incarnation as the eternal Son of God taking a true body and a reasonable soul, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary
Locate Bethlehem, Nazareth, Capernaum, the Sea of Galilee, the Jordan River, and Jerusalem on a map and connect each to an event in Jesus' life
Sequence the major events of Passion Week from the triumphal entry through the resurrection
Describe the Jewish and Roman setting of Jesus' ministry, including the synagogue, the temple, the Pharisees, the Sadducees, and Roman rule
Describe the resurrection appearances of Jesus and explain how they show that he rose bodily from the dead
Classify Jesus' miracles by the authority they reveal over nature, sickness, demons, and death and explain how John presents them as signs pointing to who Jesus is
Explain how specific events in Jesus' birth, ministry, and death fulfill Old Testament prophecies
Compare the responses of the Pharisees and of known sinners to Jesus and explain what the contrast reveals about grace and self-righteousness
Explain what Jesus taught about the kingdom of God through the parables of Matthew 13
Analyze the 'I Am' statements in the Gospel of John and explain how they connect to God's name revealed in Exodus
Compare how Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John each present the life of Jesus, noting their stated purposes and distinctive emphases
Analyze how the Sermon on the Mount describes the character and conduct of citizens of the kingdom and how Jesus relates his teaching to the Law
Connect the Transfiguration to Old Testament appearances of God's glory and explain why Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus
Explain the Reformed teaching on Christ's states of humiliation and exaltation and place the events of his life within each
Explain how the Gospels and the Reformed confessions interpret Jesus' death as a substitutionary sacrifice for sinners
Explain the significance of the Ascension, including Christ's heavenly intercession and present reign, as the Reformed confessions state it
Analyze how Jesus taught his disciples to read the Old Testament as testifying to his suffering and glory
Construct a harmony of the four Gospel accounts of Passion Week and account for differences in detail among them
Evaluate why the Reformed confessions teach that the Mediator must be true God and true man united in one person without confusion or division
Evaluate naturalistic explanations of Jesus' miracles and resurrection using the eyewitness claims of the Gospels and the apostles
Compose an essay showing how the events of Jesus' life fulfill the offices of prophet, priest, and king

BIB.3.1.9.t: Identify Abraham as the man God called to leave his home and who believed God's promise
Name Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph in the order they appear in the story of God's family
Retell how God kept his promise to give Abraham and Sarah a son in their old age
Retell the story of Joseph's coat, his brothers' jealousy, and his journey to Egypt
Retell how Joseph revealed himself to his brothers and forgave them
Recall how God renamed Jacob as Israel after Jacob wrestled with him
Summarize the call of Abraham and his journey to Canaan
Describe Jacob's dream at Bethel and the promise God repeated to him there
Describe how the text shows God was with Joseph in Potiphar's house and in prison
Identify the three parts of God's promise to Abraham as land, offspring, and blessing for all nations
Explain how Jacob deceived Isaac and Esau and describe the consequences that followed in his family
Describe Abraham's intercession for Sodom and explain what it reveals about God's justice
Explain how God cared for Hagar and Ishmael even outside the line of promise
Trace on a map the movement of the patriarchs from Ur to Haran to Canaan to Egypt
Compare Abraham's acts of faith with his failures, such as lying about Sarah and taking Hagar
Explain circumcision as the covenant sign God gave Abraham and how Paul describes it as a seal of faith
Construct a family tree of the patriarchs including their wives and the sons of Jacob
Explain the covenant ceremony of Genesis 15 and how God alone passing between the pieces shows the promise rests on him
Explain how Paul uses Genesis 15:6 to teach the Reformed doctrine of justification by faith
Analyze the testing of Abraham in Genesis 22, including God's provision of the ram and the interpretation in Hebrews
Connect the twelve sons of Jacob to the twelve tribes of Israel using Jacob's final blessings
Interpret Joseph's statements about God's purpose in his suffering as a teaching on God's providence
Explain how Judah's change of character and Jacob's blessing on Judah point forward to the kingly line of David and Christ
Explain how Melchizedek's meeting with Abraham is used in Hebrews to portray Christ's priesthood
Explain how Hebrews presents the patriarchs as strangers who lived by faith in promises not yet received
Explain the Reformed doctrine of election as Paul draws it from the choice of Isaac over Ishmael and Jacob over Esau
Evaluate how the Genesis narrator portrays polygamy and favoritism through the conflict they produce rather than by approval
Analyze how ancient Near Eastern customs such as birthright, covenant making, surrogate marriage, and household gods illuminate the patriarchal narratives
Synthesize how the Abrahamic covenant is fulfilled in Christ and extended to the church across redemptive history

BIB.3.2.1.t: Identify Jesus as the one John the Baptist called the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world
Retell how Jesus said that as the Good Shepherd he would lay down his life for his sheep
Retell how God made garments of skin to clothe Adam and Eve after they sinned
Explain from Scripture that sin separates people from God and deserves his judgment
Retell the account of Abraham and Isaac and identify the ram God provided in Isaac's place
Describe the animal sacrifices offered by Abel and Noah in the early chapters of Genesis
Retell the first Passover and explain why the blood on the doorposts spared the Israelite households
Define atonement as God's provision for covering sin and reconciling sinners to himself
Explain from Leviticus and Hebrews why the shedding of blood was required for atonement under the law
Compare the Passover lamb with Jesus as the unblemished lamb whose blood redeems his people
Describe the main Levitical offerings and the purpose Scripture gives for each
Explain the roles of the two goats on the Day of Atonement and what each pictured about the removal of sin
Explain how the Lord's Supper proclaims Christ's once-for-all sacrifice as the Reformed tradition confesses it
Explain substitution as Christ bearing the curse and penalty of sin in the place of sinners
Explain how the New Testament describes believers offering themselves as living sacrifices and sacrifices of praise in response to Christ's atonement
Analyze how Isaiah 53 presents the Suffering Servant as a substitute who bears the sins of others
Compare the repeated Levitical sacrifices with Christ's once-for-all sacrifice as Hebrews 10 presents them
Distinguish the biblical terms propitiation, expiation, reconciliation, and redemption as aspects of Christ's atoning work
Analyze how Paul presents the cross as showing God to be both just and the justifier of those who have faith in Jesus
Trace the Lamb theme from the Old Testament to Revelation and explain how each passage develops it
Evaluate why animal sacrifices could not take away sin yet were ordained by God as types pointing to Christ
Evaluate moral influence, governmental, and Christus Victor accounts of the atonement against the Reformed confession of penal substitution using Scripture
Analyze the passages the Reformed tradition uses to teach definite atonement and explain how its confessions state the doctrine
Create a written or visual synthesis tracing the theme of sacrifice from Eden to the worship of the Lamb in the new creation

BIB.3.2.2.t: Identify the tabernacle and the temple as places where God chose to live among his people Israel
Recall that God walked with Adam and Eve in the garden of Eden and that they were sent out of the garden after they sinned
Retell how Solomon built the temple and how God's glory filled it when it was dedicated
Describe how God showed his presence with Israel through the pillar of cloud and fire and the glory cloud that filled the tabernacle
Identify the main parts of the tabernacle, including the courtyard, the Holy Place, the Most Holy Place, the veil, and the ark of the covenant
Explain that the name Immanuel means God with us and that the Gospels apply this name to Jesus
Explain from Solomon's prayer how Scripture teaches both that God is present everywhere and that he chose to dwell with his people in a special way at the temple
Explain why only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place and only once a year
Explain how Scripture describes sin as separating people from the holy God and what it says is required to dwell in his presence
Explain what Paul means when he calls the church and the believer's body a temple of the Holy Spirit
Explain how Psalms 27 and 84 express the desire of God's people to dwell in his house
Explain the significance of Ezekiel's vision of God's glory departing from the temple before its destruction by Babylon
Analyze parallels between the garden of Eden and the tabernacle, such as cherubim guarding the way, the eastern entrance, and gold and precious stones
Explain the rebuilding of the second temple after the exile and Haggai's promise that its latter glory would be greater
Interpret Ezekiel's vision of the new temple, including the return of God's glory and the river flowing from the sanctuary
Explain the meaning of the tearing of the temple veil at Christ's death for access into God's presence
Analyze how John's Gospel presents Jesus as the true temple in whom God dwells with his people
Explain how Jesus's teaching on worship in spirit and truth reshapes the question of where God is to be worshiped, as the Westminster Confession summarizes it
Compare the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost with the glory filling the tabernacle and temple
Analyze why the New Jerusalem has no temple, including how its cube shape echoes the Most Holy Place
Explain how Hebrews presents the earthly tabernacle as a copy of the heavenly sanctuary where Christ now appears in God's presence
Analyze how Ephesians and 1 Peter describe the church, Jew and Gentile together, as a temple built on Christ
Create a written or visual account tracing the theme of God's dwelling presence from Eden through the tabernacle, temple, Christ, and the church to the new creation

BIB.3.2.3.t: Identify Jesus as the King promised in the Bible who rules over all things
Describe a priest as someone who goes to God on behalf of the people and prays for them
Recall that a prophet is someone God sends to speak His words to people
Retell how Samuel anointed David with oil to show that God had chosen him to be king
Identify the three offices of prophet, priest, and king that the Reformed tradition confesses Jesus fulfills
Explain that the Hebrew word Messiah and the Greek word Christ both mean Anointed One
Explain how Jesus does the work of a prophet by revealing God and His will through His teaching
Explain how Jesus does the work of a priest by standing before God for His people and interceding for them
Explain how Jesus does the work of a king by ruling, protecting, and defending His people and conquering His enemies
Summarize key Old Testament promises of a coming prophet, priest, and king
Compare Moses as prophet, Aaron as priest, and David as king with Jesus, noting both likenesses and the ways Jesus is greater
Explain how Peter applies the promise of a prophet like Moses to Jesus in his sermon in Acts
Explain how Jesus' anointing with the Spirit at His baptism and His reading of Isaiah 61 in Nazareth mark Him as the Anointed One
Analyze the anointing of prophets, priests, and kings in the Old Testament and what the anointing signified
Analyze why the offices of priest and king were kept separate in Israel and how the prophets anticipated their union in one person
Interpret Jesus' high priestly prayer as an example of His intercession for His people
Connect the priest-king Melchizedek to the eternal priesthood of Jesus as Hebrews explains it
Explain the kingship of Christ over the nations and all creation from the Psalms and the New Testament
Distinguish the political messianic expectations of Jesus' day from the kingdom Jesus proclaimed
Analyze how the Reformed tradition relates each office of Christ to a human need, such as ignorance, guilt, and bondage
Construct a profile of the threefold office of Christ using Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Evaluate how the church is described as sharing in Christ's anointing as prophets, priests, and kings
Defend from Hebrews and Revelation the claim that Jesus is the final Word, the final High Priest, and the final King
Evaluate views that present Jesus in only one office, such as a moral teacher alone, against the biblical portrait of the Messiah
Write a synthesis tracing the offices of prophet, priest, and king from the Old Testament to their fulfillment in Christ

BIB.3.2.4.t: Retell how God saved Noah and his family in the ark when the flood came on the earth
Identify God's promise to Abraham to make his family into a great people through whom all nations would be blessed
Describe how Joshua and Caleb trusted God when most of Israel refused to enter the land
Summarize the account of Elijah in which God tells him of 7,000 in Israel who had not bowed to Baal
Describe John's vision of a great multitude from every nation worshiping God as the whole people of God gathered together
Explain the biblical meaning of remnant as the part of God's people whom He preserves through judgment
Describe how God preserved a remnant of Judah through the exile and brought them back to rebuild Jerusalem
Compare the crowds who left Jesus with the disciples who stayed when His teaching became hard
Identify biblical names and images for the people of God such as flock, vine, holy nation, and bride
Explain the Reformed teaching that Christ gathers, defends, and preserves His church as the people called out by Him
Explain how the covenant promise I will be their God and they will be my people runs through the whole Bible
Analyze how the prophets join warnings of judgment on unfaithful Israel with promises of a preserved remnant
Interpret Paul's olive tree metaphor to explain how Gentile believers are grafted into the one people of God
Analyze how Paul uses the example of Elijah to show that the remnant exists by God's election of grace
Explain how the New Testament presents Jesus as the faithful Israel in whom the people of God are gathered
Distinguish the invisible church from the visible church as the Westminster Confession defines them
Explain the Reformed teaching that the visible church consists of those who profess the true religion together with their children
Explain the marks of the true church as the Reformed confessions state them and their basis in Scripture
Construct a timeline of the remnant theme from Genesis to Revelation that cites key passages and explains each stage
Evaluate episodes from church history in light of the confessional teaching that Christ will always preserve a church on earth despite error and decline
Defend from Scripture the faithfulness of God to His covenant promises in times of widespread apostasy
Compare the Reformed covenantal view of the continuity of Israel and the church with the dispensational view using key texts
Analyze the main interpretations of Paul's statement that all Israel will be saved within the argument of Romans 9 to 11

BIB.4.1.1.t: Identify a heresy as a false teaching about God that disagrees with what the Bible says
State that Jesus is both true God and true man, the truth that many early false teachers denied
Describe how early Christians tested a teaching by comparing it with the words of Scripture and the apostles
Retell how the apostles warned that false teachers would arise and how church leaders were charged to guard believers from them
Summarize the Gnostic teaching that the material world and the body are evil and that secret knowledge saves
Explain why the Arian claim that the Son was created contradicts what Scripture teaches about the Word who made all things
Explain the Docetic claim that Jesus only seemed to be human and show how the apostles answered it from his bodily life and resurrection
Compare a heresy to a counterfeit by identifying what it borrows from true teaching and what it changes
Describe Marcion's rejection of the Old Testament and its God and explain how Scripture presents one God and one story across both testaments
Distinguish modalism (Sabellianism) from the doctrine of the Trinity using passages where Father, Son, and Spirit act distinctly
Explain the Ebionite and adoptionist claims that Jesus was a mere man later made Son of God and identify texts that affirm his eternal deity
Analyze how Marcion's shortened canon pressed the early church to recognize which books belonged in Scripture
Compare Pelagius's teaching that people can obey God without inward grace with what Scripture says about sin inherited from Adam
Connect an ancient heresy to the teaching of a modern religious group, such as Arianism and the Jehovah's Witnesses' denial of Christ's deity
Explain the Donatist claim that a sacrament's validity depends on the holiness of the minister and the church's answer to it
Analyze how Montanism's claims of new prophecy challenged the sufficiency of the apostolic Scriptures
Explain why the early church held that the Redeemer must be both fully God and fully man to save, as the Reformed confessions also teach
Analyze a passage from Irenaeus's Against Heresies to identify how he answered Gnostic teaching by appeal to Scripture and the apostolic rule of faith
Classify the Christological heresies of the early centuries, including Docetism, Ebionism, Arianism, Apollinarianism, Nestorianism, and Eutychianism, by the truth about Christ's person each denies
Evaluate how the church's response to heresy led it to sharpen doctrinal language such as the term homoousios
Defend the Reformed doctrine of human inability against Pelagian and semi-Pelagian claims using Scripture and the confessions
Evaluate the criteria the early church used to distinguish orthodoxy from heresy, including Scripture, the apostolic rule of faith, and the consensus of the churches
Write an essay that traces a modern teaching to an ancient heresy and answers it from Scripture and the Reformed confessions

BIB.4.1.2.t: Identify that some of the first Christians were treated badly or hurt because they followed Jesus
Retell the story of Stephen as the first Christian killed for his witness to Jesus
Recall Jesus' teaching that the world would hate His followers as it first hated Him
Describe the catacombs as underground burial places outside Rome where early Christians buried their dead and remembered the martyrs
Explain how the apostles answered the authorities who ordered them to stop preaching about Jesus
Summarize Nero's persecution of Christians after the fire of Rome in AD 64 and the tradition of the deaths of Peter and Paul
Describe how Hebrews 13:3 calls Christians to remember and pray for believers who are persecuted and lead such a prayer in class
Explain why Romans accused Christians of atheism, cannibalism, and hatred of mankind
Describe the martyrdom of Polycarp and explain the meaning of his refusal to curse Christ
Explain from Acts how persecution scattered believers and spread the gospel to new places
Explain that the word martyr means witness and how the New Testament uses it for those who testify to Christ
Describe the account of Perpetua and Felicity and identify how their testimony expressed Christian convictions about Christ and eternal life
Explain why refusing to sacrifice to the gods or to confess Caesar as Lord was treated by Rome as disloyalty to the empire
Explain how early Christians honored and prayed for rulers while refusing to give them worship that belongs to God alone
Summarize the Roman policy described in the letters of Pliny and Trajan for how accused Christians were to be tried and punished
Analyze Tertullian's saying that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church using evidence from church growth during persecution
Explain how 1 Peter and Paul's letters connect the sufferings of believers to the sufferings of Christ
Explain the controversy over restoring Christians who denied the faith or surrendered Scriptures during persecution
Compare the Decian persecution and its sacrifice certificates with the Great Persecution under Diocletian and its attacks on Scripture and clergy
Evaluate how the legal status of Christianity changed from an unlawful superstition to a tolerated religion through the Edict of Galerius and the Edict of Milan
Construct a biblical theology of martyrdom that addresses witness, suffering, faithfulness, and the hope of the resurrection
Evaluate early church debates over whether Christians should seek martyrdom or flee persecution in light of Scripture
Evaluate the reliability and purpose of sources on persecution such as Tacitus, the martyr acts, and Eusebius
Evaluate how early Christian writers used the endurance of the martyrs as evidence for the truth of the faith
Write an essay comparing the persecution of the early church with the persecution of Christians in later and present times in light of Jesus' teaching on the cost of discipleship

BIB.4.1.3.t: Identify monks as Christians long ago who left ordinary life to spend their days praying and living simply
Retell how Anthony heard Jesus' words to the rich young man and went to live in the desert
Describe how Jesus went to quiet places to pray and how early monks tried to follow his example
Practice a short time of quiet prayer in class following Jesus' teaching on praying in secret
Name things early monks gave up such as money, houses, and marriage and explain what they hoped to gain by giving them up
Summarize the life of Anthony of Egypt as Athanasius told it
Explain why many Christians went to the desert after the persecutions ended and the church grew popular and comfortable under Constantine
Describe daily life in the communities Pachomius founded, including shared work, prayer, and meals
Compare the daily life of an early monk with the daily life of an ordinary Christian family in the early church
Describe how Basil of Caesarea organized monks to serve the poor and sick and connect his work to Jesus' teaching on caring for the needy
Distinguish eremitic hermit monasticism from cenobitic community monasticism and explain why many leaders came to favor community life
Describe how monasteries copied Scripture and preserved learning and literacy in the centuries after Rome fell
Explain the Benedictine Rule's pattern of prayer and work and compare it with Scripture's teaching on work
Analyze the strengths of early monasticism such as devotion and service alongside its dangers such as isolation and harsh self-denial
Analyze a passage from Athanasius' Life of Antony or the Sayings of the Desert Fathers for what it teaches about the Christian life
Compare Paul's teaching on singleness and marriage with the monastic view of celibacy as a higher way
Evaluate extreme ascetic practices such as Simeon Stylites living on a pillar in light of Paul's warnings about self-made religion
Explain the Reformed teaching that vows of perpetual celibacy, poverty, and obedience are not a higher degree of Christian perfection
Critique the two-tiered view of spirituality that ranks monks above laypeople using the Reformed doctrine that good works are those God commands in every lawful calling
Evaluate the impact of monasticism on Western civilization in learning, agriculture, care for the sick, and missions
Construct a biblical argument for being in the world but not of it that contrasts monastic withdrawal with the call to be salt and light
Design a plan for practicing solitude, silence, and simplicity grounded in Scripture that avoids the errors the Reformers identified in monasticism

BIB.4.1.4.t: Identify an apologist as a person who explains and defends what Christians believe
Name Justin Martyr as an early Christian teacher who wrote to explain the faith to rulers
Retell how early apologists answered false stories about Christians with truthful explanations and honest living
Explain from 1 Peter 3:15 that Christians are called to give a reason for their hope with gentleness and respect
Describe the charges of atheism, cannibalism, and disloyalty brought against Christians and how apologists explained Christian worship, the Lord's Supper, and prayer for rulers
Explain how Justin Martyr's First Apology addressed the emperor and asked that Christians be judged fairly rather than condemned for the name alone
Describe how Paul at the Areopagus began with what his hearers knew and pointed them to the Creator and the risen Christ as a model the apologists followed
Compare defending the faith by reasoned argument and godly conduct with defending it by force using examples from the apologists
Identify major early apologists such as Aristides, Justin, Athenagoras, Theophilus, Tertullian, and Origen along with the audiences they addressed
Describe how the Epistle to Diognetus presented the distinctive life of Christians as a witness to the truth of the faith
Analyze how Justin's Dialogue with Trypho used Old Testament prophecy to argue that Jesus is the promised Messiah
Explain how the apologists argued from the created order to one Creator and relate their argument to the Reformed teaching on the light of nature
Explain how Justin used the Greek idea of the Logos to present Christ and compare his use with the teaching of John 1
Analyze how Origen's Against Celsus answered educated pagan objections such as those against the incarnation and the resurrection
Summarize the Rule of Faith as stated by Irenaeus and Tertullian and explain how apologists used it as a faithful summary of apostolic teaching
Analyze the structure of argument in Justin's First Apology including appeals to justice, moral life, fulfilled prophecy, and the description of Christian worship
Evaluate the benefits and risks of the apologists' use of Greek philosophy by comparing Justin's approach with Tertullian's
Evaluate the apologists' arguments in light of the Reformed teaching that the authority of Scripture rests on God rather than on human proofs
Compare the methods of the early apologists with classical, evidential, and presuppositional approaches in modern apologetics
Create a written apology answering a contemporary objection to the Christian faith modeled on the method of an early apologist and grounded in Scripture

BIB.4.1.5.t: Identify the Apostolic Fathers as church leaders who lived soon after the apostles, some of whom learned directly from them
Name Clement, Ignatius, and Polycarp as early church leaders who wrote letters to churches
Retell how early church leaders wrote letters to teach and encourage churches, as the apostle Paul had done
Explain that Christ kept building his church after the last apostles died, using Jesus' promise in Matthew
Summarize the account of Polycarp's faithful testimony before the Roman official as told in the Martyrdom of Polycarp
Describe who Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, and Polycarp of Smyrna were and the city where each served
Distinguish the inspired writings of the apostles from the helpful but uninspired writings of the Apostolic Fathers

List the main writings in the Apostolic Fathers collection, including 1 Clement, the letters of Ignatius, Polycarp's Letter to the Philippians, the Didache, the Epistle of Barnabas, and the Shepherd of Hermas
Explain the purpose of 1 Clement as a letter urging the Corinthian church to end its division and restore its elders
Analyze the Didache's instructions on baptism, the Lord's Supper, prayer, and fasting as evidence of early Christian worship
Compare Ignatius's teaching on bishops, elders, and deacons with the New Testament pattern of church office
Explain how the Apostolic Fathers' quotations of New Testament books show which writings the early church already received as Scripture
Explain how Ignatius's letters affirm that Christ truly took on flesh, suffered, and rose from the dead
Construct a timeline placing the Apostolic Fathers and their writings in relation to the apostles and key events of the late first and early second centuries
Interpret passages from the Apostolic Fathers using their historical setting, audience, and purpose
Evaluate Clement's teaching on justification in 1 Clement 32 to 33 against Paul's teaching and the Reformed confession of justification by faith alone
Assess why some early churches read writings such as the Shepherd of Hermas publicly while the church did not receive them into the canon
Evaluate how the Reformed tradition uses the Apostolic Fathers as historical witnesses while holding them under the authority of Scripture
Construct an argument from primary sources for the continuity of the church's teaching from the apostles through the Apostolic Fathers

BIB.4.1.6.t: Identify a creed as a short statement of what the church believes from the Bible
Identify a church council as a meeting where church leaders gathered to study Scripture and settle a question
Recite the opening lines of the Apostles' Creed that name the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit
Recite the complete Apostles' Creed from memory
Describe how the apostles and elders met at the Jerusalem council to settle a question by appealing to Scripture
Explain how the Apostles' Creed is arranged around the three persons of the Trinity
Match lines of the Apostles' Creed to Bible passages that teach them
Summarize why the Council of Nicaea met in AD 325 and what it declared about Jesus being fully God
Compare a creed with a hymn in purpose, form, and use in worship
Identify the first four ecumenical councils with their dates and the central question each addressed
Explain the purposes of creeds as summaries of Scripture that unite believers, teach the faith, and guard against error
Explain how the Council of Nicaea used Scripture to answer the claim of Arius that the Son was created
Describe how Reformed churches use the ancient creeds in worship and catechesis today
Explain the meaning of homoousios and why the tradition holds that the Son being of one substance with the Father matters for salvation
Interpret the clauses on the Holy Spirit that the Council of Constantinople added to the Nicene Creed in AD 381
Explain how the Council of Ephesus affirmed that Christ is one person and why it called Mary Theotokos
Analyze the Chalcedonian Definition's phrases without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation as a statement of the hypostatic union
Explain why the Reformed tradition receives the ancient creeds as faithful summaries that remain subordinate to Scripture
Analyze the structure and teaching of the Athanasian Creed on the Trinity and the incarnation
Construct a historical overview of the first four ecumenical councils showing the occasion, key figures, and outcome of each
Compare the Eastern and Western forms of the Nicene Creed and explain the filioque clause and the Reformed position on it
Evaluate why the councils adopted precise terms not found in Scripture such as homoousios and hypostasis to express biblical teaching
Evaluate a modern teaching about the Trinity or the person of Christ using the Nicene and Chalcedonian formulations
Evaluate the role of emperors such as Constantine in calling councils in light of the Reformed teaching on church and civil authority
Produce a research study of Athanasius's defense of Nicene teaching, including his exiles and the phrase Athanasius contra mundum

BIB.4.2.1.t: Recognize that long ago most people could not read or hear the Bible in their own language and that some faithful men worked to change this
Name John Wycliffe and Jan Hus as preachers who taught that the Bible should guide the church
Retell the story of Wycliffe and his helpers translating and copying the Bible into English by hand
Describe how Jan Hus was put to death for refusing to take back his teaching and connect his story to what Jesus said about those persecuted for righteousness
Explain how Gutenberg's printing press changed how quickly and cheaply copies of the Bible could be made
Explain why Wycliffe believed ordinary people should read Scripture in their own language, using the Bereans as a biblical example and the Reformed confession of vernacular translation
Describe Peter Waldo and the Waldensians as lay preachers who spread Scripture in the common language and endured persecution
Compare the simple lives of Wycliffe's poor preachers with the wealth of many church leaders and explain the criticism Wycliffe drew from Jesus' sending of his disciples
Construct a timeline of key people and events in medieval dissent from the Waldensians through Wycliffe, Hus, and the printing press to 1517
Explain Wycliffe's teaching that Scripture is the highest authority above popes and councils and relate it to the Reformed confession of Scripture as supreme judge
Explain Hus's teaching that Christ, not the pope, is the head of the church, using the passages Reformed churches cite for this doctrine
Explain how the Avignon papacy and the Western Schism weakened confidence in church leadership and gave openings to critics like Wycliffe and Hus
Analyze the Council of Constance's actions against Hus and Wycliffe, including the broken safe-conduct and the posthumous condemnation of Wycliffe
Explain how Hus's appeal to Scripture and conscience before the council reflects the biblical teaching that God must be obeyed rather than men
Explain how Luther came to recognize continuity between his own teaching and the earlier work of Hus
Analyze excerpts from Wycliffe or Hus to identify their scriptural arguments against indulgences and transubstantiation
Explain how the humanist call to return to the sources and Erasmus's 1516 Greek New Testament prepared the way for the Reformation
Distinguish between moral reform movements such as Savonarola's preaching and doctrinal reform rooted in the authority of Scripture
Evaluate the influence and suppression of the Lollard movement in England, including the 1401 law for burning heretics
Evaluate how fully the precursors anticipated Reformation doctrine, distinguishing their clear stand on Scripture's authority from their less developed teaching on justification by faith alone
Compose an argumentative essay on the cost of reforming the church that draws on the precursors' cases and on Scripture's teaching about faithfulness under persecution

BIB.4.2.2.t: Explain that Jesus calls his people to love God with their minds as well as their hearts
Identify Anselm and Thomas Aquinas as Christian teachers who lived long ago and wrote about God
Describe how medieval Christians started cathedral schools and universities such as Paris and Oxford to study God's Word and his world
Explain the meaning of Anselm's motto faith seeking understanding and the scriptural idea of knowledge beginning with the fear of the Lord
Compare how students learned in a medieval monastery with how they learned in a medieval university
Demonstrate the scholastic method by working through a theological question with objections, a reply, and answers to the objections
Explain the goal of Scholasticism to organize Christian teaching into an ordered system, using Peter Lombard's Sentences and Aquinas' Summa Theologiae as examples
Summarize Anselm's argument in Cur Deus Homo for why the Savior had to be both truly God and truly man
Summarize Anselm's ontological argument for God's existence from the Proslogion
Explain how the rediscovery of Aristotle's writings in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries shaped scholastic theology
Summarize Aquinas' Five Ways and relate them to what Scripture teaches about God revealed in creation
Distinguish Aquinas' view of what natural reason can know from the Reformed confession that saving knowledge comes only through Scripture
Compare Anselm's satisfaction view of the atonement with the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution
Analyze how Aquinas' use of Aristotelian categories supported the doctrine of transubstantiation and why the Reformed confessions reject it
Evaluate the strengths and dangers of combining Greek philosophy with biblical theology in medieval Scholasticism
Assess how later Reformed theologians both adopted the scholastic method and corrected scholastic doctrine according to Scripture
Construct a reasoned defense of the Christian faith that draws on a classical scholastic argument while grounding it in Scripture

BIB.4.2.3.t: Identify that in the year 1054 the church divided into an Eastern church and a Western church
Name the Eastern church as the Orthodox church and the Western church as the Roman Catholic church
Locate Rome and Constantinople on a map and identify each city as the leading center of one side of the divided church
Identify Latin as the main language of the Western church and Greek as the main language of the Eastern church
Describe how the East-West split grew over many years of disagreement about church leaders and beliefs rather than happening all at once
Explain how the authority claimed by the pope in Rome differed from the role of the patriarch of Constantinople and why this difference helped cause the split
Compare worship practices of the Latin and Greek churches, such as the language of worship, leavened or unleavened bread in the Lord's Supper, and the marriage of priests
Explain how the division of the Roman Empire into eastern and western halves contributed to the cultural separation of the churches
Explain what the Filioque clause added to the Nicene Creed and why the Eastern church objected to the West adding it without an ecumenical council
Describe the events of 1054, including the mission of Cardinal Humbert to Constantinople and the mutual excommunications of Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius
Analyze how political and cultural differences between Latin and Greek Christians deepened the theological disputes between East and West
Analyze how the Crusades, including the placing of Latin bishops over Eastern cities, hardened the separation between the churches after 1054
Explain the Reformed confessional teaching that the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father and the Son
Examine in their context the biblical passages each side used in the debate over the procession of the Holy Spirit
Construct a comparison of Eastern Orthodox, Roman Catholic, and Reformed positions on the issues raised by the schism, including church authority and the procession of the Spirit
Evaluate the Filioque controversy by weighing both the doctrinal question about the Spirit and the question of who has authority to change an ecumenical creed
Evaluate the schism in light of Scripture's teaching on unity in truth and the Reformed confession of one catholic church that visible churches only partly display
Evaluate what the 1965 lifting of the 1054 excommunications by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras did and did not resolve between the churches
Produce a researched study of the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204 and its lasting effects on East-West relations

BIB.4.2.4.t: Identify the pope as the bishop who led the church in the city of Rome
Locate Rome on a map and name it as the capital city of the Roman Empire
Retell what Scripture records about Paul preaching in Rome and Jesus foretelling Peter's death, and recall the early church's report that both apostles died there
Identify from Scripture that Jesus Christ is the head of the church
Describe how the bishop of Rome came to be called pope, a title meaning father
Explain how Leo the Great's meeting with Attila the Hun in 452 raised the standing of the bishop of Rome
Explain why the church of Rome gained special honor among early churches, including its place in the capital and its link to Peter and Paul
Contrast the authority of Scripture as the church's final rule with the authority later claimed by the pope
Describe the medieval church hierarchy of pope, cardinals, bishops, and priests and the role of each
Compare the medieval hierarchy with the offices of elder and deacon described in the New Testament
Analyze the Roman Catholic reading of Matthew 16 as grounds for Petrine supremacy alongside the Reformed reading that the church is built on the confession of Christ
Explain how the collapse of Roman imperial rule in the West left the bishop of Rome as a leading civil and spiritual figure
Describe the contributions of Gregory the Great, including his mission to England, his pastoral writing, and his governing of Rome
Explain how the alliance with Frankish kings, including Pepin's donation and the crowning of Charlemagne in 800, created the Papal States and tied popes to political power
Explain how the Donation of Constantine was used to support papal claims and how Lorenzo Valla showed it to be a forgery
Analyze the Investiture Controversy between Gregory VII and Henry IV and the settlement reached at the Concordat of Worms
Evaluate the claims of Innocent III and Boniface VIII's Unam Sanctam to papal supremacy over earthly rulers in light of Jesus' teaching on his kingdom
