Defend the Reformed confessional position that no pope can be head of the church, using Scripture and the Westminster Confession
Construct a historical argument tracing the stages by which the honor of the Roman bishop grew into a claim to universal spiritual and civil jurisdiction

BIB.4.3.1.t: Identify John Calvin as a pastor who preached and taught the Bible in the city of Geneva
Locate Geneva on a map of Europe and describe it as a city where people gathered to hear the Bible taught
Recall that Calvin taught that God rules over all things and that all glory belongs to him
Retell the main events of Calvin's life, including his flight from France, his call to Geneva by Farel, his exile to Strasbourg, and his return to Geneva
Explain Calvin's teaching that ordinary work and daily life can be done for the glory of God
Name the Institutes of the Christian Religion as Calvin's major book and describe its purpose as a guide for reading and teaching the Bible
Describe how the people of Geneva sang the Psalms together using the Genevan Psalter and explain the scriptural basis for congregational psalm singing
Explain what makes a church Reformed and trace the name to the churches shaped by Calvin's teaching in Geneva
Describe the four church offices Calvin established in Geneva, namely pastors, teachers, elders, and deacons, and identify the passages he drew them from
Explain why Geneva became a refuge for Protestants fleeing persecution and how returning refugees carried Reformed teaching back to their homelands
Describe the founding of the Geneva Academy and its role in training pastors who were sent out as missionaries to France and beyond
Compare Calvin's role as an organizer and systematic teacher of the Reformation with Luther's role in beginning it
Describe Calvin's practice of preaching verse by verse through whole books of the Bible and writing commentaries on most of Scripture
Analyze the structure and main themes of the Institutes, beginning with Calvin's claim that knowledge of God and knowledge of ourselves are bound together
Explain Calvin's teaching that believers truly feed on Christ spiritually in the Lord's Supper and distinguish it from transubstantiation and a merely memorial view
Trace Calvin's influence through John Knox in Scotland, the Huguenots in France, the Puritans in England, and the Pilgrims in America
Explain the Reformed doctrine of God's sovereignty in salvation as Calvin taught it from Paul's letters
Summarize Calvin's teaching on union with Christ as the source of the twofold grace of justification and sanctification
Explain Calvin's teaching that Scripture is confirmed to believers by the inward witness of the Holy Spirit
Analyze the work of the Geneva Consistory in church discipline and the relationship between church and civil authority in Calvin's Geneva
Construct a profile of Calvin as pastor and theologian using primary sources such as his sermons, letters, and prefaces
Evaluate the trial and execution of Michael Servetus using primary sources, weighing sixteenth-century context against the teaching of Scripture
Defend the Reformed doctrine of predestination from Scripture while responding to major objections and explaining the care the confessions urge in teaching it
Distinguish Calvin's own teaching from later Calvinism as formulated at the Synod of Dort
Develop a reasoned argument assessing the legacy of Calvinism in Western history, including its effects on education, representative church government, and views of work

BIB.4.3.2.t: Identify Martin Luther as a man who lived long ago and called the church back to the Bible
Retell how Luther posted the 95 Theses on the church door in Wittenberg on October 31, 1517
Recall that Luther taught that God's forgiveness is a free gift received by faith and cannot be bought with money
Summarize the story of the thunderstorm and Luther's vow to become a monk
Describe how Luther translated the Bible into German so that ordinary people could read it in their own language
Describe Luther's work writing hymns for congregations to sing, including A Mighty Fortress Is Our God and the psalm it is drawn from
Explain what an indulgence was and why Johann Tetzel's sale of indulgences troubled Luther
Describe the late medieval church practices Luther grew up with, including penance, pilgrimages, relics, and the belief in purgatory
Describe Luther's struggle as a monk to find peace with God through fasting, confession, and good works
Describe the purpose and structure of Luther's Small Catechism as a tool for teaching families the faith
Explain the main claims of selected theses, such as Thesis 1 on lifelong repentance and Thesis 62 on the gospel as the true treasure of the church
Analyze how Luther's study of Romans 1:17 changed his understanding of the righteousness of God and of justification
Explain how the printing press spread the 95 Theses and Luther's later writings across Europe
Summarize the events of the Diet of Worms in 1521 and explain Luther's appeal to Scripture and conscience in his reply
Explain Luther's teaching on the priesthood of all believers and its basis in Scripture
Compare Luther's view of justification by faith with the late medieval church's teaching on merit and penance
Analyze primary source excerpts of the 95 Theses to trace how Luther's critique moved from indulgence abuses toward questions of papal authority
Analyze the main arguments of Luther's 1520 treatises, including The Freedom of a Christian and The Babylonian Captivity of the Church
Contrast Luther's theology of the cross with the theology of glory as set out in the Heidelberg Disputation of 1518
Evaluate Luther's later writings and actions, including his response to the Peasants' War and his writings against the Jews, in light of Scripture
Evaluate arguments for and against the necessity of Luther's break with Rome using Scripture as the final authority
Assess the lasting impact of Luther's German Bible on the German language, church life, and later vernacular translations
Construct a researched historical argument on the significance of the 95 Theses using primary and secondary sources

BIB.4.3.3.t: Recall that the Bible teaches that God saves people as a free gift and not because of the good things they do
Name the five alone phrases of the Reformation in English as Scripture alone, grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, and the glory of God alone
Identify the Bible as the only rule God has given for what to believe and how to live, using a verse that teaches it
Match each Latin sola name with its English meaning
Explain in simple words what each of the five solas means and pair each with a Bible verse that supports it
Explain why the word alone was the point of disagreement in the Reformation, since both sides affirmed Scripture, grace, faith, and Christ but differed on whether anything else was added
Explain the Reformed teaching that Jesus Christ is the only mediator between God and people and the only Savior
Describe what Soli Deo Gloria teaches and identify ways ordinary work, study, and play can be done for the glory of God
Describe the late medieval teachings on merit, the intercession of saints, church tradition, and penance that the Reformers believed obscured the gospel
Interpret Ephesians 2:1-10 in its context to explain how grace, faith, and good works relate in salvation
Analyze how each of the five solas answered a specific late medieval teaching or practice
Explain the doctrine of justification by faith alone from Romans and Galatians as the Reformed confessions state it
Distinguish the Reformation teaching of Scripture as the supreme authority over creeds and councils from the view that rejects all church tradition
Explain how the Reformed tradition connects grace alone with human inability and God's effectual calling
Analyze how Reformed confessions reconcile justification by faith alone with James 2 through the teaching that justifying faith is never alone but works by love
Explain the doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness as the ground of justification in Reformed teaching
Compare the Reformation doctrine of justification with the Council of Trent's decree on justification
Identify where each sola is stated in Reformation-era confessions and explain that the five solas as a set is a later summary of those teachings
Evaluate the claim that justification is the article on which the church stands or falls using Scripture and the Reformed confessions
Evaluate contemporary teachings such as the prosperity gospel, religious pluralism, and claims of new revelation against the five solas
Construct a reasoned defense of one sola that answers a major historical or modern objection from Scripture and the confessions
Compose an essay showing how the five solas depend on one another and point to the glory of God as their goal

BIB.4.3.4.t: Identify Ulrich Zwingli as a pastor in Zurich, Switzerland, who taught his church from the Bible
Name the Anabaptists as a group who taught that only people who confess faith should be baptized, which led others to call them rebaptizers
Retell how Zwingli began in 1519 to preach through the Gospel of Matthew verse by verse instead of following the assigned readings
Recount that early Anabaptist leaders such as Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz were punished by both Roman Catholic and Protestant authorities, including the drowning of Manz in Zurich in 1527
Describe the 1522 Affair of the Sausages and explain Zwingli's argument that Scripture does not require Christians to keep the Lenten fast
Describe how the Zurich disputations of 1523 and Zwingli's Sixty-Seven Articles sought to settle church questions by appeal to Scripture
Describe Zwingli's death at the Battle of Kappel in 1531 and Heinrich Bullinger's role in continuing the Zurich reformation
Summarize the disagreement between Luther and Zwingli over the Lord's Supper at the Marburg Colloquy of 1529, including their readings of the words this is my body
Explain the Anabaptist case for believer's baptism from the New Testament passages they cited
Explain how Zwingli reformed worship in Zurich by removing images and simplifying the service on the basis of the second commandment
Compare Zwingli's memorial view of the Lord's Supper with the later Reformed confessional teaching of a spiritual feeding on Christ by faith
Contrast the Magisterial Reformers' view that the civil magistrate should support the true church with the Anabaptist call for a church separate from the state
Explain the Reformed case for infant baptism that Zwingli set against the Anabaptists, grounded in the continuity of God's covenant with believers and their children
Trace how Menno Simons and later movements such as the Mennonites, Amish, and Hutterites descend from sixteenth-century Anabaptism
Explain why Zurich and other Protestant authorities treated Anabaptism as a threat to civil and religious order and punished its followers
Analyze the seven articles of the Schleitheim Confession of 1527 and the Scripture passages Anabaptists used to support them
Construct a comparison of Lutheran, Reformed, and Anabaptist teaching on baptism, the Lord's Supper, and the relationship of church and state
Evaluate the Anabaptist rejection of oaths, military service, and civil office in light of Scripture and the Reformed confessional position
Evaluate the Protestant persecution of Anabaptists using biblical teaching on the nature of Christ's kingdom and on living at peace with others
Evaluate the Anabaptist idea of a believers' church against the Reformed teaching that the visible church includes believers and their children
Produce a research study distinguishing the violent Münster Rebellion of 1534 to 1535 from peaceful Anabaptism and analyzing how Münster shaped later views of the movement

BIB.5.1.1.t: Identify the Buddha as a teacher who lived long ago in India and whose followers are called Buddhists
Recall that the Buddha taught that wanting things causes unhappiness and that people should live calmly and gently
Summarize the story of Siddhartha Gautama, the prince who left his palace after seeing old age, sickness, and death and later sat in meditation under a tree
Describe how Buddhists use images of the Buddha, temples, monks, and meditation in their religious practice
Explain the Buddhist idea of Nirvana as the blowing out of desire and the end of the cycle of suffering
Compare the Buddha's claim to have found a path to enlightenment with Jesus' claim to be the way, the truth, and the life
Explain the Three Jewels of Buddhism as the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha
Describe ways to speak about Buddhist beliefs accurately and respectfully when talking with Buddhist neighbors
Explain each of the Four Noble Truths and how they describe suffering, its cause in craving, its cessation, and the path to its end
Classify the eight parts of the Eightfold Path into the groups of wisdom, ethical conduct, and mental discipline
Explain the Buddhist concepts of karma, rebirth, and samsara and trace how Buddhism reshaped these ideas from its Hindu background
Contrast the Eightfold Path as a path of self-effort with the Reformed teaching that salvation is by grace through faith in Christ
Explain the three marks of existence in Buddhism, including impermanence, suffering, and no self
Compare the Buddhist teaching of anatta with the biblical teaching that each human is a created person made in God's image
Analyze the Buddhist account of the cause of suffering alongside the biblical account of suffering as a result of the fall
Evaluate the Buddhist goal of extinguishing craving and self against the Reformed teaching that humanity's chief end is to glorify and enjoy God
Construct a defense of the biblical view that suffering is real and is answered by Christ's redemption and the hope of a renewed creation
Compare the Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana traditions, including the ideals of the arhat and the bodhisattva
Evaluate popular mindfulness practices drawn from Buddhism in light of biblical meditation on God's Word

BIB.5.2.1.t: Retell a Bible story in which a person chose to do what was right even when it was hard
Recall the Golden Rule and explain how it guides the way we treat other people
Name character qualities the Bible calls good, such as kindness, patience, and self-control
Describe three questions people ask when making a moral choice: what the rule says, what will happen, and what kind of person the choice makes them
Explain from Scripture why doing something wrong to get a good result is still wrong
Compare acting out of duty to a rule with acting from good character using a story or case
Define utilitarianism as judging actions by whether they produce the greatest good for the greatest number
Define deontology as judging actions by duties and rules regardless of their outcomes
Analyze how utilitarian and deontological reasoning reach different conclusions about the same moral case
Describe virtue ethics, including Aristotle's account of virtue as a habit formed by practice and a mean between extremes
Identify the four classical cardinal virtues and the three theological virtues and locate the theological virtues in Scripture
Apply utilitarian, deontological, and virtue reasoning to a classic dilemma such as the trolley problem and explain each conclusion
Analyze biblical passages to show where Scripture appeals to commands, to consequences, and to character in its moral teaching
Explain Kant's categorical imperative in its formulations of universal law and of treating persons as ends and never merely as means
Analyze the difficulties of measuring and comparing happiness in the utilitarian theories of Bentham and Mill
Construct a critique of utilitarianism based on the dignity of every person as made in the image of God
Evaluate Kant's grounding of duty in autonomous reason against the Reformed teaching that the moral law is revealed by God and written on the heart
Evaluate how virtue ethics compares with the Reformed doctrine of sanctification, distinguishing character formed by grace from habit formed by human effort alone
Produce an argued essay on a complex bioethical issue that analyzes how each ethical system approaches it and evaluates them in light of Scripture

BIB.5.2.2.t: Identify that the Bible teaches God is good and tells people what is right and wrong
Name the Ten Commandments as the rules God gave his people to show them how to live
Retell how Jesus summarized God's law as loving God and loving your neighbor
Describe how Romans 2 explains that people who do not know the Bible still have a sense of right and wrong written on their hearts
Explain that secular ethics is an approach that decides right and wrong without reference to God or Scripture
Explain why the Bible teaches that every human life has worth because people are made in the image of God
Compare a reason for an action based on God's command with a reason based on personal feeling or preference
Identify common secular sources of moral authority such as personal feelings, cultural agreement, civil law, and human well-being
Apply the Ten Commandments to contemporary moral situations using the catechism's account of what each commandment requires and forbids
Explain the Euthyphro dilemma and the Reformed response that goodness is grounded in God's unchanging nature rather than in arbitrary will or a standard above God
Explain the moral argument for God's existence and identify its premises and conclusion
Analyze how Christian and secular accounts each ground human dignity and human rights, including the biblical teaching on the image of God
Explain individual and cultural moral relativism and identify the internal tensions in each form
Explain how the Reformed tradition accounts for real moral goodness in the actions of those who do not believe, while distinguishing it from works done in faith
Construct an argument for objective moral standards that draws on Scripture and the tradition's teaching that the moral law binds all people
Evaluate evolutionary accounts that explain morality as a product of survival and social instinct
Evaluate major objections to divine command theory and distinguish it from the Reformed view of the moral law as a perfect rule of righteousness reflecting God's character
Analyze how Scripture and the Reformed confessions relate law and love, including love as the fulfilling of the law and the uses of the law for believers
Create a comparative analysis of a contemporary ethical issue showing how a theological and a secular framework each reach and justify their conclusions

BIB.5.3.1.t: Identify Hinduism as an ancient religion that began in India and is followed by many people around the world today
Identify karma as the Hindu teaching that a person's actions bring good or bad results in this life or a future life
Describe samsara as the Hindu belief that the soul is reborn into new bodies again and again in a cycle
Explain how the Bible's teaching that each person lives once and then faces judgment differs from the Hindu belief in reincarnation
Identify the major Hindu sacred texts including the Vedas, the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, the Ramayana, and the Mahabharata
Explain dharma as the Hindu idea of duty and right order that depends on a person's place and stage in life
Describe the four traditional Hindu goals of life of dharma, artha, kama, and moksha and how they relate to one another
Compare the origin and authority Hindus give their sacred texts with the Reformed teaching that the Bible is God's inspired and sufficient written word
Analyze how the traditional varna and caste system was justified by dharma and karma and compare it with the biblical teaching that all people bear God's image and share one origin
Distinguish Brahman as ultimate reality from Atman as the inner self and explain the Upanishadic claim that Atman is Brahman
Explain moksha as release from samsara and describe the paths of knowledge, devotion, and action presented in the Bhagavad Gita
Compare the Hindu pursuit of moksha through effort and knowledge with the Reformed teaching of salvation as God's free gift of grace through faith in Christ
Contrast the Hindu cyclical view of time and ages with the biblical linear view of history from creation to new creation
Distinguish the major Hindu philosophical schools of Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita by their teaching on the relationship between Brahman and the self
Analyze a primary source passage from the Upanishads or the Bhagavad Gita to identify its teaching on dharma, karma, or the self in its literary and historical context
Evaluate pantheism and monism in light of the biblical distinction between the Creator and his creation
Evaluate the explanation of suffering given by karma against the biblical account of the Fall and God's work of redemption
Analyze how Hindu concepts such as karma, reincarnation, and monism have shaped Western culture and New Age spirituality
Construct a written argument for the distinct personhood of God and of individual humans in contrast with Hindu teaching that the self is ultimately one with Brahman
Create a respectful dialogue that accurately represents Hindu beliefs about karma and samsara and explains the Christian gospel's answer to them

BIB.5.3.2.t: Identify a Hindu temple, or mandir, as a place where Hindus bring offerings such as fruit and flowers to their gods
Describe how many Hindus in India treat the cow as a sacred animal
Recall the first and second commandments, which teach that the one true God alone is to be worshiped and not through images
Describe how Hindus use statues and images of their gods, called murtis, when they pray and worship
Identify Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva as the Hindu Trimurti and state the role of creator, preserver, or destroyer given to each
Describe how Hindus celebrate Diwali, the festival of lights, including its lamps, gifts, and story of light overcoming darkness
Identify widely worshiped Hindu deities such as Ganesha, Lakshmi, Durga, Krishna, and Rama by their common symbols
Explain the Hindu idea of an avatar as a god descending in bodily form, using Rama and Krishna as avatars of Vishnu
Describe other major Hindu festivals such as Holi and Navaratri and the deities or stories each one honors
Compare man-made idols with the living God using the descriptions of idols in Isaiah and the Psalms
Apply the second commandment, as the Reformed confessions explain it, to show why worship through images is forbidden and God is to be worshiped only as He commands
Describe the main steps of puja at a home shrine or temple, including offerings, arati, darshan, and prasad
Analyze what the practice of puja shows about the Hindu understanding of how a worshiper relates to a deity
Explain the role of the guru as a spiritual teacher and guide in Hindu devotion
Compare Hindu pilgrimage and ritual bathing in the Ganges with the biblical teaching that cleansing from sin comes through the blood of Christ
Describe Hindu devotional practices such as bhakti, mantra repetition, yoga, and meditation and the religious purposes Hindus give for them
Describe Hindu life-cycle rituals, or samskaras, such as the naming ceremony, the sacred thread ceremony, marriage, and cremation
Distinguish polytheism, henotheism, and monism as ways Hindus understand the many deities, and contrast them with biblical monotheism
Construct a comparison of the Incarnation of Christ with Hindu avatars, addressing the historical, once-for-all union of true God and true man in one person
Analyze the diversity of Hindu practice across traditions such as Vaishnavism, Shaivism, and Shaktism and in Western movements such as ISKCON
Evaluate the social practices of the caste system, including untouchability, in light of the biblical teaching that all people bear the image of God
Compose an argued essay evaluating Hindu offerings and rituals against the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ
Develop a plan for a respectful conversation with a Hindu neighbor that represents Hindu worship accurately and presents the Christian gospel

BIB.5.4.1.t: Identify Muslims as people who follow the religion of Islam
Recall that Muslims worship one god whom they call Allah
Identify Mecca in Arabia as the city where Islam began and the most holy city for Muslims
Explain that Christians also confess one God but confess this one God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
Summarize the main events of Muhammad's life including his claimed revelations, the Hijra to Medina, and his return to Mecca
Explain that the word Islam means submission and that a Muslim is understood as one who submits to Allah
Compare the Islamic view of Isa as a human prophet with the Bible's teaching that Jesus is the eternal Son of God made flesh
List the six articles of Islamic faith concerning Allah, angels, revealed books, prophets, the Day of Judgment, and divine decree
Describe the Islamic doctrine of tawhid and explain why Muslims regard belief in the Trinity as shirk
Explain how the early Muslim community spread under the first caliphs after Muhammad's death
Distinguish what Genesis records about Ishmael from later Islamic and Arab traditions that link Abraham and Ishmael to Mecca
Explain how the Sunni and Shia division arose from the dispute over succession after Muhammad and identify key differences between them
Analyze the Islamic claim that Muhammad is the seal of the prophets in light of the biblical teaching that God has spoken finally in his Son
Contrast the Islamic view of human nature and sin with the Reformed doctrine of original sin
Compare the Islamic hope of judgment by the weighing of deeds with the Reformed doctrine of justification by grace through faith
Evaluate the Islamic denial of Jesus' crucifixion using the New Testament eyewitness testimony and the Reformed teaching on why Christ's death was necessary
Evaluate the Islamic charge that the Trinity is polytheism using Scripture and the Reformed confession of one God in three persons
Develop a respectful explanation of the gospel that answers a core Islamic objection to Christian belief
Compose an argument comparing the Islamic emphasis on God's sovereign will with the Christian confession that God is love eternally within the Trinity

BIB.5.4.2.t: Identify the Quran as the holy book of Islam and the Bible as the holy book of Christians
Name prayer and giving to the poor as practices Muslims carry out
Recall that Muslims fast from food and drink during daylight hours in the month of Ramadan and celebrate Eid when it ends
List the Five Pillars of Islam (shahada, salat, zakat, sawm, hajj) and describe each in a simple sentence
Describe how Arabic calligraphy of Quranic verses is used to decorate mosques and books in place of pictures
Explain what the Hajj is, including the journey to Mecca and the role of the Kaaba
Describe the practice of salat, including the five daily times, the call to prayer, facing Mecca, and ritual washing beforehand
Compare the structure of the Quran, with its 114 suras arranged mostly by length, to the structure of the Bible, with its 66 books written by many authors across two testaments
State the content of the shahada and explain the two claims it makes about God and Muhammad
Explain the Muslim belief that the Quran is authentic only in Arabic and contrast it with the Christian practice of translating Scripture into every language
Compare the form and purpose of salat with the Christian teaching on prayer found in the Lord's Prayer
Explain how zakat is calculated and used and compare it with biblical teaching on generous giving
Compare the Ramadan fast with Jesus's teaching on fasting
Explain the role of the Hadith and Sunna as a second source of authority alongside the Quran in Muslim practice
Compare ritual washing (wudu) with Old Testament ceremonial washings and explain how Hebrews presents Christ as the one who truly cleanses
Analyze the meaning Muslims give to Hajj rituals and their link to Abraham and compare this with the Genesis account of Abraham and Isaac
Compare the Islamic reliance on Hadith tradition with the Reformed doctrine of the sufficiency and supreme authority of Scripture
Explain how Muslims interpret the Quran through tafsir and the principle of abrogation and contrast this with the Reformed principle that Scripture interprets Scripture
Compare Quranic passages about Jesus, including the denial of his crucifixion, with the Gospel accounts of his death and resurrection
Evaluate the Quran's claim that earlier scriptures were corrupted in light of the Bible's own claims about its preservation and the manuscript evidence
Explain how Sharia is derived from the Quran, Hadith, consensus, and analogy and evaluate its implications for law and freedom of conscience
Evaluate the place of the Five Pillars in Muslim hope of divine favor in light of the Reformed doctrine of justification by grace through faith
Write a gracious, Scripture-based response to a Muslim neighbor's question about why Christians do not keep fixed rules of ritual prayer, fasting, and pilgrimage

BIB.5.5.1.t: Identify that Jewish people believe there is one God who made everything
Name the Torah as the holy scroll read in the synagogue and describe how it is handled with great care
Explain why many Jewish people avoid saying or fully writing God's name and connect this practice to the third commandment
Recognize several Hebrew letters and identify that the Hebrew Scriptures are written mostly in Hebrew and read from right to left
Recite the opening words of the Shema and explain what it teaches about God being one and about loving him with all of life
List the three parts of the Tanakh as Torah, Prophets, and Writings and give an example book from each part
Explain what the Talmud is and distinguish the Mishnah from the Gemara as layers of rabbinic teaching
Describe the Jewish belief that God's covenants with Abraham and with Israel at Sinai form the foundation of Jewish peoplehood
Compare the Jewish understanding of God's oneness with the doctrine of the Trinity as confessed by Reformed churches
Explain the rabbinic teaching that an Oral Torah was given at Sinai alongside the Written Torah
Describe the concept of mitzvot, including the traditional count of 613 commandments, and explain why Judaism views Torah as a whole way of life
Summarize the main points of Maimonides' Thirteen Principles of Faith as a historic statement of Jewish belief about God, Torah, and the Messiah
Explain how the Jewish description of God's character in the thirteen attributes of mercy draws on God's self-revelation to Moses
Explain how religious leadership in Judaism shifted from Temple priests to rabbis as teachers of Torah after the destruction of the Temple in AD 70
Analyze Jesus' disputes with the Pharisees over the tradition of the elders in light of the developing Oral Law
Explain how Midrash and classic commentators such as Rashi interpret passages of the Hebrew Scriptures
Explain the Jewish view of sin and atonement without a Temple through repentance, prayer, good deeds, and Yom Kippur
Compare how Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform Judaism understand the authority of the Written Torah and the Oral Law
Compare the Jewish understanding of righteousness through covenant faithfulness and repentance with the Reformed doctrine of justification by grace through faith in Christ's sacrifice
Evaluate the rabbinic claim of an authoritative oral tradition from Sinai in light of the Reformed doctrine that Scripture alone is the supreme rule of faith
Develop a research study comparing Jewish and Reformed Christian understandings of Israel as God's chosen people using the relevant biblical texts

BIB.5.5.2.t: Identify that Jesus was a Jewish man who read and taught from the Old Testament
Name the Old Testament as the holy book that both Jewish people and Christians read
Retell how God called Abraham and promised to make his family a great nation that would bless the world
Identify the Torah as the first five books of the Bible from Genesis through Deuteronomy
Describe the three parts of the Hebrew Bible called Torah, Prophets, and Writings and explain that together they are called the Tanakh
Explain that many Jewish people today still wait for the promised Messiah while the church confesses that Jesus is that Messiah
Compare the order of books in the Tanakh with the Christian Old Testament and show that both contain the same books
Explain how Jesus and the apostles read the Old Testament as pointing to Christ
Describe how Jewish scribes preserved the Hebrew text and why the Masoretic text is the basis of modern Old Testament translations
Describe the Oral Torah and how the Mishnah and Talmud function in Judaism as authoritative interpretation alongside the written Torah
Analyze how the destruction of the Temple in AD 70 led rabbinic Judaism to reinterpret Old Testament sacrifice and priesthood
Contrast the Reformed distinction among moral, ceremonial, and judicial law with the Jewish view of the commandments of the Torah as continuing obligations
Compare how Jewish and Christian interpreters read key messianic passages such as Isaiah 53 and Psalm 22
Explain how Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform Judaism differ in their views of the authority of the Torah
Explain what the Septuagint is and how the New Testament writers used it in quoting the Old Testament
Explain the Reformed teaching of one covenant of grace under two administrations and how it shapes the Christian reading of the Old Testament
Compare covenant theology and dispensationalism on the relationship between Israel and the church
Construct a case from the Hebrew Bible for the Messiahship of Jesus that answers common Jewish objections
Evaluate how Christians should speak about and to Jewish people in light of Romans 9-11 and the church's history of antisemitism
Synthesize a written comparison of how Judaism and Reformed Christianity each receive and interpret the Hebrew Scriptures, noting shared heritage and key divergences

BIB.5.5.3.t: Identify Shabbat as the weekly day of rest that Jewish families keep from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset
Name Passover and Hanukkah as Jewish celebrations and tell one thing each one remembers
Describe common Shabbat home practices such as lighting candles, blessing bread and wine, and sharing a family meal
Recall that Jewish dietary laws called kosher permit some foods and forbid others such as pork
Describe how Jewish families celebrate Hanukkah by lighting the menorah and Purim by reading the book of Esther
Identify the items on a Passover Seder plate and explain what each represents in the Exodus story
Summarize the main kosher rules including permitted animals, the separation of meat and dairy, and the draining of blood
Describe the High Holy Days of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur and the practices of repentance and fasting connected with them
Explain Bar and Bat Mitzvah as the point at which a Jewish young person takes on responsibility for keeping the commandments
Describe the synagogue as a place of prayer, Torah reading, and community life and identify its main features
Compare the Jewish seventh-day Sabbath with the Christian Lord's Day in timing, purpose, and practice
Categorize the biblical pilgrimage festivals and the later festivals of Hanukkah and Purim by their origin and the events they remember
Explain how practices such as Sabbath, circumcision, and dietary laws have preserved Jewish identity through exile and diaspora
Analyze how the Levitical dietary laws marked Israel's separation from the nations as a holy people
Identify occasions in the Gospels when Jesus took part in Jewish festivals and explain what he taught at them
Interpret the symbolism of the Passover Seder in light of Exodus 12 and Jesus' Last Supper as a Passover meal
Explain the significance of the Western Wall and how Jewish practice shifted to prayer and synagogue worship after the destruction of the Temple
Compare how Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform Jewish communities differ in their observance of Shabbat and kashrut
Evaluate Sabbath-keeping for Christians using the Reformed teaching that the Sabbath continues as the Lord's Day on the first day of the week
Evaluate the difference between legalism and devotion in religious observance using Jesus' Sabbath teaching and the prophets' critique of empty ritual
Defend the Reformed position that Christians are free from the ceremonial law using the Jerusalem Council and related New Testament texts
Construct an account of how the Reformed tradition reads the Levitical feasts as types fulfilled in Christ's death, resurrection, and gift of the Spirit
Design a respectful approach to conversation with Jewish neighbors that represents their observances accurately and explains Christian convictions graciously

BIB.5.6.1.t: Identify a wedding as a time when a man and a woman make promises before God to be husband and wife
Recall that the Bible teaches that children are a gift from God
Name baptism as the sign the church gives to believers and their children to mark them as belonging to God's people
Retell how Hannah brought Samuel to the house of the Lord and how Mary and Joseph presented Jesus at the temple
Describe ways families in different cultures and religions celebrate the birth of a baby
Explain that every person is made in the image of God and why Christians therefore treat each new life as valuable
Summarize the Reformed teaching that baptism is a sign and seal of being joined to Christ and washed from sin
Explain the meaning of the Jewish rites of circumcision and Bar or Bat Mitzvah
Retell the account of Jesus in the temple at age twelve and explain what it shows about growing in wisdom and favor with God
Describe birth and naming customs in Islam and Hinduism such as whispering the call to prayer to a newborn and the Hindu naming ceremony
Compare a Christian wedding vow made before God with an ordinary legal contract
Explain the Reformed teaching that children of believers belong to the covenant community and receive baptism as circumcision's New Testament counterpart
Categorize rites of passage from several religions by the life stage they mark and the purpose they serve
Analyze the covenantal nature of Christian marriage as presented in Genesis, Proverbs, and Malachi
Compare coming of age rites such as Bar and Bat Mitzvah, the Hindu sacred thread ceremony, Sikh Amrit initiation, and Christian confirmation by what each signifies
Explain the Reformed practice of public profession of faith and its connection to admission to the Lord's Supper
Interpret the symbolism of water in Christian baptism and contrast it with washing rites in other religions
Explain how rituals mark changes in identity and bind communities together using biblical and other religious examples
Describe the purposes of marriage named in the Reformed confessions including mutual help, the bearing of children, and purity
Contrast the Roman Catholic view of confirmation and marriage as sacraments with the Reformed teaching of two sacraments
Explain how Scripture presents singleness as a gift and calling alongside marriage
Compare the structure and meaning of Jewish, Islamic, and Hindu weddings including the ketubah, the nikah contract, and the seven steps of the Hindu ceremony
Construct a biblical theology of the family based on Genesis 2, Deuteronomy 6, and Ephesians 5 and 6
Analyze how Ephesians 5 presents marriage as a picture of Christ and the church and connect it to the marriage supper of the Lamb
Evaluate the secular view of marriage as a contract against the biblical view of marriage as a covenant
Defend the historic Christian definition of marriage as the union of one man and one woman using Scripture and the confessions
Evaluate sociological accounts of ritual such as those of Durkheim and van Gennep in light of the theological meaning Scripture gives to covenant signs
Create a respectful presentation explaining the Christian meaning of baptism and marriage to someone from another religious tradition

BIB.5.6.2.t: Identify from the Easter account that Jesus died and rose again, defeating death
Name heaven as the place where, Scripture teaches, believers will be with Jesus
Retell how Jesus wept with Mary and Martha and then raised Lazarus from the dead
Explain from Genesis and Romans the biblical teaching that death entered the world through sin
Describe the main parts of a Christian funeral and explain how each expresses both grief and hope
Summarize the Christian teaching that believers will be raised bodily when Christ returns
Explain how the Hindu and Buddhist idea of reincarnation differs from the biblical teaching of one life followed by judgment and resurrection
Compare the funeral and mourning practices of Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, and Christianity and identify the belief about the afterlife that each practice expresses
Explain from Scripture that the final Christian hope is a renewed creation with resurrected bodies and not only a heavenly existence
Explain how 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 shapes the way Christians are taught to grieve and to comfort one another
Analyze the Reformed teaching on the intermediate state in contrast with the doctrines of purgatory and soul sleep
Explain how Scripture presents the resurrection of Christ as the firstfruits and guarantee of the future resurrection of believers
Interpret the terms Sheol and Hades in their Old and New Testament contexts and distinguish them from the final states of heaven and hell
Compare a secular naturalist view of death as final extinction with the Christian hope of resurrection and the reasons each gives for how to live
Explain the doctrine of the last judgment as taught in Scripture and the Westminster Confession
Explain why Reformed churches do not pray for the dead and contrast this with practices of prayer for the dead and ancestor veneration in other traditions
Compare annihilationism with eternal conscious punishment, the view of the Reformed confessions, by examining the key passages each view cites
Analyze Islamic teaching on death, the grave, and judgment by deeds in comparison with the Christian teaching that believers are judged as justified in Christ
Construct a biblical theology of death as an enemy that Christ has defeated and will finally destroy
Evaluate claims drawn from near-death experiences by the standard of Scripture's sufficiency
Evaluate common objections to the doctrine of hell and defend its consistency with the justice of God as the Reformed tradition teaches it
Evaluate arguments for euthanasia and assisted suicide in light of the sixth commandment and the biblical teaching that God governs life and death
Compose a short funeral meditation that expounds 1 Corinthians 15:54-57 for a grieving congregation

BIB.6.1.1.t: Name one thing a short Bible passage tells God's people to do
Give an example of how a child could obey a Bible command at home or at school
Explain that the Bible was written long ago yet still teaches God's people today
Describe how the example of Jesus in a Gospel story shows his followers how to live
Summarize the difference between what a passage meant to its first hearers and what it teaches readers today
Explain why a reader must understand what a passage means before deciding how to apply it
Explain how ordinary activities such as eating, work, and schoolwork can be done for the glory of God
Compare a cultural custom in a Bible passage with the lasting principle it expresses
Classify whether a passage calls mainly for a change in belief, attitude, or action
Apply the principle of a passage to a specific situation in school or family life
Use the Westminster Larger Catechism rules for the commandments to identify the duties and sins implied by a single commandment
Analyze a passage by stating its original meaning, the timeless principle it teaches, and a present-day application
Explain how the Bible's statements about who believers are in Christ ground the commands that follow them
Distinguish commands tied to a particular cultural or covenant setting from commands that bind in every age using evidence from the text
Contrast legalistic and lawless applications of a passage and explain how each departs from Scripture
Analyze how Christ's fulfillment of the Old Testament shapes the way an Old Testament passage is applied today
Construct a faithful application of an ancient text for a specific present-day cultural setting
Evaluate a modern ethical dilemma using principles drawn from Scripture read in context
Defend the relevance of the Old Testament for Christian living using New Testament teaching
Evaluate a published devotional or sermon for whether its application is faithful to the meaning of its passage
Produce a devotional or sermon outline that applies a text to a specific audience

BIB.6.1.2.t: Identify the beginning, middle, and end of a Bible story
Retell the events of a Bible narrative in the order they happen
State the main point of a short Bible story or parable in their own words
Find repeated words or phrases in a passage and explain what the repetition emphasizes
Summarize a chapter by dividing it into its main sections and giving each a short title
Explain how paragraphs and section breaks group related ideas within a passage
Identify the standard parts of a New Testament letter such as the greeting, thanksgiving, body, and closing
Compare the line-based structure of a psalm with the paragraph-based structure of a letter
Identify synonymous and antithetical parallelism in Hebrew poetry and explain how paired lines build meaning
State the big idea of a passage in one sentence and support it from the passage's structure
Trace the plot of a Bible narrative through its setting, conflict, climax, and resolution
Explain from Scripture why careful attention to how a passage is put together is part of handling God's word rightly
Analyze a chiasm by mapping its matching parts and identifying the central element it highlights
Interpret logical connecting words such as therefore, but, for, and so that to trace the flow of an argument
Explain how an inclusio uses matching statements at the start and end to frame a section
Explain how Paul structures a letter so that commands for Christian living follow from and rest on what God has done in Christ
Distinguish the main clause of a sentence from the clauses and phrases that support or modify it
Analyze how a Gospel writer sandwiches one story inside another so that each interprets the other
Analyze how the structural markers of a book shape and convey its message
Construct a phrase diagram of a complex Pauline sentence that shows how its clauses relate to the main verb
Evaluate proposed outlines of a book's macro-structure using the structural signals in the text
Defend an interpretation of a passage by appealing to its grammatical structure
Create an exegetical outline of a passage that shows its structure, its main point, and how the structure supports the passage's theological claim

BIB.6.1.3.t: Identify that the books of the Bible were first written down by hand by people God chose, long before printed books existed

Recall Bible verses that teach God's word will last forever
Identify Hebrew as the main language of the Old Testament and Greek as the language of the New Testament
Locate footnotes in a Bible and tell what kinds of information they give, such as other wordings found in some manuscripts
Sequence the steps by which the Bible came to us from the original writings to handwritten copies to English translations
Explain that copyists sometimes made small slips such as misspelling a word or skipping a line
Compare the number and age of New Testament manuscripts with the surviving copies of other ancient books such as Homer's writings
Define the terms manuscript, autograph, scribe, papyrus, codex, and variant
Explain how the account of King Jehoiakim burning Jeremiah's scroll shows God preserving his word
Describe the discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls and explain how the Great Isaiah Scroll bears on the accuracy of Old Testament copying
Analyze why some Bibles place brackets or notes around passages such as the longer ending of Mark and the account of the woman caught in adultery
Explain the Reformed teaching that the original Hebrew and Greek Scriptures were inspired by God and kept pure by his singular care and providence, so that the church appeals to them as final
Distinguish a textual variant among copies from an error in the original writing
Classify sample textual variants as differences of spelling, word order, omission, addition, or substitution
Explain basic principles textual critics use to weigh readings, such as age and spread of witnesses, the harder reading, and the reading that best explains the others
Distinguish differences between English versions such as the KJV, ESV, and NIV that come from textual variants from those that come from translation choices
Apply textual principles to evaluate a specific variant such as the Johannine Comma using the evidence presented in a critical apparatus
Construct an argument for the reliability of the transmitted New Testament text based on the quantity, early date, and geographic spread of its manuscripts
Evaluate the claim that textual variants alter core Christian doctrine by testing major variants against the doctrines they touch
Compare the histories of the Textus Receptus, the Majority Text, and the modern critical text, including the work of Erasmus, Westcott and Hort, and the Nestle-Aland editions
Evaluate how Reformed theologians have related the confessional doctrine of providential preservation to the practice of textual criticism

BIB.6.1.4.t: Identify one thing a Bible story shows about what God is like
Recognize that the whole Bible tells one story of God's plan to save his people through Jesus
Point out how God keeps the same promise in two different Bible stories
Compare two Bible stories to show that God acts with the same character in each
Summarize in one sentence what a short passage teaches about God, people, or salvation
Explain why the Reformed tradition holds that Scripture does not contradict itself because God is its one author
Use cross-references to locate other passages that teach the same truth as a given verse
Explain the principle that clearer passages of Scripture are used to interpret harder ones
Categorize passages under the major headings of doctrine such as God, Scripture, humanity, sin, Christ, salvation, the church, and last things
Compare a specific biblical command with the general principle that another passage shows it expresses
Trace how a theme such as the promised Redeemer unfolds from the Old Testament to its fulfillment in the New Testament
Analyze the doctrines a passage teaches directly and the doctrines it assumes
Distinguish exegesis, biblical theology, and systematic theology and explain how each builds on the others
Interpret a narrative passage in light of teaching passages that comment on it to identify its theological principle
Explain the analogy of Scripture and the analogy of faith as principles for interpreting a passage within the whole of the Bible
Explain how the Reformed confessions summarize biblical teaching while remaining subordinate to Scripture
Analyze an apparent tension between two passages and show how context and the whole of Scripture resolve it
Construct a doctrinal statement drawn from careful exegesis of several related passages
Evaluate whether a proof text is being used faithfully to its context or lifted out of it
Evaluate a doctrine such as the Trinity by gathering and weighing the full range of biblical evidence for it
Compare how the Reformed tradition and another tradition correlate passages on a disputed doctrine and evaluate which reading better accounts for the whole of Scripture
Synthesize the results of word study, structural analysis, and historical context into a doctrinal conclusion and compare it with the tradition's confessional statement

BIB.6.1.5.t: Identify key Bible words such as grace, sin, and faith when a teacher reads a passage aloud
Use a picture Bible dictionary or glossary to find what a Bible word means
Use the surrounding sentences of a verse to explain what a key word means in that passage
Use an English concordance to locate other verses that use the same word
Explain that the Bible was first written in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek and that English Bibles are translations of those words
Summarize the meaning of key doctrinal terms such as justification, adoption, and sanctification as the Reformed catechisms define them
Compare how one English word is used in different verses to show that a word can carry different meanings
Explain from Scripture why careful attention to individual words matters for understanding God's Word
Use Strong's numbers to identify the Hebrew or Greek word behind an English word in a passage
Explain why different English translations may render the same Hebrew or Greek word with different English words
Analyze the semantic range of a word and select the meaning that best fits a particular passage
Interpret a word according to how a specific biblical author uses it in his own writings
Explain the root fallacy and why a word's etymology does not determine its meaning in a passage
Distinguish the Greek words for love in their contexts without overstating the difference between them
Use a standard lexicon and theological wordbook to gather the range of meanings for a Hebrew or Greek word
Identify common word study errors such as reading later meanings back into a word or importing every possible meaning into one verse
Construct a basic word study on a key theological term by moving from concordance search to context to a supported definition
Evaluate how a word's use in the Septuagint informs its meaning in the New Testament
Defend the importance of precise definitions in theology using the Reformed understanding of justify as declare righteous
Evaluate a published word study or sermon illustration for accurate use of the original languages
Produce a study of a biblical concept across an author's writings that distinguishes the concept from any single word used for it

BIB.6.2.1.t: Identify the Bible as one book from God that tells one true story from beginning to end
Name the Bible itself as the best helper for understanding other parts of the Bible
Explain that the parts of the Bible always agree with each other because God, who gave it, always tells the truth
Match a short Bible verse with another verse that teaches the same truth
State the rule that Scripture interprets Scripture in your own words and give an example of one passage explaining another
Explain why Reformed interpreters use clearer passages to help understand passages that are harder to understand
Locate related passages using the cross-reference notes in a study Bible
Compare two passages on the same subject and write a summary that includes what each contributes
Describe how Jesus answered a misused Scripture by setting it beside another Scripture during his temptation
Gather passages with a concordance on a key word and explain why a shared word does not always carry the same meaning in every passage
Compare parallel Gospel accounts of the same event and explain how the details fit together into a fuller picture
Analyze the apparent contradiction between Paul and James on justification by comparing how each uses the words faith, works, and justify
Explain how the Reformed tradition grounds the analogy of Scripture in the single divine authorship of the whole Bible
Evaluate an interpretation that builds a teaching on one isolated verse against the wider testimony of Scripture
Differentiate the analogy of Scripture from the analogy of faith and explain how creeds summarize the rule of faith drawn from Scripture
Construct a doctrinal summary on a topic such as the Trinity by gathering, comparing, and ordering passages from across the Bible
Explain why the Reformed tradition treats Scripture as the supreme judge over councils, traditions, and private interpretations
Evaluate how a New Testament author interprets an Old Testament passage by comparing the original text with its apostolic use
Evaluate a common claim that the Bible contradicts itself and defend its internal consistency using the principles of the analogy of Scripture
Produce a written study that reconciles a difficult set of parallel passages such as the accounts of David's census in Samuel and Chronicles

BIB.6.2.2.t: Identify that God used people to write the books of the Bible
Name the human writer of a familiar Bible book, such as Moses, David, Luke, or Paul
Recall a verse where a Bible writer tells readers why he wrote his book
Ask the question what did the writer want his first readers to know when reading a Bible passage
Summarize in their own words the main point an author makes in a short Bible passage
Explain why readers may not make a Bible passage mean whatever they want it to mean
Distinguish a reader's personal reaction to a verse from what its author actually stated
Apply the principle that a passage has one meaning intended by its author but many faithful applications
Analyze the occasion that prompted an author to write a New Testament letter, such as Paul's reasons for writing Galatians
Analyze how an author's purpose statements, repeated words, and structure reveal his intent across a whole book
Compare an authorial intent approach to interpretation with a reader response approach
Explain the Reformed doctrine of dual authorship, in which the Holy Spirit and human writers together produced Scripture
Analyze how the divine author's intent can be fuller than a human author's understanding without contradicting what the human author meant
Construct a thesis statement on the purpose of a specific Bible book and support it with evidence from the text
Evaluate the postmodern claim that the author is dead and meaning is created by readers
Defend the Reformed position that Scripture has a single, knowable meaning that settles interpretive disputes
Analyze how the distinct styles and personalities of different human authors show that inspiration worked through them rather than overriding them
Evaluate competing interpretations of a passage by measuring each against the author's demonstrable intent

BIB.6.2.3.t: Identify whether a Bible passage read aloud is a story or a song
Recognize that the Bible is one book made up of many kinds of writing, such as stories, songs, laws, and letters
Distinguish a law that tells God's people what to do from a letter written to a church
Identify picture words in a psalm and tell what each picture teaches about God
Explain that a parable is a story Jesus told to teach a truth about God's kingdom
Distinguish history writing that reports what happened from prophecy that delivers God's message through a prophet
Explain that the Gospels are historical accounts of Jesus written so that readers may know and believe the truth about him
Sort the books of the Bible into their main genres, including law, history, poetry and wisdom, prophecy, gospel, epistle, and apocalyptic
Identify the features of a parable, such as an everyday setting, a central point, and a surprising twist
Compare how a reader should handle a psalm of praise with how a reader should handle a commandment
Describe common forms of prophetic speech, such as the covenant lawsuit, the woe oracle, and the promise of restoration
Identify synonymous, contrasting, and building parallelism in lines of Hebrew poetry
Describe the standard parts of a New Testament letter, including greeting, thanksgiving, body, and closing
Explain why proverbs state general patterns of wise living rather than unconditional promises

Explain how the occasional nature of the epistles, written to answer specific questions and problems, shapes the way they are interpreted
Analyze how the structure of a lament psalm moves from complaint to petition to trust and praise
Distinguish descriptive narrative from prescriptive teaching and explain why a narrative that reports an action does not necessarily commend it
Analyze the forms of Old Testament law and explain the Reformed tradition's distinction between moral, ceremonial, and judicial law
Evaluate interpretations that classify biblical narratives as myth by examining the genre markers of historical writing in the text
Evaluate how speeches within dialogue wisdom books such as Job and Ecclesiastes must be read in light of the book's overall design and conclusion
Analyze passages where genres are blended, such as a victory song set within a narrative, and explain how each genre contributes to the passage's meaning
Create a genre analysis of a chosen biblical book that identifies its genres, literary features, and the interpretive guidelines they require

BIB.6.2.4.t: Identify that God told his people more and more about his plan over time, from Adam all the way to Jesus
Name Jesus as the fullest and final word God has spoken to his people
Retell how God's first promise of a rescuer was made clearer through later promises to Abraham and David
Describe how God's plan grows from the Garden in Genesis to the city in Revelation like a seed growing into a tree
Explain that Old Testament sacrifices and feasts were shadows that pointed forward to Christ as the substance
Compare what Moses and the prophets knew about the Messiah with what the apostles proclaimed after Christ came
Explain what Paul means by the fullness of time and why God sent his Son at that point in the story of redemption
Distinguish progressive revelation as a clearer unfolding of truth from the mistaken idea that earlier revelation was false or corrected
Trace the unfolding of God's covenant promises of seed, land, king, and worldwide blessing across Scripture
Interpret Paul's teaching on the mystery hidden in former ages and now revealed, including the joining of Gentiles to God's people
Analyze how Hebrews presents the repeated Levitical sacrifices as fulfilled by Christ's once-for-all offering

Synthesize the organic unity of Scripture in an essay tracing one biblical theme from its first promise to its fulfillment in Christ

BIB.6.2.5.t: Identify that the Bible tells about real people, places, and events that truly happened

Explain that every word of Scripture matters and should be read carefully without adding to it
Locate the places named in a Bible story on a simple map of Bible lands
Summarize the plain meaning of a short Bible passage in your own words
Describe details of everyday life in Bible times, such as houses, farming, or travel, that help explain what happens in a passage
Explain that a passage must first be understood as its original readers would have understood it before it is applied today
Identify the subject, action, and object in a Bible sentence to tell who does what to whom
Use a Bible dictionary or atlas to find background information about a person, place, or custom in a passage
Contrast a reading that follows the actual words of a passage with an invented meaning read into it
Apply the Reformed teaching that each Scripture has one true sense by testing proposed readings of a verse against its plain meaning
Identify how pronouns, connecting words such as therefore and because, and verb tense change the meaning of a verse

Analyze the historical setting of a Bible book by determining its author, approximate date, original audience, and occasion
Interpret a passage by diagramming its grammatical structure, separating main clauses from the clauses that modify them

Examine a Hebrew or Greek term with an interlinear and lexicon and assess how different English translations render it

BIB.6.2.6.t: Tell what happened just before and just after a familiar event in a Bible story

Identify who is speaking and who is being spoken to in a Bible passage
Summarize the paragraph surrounding a given verse in your own words
Explain how taking a verse out of its context can change what it seems to mean
Explain why a statement in Scripture must be read in light of its speaker, using the words of Job's friends as an example
Compare what the immediate context and the context of the whole book each show about the meaning of a verse
Use the surrounding verses to correct a common misreading of Philippians 4:13
Trace the logical flow of an argument in an epistle by following connecting words such as therefore, for, and but
Identify the stated purpose of a biblical book and use it to explain a passage within that book
Interpret a difficult verse by reading it within the argument of its whole chapter
Explain the three circles of context, immediate, book, and canonical, and how each one narrows the possible meaning of a verse
Explain why chapter and verse divisions are later additions and identify a passage whose thought continues across a chapter break
Analyze how Jesus answered Satan's misuse of a psalm by setting Scripture in its proper context
Construct a context chart for a biblical book showing its purpose, major sections, and the flow between them
Evaluate popular uses of isolated verses by comparing them with the meaning their contexts require
Defend the Reformed principle that a passage has one true sense which its context helps determine
Produce an exegetical outline of a passage that traces the author's line of thought from its context

BIB.7.1.1.t: Put pictures of Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and Jesus in the order the Bible tells their stories
Describe the Bible as a true account of real events that took place over a very long time, from creation to Jesus
Explain from Galatians 4:4 that God sent his Son at the exact time he had planned
Summarize the main eras of Old Testament history in order: creation, patriarchs, exodus and wilderness, judges, kings, exile, and return
Place major Bible figures on a class timeline to show who lived before whom
Explain the meaning of BC, AD, BCE, and CE and why years before Christ count down while years after count up
Calculate the number of years between two dated events, including spans that cross from BC to AD with no year zero
Locate key anchor dates on a timeline, including David's reign, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and the return under Cyrus in 538 BC
Identify the ways the Bible itself marks time, such as regnal years, genealogies, and references to well-known events
Explain how dated promises and their fulfillment show the Reformed teaching that God governs real history according to his plan
Analyze the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11 to explain how ages and the term fathered are used and why biblical genealogies may sometimes skip generations
Interpret the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 and explain how it is used to date the Exodus from Solomon's reign
Connect biblical events to dates fixed by outside records, such as the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BC and Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC
Explain how archaeologists date ancient material through stratigraphy, pottery, inscriptions, and radiocarbon, and describe the limits of each method
Compare the arguments for the early date and the late date of the Exodus, weighing the biblical numbers and archaeological evidence each side uses
Compare the 400 and 430 year time spans given for Israel's sojourn and explain the main proposals for reconciling them
Analyze apparent conflicts in the regnal numbers of Kings by applying coregencies, accession and non-accession reckoning, and differing calendar years
Construct a synchronized timeline of the kings of Israel and Judah alongside Assyrian and Babylonian rulers using the cross-references in Kings
Analyze how prophetic time markers such as Jeremiah's seventy years relate to the dated events of the exile and return
Evaluate the differences among Masoretic, Septuagint, and Samaritan numbers in the Genesis genealogies and their effect on dating the flood and creation
Evaluate Ussher's chronology and other approaches to dating early Genesis, describing how Reformed interpreters have reasoned about the question
Evaluate minimalist claims that the Israelite monarchy is not historical by weighing inscriptions such as the Tel Dan Stele, Mesha Stele, and Shishak's list against the biblical record
Produce a study tracing the Persian, Greek, Hasmonean, and Roman periods between the testaments and how they set the stage for Christ's coming

BIB.7.1.2.t: Identify God as the one who made everything by speaking
Name the sun, moon, and stars as lights God made to give light and mark time, not gods to be worshiped
Retell how many ancient peoples told stories of gods fighting to make the world, while Genesis tells of one God who made everything good
Summarize the difference between belief in one God (monotheism) and belief in many gods (polytheism)
Explain that Genesis presents humans as made in God's image to rule and care for creation, while ancient myths described humans as made to do the gods' labor
Compare the orderly creation by God's word in Genesis with the violent conflict found in other ancient creation stories
Describe the ancient picture of the cosmos as heavens, earth, and waters and identify where Scripture uses this everyday language
Explain why Scripture forbids astrology and divination by showing that the stars are creatures governed by God rather than controllers of human fate
Analyze the Enuma Elish by summarizing its account of Marduk and Tiamat and contrasting its view of God, matter, and humanity with Genesis 1
Compare Egyptian creation accounts such as those of Atum and Ptah with the Genesis account of creation by one God
Explain the doctrine of creation out of nothing and contrast it with ancient myths in which the world is formed from preexisting matter or a slain god
Interpret details of Genesis 1, such as the unnamed greater and lesser lights and the great sea creatures, as a polemic against pagan worldviews
Explain the ancient idea of the cosmos as a temple and identify temple and rest imagery in the creation account
Explain how the biblical view of nature as an orderly creation distinct from God has been argued to support scientific inquiry
Compare the Genesis flood account with the Atrahasis and Gilgamesh flood stories in terms of the reason for the flood and the character of the deity
Construct a comparison of ancient paganism, biblical theism, and modern materialism on the origin of the world, the nature of the divine, and the purpose of humanity
Evaluate how Scripture uses the chaos monster imagery of Leviathan and Rahab differently from its use in ancient Near Eastern mythology
Defend the Reformed teaching of God's transcendence and immanence against pantheism and nature worship
Evaluate scholarly explanations for similarities between Genesis and ancient Near Eastern texts in light of the Reformed doctrine of the inspiration of Scripture
Analyze how Paul applies the doctrine of creation to a pagan audience in his speech at the Areopagus
Produce an essay explaining how the biblical teaching that every person bears God's image, rather than only the king, dignifies humanity in contrast to ancient Near Eastern thought

BIB.7.1.3.t: Identify that most of the Old Testament was first written in the Hebrew language
Name the meanings of Hebrew words still used in worship today, such as shalom, amen, and hallelujah
Recall that Jesus spoke Aramaic and identify Aramaic words kept in the Gospels, such as Abba and Talitha cumi
Describe how Hebrew is written from right to left using an alphabet of twenty-two letters
Explain that our English Bible is translated from the original Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek so that people can read God's Word in their own language
Locate the passages of the Old Testament written in Aramaic and explain why those sections fit an Aramaic-speaking setting
Explain how Hebrew names carry meanings that connect to the stories and promises of Scripture
Compare how two English translations render the same verse and explain why translators must choose between possible words
Analyze how the Dead Sea Scrolls, such as the Great Isaiah Scroll, give evidence for the careful transmission of the Hebrew text
Describe Hebrew as a Semitic language related to Aramaic, Ugaritic, Phoenician, and Akkadian
Compare word-for-word and thought-for-thought translation approaches and evaluate the strengths of each for Bible study
Explain why Jews translated the Old Testament into Greek in the Septuagint and how New Testament writers quote it
Describe the discovery of the Ugaritic texts at Ras Shamra and explain how they help clarify rare Hebrew words and poetic patterns
Explain how the Masoretes preserved the Hebrew text by adding vowel points and careful scribal notes
Conduct a Hebrew word study using a concordance and lexicon to trace a word's meaning across several passages
Analyze how biblical poets use Canaanite language known from Ugaritic texts to declare the LORD's supremacy over Baal
Explain the Reformed teaching that Scripture in its original languages is the final authority, providentially preserved, and to be translated for all peoples
Evaluate how understanding Hebrew terms such as hesed and berit enriches the meaning of key doctrinal passages
Evaluate arguments for the reliable preservation of the Old Testament text using manuscript evidence
Analyze the spread of Aramaic as the common language of the ancient Near East using evidence from the Old Testament
Compare readings of a passage in the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint, and the Dead Sea Scrolls and explain how scholars weigh textual differences

BIB.7.1.4.t: Recall that God gave His people the Ten Commandments written on two tablets of stone
Name the Ten Commandments as the rules God gave His people at Mount Sinai
Recall that kings in Bible times, such as Hammurabi of Babylon, carved their laws on large stones for people to see
Explain why God reminded Israel that He had rescued them from Egypt before giving them His commandments
Summarize the rule of eye for eye as a command for judges to make a punishment fit the wrong rather than permission for personal revenge
Explain what an ancient treaty was as a formal agreement in which a great king and a lesser king or people made promises and accepted obligations
Compare the penalties for theft in Hammurabi's code with the restitution required in the law of Moses
Explain how the covenant at Sinai presents God as Israel's great King and Israel as His treasured people
Identify the main parts of a second millennium suzerain-vassal treaty, including preamble, historical prologue, stipulations, deposit and reading, witnesses, and blessings and curses
Analyze how the book of Deuteronomy follows the outline of an ancient suzerain-vassal treaty
Distinguish apodictic law from casuistic law by classifying examples from the Book of the Covenant
Connect the blessings and curses of the Mosaic covenant to the sanctions that closed ancient treaties
Explain why the tablets of the covenant and the Book of the Law were placed in or beside the ark in light of the ancient practice of depositing treaty copies in a sanctuary
Explain how the Mosaic law protected servants, sojourners, widows, and orphans in ways that differed from other ancient Near Eastern law codes
Compare how ancient Near Eastern law codes and the Torah treat the value of human life, using cases such as the goring ox and class-based penalties
Analyze how the prophets bring a covenant lawsuit against Israel by calling witnesses and charging the people with breaking the covenant
Analyze a Hittite vassal treaty in translation alongside the covenant renewal at Shechem to identify shared covenant elements and key differences
Evaluate the law of retaliation as a principle that limited vengeance and applied equal justice to native Israelite and sojourner alike
Explain how the Westminster Confession's distinction of moral, ceremonial, and judicial law applies to the case laws of Moses that resemble ancient Near Eastern codes
Write an argument showing how Israel's law, unlike royal law codes, is grounded in the holy character of God as its giver

BIB.7.1.5.t: Identify Egypt as a land along the Nile River where Joseph and Moses lived
Name Ur of the Chaldeans as Abraham's first home and retell how God called him to leave it
Describe how people in Abraham's world built cities and towers out of baked mud bricks
Locate the Fertile Crescent, the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, and the Nile River on a map
Describe what a Mesopotamian ziggurat looked like and explain how the tower of Babel account reflects this kind of building
Explain how the yearly flooding of the Nile supplied Egypt with food and why famine sent Jacob's family to Egypt
Compare the life of an Israelite shepherd with the life of an Egyptian city dweller using details from the Joseph narrative
Identify Egyptian court customs in the Joseph narrative such as the signet ring, linen garments, chariots, and Egyptian names
Locate Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, and Persia on a Bible map and explain why Israel's location placed it between these powers
Describe the role of Pharaoh as a king regarded as divine and explain how Exodus presents the conflict between Pharaoh and the LORD
Describe Egyptian forced labor and royal building projects as background to Israel's bondage
Analyze the struggle between the northern empires of Assyria and Babylon and the southern power of Egypt and how Judah's kings were pulled between them
Explain how the plagues of Egypt are presented as the LORD's judgment on the gods of Egypt
Explain the Assyrian policy of deporting and resettling conquered peoples and how it shaped the fall of Samaria
Explain how Babylon deported and retrained the leading people of Judah as background to the book of Daniel
Analyze Sennacherib's campaign against Judah by comparing the biblical account with Assyrian royal records
Analyze how the prophets describe Assyria and Babylon as instruments in God's hand who are still accountable for their pride and cruelty
Evaluate the archaeological and textual evidence bearing on Israel's sojourn in Egypt
Evaluate how Mesopotamian records such as the Babylonian Chronicles, the Jehoiachin ration tablets, and the Cyrus Cylinder relate to the biblical accounts
Construct an account of the rise and fall of the ancient Near Eastern empires that connects them to the Reformed reading of God's sovereignty in Daniel's visions

BIB.7.2.1.t: Identify pictures of the ways people traveled in Bible times, such as walking on stone roads and sailing in boats
Retell how Paul traveled by road and by ship to tell people in many places about Jesus
Describe what a Roman road looked like and explain why the Romans built such strong, straight roads
Explain in your own words that Pax Romana means Roman Peace, a long period when Rome kept order across many lands beginning in the time of Caesar Augustus
Explain how roads, sea routes, and peace across the empire helped early missionaries carry the gospel from city to city
Compare travel in the first century with travel today in speed, cost, comfort, and danger
Trace Paul's first missionary journey on a map, naming the cities he visited and whether he traveled by land or sea
Describe how Rome's control of the Mediterranean, including the clearing of pirates and the grain ships from Alexandria, shaped sea travel in Paul's day
Explain how Roman administration, such as the census, required people to travel, using the journey of Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem
Analyze how major Roman roads such as the Via Egnatia and the Via Appia connected the cities named in Acts
Explain how the shared Koine Greek language allowed travelers and missionaries to communicate across the eastern empire
