Interpret the phrase fullness of time in its context in Galatians and explain why many interpreters connect it to the conditions of the Roman world
Explain the role of Roman colonies like Philippi as settlements of Roman citizens along major roads and how Luke describes the city
Describe how Jewish communities and synagogues in cities along trade routes served as starting points for Paul's preaching
Analyze how Roman travel networks made it possible for letters and messengers to link scattered churches
Construct a map of Paul's journeys showing the roads and sea routes he likely used, citing the passages in Acts that support each route
Explain the Reformed doctrine that God governs history through ordinary means and apply it to the conditions surrounding Christ's coming and the spread of the gospel
Evaluate the cost and danger of first-century travel despite the Roman peace, using Paul's own account of his hardships
Evaluate historical arguments that credit the early church's growth to Roman conditions, distinguishing secondary causes from God's providence as the Reformed tradition confesses it
Synthesize the roads, sea routes, common language, colonies, and peace of the Roman world into a written argument about how they shaped the early church's mission

BIB.7.2.2.t: Identify that people in the Roman world made statues of many gods and bowed down to them, while the Bible teaches that there is only one true God
Identify Caesar as the emperor who ruled the Roman world when Jesus was born
Recall that the earliest Christians confessed Jesus is Lord as a short statement of what they believed about Jesus
Explain that the Romans worshiped many gods and name major Roman gods such as Jupiter, Mars, and Venus with what each was believed to control
Describe how Roman religion was practiced through temples, sacrifices, household gods, and city festivals, using the riot over Artemis in Ephesus as an example
Explain why Christians in the Roman world got in trouble for refusing to worship the emperor or offer sacrifice to the gods
Retell Jesus' answer about paying taxes to Caesar and explain how the coin's image and inscription shaped the meaning of his reply
Compare the living God described in Scripture with the idols of the nations
Describe the imperial cult, including temples to Rome and Augustus and titles such as lord, savior, and son of god claimed for the emperor
Analyze how the New Testament applies the titles Lord, Savior, and Son of God to Jesus in a world where Caesar claimed those same titles
Analyze how Paul responded to the idols and altars of Athens in his speech at the Areopagus
Explain the syncretism of Roman religion and why the first commandment kept Christians from adding Christ to the gods of Rome
Explain the question of food sacrificed to idols in Corinth and summarize the guidance Paul gave to believers
Interpret emperor worship as an act of political loyalty and explain why refusing it was treated as disloyalty to Rome
Explain why Romans charged Christians with atheism for worshiping a God without images or sacrifices and for withdrawing from civic religion
Analyze the imagery of Revelation, including the beast and the throne of Satan at Pergamum, in light of the imperial cult in Asia Minor
Analyze primary sources such as Pliny's letter to Trajan to describe how Roman officials tested and punished Christians
Contrast the claims and character of the kingdom of Caesar with the kingdom of Christ as Scripture presents it
Evaluate the claim that early Christianity borrowed from the mystery religions by comparing their rites and myths with the historical gospel
Evaluate how the New Testament commands to honor the emperor fit with the Christian refusal to worship him
Construct an argument for the exclusivity of Christ as the Reformed tradition confesses it, set against the religious pluralism of the Roman world
Create a written synthesis relating the early church's response to pressure to conform under Rome with Scripture's call to holiness in any culture

BIB.7.2.3.t: Identify the servant and the master in a Bible story such as Jesus healing the centurion's servant
Recall from Scripture that God made both rich people and poor people
Retell how Jesus washed his disciples' feet, a job usually done by a servant
Describe the main social groups of the Roman world, including senators, wealthy landowners, citizens, freed people, and slaves
Explain what Roman citizenship meant and how Paul used his citizenship when he was arrested
Describe how people became slaves in the Roman world and the kinds of work slaves did
Retell the story of Onesimus and explain what Paul asked Philemon to do for him
Describe how the first believers in Jerusalem shared their goods so that no one among them was in need
Describe the structure of a Roman household, including the head of the household, family members, and slaves, and explain why whole households joined the church together
Contrast Jesus' teaching on greatness through service with the way Roman rulers exercised authority
Explain how honor and shame shaped social life in the Roman world and identify examples in the Gospels
Explain how Jesus' instruction to invite those who cannot repay challenged the expectations of patronage
Analyze the patron and client system of gifts, loyalty, and obligation in Roman society
Explain how divisions between rich and poor at Corinthian church meals led Paul to rebuke their practice of the Lord's Supper
Explain why Paul reminded the Corinthians that not many of them were wise, powerful, or of noble birth
Interpret Paul's statement that there is neither slave nor free in Christ within its first-century setting
Apply James' warning against favoring the rich to a first-century scene of seating in a gathering of believers
Identify women of means who acted as patrons of Jesus and the early church, such as Phoebe, Lydia, and the women of Luke 8, and explain their role
Compare Roman slavery with race-based chattel slavery in American history, identifying both differences and shared injustices
Analyze how New Testament writers used the language of slavery, purchase, and freedom to describe redemption in Christ
Explain the significance of Christ taking the form of a slave and dying by crucifixion, a punishment associated with slaves
Analyze the New Testament household codes in their Roman context, noting how they address slaves as moral agents and place duties on masters
Compare the Roman ideal of benefaction that expected a return with the New Testament teaching of grace given freely
Evaluate how Paul's teaching in Philemon, his counsel to gain freedom, and his condemnation of enslavers undermined the foundations of slavery
Evaluate how defenders of slavery and abolitionists in American history used the household codes, judging which reading fits the text in its context
Compose an essay explaining how the early church formed a community across lines of status, wealth, and citizenship, drawing on Scripture and the Reformed confession of the communion of saints

BIB.7.2.4.t: Identify Athens as a city where people gathered to talk about big questions and where Paul went to tell about Jesus
Retell how Paul spoke to the thinkers of Athens at the Areopagus, also called Mars Hill
Recall that Paul told the people of Athens that God made the world and everything in it and gives life to all people
Describe what a philosopher is and why the people of Athens liked to hear and discuss new ideas
Summarize the Epicurean teaching that the goal of life is a calm and pleasant life free from fear and pain
Summarize the Stoic teaching that a person should live by reason, practice self-control, and calmly accept whatever happens
Explain what Paul meant when he told the Athenians that they worshiped what they did not know
Compare the Epicurean belief that the gods are distant and uninvolved with the Stoic belief that a divine reason fills all things
Explain why some Athenians called Paul a babbler and thought he was preaching foreign gods
Identify the Greek poets Paul quoted at Athens and explain why he used words his listeners already knew
Analyze how Paul's teaching on creation and providence answered both the distant gods of the Epicureans and the all-pervading divine reason of the Stoics
Analyze the structure of Paul's Areopagus speech as it moves from creation to providence, repentance, judgment, and resurrection
Explain why Greek listeners shaped by Epicurean and Stoic views of death mocked the bodily resurrection Paul preached
Compare the Stoic idea of the Logos as impersonal world reason with John's teaching that the Logos is the eternal, personal Word who became flesh
Contrast the Epicurean pursuit of ataraxia and the Stoic pursuit of freedom from passion with the peace with God that Scripture says comes through Christ
Analyze how Paul uses the Stoic idea of self-sufficient contentment in Philippians and grounds it in the strength of Christ rather than in the self
Analyze Paul's use of the saying let us eat and drink for tomorrow we die as his answer to a life lived without hope of resurrection
Compare Christian ethics with Stoic ethics in their views of virtue, emotion, self-control, and the motive and source of good works
Explain how Paul appeals to what all people can know of God through creation at Athens and why the Reformed tradition holds that this knowledge is not sufficient for salvation
Evaluate Paul's contrast between the wisdom of the world and the wisdom of God and his warning against philosophy according to human tradition
Evaluate Paul's method at Athens of using common ground while calling for repentance as a model for engaging an intellectual culture
Construct a written response to a modern form of Stoic or Epicurean thinking using Paul's Areopagus speech and Reformed teaching on creation and resurrection

BIB.7.3.1.t: Identify the Temple in Jerusalem as the place where the Jewish people worshiped God in the days of Jesus
Name the Pharisees and the Sadducees as groups of Jewish teachers and leaders who appear in the stories about Jesus
Retell how God's people returned from exile and rebuilt the Temple, which began the Second Temple period
Recount a Gospel story in which Jesus answered the Pharisees about keeping the Sabbath
Describe the work of the scribes as students, copyists, and teachers of the law of Moses
Summarize the main differences between the Pharisees and the Sadducees in their beliefs about the resurrection, angels, and spirits
Explain how Jesus' parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector contrasts trust in one's own righteousness with humble dependence on God's mercy
Explain how Herod expanded the Second Temple and how Jesus foretold its destruction
Compare the Zealots, the Essenes, and the Herodians with the Pharisees and Sadducees in how each group related to Rome and to the Temple
Describe how Greek rule and the Maccabean revolt in the intertestamental period shaped Jewish zeal for the law and the Temple
Explain the tradition of the elders and how Jesus distinguished it from the commandment of God in the dispute over handwashing and Corban
Connect the Sadducees to the high priestly families and their control of the Temple using their opposition to the apostles in Acts
Explain how Jesus answered the Sadducees' denial of the resurrection from the Scriptures and how the Reformed confessions state the doctrine of the resurrection of the body
Analyze Jesus' woes against the scribes and Pharisees by distinguishing his respect for the teaching of Moses from his rebuke of hypocrisy and neglect of justice, mercy, and faithfulness
Explain who the Qumran community was and how the Dead Sea Scrolls bear on the faithful transmission of the Old Testament text
Compare Paul's former life as a zealous Pharisee with his later teaching on righteousness through faith in Christ
Evaluate common stereotypes of the Pharisees using New Testament accounts of Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Pharisees who warned Jesus
Analyze how extrabiblical sources such as Josephus describe the Jewish sects and compare their accounts with the New Testament
Evaluate the Reformed teaching that worship and good works must rest on God's commands rather than human traditions in light of Jesus' critique of the Pharisees

Construct an account of the diversity of Second Temple Judaism that explains how each major group responded to the Law, the Temple, and Rome and how this context illumines the conflicts in the Gospels

BIB.7.3.2.t: Identify a synagogue as a place where Jewish people gathered on the Sabbath to hear God's Word read and to pray
Retell how Jesus went to the synagogue in Nazareth on the Sabbath and read from the scroll of Isaiah
Name the people who served in a synagogue, such as the ruler who led the gathering and the attendant who cared for the scrolls
Summarize the main parts of a synagogue gathering, including reading the Law and the Prophets, teaching, and prayer
Identify the Sanhedrin as the ruling council of the Jews in Jerusalem, led by the high priest
Explain the difference between the Temple in Jerusalem as the one place of sacrifice and the synagogues in many towns as places of reading, teaching, and prayer
Explain how Ezra's public reading and explanation of the Law gave a pattern for reading and teaching Scripture in the synagogue
Compare the role of a synagogue ruler with the role of a priest serving in the Temple
Explain what Jesus meant when he said the scribes and Pharisees sit on the seat of Moses
Describe how Jesus and Paul used the synagogue as a setting to teach Scripture and proclaim the gospel
Describe how members of the council such as Caiaphas, Nicodemus, and Joseph of Arimathea responded differently to Jesus
Analyze the Sanhedrin's role in the trial of Jesus, including its search for testimony and its charge of blasphemy
Explain how synagogues allowed Jews scattered in the Diaspora to keep hearing the Law and why Paul often began his mission work there
Explain what being put out of the synagogue meant and why it was a serious threat to those who confessed Jesus
Analyze how the apostles answered the Sanhedrin's command to stop preaching in the name of Jesus
Distinguish synagogue practices shown in the New Testament from customs such as the minyan that are described in later rabbinic sources
Construct a diagram of the Sanhedrin's makeup, including the high priest, chief priests, elders, and scribes and the parties represented among them
Analyze how the synagogue pattern of public reading, exhortation, and prayer shaped the worship of the early church
Evaluate the legal authority of the Sanhedrin under Roman rule, including why it brought Jesus to Pilate
Evaluate the Sanhedrin's judgment of Jesus against the Old Testament standards for just judges and reliable witnesses
Develop an account of how the synagogue's focus on Torah helped Judaism endure after the Temple fell, contrasted with the Reformed teaching that Christ fulfills the Temple

BIB.7.3.3.t: Identify Passover as the meal God commanded Israel to eat to remember how He rescued them from Egypt
Retell that God gave Israel a weekly day of rest called the Sabbath
Recall that God commanded Israel's feasts so His people would remember His works and give thanks to Him
Describe how Israelites lived in booths during the Feast of Tabernacles and tell what the booths helped them remember
Identify Hanukkah as the Feast of Dedication that celebrated the rededication of the temple and recall that Jesus was in the temple during this feast
Describe how Jesus traveled with His family to Jerusalem to keep the Passover as a boy
Summarize the parts of the first Passover, including the lamb, the blood on the doorposts, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs, and explain what each recalled
Explain why the Jews celebrate Purim using the account in the book of Esther
Identify the three pilgrimage feasts and explain why Israelites traveled to Jerusalem to keep them
Explain the Feast of Weeks as a harvest festival of firstfruits held fifty days after the Passover season
Describe how the Jewish calendar follows the moon, beginning each month at the new moon and the religious year in the spring month of Abib or Nisan
Compare the weekly Sabbath with Israel's yearly festivals in purpose and practice
Explain the rituals of the Day of Atonement, including the high priest entering the Most Holy Place and the sending away of the scapegoat
Describe the commands for the Feast of Firstfruits and the Feast of Trumpets
Explain the sabbatical year and the Year of Jubilee and how Jesus applied jubilee language to His ministry
Construct a calendar of Israel's appointed feasts showing their months, agricultural seasons, and the events of redemption each recalled
Explain how Hanukkah arose from the Maccabean revolt against Antiochus IV, treating 1 Maccabees as a useful historical source that is not inspired Scripture
Interpret Jesus as the fulfillment of the Passover by connecting the Last Supper and the apostolic teaching that Christ is our Passover lamb
Analyze how the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost connects to the Feast of Weeks as a firstfruits harvest
Analyze how Jesus used the water and light imagery of the Feast of Tabernacles to reveal who He is
Analyze how Hebrews presents Christ's priestly work as the fulfillment of the Day of Atonement
Explain the Reformed teaching that Israel's feasts belonged to the ceremonial law, foreshadowed Christ, and are now fulfilled and abrogated
Explain how the Reformed tradition understands the Lord's Supper in relation to the Passover and the Lord's Day in relation to the Sabbath
Compare the feast commands of the Torah with practices that developed by the Second Temple period, such as Passover Seder customs and the water-pouring rite at Tabernacles
Evaluate interpretations of feast typology by distinguishing types the New Testament itself establishes from speculative prophetic schemes
Evaluate arguments about whether Christians are bound to keep the Jewish feasts using Paul's teaching and the Reformed confession on Christian liberty
Create a presentation or essay tracing how Israel's cycle of feasts retells the history of redemption and points to its completion in the new creation

BIB.7.3.4.t: Identify that God promised to send a King to rescue his people and that many people were waiting for him
Recall that the words Messiah and Christ both mean anointed one and name Jesus as the promised Messiah
Retell how Simeon and Anna waited in the temple for the promised one and recognized the baby Jesus
Explain why many people expected the Messiah to defeat the Romans and why Jesus riding into Jerusalem on a donkey surprised them
Explain the title Son of David and connect it to God's covenant promise of an everlasting throne
Compare the popular hope for a warrior king with the suffering servant described in Isaiah
Describe how the Old Testament anointing of prophets, priests, and kings shaped the hope for a Messiah who would fulfill all three offices
Identify the hope of bodily resurrection at the end of the age in Daniel and in Martha's words to Jesus
Summarize how the Maccabean revolt and the later Roman conquest of Judea intensified political hopes for a deliverer
Distinguish canonical Scripture from intertestamental writings such as 1 Maccabees and 1 Enoch and explain how the Reformed tradition uses the latter as historical sources rather than as Scripture
Explain the main features of apocalyptic literature such as visions, symbolic beasts, cosmic conflict, and God's final triumph using examples from Daniel
Interpret the Son of Man figure in Daniel and analyze how Jesus applied the title to himself at his trial
Explain the Jewish framework of the present age and the age to come and identify where the New Testament uses it
Analyze how Daniel's seventy weeks prophecy fed first century expectations and how the Reformed tradition reads it as fulfilled in Christ
Compare the different figures first century Jews expected, including a Davidic king, a prophet like Moses, and a returning Elijah
Analyze the disciples' hope for the restoration of Israel's kingdom and how the risen Jesus responded to it
Examine accounts of revolutionary leaders such as Theudas and Judas the Galilean and explain what they reveal about popular messianic movements
Evaluate how Jesus redefined messiahship through suffering, death, and exaltation using the Gospel accounts and Isaiah's servant songs
Synthesize how Jewish hopes for resurrection, judgment, and new creation are taken up in the Reformed confession of Christ's return and the last things

BIB.8.1.1.t: Retell the story of the Holy Spirit coming at Pentecost with the sound of a rushing wind and tongues of fire
Name the Holy Spirit as the Helper whom Jesus promised to send to his disciples
Recall that Jesus told his disciples to wait in Jerusalem until the Holy Spirit came
Recall that Peter preached about Jesus at Pentecost and that about three thousand people were baptized
Summarize the events of Acts 2 in order from the coming of the Spirit to the baptism of the new believers
Locate on a map several of the nations listed in Acts 2 to show that people from many lands heard the gospel in their own languages
Explain how the gift of languages at Pentecost contrasts with the confusion of languages at Babel
Explain the setting of Pentecost as a Jewish harvest feast held fifty days after Passover
Explain that the Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity, true God equal with the Father and the Son
Compare Peter's denial of Jesus with his boldness at Pentecost and identify how Luke attributes the change to the Holy Spirit
Trace how the pattern of Acts 1:8 from Jerusalem to Samaria to the ends of the earth unfolds through the Spirit's work in Acts
Explain why Jesus said it was better for his disciples that he go away and how his ascension relates to the sending of the Spirit
Explain why the Reformed tradition describes Pentecost as a once-for-all event in redemptive history that marks the beginning of the new covenant church
Analyze how Peter uses Joel 2, Psalm 16, and Psalm 110 to argue that Jesus is both Lord and Christ
Explain from Scripture that the Spirit gives gifts to believers for the common good of the church
Interpret how Pentecost fulfills Joel's prophecy of the Spirit poured out on all flesh regardless of age, sex, or social status
Explain the response Peter called for in Acts 2:37-41 and how the Reformed tradition reads the promise to believers and their children in support of covenant baptism
Explain the Spirit's work of convicting the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment
Describe how the Spirit produces fruit in believers as part of the work the Reformed tradition calls sanctification
Explain how the Reformed tradition teaches that the Spirit applies Christ's redemption by uniting believers to him through faith
Explain the Spirit's work of illumination in enabling readers to understand Scripture
Construct an explanation of the Holy Spirit's role in missions from passages where the Spirit directs and empowers witness in Acts
Evaluate the distinction between the Spirit's permanent indwelling of every believer and the repeated filling of the Spirit described in Acts and Ephesians
Defend the personhood and deity of the Holy Spirit from Scripture against views that treat the Spirit as an impersonal force
Evaluate continuationist and cessationist interpretations of tongues and prophecy using Acts, 1 Corinthians, and the Westminster Confession
Synthesize the connection between Christ's Great Commission and the Spirit's empowering at Pentecost in a written argument

BIB.8.1.2.t: Identify ways the first Christians in Jerusalem shared their food and belongings with one another
Name Stephen as the first follower of Jesus to die for his faith and retell how he prayed for the people who killed him
List the four things the Jerusalem believers devoted themselves to: the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers
Retell the healing of the lame man at the temple gate and the arrest of Peter and John that followed
Explain why Peter and John said they must obey God rather than men when the leaders ordered them to stop speaking about Jesus
Retell how God freed the apostles from prison and later answered the church's prayer for Peter's release
Explain why the apostles rejoiced after being beaten by connecting their response to Jesus' teaching about persecution
Compare the generous gift of Barnabas with the deception of Ananias and Sapphira and explain why Peter called their sin lying to the Holy Spirit
Describe Saul's part in the persecution after Stephen's death and how the scattering of believers carried the gospel into Judea and Samaria as Jesus had said
Identify Luke's summary statements of the church's growth in Jerusalem and explain what they show about the Lord's role in adding to the church
Analyze the church's prayer under threat in Acts 4, including its use of Psalm 2 and its appeal to God's sovereign plan
Explain how the appointment of the seven resolved the neglect of widows while guarding the apostles' ministry of the word and prayer, and how Reformed churches have drawn the office of deacon from it
Explain the significance of Stephen's vision of the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God in light of Daniel's prophecy and Christ's exaltation
Explain Gamaliel's counsel to the Sanhedrin and evaluate its reasoning in light of how the rest of Acts unfolds
Trace the argument of Stephen's speech through Israel's history and explain how it answered the charges brought against him
Analyze the meaning of koinonia in the Jerusalem church and relate it to the communion of saints as confessed by the Reformed churches
Analyze the tension between the Jerusalem believers' continued temple worship and the charge that Stephen spoke against the temple and the law
Evaluate the claim that the early church practiced compulsory socialism by examining evidence that its sharing was voluntary
Construct a written argument assessing the saying that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church against the pattern of persecution and growth in Acts

BIB.8.1.3.t: Identify Paul as a man God sent to travel to many places to tell people about Jesus
Name Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, and Luke as helpers who traveled with Paul
Retell the story of Paul's shipwreck and how God kept everyone on the ship alive as He had promised
Retell how Paul and Silas prayed and sang in the Philippian jail and how the jailer and his household came to believe
Describe Paul's pattern of preaching first in the synagogue and then turning to the Gentiles
Trace on a map the cities Paul and Barnabas visited on the first missionary journey
Explain how Paul and Barnabas responded when the crowd at Lystra tried to worship them as gods
Explain why Paul often stayed and preached in large cities such as Corinth and Ephesus
Describe how Paul worked as a tentmaker to support himself so he would not burden the churches
Explain how the Holy Spirit called Paul and Barnabas and how the church at Antioch sent them out with prayer and fasting
Compare how the Jews of Berea and Thessalonica responded to Paul's preaching, including the Bereans' daily examination of the Scriptures
Explain how the Spirit closed doors in Asia and Bithynia and how the Macedonian vision directed Paul into Europe
Describe how Paul returned to strengthen new churches and appointed elders to lead them
Construct a map of Paul's three missionary journeys and his voyage to Rome with key events labeled
Analyze how Paul's Areopagus speech moves from creation and the Athenians' own altar and poets to the call to repent and the resurrection
Analyze how the riot at Ephesus shows the gospel confronting idolatry and the trade built around it
Connect the founding of churches in Acts to the letters Paul later wrote to those same churches
Explain how Paul used his Roman citizenship and appeals to Roman law to protect the mission and bring the gospel before rulers
Analyze Paul's farewell address to the Ephesian elders as a summary of his ministry aims and methods
Analyze how Luke's account of Paul's journeys shows the gospel advancing from Jerusalem to Rome as Jesus foretold
Explain how the Reformed tradition relates God's sovereign election to Paul's urgent preaching, using texts where God's choosing and the preaching of the gospel appear together
Evaluate how Paul adapted his approach for Jewish and Gentile audiences while keeping the message of the cross and resurrection unchanged
Evaluate which features of Paul's strategy, such as urban centers, teams, and local elders, can guide missions today, distinguishing what Acts describes from what it commands
Develop a written theological account of suffering in Christian mission drawn from Paul's hardships and his own explanation of them

BIB.8.1.4.t: Identify from the story of Cornelius that people who were not Jewish believed in Jesus and received the Holy Spirit
Retell Peter's vision of the sheet filled with animals and what God taught Peter through it
Recall God's promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him
Describe how the church at Antioch grew as believers shared the good news about Jesus with Greeks
Summarize the question the Council met to settle about whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved
Identify Peter, Barnabas, Paul, and James as speakers at the Council and state what each one contributed
Explain Peter's conclusion that Jews and Gentiles are saved in the same way, through the grace of the Lord Jesus
Explain why Peter's report about Cornelius led the Jerusalem believers to conclude that God had granted repentance to the Gentiles
Describe how the Council's decision was carried to the churches and how the Gentile believers received it
Compare Old Testament ceremonial laws on food and circumcision with their fulfillment in Christ using the Reformed distinction among moral, ceremonial, and judicial laws
Analyze how James uses Amos 9:11-12 to show that the inclusion of the Gentiles fulfills Old Testament prophecy
Interpret the four requests in the Council's letter and explain why they were asked of Gentile believers living among Jewish neighbors
Analyze how the Council weighed reports of God's work among the Gentiles alongside the testimony of the Scriptures in reaching its decision
Explain the Reformed teaching on Christian liberty and the call to limit one's liberty so as not to cause a fellow believer to stumble
Compare the account of the Council in Acts 15 with Paul's account of the circumcision controversy and Peter's withdrawal at Antioch in Galatians 2
Construct an argument from Acts 15 and Galatians for justification by grace through faith apart from works of the law as the Reformed confessions teach
Evaluate the Council as a model for how the church resolves doctrinal disputes in light of the Reformed teaching on synods and councils
Defend from Scripture the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in one body and apply it to the church's unity across ethnic lines today
Evaluate the significance of the Council's decision for the church's mission to make disciples of all nations
Develop an explanation of how believers are free from the Mosaic law as a covenant of works yet remain under the law of Christ

BIB.8.2.1.t: Identify Jesus as the one the whole Bible points to and tells about
Retell a Bible story in order by naming who was in it, what happened, and what it shows about God
Name the Bible as God's Word, written by people whom God's Spirit guided
Recall that God gives his Word to tell us what to believe about him and how he wants us to live
Answer the question of what a Bible passage teaches about God using details from the passage
Explain how the verses before and after a passage help show what it means
Distinguish what a passage meant to its first hearers from how it applies to readers today
Identify the author, first audience, and purpose of a New Testament book using clues within the text
Compare how a Gospel, a historical narrative, a letter, and apocalyptic writing are each read
Apply the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture by using a clearer passage to explain a harder one
Use cross-references and a concordance to locate passages related to a text being studied
Identify figures of speech such as metaphor, simile, and hyperbole in Jesus' teaching and explain their intended meaning
Analyze a passage using the steps of observation, interpretation, and application
Explain how cultural and historical background clarifies the meaning of a text without overriding what the text says
Interpret a parable by identifying its main point in light of its setting and audience rather than as historical narrative
Explain how New Testament writers read Old Testament passages as fulfilled in Christ
Analyze an example of a verse taken out of context and show how its context corrects the misreading
Trace the argument of a paragraph in an epistle by identifying connecting words such as therefore, because, and so that
Explain the Reformed teaching that the Holy Spirit illumines readers to understand Scripture while careful study remains necessary
Conduct a word study that determines a word's meaning from its use in context rather than from its root alone
Distinguish descriptive passages that report what happened from prescriptive passages that command what should be done
Construct an exegetical outline that shows the structure and main idea of a New Testament passage
Explain the Reformed view that creeds and confessions guide interpretation while remaining subordinate to Scripture as the supreme judge
Evaluate competing interpretations of a passage using context, genre, and the analogy of Scripture
Defend the Reformed doctrine of the perspicuity of Scripture for what is necessary to salvation
Compare the grammatical-historical method with allegorical and reader-centered approaches to interpretation
Write an interpretation of a New Testament passage that applies the grammatical-historical method from observation through application

BIB.8.2.2.t: Identify the Temple in Jerusalem as the place where God's people gathered to worship him, pray, and offer sacrifices
Identify Jesus as a Jewish boy who grew up in Nazareth in the land of Israel and traveled with his family to Jerusalem for Passover
Recall that faithful Jewish people such as Simeon and Anna were waiting for the Messiah God had promised
Describe what happened in a synagogue on the Sabbath, including the reading of the Scriptures from scrolls
Explain the difference between the Temple and a synagogue in Jewish worship
Describe the major Jewish feasts that Jesus attended, such as Passover, Tabernacles, and Dedication
Explain who the Pharisees and Sadducees were and name a belief that set them apart from each other
Describe the roles of priests, Levites, scribes, and the Sanhedrin in Jewish religious life
Explain why Jesus drove the money changers and sellers out of the Temple courts
Locate Judea, Samaria, Galilee, and Jerusalem on a map and explain why Jews and Samaritans avoided one another
Compare the first-century hope for a political king with the kind of king Jesus showed himself to be
Explain how the Law of Moses shaped daily Jewish life through practices such as Sabbath keeping, food laws, ritual purity, and circumcision
Explain the span of the Second Temple period from the rebuilding of the Temple after the exile to its destruction in AD 70
Analyze how Jesus responded to the tradition of the elders and how he distinguished it from the commandment of God
Analyze how the Jewish Diaspora, its synagogues, and Gentile God-fearers opened pathways for the spread of the gospel
Compare the range of first-century messianic expectations with the way Jesus fulfilled the Old Testament promises as prophet, priest, and king
Compare the beliefs and aims of the major Jewish groups of Jesus' day, including Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes, Zealots, and Herodians
Analyze how Paul describes his training as a Pharisee and how he reassesses it in light of knowing Christ
Evaluate the influence of Hellenistic culture on first-century Judaism as seen in the Greek-speaking Jews of the New Testament
Evaluate how sources outside the Bible such as Josephus and the Dead Sea Scrolls illuminate the New Testament world while Scripture remains the final authority
Evaluate claims of the New Perspective on Paul about Second Temple Judaism in light of Paul's teaching on justification as confessed in the Reformed tradition
Compose a synthesis explaining how the religious setting of Second Temple Judaism formed the setting into which God sent his Son in the fullness of time

BIB.8.2.3.t: Identify the Bible as God's Word given to his people
Name the two main parts of the Bible as the Old Testament and the New Testament
Recall that God moved human writers, including apostles such as Paul, Peter, and John, to write the books of the New Testament
Identify the 27 books of the New Testament and sort them into Gospels, Acts, Letters, and Revelation
Explain that the word canon means a measuring rule and why the church calls the books of Scripture its rule of faith and life
Describe how the apostles' letters were read aloud in the churches and shared from one congregation to another
Explain how Scripture differs from other helpful Christian books in its inspiration and authority
Categorize the New Testament books by author and describe how early collections such as Paul's letters were gathered
Analyze the marks the early church used to recognize canonical books, including apostolic origin, agreement with apostolic teaching, and widespread use in the churches
Explain the Reformed teaching that the church recognized the canon rather than created it, because Scripture's authority rests on God its author
Describe how Athanasius' Festal Letter of 367 and the councils of Hippo and Carthage confirmed books the churches were already using
Explain why Reformed churches do not receive the Apocrypha as part of the canon
Analyze why the Gnostic gospels were not received by the church by comparing their teaching with the apostolic witness to Christ
Construct a defense of the closed canon from the finality of God's revelation in Christ and the apostolic foundation of the church
Compare the Reformed, Roman Catholic, and Eastern Orthodox accounts of how the canon relates to the authority of the church
Evaluate the Muratorian Fragment and other early lists as evidence for how the canon was recognized, including the books once disputed such as Hebrews, James, and 2 Peter
Write a study that explains and evaluates the Reformed doctrine that Scripture is self-attesting and that the Holy Spirit's witness through the Word is the final ground for receiving the canon

BIB.8.2.4.t: Identify that a long time passed between the last Old Testament prophet and the birth of Jesus
Name Malachi as the last book of the Old Testament and Matthew as the first book of the New Testament
Recall from Scripture that faithful people like Simeon and Anna were waiting for the promised Messiah when Jesus was born
Explain why the time between the Testaments is often called the 400 silent years because God sent no new prophet and no new Scripture was written
Explain from Scripture that God continued to rule over kings and nations during the years when He sent no new prophet
Retell the story of the Maccabean revolt and the rededication of the temple that is remembered at Hanukkah
Sequence the powers that ruled Judea between Malachi and Matthew from Persia through Greece, the Ptolemies, the Seleucids, and the Hasmoneans to Rome
Analyze how the conquests of Alexander the Great spread the Greek language and culture across the lands of the Bible
Compare Daniel's visions of successive kingdoms with the empires that rose and fell between the Testaments as Reformed interpreters have read them
Describe the origin of the Septuagint and trace examples of New Testament writers quoting it
Interpret the desecration of the temple by Antiochus IV Epiphanes in light of Daniel's prophecy of the abomination of desolation and Jesus' later use of that phrase
Describe the rise and fall of the Hasmonean dynasty ending with Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC
Explain how the spread of Jewish communities across the Greek and Persian world during this period prepared places where the gospel was later preached
Construct an annotated timeline of the intertestamental period from Malachi to the birth of Christ marking its key rulers and events
Evaluate the books of the Maccabees as historical sources for this period while distinguishing them from inspired Scripture as the Reformed confessions teach
Defend the continuity of God's plan across the silent years by tracing Malachi's promise of a coming messenger to its fulfillment in John the Baptist
Compose an essay arguing how the political, linguistic, and religious developments of the intertestamental period set the stage for the fullness of time

BIB.8.2.5.t: Identify a Roman soldier or centurion in a Bible story such as the centurion who asked Jesus to heal his servant
Recall that Caesar Augustus ruled the Roman Empire and ordered the census that brought Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem
Describe how Roman roads and sea routes helped travelers like Paul move from city to city
Explain what Jesus taught when he was shown a Roman coin bearing Caesar's image
Summarize the Pax Romana and describe how it made travel and trade safer across the empire
Explain why Jewish tax collectors working for Rome were despised, using the account of Zacchaeus
Describe crucifixion as a Roman punishment and identify the Roman officials and soldiers involved in Jesus' death
Compare the roles of Pilate as Roman governor and Herod Antipas as a client ruler in the trial of Jesus
Explain how Koine Greek as a common language of the Roman world helped the gospel spread among many peoples
Distinguish the members of the Herodian family who appear in the New Testament and their relationship to Rome
Describe Greco-Roman polytheism and identify the pagan gods and temple practices the apostles encountered in Acts
Explain the Reformed teaching that God in his providence prepared the Roman world for the coming of Christ in the fullness of time
Analyze how Roman roads, peace, and law contributed to the course of Paul's missionary journeys
Explain how Luke dates the events of Jesus' life by naming Roman rulers and officials
Explain the imperial cult and why refusing to honor Caesar as divine placed early Christians in danger
Analyze how Paul used his Roman citizenship and legal rights in the course of his ministry
Explain the social hierarchy of the Roman world, including citizens, freedmen, and slaves, and how apostolic teaching addressed it
Analyze how Paul engaged Stoic and Epicurean philosophers at Athens
Explain the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 and how Jesus foretold it
Analyze how apostolic commands to submit to governing authorities applied to Christians living under Roman rule
Construct an annotated map of the Roman provinces where key New Testament events took place
Analyze the Roman patronage system and its bearing on New Testament teaching about benefactors and service
Evaluate the conflict between the Christian confession that Jesus is Lord and the claims of Caesar
Write an analysis of how Roman political, social, and religious structures shape the narrative of a Gospel or Acts

BIB.8.3.1.t: Identify that the risen Jesus told John to write letters to seven churches
Describe John's vision of Jesus standing among seven golden lampstands and holding seven stars
Recall that Jesus tells each church that he knows their works
Name the seven churches of Asia Minor in the order Jesus addresses them
Identify the warning and the promise Jesus gives in a single letter such as the letter to Smyrna
Describe the common pattern of the letters including the title of Christ, commendation, rebuke, call to repent, call to hear, and promise to the one who conquers
Explain what Jesus means by calling the church in Laodicea lukewarm in light of its claim to be rich and in need of nothing
Explain the rebuke to Ephesus for abandoning its first love and the threefold remedy to remember, repent, and do the works it did at first
Compare the church in Smyrna, which was poor and suffering yet called rich, with the church in Sardis, which had a reputation for being alive yet was called dead
Explain how Revelation interprets the stars as the angels of the churches and the lampstands as the churches themselves
Locate the seven cities on a map of the Roman province of Asia and trace the route a messenger would travel to deliver the letters
Analyze how the title of Christ that opens each letter draws on the vision of chapter one and fits the needs of that church
Analyze how historical details of the cities such as emperor worship in Pergamum and the wealth and lukewarm water of Laodicea illuminate the letters
Identify the false teachings and compromises the letters name, including the Nicolaitans, the teaching of Balaam, and the woman Jezebel, and explain the danger each posed
Interpret the promises to the one who conquers and trace how several of them are fulfilled in the closing chapters of Revelation
Explain why the repeated call to hear what the Spirit says to the churches shows that the letters address the whole church in every age
Compare Ephesus, which guarded sound doctrine but lost its love, with Pergamum and Thyatira, which showed love and service but tolerated false teaching
Analyze the meaning of Jesus standing at the door and knocking when the verse is read in its context as a call to the church in Laodicea
Explain how the call to Smyrna to be faithful unto death and the promise to keep Philadelphia relate to the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints
Analyze how Christ's calls to repent and his warning to remove a church's lampstand relate to the Reformed teaching on church discipline and the marks of a true church
Evaluate how Christ holding the stars and walking among the lampstands supports the Reformed confession that Christ alone is head of the church
Evaluate how the warnings to the seven churches apply to congregations today by drawing principles from the original context rather than reading modern situations into the text
Evaluate major interpretive approaches to the seven churches, including letters to historical congregations, successive ages of church history, and timeless types, using evidence from the text
Create a study guide that examines a congregation using the categories the letters themselves use, such as works, love, doctrinal faithfulness, holiness, and endurance

BIB.8.3.2.t: Identify Jesus as both the Lion of the tribe of Judah and the Lamb in John's vision
Name the great dragon in Revelation as Satan, the enemy of God and his people
Recall that numbers in Revelation carry meaning, such as seven standing for fullness or completeness
Describe the throne room vision, including the throne, the rainbow, the elders, and the living creatures full of eyes and wings
Explain why Jesus is called the Lamb who was slain by connecting the title to the Passover lamb and his sacrifice for sinners
Compare the four living creatures around God's throne with the creatures in Ezekiel's vision and the seraphim in Isaiah's vision
Identify symbols that Revelation explains within the text, such as lampstands as churches, incense as prayers, and the dragon as Satan
Identify the Four Horsemen and explain their background in the horsemen and chariots of Zechariah's visions
Contrast the Beast with the Lamb by showing how the Beast imitates the Lamb's death, resurrection, and authority
Analyze how Revelation draws on Daniel's vision of the four beasts and the Son of Man in its portraits of Christ and the Beast
Interpret Babylon in Revelation as a symbol of the world system opposed to God, drawing on the prophets' oracles against historical Babylon
Analyze how John's eating of the little scroll reworks Ezekiel's commissioning to show the prophet's calling
Connect the bowl judgments in Revelation to the plagues of the Exodus and explain what the parallel teaches about God's deliverance of his people
Describe the features of apocalyptic literature, including visions, angelic interpreters, symbolic numbers and creatures, and cosmic conflict, using Daniel and Revelation as examples
Compare the mark of the Beast with the seal of God using the Old Testament background of marking on the forehead and hand
Apply the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture by tracing an image in Revelation back to its Old Testament source to explain its meaning
Create a reference guide to symbolic numbers in Revelation, such as 7, 12, 144,000, 1,000, and the forty-two months, that explains each with its biblical background
Analyze how reading Revelation as apocalyptic prophecy sent as a letter shapes its interpretation differently from reading it as straightforward narrative
Evaluate the preterist, historicist, futurist, and idealist approaches to Revelation, including how each handles literal and symbolic readings of its imagery
Trace the conflict between the seed of the woman and the serpent from Genesis 3:15 through the vision of the woman and the dragon in Revelation 12

BIB.8.3.3.t: Identify Jesus as the Lamb who wins the victory over evil in Revelation
Name Jesus as the rider on the white horse who is called Faithful and True and King of kings and Lord of lords
Recall that God will one day throw Satan away forever so that he can never harm God's people again
Retell how God's people in heaven sing praise because the Lamb has won the victory
Explain that Jesus won his victory over sin and Satan by dying on the cross and rising again, as shown by the Lamb who was slain
Summarize the Marriage Supper of the Lamb and what it shows about Christ's love for his church
Explain from Scripture that death itself will be defeated and thrown into the lake of fire
Describe how the followers of the Lamb overcome the dragon by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony
Compare the temporary and limited power of evil with the eternal reign of God as Revelation presents them
Identify the main events of Christ's final defeat of the beast, the false prophet, and Satan in Revelation 19 and 20
Explain the Reformed teaching that Christ as King restrains and conquers all his and his people's enemies
Describe the amillennial, postmillennial, and premillennial views and the reading of Revelation 20:1-6 that each one holds
Explain how the Great White Throne judgment displays God's justice through judgment according to works and the Book of Life
Analyze the binding of Satan in Revelation 20:1-3 by connecting it to Jesus' teaching on binding the strong man and casting out the ruler of this world
Explain the meaning of the second death and contrast it with the first resurrection
Explain from Scripture why believers are openly acknowledged and acquitted in the day of judgment through Christ
Explain the Reformed teaching that the day of judgment is certain while its hour is unknown and why Scripture therefore calls believers to watchfulness
Compare the main millennial views by constructing a timeline of the last things for each and evaluating how each handles the text of Revelation 19 and 20
Analyze how Revelation's message of the Lamb's victory answers the cry of persecuted believers for justice
Defend from Scripture the bodily and visible return of Christ as the church has confessed it
Evaluate how God's final judgment vindicates his holiness and displays both his mercy and his justice
Construct a biblically supported account of Christ's victory that traces it from the cross to the final defeat of every enemy

BIB.8.3.4.t: Identify from Revelation 21:2-3 that God promises a holy city where he will live with his people forever
Name the things Revelation 21:4 says God will take away in the new creation, such as tears, death, crying, and pain
Identify the river of the water of life and the tree of life in the description of the city in Revelation 22:1-2
Retell in your own words God's promise in Revelation 21:5 that he is making all things new
Explain from Revelation 21:23 and 22:5 why the city needs no sun or lamp
Explain from Revelation 21:27 that those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life enter the city
Describe what Revelation 22:3-5 says God's servants will do in the city, including seeing his face, serving him, and reigning forever
Compare the Garden of Eden in Genesis 2 and 3 with the garden city of Revelation 22, noting what is restored and what surpasses Eden
Explain what Revelation teaches about the nations bringing their glory into the city and the leaves of the tree of life bringing healing to the nations
Explain how the names of the twelve tribes on the gates and the twelve apostles on the foundations show the one people of God from both testaments
Explain how the New Testament connects the hope of the new heavens and new earth to holy living in the present
Analyze how the cube-shaped dimensions of the city connect it to the Most Holy Place of the temple
Interpret the absence of a temple in the city in light of God and the Lamb being its temple
Connect the image of the city as the bride of the Lamb to the New Testament teaching on the church as the bride of Christ
Explain the doctrine of the beatific vision as the promise that God's people will see God and enjoy him fully
Distinguish the intermediate state of believers after death from their final state in the resurrection and new creation as the Reformed confessions teach
Analyze the continuity and difference between the present body and the resurrection body using 1 Corinthians 15 and the risen Christ
Analyze whether Scripture presents the new heavens and new earth as a renewal or a replacement of the present creation
Evaluate popular depictions of heaven, such as floating on clouds with harps, against the biblical teaching of resurrected people on a renewed earth
Write a description of eternal life with God in the new creation that is grounded in and cites specific passages of Scripture
Develop an argument tracing the biblical theme of God dwelling with his people from Eden through the tabernacle and incarnation to the New Jerusalem, where God is all in all

BIB.8.4.1.t: Identify James as a letter in the Bible written by James, the brother of Jesus, to teach believers how to live
Retell James's picture of the tongue as a small spark that can set a great forest on fire
Recall James's promise that God gives wisdom generously to those who ask him in faith
Recall James's teaching that faith without works is dead
Describe what it looks like in daily life to be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger
Summarize James's teaching that trials test faith and produce steadfastness, so believers can count them joy
Explain James's teaching that temptation comes from our own desires and not from God, while every good gift comes from the unchanging Father
Explain why showing favoritism to the rich breaks the royal law to love your neighbor as yourself
Describe James's definition of pure religion as controlling the tongue, caring for orphans and widows, and keeping oneself unstained from the world
Compare hearing the word with doing the word using James's illustration of the person who looks in a mirror and forgets
Explain how James uses Abraham and Rahab as examples of faith shown by works
Explain James's warnings against speaking evil of a brother and against boasting about tomorrow instead of saying if the Lord wills
Describe James's call to restore a believer who wanders from the truth
Contrast the wisdom from above with earthly wisdom using the qualities and fruits James lists
Analyze how James traces quarrels to selfish desires and calls readers to humble submission to God
Explain James's instructions on prayer for the sick, confession of sins to one another, and the example of Elijah's prayer
Apply James's teaching on taming the tongue, including the stricter judgment of teachers and the inconsistency of blessing and cursing, to examples of everyday speech
Analyze how James and Paul use the words faith, works, and justified so that their teaching agrees rather than conflicts, as the Reformed confessions explain
Explain James's phrase the perfect law of liberty and how the Reformed tradition understands the moral law as a rule of life for believers
Explain James's warning to rich oppressors and his call for patient endurance until the coming of the Lord, using the examples of the farmer, the prophets, and Job
Analyze the features of James as wisdom writing addressed to Jewish Christians of the dispersion, including its short exhortations and vivid images
Compare parallel teachings in James and the Sermon on the Mount on trials, mercy, judging, and oaths
Evaluate historical debates over James, including Luther's hesitations, in light of the Reformed confessions' acceptance of James as canonical Scripture
Construct an explanation of how good works serve as the fruit and evidence of true faith rather than its ground, drawing on James, Paul, Jesus, and the confessions

BIB.8.4.2.t: Identify Peter as the disciple who denied Jesus three times and was restored by Jesus to care for his sheep
Name Peter's picture of believers as living stones built on Jesus the cornerstone
Recall Peter's teaching that suffering for doing good is blessed because Jesus suffered for us and left an example
Describe Peter's instruction to cast all anxieties on God because he cares for his people
Describe Peter's picture of the devil as a roaring lion and his call to be watchful and resist him firm in the faith
Summarize the living hope and imperishable inheritance that Peter says believers have through the resurrection of Jesus
Explain the command to be holy because God is holy and trace it back to its source in Leviticus
Explain how Peter describes believers as ransomed by the precious blood of Christ who bore their sins
List the qualities Peter tells believers to add to their faith and explain how God's promises supply what is needed for godliness
Compare temporary trials with eternal glory using Peter's image of faith refined like gold
Identify the marks of false teachers described in 2 Peter such as denying the Master, greed, and sensuality
Explain how Peter applies Israel's titles of royal priesthood and holy nation to the church
Prepare a respectful answer for the hope Christians hold, following Peter's instruction to speak with gentleness and a good conscience
Analyze Peter's description of believers as exiles and sojourners and how it shapes their conduct among unbelievers
Interpret Peter's explanation of the apparent delay of the Lord's return as God's patience toward sinners
Explain how Peter connects Noah's rescue through the flood to baptism as a sign rather than a mere outward washing
Explain how Peter uses his eyewitness account of the transfiguration to show that the apostolic message is not a cleverly devised myth
Explain how Peter's examples of the flood, Sodom, Noah, and Lot show both God's judgment on the wicked and his rescue of the godly
Analyze how 1 Peter presents Christ's suffering as both a substitutionary atonement and an example for believers, drawing on Isaiah 53
Construct a summary of the theology of suffering taught across 1 Peter
Analyze Peter's teaching on the day of the Lord and the new heavens and new earth, including how translation choices affect its reading
Evaluate Peter's call to submission to civil rulers, masters, and husbands in light of its stated purposes and its limits elsewhere in Scripture
Defend the Reformed doctrine of the inspiration of Scripture using Peter's teaching on prophets carried along by the Spirit and his recognition of Paul's letters as Scripture
Analyze Peter's charge to elders to shepherd the flock under the Chief Shepherd and relate it to his own restoration by Jesus
Compare the main interpretations of Christ preaching to the spirits in prison and evaluate them against the context of 1 Peter
Evaluate scholarly arguments about the authorship and date of 2 Peter in light of the letter's own claims

BIB.8.4.3.t: Identify from 1 John that God is love and that he showed his love by sending his Son
Recite 1 John 4:19 and tell how God's love for us comes before our love for him and for others
Identify from 1 John that God is light with no darkness in him
Recite 1 John 1:9 and explain that John teaches we should confess our sins to God, who promises to forgive
Describe practical ways to love others in deed and truth as John commands, using Jesus laying down his life as the pattern
Explain what it means that Jesus is our Advocate with the Father when believers sin
Summarize John's contrast between walking in the light and walking in the darkness
Explain from 1 John 3 what it means to be called children of God and how the tradition confesses this as adoption
Explain how John presents keeping God's commandments and loving fellow believers as evidence of knowing God
Explain how John says faith in Jesus as the Son of God overcomes the world
Describe John's teaching on confident prayer according to God's will and practice writing a prayer shaped by it
Compare love of the world with love of the Father using the three desires John names
Identify the traditional author, audience, and occasion of 1, 2, and 3 John, including the role of the elder
Identify the spirit of antichrist as John describes it, especially the denial that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh
Explain the meaning of propitiation in 1 John and how it shows the source of God's love
Explain John's teaching on fellowship with the Father, the Son, and one another and what breaks it
Analyze the recurring tests of true belief in 1 John, namely right belief about Christ, obedience, and love
Interpret the statement that perfect love casts out fear within its context of confidence on the day of judgment
Compare the prologue of 1 John with the prologue of the Gospel of John, noting shared themes of the Word, life, and eyewitness testimony
Contrast the purpose statement of 1 John with that of the Gospel of John
Interpret John's statements about not practicing sin and about the sin leading to death in light of his teaching that believers still sin
Compare the conduct of Gaius, Diotrephes, and Demetrius in 3 John and what each shows about faithful church life
Analyze the textual evidence for the longer reading of 1 John 5:7-8 and explain why the doctrine of the Trinity does not depend on it
Construct a biblical definition of agape love from the Johannine epistles
Evaluate the grounds of assurance of salvation that John gives and compare them with the Reformed confession of assurance
Defend the true humanity and incarnation of Christ from the Johannine epistles against docetic and proto-Gnostic teaching
Synthesize the teaching of 2 and 3 John on when to extend and when to withhold hospitality for the sake of truth

BIB.8.4.4.t: Identify Jude as the writer of a short New Testament letter who called himself a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James
Recall from Jude's closing words that God is able to keep his people from stumbling
Recite the doxology of Jude from memory and name the things it gives to God
Identify the three words Jude uses to describe believers in his greeting as called, beloved, and kept
Explain in their own words what Jude means by urging believers to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints
Describe how Jude says false teachers crept into the church unnoticed and what two errors he says they taught
Retell the three Old Testament examples of judgment Jude uses and explain what each one warns about
Explain the meaning of Jude's word pictures of hidden reefs, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, and wandering stars
Compare the way of Cain, the error of Balaam, and the rebellion of Korah using their Old Testament accounts
Contrast the restraint of the archangel Michael with the slander of the false teachers in Jude
Explain the four commands Jude gives for believers to build themselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and wait for Christ's mercy
Analyze how Jude quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch and explain why the Reformed tradition holds that quoting a book does not make that book part of the canon
Explain how Jude uses the apostles' earlier predictions of scoffers to show that false teaching in the church was expected
Describe the different responses Jude commands toward those who doubt, those who must be snatched from the fire, and those to be shown mercy with fear
Construct a profile of the false teachers in Jude from the traits the letter assigns to them in belief, conduct, and speech
Evaluate the claim that grace permits sinful living by comparing Jude's warning with Paul's teaching and the Reformed confessions
Defend from Jude 1:3 and related texts the Reformed teaching that the faith was delivered once for all and is not added to by new revelations
Develop a plan for answering a false teaching that follows Jude's pattern of holding firm to truth while showing mercy to those who doubt
Synthesize Jude's warnings of judgment with his repeated theme of God keeping his people and explain how the tradition's doctrine of perseverance draws on the letter

BIB.8.5.1.t: Retell the story of Jesus being born in Bethlehem and laid in a manger, naming Mary, Joseph, and baby Jesus
Recall the good news the angels told the shepherds and what the shepherds did after hearing it
Retell the visit of the wise men who followed the star and the gifts they brought to Jesus
Describe the angel's announcements to Mary and to Joseph and explain that the name Jesus was given because he would save his people from their sins
Explain the church's teaching that Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary
Explain that the name Immanuel means God with us and connect it to Isaiah's prophecy
Explain from Scripture why the Son of God became truly human to save his people
Describe the boy Jesus in the temple and explain how Luke 2:52 shows that Jesus grew as a true human being
Locate Bethlehem and Nazareth on a map and explain why Bethlehem as the city of David matters for the Messiah's birth
Compare the humble circumstances of Jesus' birth with the glory announced by the angels and explain what this shows about his humiliation
Describe how Simeon and Anna recognized the infant Jesus in the temple as the promised salvation for Israel and the Gentiles
Identify the Old Testament prophecies Matthew cites in his birth narrative and explain what each claims about Jesus
Compare the nativity accounts of Matthew and Luke, identifying the events and emphases unique to each Gospel
Analyze the genealogies in Matthew and Luke to explain how each presents Jesus as son of David and son of Abraham or son of Adam
Analyze how Matthew's use of Hosea 11:1 in the flight to Egypt presents Jesus as the true Son who relives Israel's story
Explain how Zechariah's Benedictus links the births of John and Jesus to God's covenant promises to David and Abraham
Interpret the Magnificat by comparing its themes of reversal and covenant faithfulness with Hannah's song
Explain how the prologue of John's Gospel presents the eternal Word who became flesh
Explain the doctrine of the hypostatic union as two whole natures joined in one person without conversion, composition, or confusion
Distinguish the church's confession of Christ's person from early errors such as Docetism, Arianism, Nestorianism, and Eutychianism using Scripture
Defend from Scripture and the catechisms the Reformed teaching that the Mediator had to be both truly human and truly God
Defend the Virgin Birth and its significance for Christ's sinless human nature as taught in the Reformed confessions
Evaluate the historical questions surrounding Luke's census under Quirinius using ancient evidence and proposed scholarly resolutions
Evaluate kenotic interpretations of Philippians 2:5-11 in light of the Reformed confession that Christ remained fully God in taking human nature
Create a study tracing the promised seed and Davidic king from Genesis through the prophets to their fulfillment in the nativity accounts

BIB.8.5.2.t: Identify a parable as a story Jesus told to teach about God and his kingdom
Retell the parable of the lost sheep and tell how the shepherd searched for the one that was lost
Retell the parable of the Good Samaritan and name the person who acted as a neighbor
Recite the Lord's Prayer and identify the petition that asks for God's kingdom to come
Retell the parable of the prodigal son and describe how the father welcomed his son home
State Jesus' announcement that the kingdom of God is at hand and his call to repent and believe the gospel
Compare the wise and foolish builders and explain what it means to hear and do Jesus' words
Identify the Golden Rule and give examples of how it applies in everyday situations
Explain the parable of the sower by matching each kind of soil to a way people respond to God's word
Describe the Beatitudes and explain the kind of people Jesus calls blessed in his kingdom
Explain what the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven teach about the small beginning and great growth of the kingdom
Explain what the parables of the hidden treasure and the pearl teach about the surpassing worth of the kingdom
Explain the meaning of each petition of the Lord's Prayer using the answers of the Westminster Shorter Catechism
Explain what the parable of the unforgiving servant teaches about forgiving others as God has forgiven us
Explain how Jesus teaches the full meaning of the law in the sayings of the Sermon on the Mount that begin you have heard that it was said
Analyze how the audience and occasion of a parable shape its main point, using the grumbling Pharisees in Luke 15 as an example
Analyze the theme of reversal in Jesus' kingdom teaching where the last are first and the humble are exalted
Explain what the parables of the weeds, the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and goats teach about final judgment and readiness for Christ's return
Analyze why Jesus taught in parables by explaining how they revealed the kingdom to disciples and concealed it from hardened hearers
Explain the cost of discipleship as Jesus teaches it through the tower builder and the king going to war
Explain the Reformed understanding of the kingdom of God as God's saving reign in Christ that advances through the word and Spirit
Evaluate competing interpretations of a parable by testing them against its literary context, its main point, and the rest of Scripture
Compose an essay explaining the ethic of the Sermon on the Mount and its relation to the law and to God's grace
Compare the parables of the Pharisee and tax collector and the laborers in the vineyard with the Reformed doctrine of justification by grace
Evaluate Jesus' command to love enemies in light of Old Testament law and the Reformed teaching on the sixth commandment
Defend Jesus' authority to interpret the law using the response of the crowds and his claim to fulfill the law and the prophets
Compare the Reformed view of the kingdom with views that reduce it to social reform or place it wholly in the future
Construct a synthesis of the already and not yet character of the kingdom drawn from Jesus' parables and kingdom sayings

BIB.8.5.3.t: Retell the account of Jesus giving sight to a man born blind
Retell the account of Jesus walking on the water and name what the disciples said about him afterward
Recall how Jesus fed more than five thousand people with a boy's five loaves and two fish and had food left over
Describe how Jesus raised Lazarus from the tomb and what Jesus said about himself before doing it
Summarize two reasons the Gospels give for Jesus' miracles, his compassion for people and his revealing of who he is
Explain what Jesus calming the storm shows about his authority over wind and sea
Distinguish a miracle as God's direct work above ordinary means from a magic trick that relies on deception or hidden technique
Explain how Jesus used the healing of the paralyzed man to show his authority to forgive sins
Explain how Jesus pointed to his miracles to show John the Baptist that Isaiah's promises of the coming kingdom were being fulfilled
Analyze how Jesus' healings and nature miracles reverse effects of the fall such as sickness, hunger, and death
Explain how Jesus' casting out of demons demonstrates that the kingdom of God has come and that Satan is being overthrown
Analyze the signs in John's Gospel by tracing how each one reveals Jesus' glory and serves John's stated purpose for writing
Explain the transfiguration as a preview of the King's glory and connect it to Jesus' promise that some would see the kingdom come in power
Explain why Jesus refused to perform signs on demand and how the Gospels relate miracles to faith
Classify Jesus' miracles as nature miracles, healings, exorcisms, and raisings from the dead and explain what each category reveals about his kingdom
Compare Jesus' miracles with miracles performed through Moses, Elijah, and Elisha to show how the Gospels present Jesus as greater than the prophets
Evaluate the responses of the Pharisees, the crowds, and the disciples to Jesus' miracles and what those responses reveal about unbelief and faith
Evaluate common naturalistic objections to the Gospel miracles and defend their historicity using eyewitness testimony and the public nature of the events
Explain the Reformed position that miracles chiefly attested Christ and the apostolic message and relate it to the tradition's teaching that former ways of revealing God's will have ceased
Compose a theological argument presenting Jesus' miracles as a foretaste of the new heavens and new earth, drawing on Old Testament promises and the Bible's closing vision

BIB.8.5.4.t: Retell how the crowds welcomed Jesus into Jerusalem by waving branches and shouting Hosanna
Recall that Jesus died on the cross, was buried, and rose again on the third day, leaving the tomb empty
Describe how Jesus washed his disciples' feet and explain the example of service he told them to follow
Summarize the Last Supper and explain what Jesus said the bread and the cup represent
Describe Jesus' prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane and what it shows about his submission to the Father's will
Identify people to whom the risen Jesus appeared, including Mary Magdalene, the travelers to Emmaus, and Thomas
Explain the Reformed teaching that Jesus died as a substitute, bearing the punishment for the sins of his people
Construct a timeline of the major events of Passion Week from the triumphal entry to the resurrection
Compare Judas' betrayal and Peter's denial, including how each story ends
Identify Jesus' predictions of his death and resurrection and describe how the disciples responded to them
Explain how Jesus' clearing of the temple during Passion Week intensified the religious leaders' opposition to him
Explain how events of the Passion fulfill Old Testament prophecies
Analyze the Jewish and Roman trials of Jesus, including the charges brought and the roles of Caiaphas, Pilate, and Herod
Analyze the seven sayings of Jesus from the cross in light of their Gospel context and Old Testament background
Compare the Passover in Exodus with the Last Supper and the crucifixion to explain why Scripture calls Christ our Passover lamb
Explain the meaning of the darkness and the tearing of the temple curtain at Jesus' death
Explain the significance of the resurrection for justification and for the future resurrection of believers
Distinguish Christ's state of humiliation from his state of exaltation as the Westminster Standards describe them
Explain how the Reformed tradition interprets the Apostles' Creed phrases about Christ's burial and descent into hell
Compare the four Gospel accounts of the crucifixion and identify the distinct emphasis of each evangelist
Analyze the Gospel accounts and Roman crucifixion practice as evidence that Jesus truly died
Evaluate the historical evidence for the resurrection against alternative explanations such as theft, swoon, and hallucination
Evaluate major theories of the atonement against Scripture, explaining why the Reformed tradition holds penal substitution as central
Explain the Reformed doctrine of definite atonement and the passages its defenders cite
Create a written or oral synthesis explaining how the cross and the empty tomb together accomplish redemption and union with Christ

BIB.8.6.1.t: Identify from Romans 3:23 that every person has sinned against God
Name eternal life in Christ as a free gift from God that no one can earn
Recall from Galatians that God saves people through faith in Jesus and not by their good works
Retell how God showed his love by sending Christ to die for people while they were still sinners
Recite the Roman Road verses in order and explain what each one teaches about salvation
Explain justification as God declaring a sinner righteous because of Christ and not because of the sinner's goodness
Explain why Paul calls the gospel the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes
Compare the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit using examples from Galatians 5
Summarize Paul's account in Galatians of receiving the gospel by revelation and confronting Peter at Antioch
Explain the tradition's teaching that saving faith receives and rests on Christ alone for salvation
Describe how Romans 12:1-2 calls those saved by God's mercy to respond with whole-life worship
Analyze Paul's argument in Romans 1 to 3 that both Gentiles and Jews stand guilty before God
Outline the overall structure of Romans and locate its major sections on sin, justification, new life, Israel, and Christian living
Explain how Paul uses Abraham to show that righteousness has always been credited by faith
Interpret Romans 8 to explain what Paul teaches about no condemnation and life in the Spirit
Compare the work of Adam and the work of Christ as Paul presents them in Romans 5
Explain adoption as Romans and Galatians present it, including the believer's status as God's child and heir
Explain how Romans 6 grounds the believer's new life in union with Christ in his death and resurrection
Distinguish justification from sanctification using Romans and the Westminster Standards
Explain how Romans 3:25-26 presents Christ's death as a propitiation that shows God to be both just and the justifier
Analyze the doctrine of imputation as Paul develops it in Romans 4 and 5
Construct a definition of the gospel drawn from the opening of Romans and Galatians
Explain Paul's teaching in Romans 9 to 11 on the place of Israel and the Gentiles in God's saving plan
Compare major interpretations of the struggle with sin described in Romans 7
Analyze how Romans 8 and 9 present God's sovereign purpose in salvation as the Reformed tradition confesses it
Evaluate the Judaizers' teaching in Galatia using Paul's arguments against adding works of the law to faith
Defend the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone from Romans and Galatians in contrast to the Council of Trent
Explain how Paul's teaching on justification in Romans 4 harmonizes with James 2 on faith and works
Explain Paul's teaching on Christian freedom and how it guards against both legalism and license
Synthesize Paul's teaching on the purposes of the law and its relationship to grace in Romans and Galatians

BIB.8.6.2.t: Identify the church as one body with many members who each belong and care for one another
Name the churches in Corinth and Thessalonica as churches that Paul wrote letters to
