Describe the qualities of love that Paul lists and name love as the greatest of faith, hope, and love
Explain Paul's teaching that church workers are fellow workers who plant and water while God gives the growth
Retell Paul's teaching that Jesus will return, the dead in Christ will rise, and believers will be with the Lord forever
Summarize the words of Jesus at the Lord's Supper as Paul passed them on to the Corinthian church
Explain that the Holy Spirit gives different gifts to church members for the common good
Explain Paul's teaching that the church and the believer's body are a temple of the Holy Spirit
Describe how Paul taught the Corinthians to give generously and cheerfully to meet the needs of other believers
Compare the wisdom of the world with the wisdom of God shown in the message of the cross
Outline Paul's argument that the resurrection of Christ is the foundation of the gospel and of Christian hope
Explain how the comfort God gives in suffering equips believers to comfort others in the church
Explain Paul's command to work quietly and not be idle while the church waits for the Lord's return
Analyze the divisions, immorality, and lawsuits in the Corinthian church and the corrections Paul gives for each
Explain how Paul directs church discipline toward repentance, restoration, and the purity of the congregation
Explain what it means for believers to be ambassadors for Christ entrusted with the message of reconciliation
Analyze Paul's teaching about the man of lawlessness in light of his purpose to correct the false claim that the day of the Lord had already come
Explain Paul's principles for orderly worship that builds up the whole congregation
Analyze how Paul's teaching on strength in weakness answers the boasting of the false apostles in Corinth
Explain the Reformed teaching on worthy reception of the Lord's Supper through self-examination and discerning the body
Construct an explanation of the resurrection body using Paul's seed analogy and his contrasts between the natural and spiritual body
Compare the Reformed teaching on Christ's spiritual presence in the Lord's Supper with other views using Paul's language of participation
Evaluate uses of Christian liberty according to Paul's principle of love for the weaker brother and the glory of God
Defend the bodily resurrection of believers against its denial using Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 15
Evaluate continuationist and cessationist readings of Paul's teaching on spiritual gifts in light of the Reformed tradition's position
Compose a synthesis of Paul's call to holy living in light of the certain but unknown day of Christ's return

BIB.8.6.3.t: Identify Jesus as the head of the church using Paul's picture of a head and its body
Retell how Jesus humbled himself to become a servant and die on the cross
Recite Philippians 4:4 and explain that Paul told believers to rejoice in the Lord even while he was in prison
Retell the story of Onesimus and identify how Paul asked Philemon to welcome him as a brother in Christ
Identify from Colossians that Jesus made all things and holds all things together
Name the pieces of the armor of God and explain that believers stand firm in the strength of the Lord
Identify Paul as the author of the four Prison Epistles, describe his circumstances in prison, and name the recipients of each letter
Describe the two movements of Christ's humiliation and exaltation in Philippians 2
Explain what Paul means by being in Christ by listing the spiritual blessings he names in Ephesians 1
Compare the old self and the new self and explain how Paul grounds the new life in being raised with Christ
Explain Paul's comparison between his former credentials and the surpassing worth of knowing Christ
Analyze the titles and claims Paul makes about Christ in the Colossian hymn, including image, firstborn, head, and fullness
Explain how the mystery revealed in Christ brings Jews and Gentiles together into one new humanity through the cross
Explain how Paul presents Christ's victory over the rulers and authorities through his cross, resurrection, and ascension
Interpret Philippians 4:13 within its context of contentment in every circumstance
Analyze how Paul answers the false teaching at Colossae by asserting the fullness and sufficiency of Christ
Explain how the ascended Christ gives gifts to build up his body in unity and maturity
Analyze how the structure of Ephesians moves from what God has done in Christ to how believers are to walk
Analyze how Paul applies the lordship of Christ to household relationships, including the case of Philemon and Onesimus
Evaluate kenotic Christology in light of Philippians 2 and Colossians 2 and the Reformed confession of Christ's two natures
Construct a scriptural argument from the Prison Epistles for the full deity and true humanity of Christ in one person
Synthesize the Christology of the four Prison Epistles into a summary of Christ's person and his offices as prophet, priest, and king

BIB.8.6.4.t: Identify Timothy as the young helper whom Paul taught and called his child in the faith
Retell how Timothy learned the Scriptures from childhood through his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice
State that all Scripture is breathed out by God and is useful for teaching and training
Name the five ways Paul told young Timothy to set an example for believers in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity
Describe Paul's pictures of the Christian life as fighting the good fight and finishing the race
Explain why Paul instructed the church to pray for kings and all who are in authority
Explain what Paul means by godliness with contentment and why he warns against the love of money
Interpret the images of the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer that Paul uses to describe faithful service
Summarize the qualifications Paul gives for elders by sorting them into character, family, and teaching
Compare the sound teaching Paul commends with the myths and false teaching he warns Timothy and Titus against
Explain the role and qualifications of deacons and how their service differs from that of elders
Explain how Paul uses his own story as the foremost of sinners to show the mercy of Christ Jesus
Trace the chain of faithful teachers Paul describes for passing the gospel from one generation to the next
Explain the Reformed doctrine of the inspiration, authority, and sufficiency of Scripture from Paul's words to Timothy
Describe Paul's instructions for older men, older women, younger women, younger men, and bondservants and the reason he gives for each
Explain Paul's instructions for the church's care of widows and its honor and correction of elders
Explain how Paul connects God's grace and sound doctrine to a life devoted to good works in Titus
Apply Paul's charge to rightly handle the word of truth by interpreting a passage from the Pastoral Epistles in its context
Explain the Reformed understanding of church government by elders and deacons drawn from the Pastoral Epistles
Explain the confession that Christ Jesus is the one mediator between God and men as Paul states it to Timothy
Analyze how Paul prepares Timothy to share in suffering for the gospel and to expect persecution
Analyze Paul's charge to preach the word in season and out of season and how the Reformed tradition confesses the place of preaching
Evaluate how Paul directs leaders to correct opponents with gentleness and to deal with divisive people
Compare the Reformed tradition's reading of Paul's instructions on men and women in worship and office with other interpretations of the same texts
Evaluate the priority Paul places on character over skill in the qualifications for church leaders
Defend from the Pastoral Epistles the duty to guard the deposit of faith without adding to it
Create a written charge to a church leader that synthesizes the major themes of 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus, including Paul's final charge

BIB.9.1.1.t: Identify 1 and 2 Chronicles as books that tell about the kings God gave to rule his people, especially King David and King Solomon
Recall that King Solomon built a temple in Jerusalem where God's people gathered to worship him
Retell how King David brought the ark of God to Jerusalem with singing and music and gave thanks to the Lord
Retell how King Jehoshaphat prayed when enemies came and how God told the people that the battle was his
Explain that the long lists of names at the start of Chronicles trace God's people from Adam to the families who returned to Jerusalem
Describe how King Josiah found the Book of the Law, read it to the people, and led them to renew the covenant
Explain that Chronicles retells much of the history found in Samuel and Kings from a different point of view
Summarize Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple and God's answer when his glory filled the house
Explain the theme of seeking the Lord in Chronicles using the example of King Asa's faithfulness and later decline
Summarize the promise God made to David about a son whose throne would be established forever
Explain how the account of Manasseh's humbling and restoration shows God's mercy to a repentant sinner
Analyze the prayers of Jabez and Jehoshaphat in their contexts to identify what each asks of God and on what basis
Explain from the accounts of Uzzah and the second ark procession why Chronicles stresses worship carried out in the way God prescribed
Compare parallel accounts in Samuel and Chronicles, such as David's sin with Bathsheba and the census, to identify what Chronicles includes, omits, or changes
Analyze how the ending of Chronicles, from the exile to the decree of Cyrus, shows the book was written for the community returning from exile
Describe how David organized the Levites, priests, and musicians for temple service and explain the purpose of this order
Interpret why Chronicles centers on Judah and David's line while still inviting all Israel to return to the Lord
Connect the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 1 to 9 to the identity and hope of the post-exilic community
Explain how Uzziah's judgment for burning incense shows the distinction Chronicles draws between the offices of king and priest
Analyze the pattern of blessing for seeking God and judgment for forsaking him in the reigns of Judah's kings and identify where Chronicles tempers it with mercy
Interpret 2 Chronicles 7:14 within its temple and covenant setting and evaluate common ways it is applied today
Construct a comparison of Kings as prophetic history explaining the exile and Chronicles as priestly history encouraging renewed worship
Explain the significance of Chronicles as the final book of the Hebrew canon and how Jesus' reference to Abel and Zechariah reflects that order
Research the Persian period setting of Chronicles using historical sources and explain how that setting shapes the book's concerns
Evaluate the theological purpose of the idealized portrait of David and Solomon as builders of the temple and models of the coming king
Synthesize how the hope for the Son of David and the house of God in Chronicles is fulfilled in Jesus Christ as king and true temple

BIB.9.1.2.t: Identify Solomon as the king who asked God for wisdom and built the Temple in Jerusalem
Retell how God provided food for Elijah through the ravens and the widow of Zarephath
Describe how Elijah was taken up to heaven and how Elisha carried on his work as prophet
Recall that after Solomon the kingdom split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
Summarize the contest between Elijah and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel
Retell the healing of Naaman and explain what it shows about God's power reaching beyond Israel
Explain how Solomon's sin and Rehoboam's harsh answer led to the division of the kingdom
Describe Hezekiah's prayer when Jerusalem was threatened by Assyria and how God answered it
Compare the Northern Kingdom of Israel and the Southern Kingdom of Judah in their capitals, royal lines, and places of worship
Trace how Solomon's many wives and wealth turned his heart from the LORD in light of the law for kings
Classify kings such as Hezekiah, Josiah, Ahab, and Manasseh using the narrator's verdict of doing right or evil in the sight of the LORD
Explain what God's appearance to Elijah at Horeb in the low whisper teaches about God's preservation of a faithful remnant
Analyze the ministries of Elijah and Elisha as prophets who confronted kings and performed signs that called Israel back to the covenant
Connect Josiah's reforms to the finding of the Book of the Law in the Temple
Identify the pattern of prophecy and fulfillment in Kings using the prophecy against Bethel's altar and its fulfillment under Josiah
Explain the sin of Jeroboam's golden calves as a violation of the second commandment and trace its effect on later northern kings
Analyze the account of Naboth's vineyard to show how Ahab and Jezebel abused royal power against God's law
Explain how Kings shows God keeping his promise to David through the preserved line of Judah and the release of Jehoiachin
Construct a synchronized timeline of the kings of Israel and Judah using the regnal formulas of Kings alongside Assyrian and Babylonian history
Evaluate the role of the prophet in relation to the king in Kings using Nathan, Elijah, Micaiah, and Isaiah
Defend the Reformed reading of the fall of Samaria and Jerusalem as God's just judgment under the covenant curses of Deuteronomy
Explain how the New Testament presents Jesus as greater than Solomon and links John the Baptist to Elijah
Produce a study of the contest between the LORD and Baal across Kings showing why the narrative condemns idolatry

BIB.9.1.3.t: Retell how God called the boy Samuel in the night and how Samuel answered, "Speak, for your servant hears"
Retell how David trusted the Lord to fight for him when he faced Goliath
Retell how Hannah prayed to the Lord for a son and gave Samuel back to serve the Lord
Identify Saul as Israel's first king and David as the king the Lord chose and Samuel anointed to replace him
Explain what the Lord's words to Samuel in 1 Samuel 16:7 teach about how God chose David
Describe the covenant friendship of David and Jonathan using examples from the text
Describe how David showed kindness to Mephibosheth because of his promise to Jonathan
Explain why Israel's request for a king like all the nations displeased Samuel and the Lord
Explain why David refused to harm Saul when he had the chance, using David's own words
Compare Saul's response to Samuel's rebuke with David's response to Nathan's rebuke
Explain what Samuel meant when he told Saul that to obey is better than sacrifice
Outline the structure of 1 and 2 Samuel around the careers of Samuel, Saul, and David
Describe how David united the tribes, made Jerusalem his capital, and brought the ark into the city
Analyze what the capture of the ark and the death of Uzzah reveal about the holiness of God and the danger of treating his presence as a tool
Analyze the promises the Lord made to David in the Davidic covenant concerning his house, his offspring, and his throne
Trace how David's sin with Bathsheba led to the consequences Nathan announced within David's own family
Analyze how the New Testament presents Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of the promise to David of an everlasting king
Analyze the contrast between kingship under God's law and kingship like that of the nations as presented in Samuel
Evaluate the character of Absalom and David's response to his rebellion using evidence from the narrative
Analyze the role of the prophets Samuel, Nathan, and Gad in confronting and holding Israel's kings accountable to the word of the Lord
Evaluate scholarly theories about the composition of Samuel, such as the Court History or Succession Narrative, in light of the Reformed doctrine of Scripture's inspiration and authority
Compose an essay tracing the messianic themes that frame 1 and 2 Samuel in the Song of Hannah and the last words of David

BIB.9.1.4.t: Identify Esther as a Jewish young woman whom God placed as queen in the land of Persia
Name the main people in the book of Esther, including Esther, Mordecai, King Ahasuerus, and Haman
Retell how Esther went to the king without being called in order to ask help for her people, even though it put her life in danger
Sequence the main events of Esther from Vashti's removal through the deliverance of the Jews
Explain why Haman plotted to destroy all the Jews in the Persian empire
Locate the book of Esther in history as taking place in the Persian empire after the exile, among Jews who had not returned to Judah
Describe the fast Esther asked the Jews to keep and explain what it shows about their dependence on God in a crisis
Compare Haman's pride and downfall with Mordecai's faithfulness and exaltation using the book's own details
Explain Mordecai's words for such a time as this in their context, including his confidence that deliverance would come for the Jews
Identify the reversals in the plot of Esther, such as Haman honoring Mordecai, Haman hanged on his own gallows, and the decree of destruction turned to victory
Analyze how the book of Esther displays God's providence through ordinary events even though God's name is never mentioned
Describe the origin, name, and purpose of the feast of Purim as Esther and Mordecai established it
Explain the significance of Haman as an Agagite and Mordecai as a Benjaminite descendant of Kish in light of Israel's earlier conflict with Amalek
Analyze how the irrevocable law of the Medes and Persians shaped the danger of the Jews and the way their deliverance was achieved
Explain how the preservation of the Jews in Esther fits God's covenant promise to preserve Abraham's offspring through whom the Messiah would come
Compare Esther's intercession for her people with Christ's work as mediator and intercessor, noting both likenesses and differences
Evaluate historical objections to Esther's place in the canon and explain the Reformed position that the Hebrew book is Scripture while the Greek additions are not
Evaluate the morally complex choices of Esther, Mordecai, and the Jews by distinguishing what the narrative describes from what Scripture elsewhere commands
Construct a defense of the Reformed doctrine of providence that uses Esther to show how God governs human choices and ordinary means without being the author of sin
Write an essay tracing the theme of hostility toward God's people from Exodus through Esther and explaining how the book's deliverance displays God's care for His church

BIB.9.1.5.t: Identify Ezra as a man who studied God's Word, obeyed it, and taught it to God's people
Recall that God brought his people home from Babylon to Jerusalem
Name the temple as the house of God that the returning people rebuilt
Describe how the people sang praise to God and how some older people wept when the temple foundation was laid
Summarize the decree of Cyrus allowing the people to return and explain how it fulfilled the word God spoke through Jeremiah
Describe how Ezra and the people fasted and prayed for God's protection before their journey to Jerusalem
Explain who opposed the rebuilding of the temple and the ways they tried to stop the work
Explain how the prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the people to start building the temple again
Describe how the people dedicated the finished temple and celebrated the Passover
Compare the first return under Zerubbabel and Jeshua with the second return under Ezra in their leaders, purposes, and accomplishments
Explain why the returnees rebuilt the altar and offered sacrifices as the Law of Moses commanded before the temple was finished
Outline the two main parts of Ezra, the rebuilding of the temple and the reform of the people under Ezra
Explain how Ezra shows God directing pagan kings to accomplish his purposes for his people, as the Reformed tradition confesses in its doctrine of providence
Apply Ezra's pattern of studying, doing, and teaching God's law by preparing and presenting a short study of a Bible passage
Trace the repeated phrase about the good hand of God being on Ezra and explain what it teaches about God's guidance of his servants
Explain the role of a scribe in post-exilic Israel using the description of Ezra as a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses
Analyze Ezra's prayer of confession to show how it acknowledges the people's sin, God's justice, and God's mercy to the remnant
Interpret the intermarriage crisis in light of the Mosaic prohibition against marrying idolatrous nations and its threat to covenant faithfulness
Identify the Aramaic sections of Ezra and explain why official Persian correspondence was recorded in that language
Construct a timeline of the Persian kings named in Ezra and place the book's events on it, including the gap between the temple's completion and Ezra's arrival
Analyze why Ezra 4 groups opposition from later reigns together out of chronological order and what theme this arrangement highlights
Compare the opening of Ezra with the closing of Chronicles and explain how the repeated decree links the exile to the restoration

Evaluate whether the community's separation from the peoples of the land was ethnic exclusivity or covenant faithfulness, using the text's own grounds including its welcome of those who separated from idolatry
Defend the Reformed reading that God kept his covenant promises after the exile though no Davidic king reigned, using remnant language and Zerubbabel's place in the line of David
Analyze how the rebuilt but humbler second temple pointed beyond itself to Christ as the true temple

BIB.9.1.6.t: Identify Joshua as the leader God chose after Moses to bring Israel into the promised land
Retell how the walls of Jericho fell when Israel followed God's instructions to march and shout
Recall that Rahab hid the spies and that she and her family were saved when Jericho fell
Retell how Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground and set up twelve stones to remember what God had done
Explain from Joshua how God kept His promise to give Israel the land He had sworn to Abraham
Explain how God's command to Joshua to be strong and courageous rests on God's presence and on meditating on His Law
Explain Achan's sin and how it brought defeat at Ai and judgment on his household
Outline the four main sections of Joshua as entering the land, conquering the land, dividing the land, and renewing the covenant
Explain why Israel was circumcised and kept the Passover at Gilgal before the conquest began
Compare the report of the spies in Joshua 2 with the report of the spies in Numbers 13 and 14
Describe Joshua's encounter with the commander of the LORD's army and what it shows about who leads Israel's battles
Explain how the Gibeonites deceived Israel and why the text faults Israel for not asking counsel of the LORD
Analyze the central, southern, and northern campaigns of the conquest using a map of Canaan
Analyze Rahab's confession of the LORD and how the New Testament presents her as an example of faith and an ancestor of Christ
Explain the purpose of the cities of refuge and the Levitical cities in Israel's life in the land
Interpret the account of the sun standing still in its literary context and compare ways Reformed interpreters have explained it
Connect the allotment of tribal territories to God's promises to the patriarchs and to Caleb's inheritance
Explain the meaning of herem, things devoted to destruction, from its commands in Deuteronomy and its use in Joshua
Analyze the dispute over the altar of witness and how the tribes resolved it to preserve the unity of worship
Analyze how Joshua's statements of total conquest relate to its notices of land that remained unconquered
Analyze the covenant renewals at Mount Ebal and Shechem and Joshua's charge to choose whom Israel will serve
Evaluate arguments about the justice of the Canaanite conquest using the biblical reasons given for judgment and the sparing of Rahab and Gibeon
Analyze ways the Reformed tradition reads Joshua as a type of Christ who leads His people into their inheritance
Evaluate how archaeological evidence from sites such as Jericho, Ai, and Hazor bears on the dating and history of the conquest
Evaluate how ancient Near Eastern sources such as the Amarna Letters and their references to the Habiru inform the setting of Joshua
Synthesize the theme of rest from Joshua with its development in the Psalms and Hebrews in a written argument

BIB.9.1.7.t: Identify Gideon, Deborah, and Samson as people God used to rescue Israel in the book of Judges
Name the judges as leaders God raised up for Israel in the time before Israel had kings
Retell how the people of Israel forgot God and how God sent a judge to save them when they cried out to him
Summarize the repeating cycle in Judges of sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance
Explain how God gave Gideon victory over the Midianites with a small army so that Israel would know the victory came from the LORD
Describe the roles of Deborah, Barak, and Jael in Israel's deliverance from Sisera and the Canaanites
Compare the strength God gave Samson with his repeated disobedience and his broken Nazirite vow
Explain how Israel's failure to drive out the Canaanites and its intermarriage with them led to idolatry
Construct a chart of the major judges showing each judge's enemy, tribe or region, and years of rest
Explain what Judges means when it says the Spirit of the LORD came upon a judge to equip him for the task of deliverance
Analyze the refrain that in those days there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes
Interpret Jephthah's vow and its outcome in light of God's law about vows and child sacrifice
Connect Israel's moral decline to its religious compromise using the accounts of Micah's idol and the tribe of Dan
Explain how the LORD's compassion toward Israel in its distress shows his covenant faithfulness to an unfaithful people
Analyze Gideon's refusal of kingship alongside his ephod and the rise of Abimelech to explain what Judges teaches about the LORD as Israel's true king
Explain why Hebrews names Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among examples of faith despite their failures
Analyze how the judges grow progressively more flawed from Othniel to Samson and how this shapes the book's downward structure
Evaluate the closing chapters of Judges, including the outrage at Gibeah and the civil war against Benjamin, as the climax of Israel's apostasy
Defend the Reformed teaching that God sovereignly accomplishes his purposes through flawed and sinful human instruments without being the author of their sin
Compose an essay tracing the spiral of apostasy in Judges and how the book's longing for a righteous king anticipates the kingship of Christ

BIB.9.1.8.t: Identify Nehemiah as the cupbearer who served the king of Persia
Retell that Nehemiah led God's people to rebuild the broken walls of Jerusalem
Recall that the builders worked with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other
Describe how Nehemiah prayed to God before he answered the king's question
Summarize how Nehemiah organized the people so that each group repaired a section of the wall, often near its own house
Explain why an ancient city needed walls and why Jerusalem's broken walls were a disgrace to God's people
Describe how the people listened, wept, and then rejoiced when Ezra read the Law aloud
Identify the parts of Nehemiah's prayer in chapter 1, including praise, confession of sin, remembering God's promise, and making a request
Describe how the people dedicated the finished wall with thanksgiving, singing, and great joy
Locate Susa and Jerusalem on a map and describe Nehemiah's journey from the Persian court to Judah
Identify Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem and describe the tactics of mockery, threats, and deception they used against the work
Explain how Nehemiah answered opposition by both praying to God and setting a guard
Outline the book of Nehemiah in two main movements, the rebuilding of the wall and the renewal of the people
Explain how the book shows God's providence working through a pagan king and through the swift completion of the wall
Describe Nehemiah's leadership actions, such as inspecting the walls, casting vision, organizing workers, and refusing the governor's food allowance, citing the text for each
Place Nehemiah's mission in the Persian period under Artaxerxes I and explain how it followed the earlier returns under Zerubbabel and Ezra
Interpret the statement that the joy of the LORD is your strength in its context of hearing the Law and keeping the feast
Analyze the economic injustice described in Nehemiah 5 and explain how Nehemiah's response applied the Law's teaching on lending to the poor
Explain how the Levites read the Law clearly and gave its sense so the people understood, and relate this to the Reformed teaching on the reading and preaching of the Word
Analyze the prayer of confession in Nehemiah 9 as a retelling of Israel's history that contrasts God's faithfulness with the people's repeated rebellion
Explain how the public reading of the Law led to confession and a written covenant pledge, and list the specific commitments the people made
Explain that Ezra and Nehemiah form one book in the Hebrew canon and describe how Nehemiah's first-person memoir and its lists shape the book
Compare the roles of Nehemiah as governor and Ezra as priest and scribe in the restoration community
Explain Nehemiah's Sabbath reform and relate it to the fourth commandment as the Reformed confessions teach it
Construct a profile of godly leadership from Nehemiah that weighs both his strengths and his faults, supported with textual evidence
Analyze Nehemiah's recurring prayers for God to remember him and what they show about his reliance on God's steadfast love
Evaluate whether the reforms lasted by comparing the covenant pledges of chapter 10 with the failures Nehemiah found in chapter 13
Evaluate how the unresolved ending of Nehemiah points beyond itself to the need for the new covenant fulfilled in Christ
Compose an essay tracing how prayer and practical action work together throughout the book of Nehemiah in light of the Reformed doctrine of God working through means

BIB.9.1.9.t: Name Naomi, Ruth, and Boaz as the main people in the book of Ruth and tell one thing each person did
Recall Ruth's promise to go with Naomi and to make Naomi's people and God her own
Describe how Boaz showed kindness to Ruth while she gathered grain in his field
Identify actions in Ruth's story that show loyal kindness and give examples of similar actions toward family and friends
Retell the story of Ruth in order from the famine and Naomi's return to Bethlehem through the birth of Obed
Explain how God's law about gleaning provided food for poor people and foreigners like Ruth
Identify Obed, the son of Ruth and Boaz, as the grandfather of King David
Compare Orpah's choice to return to Moab with Ruth's choice to stay with Naomi using details from the text
Explain what a kinsman redeemer was in Israel and how Boaz filled that role for Naomi and Ruth
Trace how Naomi moves from emptiness and bitterness at her return to fullness at the birth of Obed
Explain the meaning of the Hebrew word hesed and identify where Ruth, Boaz, and the LORD each show it in the book
Locate Moab and Bethlehem on a map and explain why Ruth's identity as a Moabite mattered in Israel
Connect the setting of Ruth to the period of the judges and contrast its faithful characters with the disorder of that time
Analyze the literary structure of Ruth by outlining its four scenes and showing how the opening and closing sections mirror each other
Explain the levirate marriage custom and how it relates to Boaz's redemption of Elimelech's land and name
Interpret the significance of a Moabite woman appearing in the genealogy of Jesus Christ
Explain Ruth's place among the Writings in the Hebrew canon and its traditional reading at the Feast of Weeks compared with its place in English Bibles
Analyze the legal proceedings at the city gate including the elders, the witnesses, and the sandal exchange
Analyze how Ruth's words and actions present her as a Gentile who takes refuge under the wings of Israel's God
Evaluate the ways Boaz as kinsman redeemer foreshadows Christ as the Redeemer of God's people and where the comparison has limits
Evaluate how the book of Ruth displays God's providence working through ordinary events and human choices while rarely describing God acting directly
Defend from Ruth and related Scripture the Reformed teaching that God's saving purpose includes people from the nations
Synthesize the book of Ruth as a bridge from the period of the judges to the Davidic monarchy using its setting and closing genealogy

BIB.9.2.1.t: Retell how Daniel kept praying to God and how God shut the lions' mouths to protect him
Name Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and recall that they would not bow down to the king's golden statue
Recall from Daniel that God rules over all kings and kingdoms
Describe how Daniel and his friends refused the king's food and how God blessed them with health and wisdom
Summarize the story of the fiery furnace, including the fourth figure in the fire and the king's response
Retell the story of the writing on the wall and explain what the words meant for King Belshazzar
Explain Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the statue made of metals, including the four kingdoms and the stone that becomes God's everlasting kingdom
Describe the historical setting of Daniel, including the exile of Judah to Babylon and Daniel's service under Babylonian and Persian kings
Compare the pride and humbling of Nebuchadnezzar with Daniel's humility in giving credit to God
Explain how Daniel and his friends served faithfully in a pagan government while refusing to compromise their worship of God
Identify the structure of Daniel as court narratives followed by visions and note the shift between Hebrew and Aramaic
Analyze how the theme of God's sovereignty over the nations is developed across the narratives of Daniel
Explain how Jesus identified himself with the Son of Man of Daniel 7 and how this reveals his kingship
Interpret the vision of the four beasts and the Ancient of Days and compare it with the statue dream of chapter 2
Explain the main features of apocalyptic literature using examples from the visions of Daniel
Analyze Daniel's prayer of confession as a response to God's covenant promises spoken through Jeremiah
Explain how Daniel 12 teaches the bodily resurrection and final judgment and connect it to the teaching of Jesus
Interpret the vision of the ram and the goat using the angel's explanation and identify the historical kingdoms it describes
Construct a timeline of the seventy weeks prophecy that compares the traditional messianic reading with other major interpretations
Analyze the portrayal of heavenly conflict and the role of angels such as Michael in Daniel's final vision
Evaluate arguments for a sixth-century and a Maccabean dating of Daniel, including the role of assumptions about predictive prophecy
Trace how the book of Revelation draws on the imagery of Daniel's visions
Create a study on living faithfully as exiles that draws on Daniel and connects it to New Testament teaching for believers

BIB.9.2.2.t: Identify Ezekiel as a prophet whom God sent to speak His words to His people
Retell the story of the valley of dry bones that came to life when Ezekiel spoke God's word and God gave them breath
Describe how God promises in Ezekiel to be the Shepherd who searches for and cares for His lost sheep
Describe the main features of Ezekiel's opening vision of God's glory, including the living creatures, the wheels, and the throne
Explain why Ezekiel acted out some of his messages with sign-acts such as the brick siege model and the exile's baggage
Explain from Ezekiel's temple visions that God's glory departed from the temple because of the people's idolatry
Locate Ezekiel's ministry among the exiles in Babylon in relation to the deportation of 597 BC and the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC
Compare the heart of stone with the heart of flesh and explain what God promises to do in giving a new heart and His Spirit
Outline the three-part structure of Ezekiel as oracles of judgment on Judah, oracles against the nations, and messages of restoration
Explain the role of the watchman and the responsibility it placed on Ezekiel to warn the people
Explain what the title son of man emphasizes about Ezekiel when God addresses him by it
Analyze how the repeated phrase then they will know that I am the LORD expresses the purpose of both God's judgments and His restorations in Ezekiel
Explain how the oracle against Israel's false shepherds and the promise of David as one shepherd point forward to Christ the Good Shepherd
Explain how the sign of the two sticks promises the reunion of Israel and Judah under one king in an everlasting covenant of peace
Interpret the allegory of the unfaithful wife as a picture of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness and God's everlasting covenant grace
Explain how Ezekiel 18 corrects the proverb of the sour grapes by teaching individual accountability for sin and God's call to repent and live
Explain why God says He restores Israel for the sake of His holy name rather than for their own merit
Analyze the lament over the king of Tyre and evaluate interpretations that connect its imagery to the fall of Satan
Construct a diagram tracing the departure of God's glory from the temple and its return in the restoration vision
Defend the Reformed teaching that regeneration is a sovereign work of the Spirit using the new heart promise and the vision of the dry bones
Evaluate the apocalyptic imagery of the Gog and Magog oracles and compare major interpretive approaches to them
Evaluate literal and typological readings of Ezekiel's new temple vision and synthesize its river and its closing name with their fulfillment in the New Testament

BIB.9.2.3.t: Identify Isaiah as a prophet who saw the Lord seated on a high throne while angels called out that God is holy
Recall that Isaiah promised a child called Immanuel, meaning God with us, and that Matthew says this promise came true in Jesus
Recall that Isaiah said the Servant would be wounded for our transgressions and that Christians read this as a promise of Jesus' death for sinners
Retell the story of Isaiah's call, including his confession of sin, the burning coal touching his lips, and his answer Here am I, send me
Name the titles Isaiah gives the promised child, such as Wonderful Counselor and Prince of Peace, and explain what each tells about the coming King
Describe Isaiah's picture of the peaceful kingdom of the Branch from Jesse, where the wolf lives with the lamb
Explain how Isaiah 53 describes the Servant suffering in the place of others and how the Reformed tradition connects this to Christ's sacrificial death
Explain Isaiah's message of comfort to God's people and how the Gospels identify John the Baptist as the voice crying in the wilderness
Compare Isaiah's mockery of handmade idols with his portrait of the Lord as the incomparable Creator
Locate passages from Isaiah quoted in the New Testament and explain how Jesus and the apostles use them
Explain Isaiah's charge against empty worship and his call for repentance and justice for the oppressed
Analyze the structure of Isaiah by comparing the emphasis on judgment in chapters 1 to 39 with the emphasis on comfort and restoration in chapters 40 to 66
Analyze how Isaiah's vision of God's holiness exposes human sin and how the cleansing of his lips points to atonement provided by God
Interpret a messianic prophecy such as the Immanuel sign by explaining its meaning for Ahaz in its own time and its fulfillment in Christ
Explain the historical setting of Isaiah's ministry, including the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, Sennacherib's invasion, Hezekiah's prayer, and the prediction of exile to Babylon
Analyze the Servant Songs to distinguish where the servant is the nation of Israel and where the Servant is an individual who redeems Israel
Explain Isaiah's call for Judah to trust the Lord rather than seek security in alliances with Egypt
Analyze Isaiah's teaching on God's sovereignty over the nations, including Assyria as the rod of his anger and Cyrus as his anointed instrument
Construct a written account of Isaiah's theology of the Holy One of Israel by tracing the title through both halves of the book
Analyze Isaiah's vision of the nations coming to worship the Lord and how the apostles apply it to the mission to the Gentiles
Evaluate critical theories that divide Isaiah among multiple authors by weighing them against evidence for the book's unity, including New Testament attribution and the Great Isaiah Scroll
Synthesize Isaiah's vision of the new heavens and new earth with its fulfillment in Revelation in a written or presented account of biblical hope

BIB.9.2.4.t: Identify Jeremiah as a prophet God sent to speak his words to Judah, known as the weeping prophet because he grieved over his people
Retell the story of Jeremiah at the potter's house and tell what it shows about God as the potter and his people as the clay
Recount how God called Jeremiah when he was young and promised to be with him even though Jeremiah felt unable to speak
Describe Jeremiah's message calling the people of Judah to turn away from idols and return to the Lord
Retell how Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern for preaching God's word and was rescued by Ebed-melech
Summarize the account of King Jehoiakim burning Jeremiah's scroll and explain how God's word was written again
Place Jeremiah's ministry on a timeline of Judah's last kings from Josiah to Zedekiah and the rise of Babylon
Explain God's promise of a new covenant in which he writes his law on his people's hearts and forgives their sin
Explain the instructions in Jeremiah's letter to the exiles to build houses, seek the welfare of Babylon, and wait seventy years for God's restoration
Compare Jeremiah's message with that of the false prophets who promised peace, using the conflict with Hananiah as an example
Describe Jeremiah's purchase of a field during the siege and explain how it signaled God's promise to restore the land
Explain how Jeremiah announced judgment on Judah as the consequence of breaking the covenant made at Sinai
Analyze Jeremiah's acted parables, such as the linen belt, the broken flask, and the yoke, to explain the message each sign conveyed
Interpret the Temple Sermon as a warning against trusting in the temple and its rituals while disobeying God
Explain the historical events of Babylon's siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC using the accounts in Jeremiah and Kings
Explain the promise of a righteous Branch from David's line called The LORD Is Our Righteousness and identify its fulfillment in Christ
Explain Jeremiah's diagnosis of the deceitful human heart and relate it to the Reformed doctrine of the corruption of human nature
Analyze Jeremiah's confessions as laments in which the prophet brings his complaints against his persecutors and his calling before God
Describe the arrangement of the book of Jeremiah, including its non-chronological ordering, its narrative sections, and its oracles against the nations
Trace how the New Testament applies Jeremiah's new covenant promise to the ministry, death, and priesthood of Christ
Compare Jeremiah's rejection and suffering with the suffering of Jesus, including Jesus' use of Jeremiah's words in cleansing the temple
Explain how Jeremiah presents God as sovereign over the nations, using Babylon as his servant and then judging Babylon in turn
Evaluate the case Jeremiah makes for the justice of God's judgment on Judah, citing the covenant charges brought against the nation
Evaluate differing Christian interpretations of the new covenant in Jeremiah 31 in light of the Reformed understanding of one covenant of grace under different administrations
Produce a study of prophetic conflict in Jeremiah's day that applies the biblical tests for true and false prophecy

BIB.9.3.10.t: Identify Obadiah as the shortest book in the Old Testament and as a prophet who received a message from God
Retell that Jacob and Esau were twin brothers whose families grew into the nations of Israel and Edom
Describe what Edom did wrong when Jerusalem was attacked and explain from Scripture why God's people should not be glad when others are hurt
Identify God's promise in Obadiah to rescue His people on Mount Zion and to rule as King
Summarize the conflict between Jacob and Esau in Genesis, including the birthright, the stolen blessing, and their later meeting
Explain how Edom's pride in its high rocky home deceived it and how Scripture teaches that God brings the proud low
Locate Edom on a map of the ancient Near East and describe how its mountainous terrain made it feel secure
Outline the structure of Obadiah as judgment on Edom, the day of the Lord on the nations, and the restoration of Zion
Explain why Obadiah treats Edom's violence as a sin against a brother using God's earlier instruction about Edom
Analyze the historical setting of Obadiah and weigh the evidence for linking it to the Babylonian fall of Jerusalem
Connect the judgment of Edom to the deliverance and holiness promised for Mount Zion and the house of Jacob
Interpret the announcement that the day of the Lord is near upon all the nations, including the image of drinking the cup of judgment
Explain the principle that as you have done it shall be done to you and compare it with other biblical statements of reciprocal justice
Construct a timeline of relations between Israel and Edom from the patriarchs through the exile using biblical texts
Distinguish God's just judgment of Edom from personal revenge using the New Testament teaching on vengeance and love of enemies
Compare Obadiah's oracle with the parallel oracle against Edom in Jeremiah and identify shared wording and distinct emphases
Analyze the escalating sins of Edom in Obadiah from standing aloof to gloating, looting, and handing over survivors as failures to love one's neighbor
Defend the Reformed teaching that God justly governs and judges the nations using Obadiah and related texts
Explain how the promise that the kingdom shall be the Lord's is developed through the prophets and fulfilled in Christ's reign, including the gathering of the nations

BIB.9.3.11.t: Identify Zechariah as a prophet God sent to encourage his people while they rebuilt the temple
Retell Zechariah's promise that Jerusalem's King would come riding on a donkey and match it to Jesus entering Jerusalem
Recite Zechariah 4:6 and explain that God's work is accomplished by his Spirit rather than by human strength
Describe God's call through Zechariah for his people to return to him and his promise to return to them
Describe how the LORD removed Joshua the high priest's filthy garments and clothed him in clean ones as a picture of God taking away sin
Explain the vision of the lampstand and two olive trees and its message to Zerubbabel about not despising the day of small things
Summarize Zechariah's answer to the question about fasting by listing the justice, mercy, and truthfulness God required of his people
Locate Zechariah in the history of the return from exile and explain how he and Haggai together urged the rebuilding of the temple
Compare the worthless shepherds of Zechariah 11 with the Good Shepherd Jesus describes in John 10
Summarize each of the eight night visions and state the message of comfort or warning each gave the returned exiles
Explain Zechariah's promise that many nations would join themselves to the LORD and connect it to the spread of the gospel to the Gentiles
Analyze how the cleansing of Joshua in Zechariah 3 illustrates the Reformed doctrine of justification by imputed righteousness
Explain how the Branch of Zechariah 3 and 6 unites the offices of priest and king and how the church has read this as fulfilled in Christ
Interpret the symbols of the night visions using the explanations the angel gives within the text as a method for reading apocalyptic literature
Trace the New Testament quotations of Zechariah in the Gospel passion narratives and explain what each shows about Jesus
Analyze how the prophecy of mourning for the pierced one and the fountain opened for cleansing portrays repentance and forgiveness
Evaluate proposed explanations for Matthew's attribution of the thirty pieces of silver prophecy to Jeremiah
Evaluate how the Book of Revelation takes up and transforms Zechariah's imagery of horses, lampstands, olive trees, and measuring
Evaluate arguments about the unity and authorship of Zechariah 1-8 and 9-14 and defend the traditional view of the book as one prophetic work
Compare major interpretive approaches to the Day of the LORD in Zechariah 14 and explain the significance of Holiness to the LORD extending to all of life
Compose an essay synthesizing how Zechariah's portraits of the lowly King, the stricken Shepherd, and the pierced One anticipate the suffering and reign of the Messiah

BIB.9.3.12.t: Identify Zephaniah as a prophet God sent to speak His message to His people
Recall that Zephaniah says the Lord rejoices over His people with singing
Name the day of the Lord as the day Zephaniah warned God would come to judge sin
Retell the movement of Zephaniah from a warning of judgment on the whole earth to a promise of joy for God's people
Describe the remnant in Zephaniah as the humble people who take refuge in the name of the Lord
Compare the day of the Lord as Zephaniah describes it for the proud with the day of rejoicing promised to the remnant
Locate on a map the nations named in Zephaniah's oracles and explain why the prophet announces judgment on them as well as on Judah
Recite Zephaniah 3:17 and explain what each of its phrases teaches about the Lord's presence and delight among His people
Explain the idolatry and complacency Zephaniah condemned in Judah
Analyze how the judgment language of Zephaniah 1 reverses the order of creation in Genesis 1
Interpret the call to seek the Lord, righteousness, and humility as a summons to repentance before the day of the Lord
Relate the setting of Zephaniah to the reign and reforms of King Josiah
Explain the image of the Lord as a mighty warrior who saves and dwells in the midst of His people
Analyze how the promise of purified speech for the peoples reverses the scattering at Babel
Analyze the charges Zephaniah brings against Jerusalem's officials, judges, prophets, and priests
Trace the day of the Lord theme from Zephaniah to the New Testament teaching on Christ's return and final judgment
Evaluate the syncretism condemned in Zephaniah in light of the first commandment
Defend from Zephaniah the Reformed teaching that God's judgment on sin and His restoration of a purified people together display His justice and mercy
Write an essay that synthesizes the restoration promises of Zephaniah 3 with their New Testament fulfillment in Christ and the new creation

BIB.9.3.1.t: Identify Amos as a shepherd and fig farmer whom God called to carry his message to Israel
Retell that God sent Amos to warn people who were cheating the poor and treating them unkindly
Explain that God sees whether people treat others fairly, using the example of sellers who cheated with dishonest scales
Locate Tekoa in Judah and Bethel in Israel on a map of the divided kingdom and explain that Amos traveled from the south to preach in the north
Summarize Amos's warnings to the wealthy who lived in luxury while they oppressed the needy
Explain the meaning of let justice roll down like waters by comparing it to a stream that never runs dry
Explain what the call to seek the LORD and live required of Israel according to Amos
Retell the conflict between Amos and Amaziah the priest at Bethel and explain why Amos said his authority came from God's call
Compare Israel's festivals, offerings, and songs with the obedience God required of his people in Amos
Describe the five visions of Amos and state what each one reveals about God's dealings with Israel
Describe practical ways of honest dealing and care for the needy that obey the commands Amos says Israel broke
Explain how the hymns in Amos present the LORD as the Creator who rules nature and history and therefore has the right to judge
Analyze how the repeated pattern for three transgressions and for four in the oracles against the nations builds toward the judgment on Judah and Israel
Interpret the vision of the plumb line as an image of God measuring Israel against his own standard
Explain how Amos teaches that Israel's special relationship with God brought greater accountability rather than protection from judgment
Explain the famine of hearing the words of the LORD as a judgment on a people who silenced God's prophets
Explain Amos's warning that the Day of the LORD would bring darkness rather than light to those who presumed upon it
Analyze why Amos treats injustice toward neighbors as making Israel's worship unacceptable, relating his message to love of God and love of neighbor in the law
Identify literary forms in Amos such as the funeral lament, woe oracle, ironic call to worship, and vision report and explain how each shapes the message
Explain from Amos 3 why a true prophet must speak when the LORD speaks and how God reveals his purposes through his prophets
Analyze the refrain yet you did not return to me as a record of God's disciplines meant to call Israel to repentance
Relate Amos's prophecies of exile to their fulfillment in Assyria's conquest of the northern kingdom
Analyze how the Reformed tradition reads the statements that the LORD relented in Amos alongside its confession that God is unchanging
Interpret the promise to raise up the fallen booth of David and explain how James applies it to the inclusion of the Gentiles
Evaluate how Israel's economic prosperity under Jeroboam II masked moral and spiritual decline according to Amos
Evaluate how Amos's indictment of corrupt courts and bribery applies to the pursuit of righteousness in public life today
Synthesize Amos's teaching on courts, markets, and the poor into an account of the duties and sins the Reformed tradition confesses under the eighth commandment
Compose an essay on the danger of religious hypocrisy that draws evidence from Amos and from the New Testament

BIB.9.3.2.t: Identify Habakkuk as a prophet who brought his questions to God in prayer
Retell how Habakkuk stood at his watchpost to wait for God's answer
Recite the words of Habakkuk 2:4 that the righteous shall live by his faith
Describe what Habakkuk said he would do even if the fig tree, vines, fields, and flocks all failed
Summarize Habakkuk's first complaint about violence and injustice going unpunished in Judah
Explain God's first answer that he was raising up the Chaldeans to bring judgment on Judah
Summarize Habakkuk's second complaint asking how a holy God could use a nation more wicked than Judah
Explain God's command to write the vision plainly and wait for it because it will surely come at the appointed time
Compare Habakkuk's honest questions addressed to God with Israel's grumbling against God in the wilderness
Identify how Habakkuk's prayer recalls God's past saving acts such as the Exodus and asks him in wrath to remember mercy
Outline the book of Habakkuk as a dialogue with God, a series of woes, and a closing prayer-psalm
Explain how Habakkuk 3:17-19 grounds praise in God's character and salvation rather than in outward circumstances
Analyze how the dialogue between the prophet and God moves Habakkuk from complaint to confident trust
Situate Habakkuk in the late seventh century BC as Babylon rose to power before invading Judah
Interpret Habakkuk 2:4 in context by contrasting the puffed-up soul of the proud with the righteous who live by faith
Explain the five woe oracles against the Chaldeans and identify the sin each one condemns
Explain how the promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord's glory and the call for silence before him frame the woes
Explain the Reformed doctrine of providence as Habakkuk shows God ordaining Babylon's rise while holding Babylon guilty for its sin
Construct a biblical response to the problem of evil drawing on God's answers to Habakkuk
Evaluate objections to God's sovereignty in using wicked nations by testing them against Habakkuk and related texts
Evaluate how Paul and Hebrews use Habakkuk 2:4 to teach justification by faith and persevering faith
Compose a prayer modeled on Habakkuk's pattern of honest lament, remembrance of God's works, and declared trust

BIB.9.3.3.t: Identify Haggai as a prophet God sent to His people after they came home from exile to tell them to rebuild the temple
Retell how the people built their own houses while God's house stayed in ruins
Recall the promise "I am with you" that God gave the builders through Haggai
Describe how Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people responded to Haggai's message by obeying and returning to work on the temple
Explain what Haggai meant when he told the people to "consider your ways"
Explain how the drought and poor harvests in Haggai show that God rules over rain, crops, and all creation
Explain why some of the people were discouraged when they compared the new temple with Solomon's temple and how God answered their discouragement
Explain from Haggai the tradition's teaching that God's Spirit stirs up and strengthens His people to do the work He gives them
Identify the four dated messages in Haggai and summarize the main point of each
Construct a timeline of the post-exilic period that places Haggai's messages among the events recorded in Ezra, including the return, the halted work, and the temple's completion
Analyze how Haggai connects the people's neglect and obedience with curse and blessing in light of the covenant warnings of Deuteronomy
Explain the priestly ruling about holy and unclean things in Haggai 2 and how Haggai applied it to the people's offerings
Interpret the promise that the latter glory of the temple will be greater than the former in light of Christ's coming as God's presence with His people
Analyze how Hebrews interprets Haggai's prophecy of the shaking of the heavens and the earth as pointing to an unshakable kingdom
Analyze Haggai's literary features, including its dated oracles and repeated calls to "consider" and "be strong", to show how they shape its message
Evaluate the messianic significance of the signet ring promise to Zerubbabel by comparing it with the judgment on Jehoiachin and its fulfillment in Christ the Son of David
Evaluate how the New Testament develops Haggai's temple theme into the teaching that the church is God's temple, as the Reformed tradition confesses about the visible church
Evaluate how Haggai's call to put God's house first addresses neglect of worship and the work of the church among God's people today
Create an expository outline of one of Haggai's messages that explains its historical setting, its main point, and its fulfillment in Christ

BIB.9.3.4.t: Identify Hosea as a prophet whom God told to marry Gomer and to keep loving her when she was unfaithful
Retell how Hosea bought Gomer back as a picture of God's love that keeps going for His people
Recall that God called His wandering people to return to Him and promised to heal them
Describe how Hosea pictures God caring for Israel like a parent teaching a little child to walk
Name Hosea's three children and tell what each name means
Explain how God promised to turn 'Not my people' into 'Children of the living God'
Identify Hosea as a prophet sent to the northern kingdom of Israel and locate it on a map of the divided kingdom
Explain why Hosea compares Israel's worship of idols to a wife leaving her husband
Identify the golden calves and foreign alliances in Hosea as ways Israel trusted something other than the Lord
Explain Hosea's charge that God's people were destroyed for lack of knowledge of Him
Explain the image of sowing the wind and reaping the whirlwind as Hosea's picture of the consequences of sin
Write a prayer of confession and return modeled on the words God gives Israel in Hosea 14
Outline the structure of Hosea as a marriage narrative followed by oracles of judgment and hope ending in a call to wisdom
Contrast the shallow repentance of Hosea 6 with the true return of Hosea 14 using the catechism's definition of repentance
Analyze how Hosea develops the marriage metaphor through accusation, discipline, and renewed betrothal
Explain how Jesus uses Hosea 6:6 to show that God desires steadfast love rather than empty ritual
Analyze how the promise of the Valley of Achor as a door of hope reverses the judgment of Joshua 7
Analyze how Hosea's redemption of Gomer foreshadows Christ redeeming His bride the church
Explain how the promise that Israel will seek David their king in the latter days points to the Messiah
Relate Hosea's warnings to the prosperity of Jeroboam II, the political instability that followed, and the fall of Samaria
Analyze how Matthew applies 'Out of Egypt I called my son' to Jesus as the true Son and true Israel
Explain the meaning of hesed in Hosea as God's steadfast covenant love and the loyalty He requires of His people
Analyze how Paul and Peter apply Hosea's reversal of 'Not my people' to Gentiles brought into the church
Analyze how Paul uses Hosea 13:14 to proclaim Christ's victory over death
Analyze how Hosea uses episodes from the life of Jacob to call Israel to repentance
Evaluate how Hosea 11:8-9 portrays God's compassion and holiness, interpreting its language in light of the Reformed confession that God is without passions
Evaluate major interpretations of Hosea's marriage as literal event or vision and the purpose of its shocking prophetic sign act
Synthesize Hosea's marriage message with New Testament bride imagery in a written or oral presentation

BIB.9.3.5.t: Retell how a huge swarm of locusts ate the crops of Judah and left the land empty
Recall that God told His people to tell their children and grandchildren what He had done
Identify God's call through Joel for His people to return to Him with all their heart
Recall that God promised to give back to His people the years the locusts had eaten
Describe God's promise to pour out His Spirit on all kinds of people, including sons and daughters, old and young, and servants
Summarize the movement of the book of Joel from disaster, to a call to repent, to promises of restoration and the Spirit
Write a short prayer asking God for help in a time of trouble, modeled on Joel's cry to the Lord
Explain what rend your hearts and not your garments means by contrasting outward signs of sorrow with true inward repentance
Identify the attributes of God named in Joel 2:13 and trace them back to God's self-description to Moses
Explain the Day of the Lord in Joel as a day of God's judgment that is also a day of rescue for those who call on His name
Compare the locust plague of Joel 1 with the invading army of Joel 2 and explain how Joel uses a present disaster to warn of a greater coming judgment
Analyze Joel 1 as a communal lament by identifying each group called to mourn and the reason given for their mourning
Explain the biblical basis for corporate fasting and solemn assembly as called for in Joel and as the Reformed tradition confesses it
Explain how Paul applies Joel 2:32 to teach that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord, Jew or Gentile, will be saved
Analyze how Peter interprets Joel 2:28-32 as fulfilled in the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost
Analyze the reasons Joel gives for God's judgment on the nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat
Contrast Joel's command to beat plowshares into swords with the reversed image in Isaiah and Micah and explain what each passage signals about the Day of the Lord
Evaluate proposals for the date of Joel using internal evidence such as the absence of a named king and the prominence of priests, elders, and the temple
Explain the Reformed reading of the Day of the Lord as begun at Pentecost and completed at Christ's return in final judgment

Evaluate how the Reformed tradition reads Joel's promises of restored land and God dwelling in Zion as fulfilled in Christ, His church, and the new creation, in comparison with readings that expect a separate future fulfillment for national Israel
Create a teaching outline that traces the pattern of judgment, repentance, and restoration in Joel through its fulfillment in Christ and the gift of the Spirit

BIB.9.3.6.t: Identify Jonah as the prophet God sent to Nineveh who was swallowed by a great fish
Name Nineveh as the great city God sent Jonah to and Tarshish as the place he tried to flee to
Retell in order the main events of Jonah's flight, rescue, preaching, and complaint
Describe how God directed the storm, the fish, the plant, and the worm to show that he rules over all creation
Explain from Jonah's flight that no one can escape God's presence
Describe how the pagan sailors came to fear and worship the LORD during the storm
Describe how the king and people of Nineveh responded to Jonah's message and how God spared the city
Explain why Jonah was angry at God's mercy using his own words in chapter 4
Compare God's compassion for Nineveh with Jonah's concern for the plant
Explain how God's concern for Nineveh relates to Jesus' command to love one's enemies
Connect Jonah's description of God in Jonah 4:2 to the LORD's self-revelation to Moses
Locate Jonah's ministry in the reign of Jeroboam II and describe Assyria's place as Israel's rising enemy
Analyze Jonah's prayer from the fish as a psalm of thanksgiving, noting its echoes of the Psalms and its climax that salvation belongs to the LORD
Interpret the sign of Jonah as Jesus applied it to his death, resurrection, and the judgment of his generation
Analyze how Jonah's conduct reflects Israel's calling to bless the nations and its failure to fulfill that calling
Analyze the irony in the narrative, including the prophet's repeated going down and the quick obedience of pagans contrasted with the prophet's resistance
Analyze how God's relenting from judgment on Nineveh fits with the Reformed confession of God's unchanging nature and decree
Use biblical and historical evidence of Assyrian cruelty to explain Jonah's reluctance to preach to Nineveh
Compare Jonah's mission to Nineveh with Peter's mission from Joppa to the Gentile Cornelius
Evaluate the purpose of the book ending with God's unanswered question to Jonah
Evaluate historical and parable readings of the book and articulate the Reformed tradition's case for its historicity
Construct an account tracing God's purpose to save people from the nations from Abraham through Jonah to the Great Commission

BIB.9.3.7.t: Identify Malachi as the last book of the Old Testament in the order of the English Bible
Recall that in Malachi God calls himself a Father and Master who deserves honor from his people
Retell how God told the people they were robbing him by holding back their tithes and offerings
Recall that God promised to send the prophet Elijah before the great day of the Lord
Summarize the main complaints God brings against the people and the questions they ask in reply
Explain how the Gospels identify John the Baptist as the messenger God promised to send ahead of the Lord
Describe the book of remembrance and what it shows about God's care for those who fear him
Compare the blemished sacrifices and careless attitude of the priests with the honoring worship God required
Explain the principle behind God's command about tithes and offerings and the promise attached to it
Place Malachi in its post-exilic setting by relating its concerns to the problems Nehemiah confronted
Explain the images of the refiner's fire and fuller's soap and what they teach about the Lord's coming to purify his people
Analyze the disputation pattern of statement, objection, and reply that structures the book
Connect the promise of the sun of righteousness rising with healing to the coming of Jesus Christ
Interpret the statement I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated in light of its covenant context and Paul's use of it
Explain Malachi's teaching on intermarriage with idolaters and on divorce as faithlessness to the covenant
Explain how Malachi's promise that God's name will be great among the nations anticipates worship of God by the Gentiles
Analyze the covenant with Levi and how the priests failed in their calling to teach true instruction
Explain how Malachi presents the day of the Lord as both judgment on the wicked and deliverance for the righteous
Construct a profile of the spiritual complacency of the post-exilic community using evidence from the text
Evaluate the claim that the promised Elijah was fulfilled in John the Baptist using Jesus' own words
Defend the Reformed doctrine of God's immutability from Malachi's declaration I the Lord do not change
Synthesize how Malachi's closing call to remember the law of Moses and await Elijah links the Old Testament canon to the opening of the New Testament

BIB.9.3.8.t: Identify Micah as a prophet who spoke God's words to God's people
Name Bethlehem as the small town Micah said a ruler would come from and tell that Jesus was born there
Recite Micah 6:8 and name the three things it says the LORD requires
Describe Micah's picture of God throwing sins into the depths of the sea and tell what it shows about God's forgiveness
Give examples of acting justly, loving kindness, and walking humbly with God in home and school life based on Micah 6:8
Describe the wrongs Micah condemned, including seizing fields and houses, taking bribes, and prophesying for money
Explain how the chief priests and scribes used Micah 5:2 in Matthew 2 to point to the birthplace of the promised ruler
Compare the corrupt rulers of Micah 3 with the shepherd ruler promised in Micah 5
Locate Micah in history as a prophet from Moresheth during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah and a contemporary of Isaiah before the fall of Samaria
Explain why Micah 6:6-7 sets aside lavish sacrifices and how Micah 6:8 summarizes the obedience God has already made known
Explain how Micah's resolve to watch and wait for the LORD in Micah 7:7-9 expresses hope in God's justice in a time of judgment
Analyze the courtroom lawsuit of Micah 6:1-5 by identifying the witnesses, the charge, and the saving acts God recounts as evidence
Outline the structure of Micah as three cycles that each open with a call to hear and move from judgment to hope
Interpret the prophecy of the mountain of the LORD in Micah 4:1-5 and compare it with the parallel in Isaiah 2:2-4
Explain Micah's promise of a gathered remnant and trace how it turns judgment toward restoration
Contrast Micah's Spirit-given boldness with the false prophets of his day using the biblical tests of a true prophet
Analyze how Jeremiah 26 recalls Micah's warning against Zion and Hezekiah's response to show how prophetic warnings call for repentance
Evaluate the claim that Micah 6:8 teaches salvation by good deeds in light of God's prior redemption in Micah 6:4-5 and the tradition's teaching on good works as the fruit of faith
Evaluate interpretations of Micah 5:2-5 and defend the tradition's reading of the ruler whose origin is from of old as the eternal Son who became the shepherd-king
Defend the consistency of God's justice and mercy in Micah using his judgments and his pardon together with their fulfillment at the cross
Compose an exposition of Micah 7:18-20 that explains the wordplay on Micah's name, the pardon of sin, and God's oath to Abraham and Jacob, and connects them to forgiveness in Christ

BIB.9.3.9.t: Identify Nahum as a prophet God sent with a message about the city of Nineveh
Recite Nahum 1:7 and tell what it says God is like for those who trust Him
Locate Nineveh on a map as the capital of Assyria and recognize it as the same city Jonah preached to
Retell in your own words that the LORD is slow to anger and great in power and will not leave the guilty unpunished
Summarize the main message of each of Nahum's three chapters
Explain that the name Nahum means comfort and describe how his message offered comfort to Judah
Describe how Nineveh turned back to wickedness after repenting in Jonah's day by naming the sins listed in Nahum 3
Identify the images from nature in Nahum 1:3-6 and explain what each shows about God's power
Compare the picture of God as a stronghold with the picture of God as an overflowing flood and explain how the same God is refuge to some and judgment to others
Explain the Assyrian empire's conquest of Israel and threat to Judah as the historical background to Nahum
Explain from Nahum and Romans why vengeance belongs to God and how the Reformed tradition teaches believers to respond to wrongs without seeking revenge
Analyze the poetic devices Nahum uses to portray the siege of Nineveh, such as vivid imagery, rapid commands, the lion metaphor, and the taunt
Trace how Nahum 1:3 echoes God's self-description in Exodus 34:6-7 and explain which part of that description Nahum emphasizes
Connect Nahum's description of Nineveh's fall to historical records of its destruction in 612 BC such as the Babylonian Chronicle
Explain how Nahum displays the Reformed doctrine of God's providential rule over the rise and fall of nations
Explain why God's patience toward the unrepentant eventually ends, using Nahum and Paul's teaching on stored-up wrath
Analyze the comparison between Nineveh and Thebes in Nahum 3:8-10 and explain the argument it makes against Nineveh's pride
Explain how scholars identify a partial alphabetic acrostic in Nahum 1:2-8 and how its structure frames the poem about God's character
Compare Jonah and Nahum to show how both books reveal the same God's mercy and justice toward Nineveh
Trace the use of Nahum 1:15 in Isaiah 52:7 and Romans 10:15 and explain how the announcement of deliverance points forward to the gospel
Evaluate objections to the violent imagery of Nahum and defend the Reformed teaching that God's wrath against cruelty expresses His justice
Write an explanation of how Nahum's message of judgment on oppressors brings comfort to God's people and anticipates the final judgment

BIB.9.4.1.t: Identify Moses as the leader who spoke God's words to Israel just before they entered the promised land
Recite the command to love the LORD your God with all your heart, soul, and might
Identify Joshua as the leader God chose to bring Israel into the land after Moses
Retell how God told Israel's parents to talk about his words at home, on the road, at bedtime, and in the morning
Explain what the Shema teaches about God being the one and only LORD
Explain why Moses repeated the Ten Commandments to a new generation and how this connects to the name Deuteronomy, meaning second law
Explain from Deuteronomy that God chose Israel because of his own love and promise and not because of their size or righteousness
Describe the laws in Deuteronomy that protect widows, orphans, sojourners, and the poor and explain how they reflect God's own character
Compare the covenant blessings promised for obedience with the curses warned for disobedience
Explain how Jesus answered each of Satan's temptations by quoting Deuteronomy
Outline Deuteronomy as a series of speeches by Moses using the headings that open each section
Explain the call to choose life in its setting of covenant renewal on the plains of Moab
Explain why Moses died on Mount Nebo outside the land and what the closing epitaph says about his unique role
Explain the promise of a prophet like Moses and how the New Testament identifies its fulfillment in Christ
Analyze the law of the king and use it to evaluate Solomon's reign
Explain the command to worship at the place the LORD will choose and trace how it points to the temple and to Jesus' teaching on true worship
Analyze the Song of Moses as a witness that rehearses God's faithfulness and Israel's coming unfaithfulness
Analyze how Deuteronomy follows the pattern of ancient Near Eastern suzerain-vassal treaties and what that pattern shows about God's covenant with Israel
Explain how the Reformed tradition uses Deuteronomy's commands not to add to or take from God's word to support the sufficiency of Scripture
Trace the theme of the heart in Deuteronomy from the command to circumcise one's heart to the promise that God himself will do it
Analyze how Deuteronomy's warnings of exile and promises of return anticipate the later history of Israel
Evaluate the Deuteronomistic History hypothesis and critical dating theories against the book's own claims about Moses writing the law
Compose an essay tracing how the Prophets, Jesus, and Paul draw on Deuteronomy and arguing for its place in the theology of the whole canon

BIB.9.4.2.t: Identify Exodus as the book of the Bible that tells how God brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt
Retell how God protected baby Moses in a basket on the Nile River
Name Moses as the leader God called at the burning bush to bring Israel out of Egypt
Recall how God parted the Red Sea so Israel could cross on dry ground
Describe how God provided manna, quail, and water for Israel in the wilderness before Sinai
Recite the Ten Commandments in order as God gave them at Mount Sinai
Summarize the ten plagues and explain how they showed God's power over Pharaoh and the gods of Egypt
Explain the meaning of the word exodus as a going out and show how the title fits the book
Explain what God commanded Israel to do at the first Passover and why the blood on the doorposts spared their firstborn
Explain how God's covenant promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are the reason Exodus gives for the rescue from Egypt
Explain why the Ten Commandments begin by recalling God's rescue from Egypt before giving any command
Explain how the Song of the Sea praises the LORD as warrior and king after the crossing
Explain how the golden calf account shows Israel's idolatry, Moses' intercession, and God's mercy in renewing the covenant
Explain the terms of the Sinai covenant, including Israel's calling to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation and the ratifying blood ceremony
Analyze the structure of Exodus in three movements of deliverance from Egypt, covenant at Sinai, and the building of the tabernacle
Interpret the divine name revealed at the burning bush and explain what it teaches about God's self-existence and covenant faithfulness
Analyze how the New Testament presents Christ as the fulfillment of the Passover lamb
Explain the purpose of the tabernacle as God's dwelling among his people and how its layout and furnishings expressed his holiness
Analyze how Exodus describes the hardening of Pharaoh's heart as both Pharaoh's own act and God's judicial act
Construct a map of the proposed routes of the Exodus and explain the textual and geographical clues behind each
Analyze how New Testament writers use tabernacle imagery to describe the person and work of Christ
Compare the laws of the Book of the Covenant with ancient Near Eastern law codes such as the Code of Hammurabi
Evaluate the biblical and archaeological arguments for the early and late dates of the Exodus
Evaluate minimalist claims against the historicity of the Exodus using textual and archaeological evidence
Compose an essay tracing how later Scripture uses the Exodus as a pattern of redemption for the return from exile and the work of Christ

BIB.9.4.3.t: Identify Genesis as the first book of the Bible and the book that tells how the world began
Recall that God made everything out of nothing and called what he made good
Retell in order what God made on each of the six days of creation and his rest on the seventh day
Name Adam and Eve as the first man and woman and explain that God made them in his image
