Retell the account of Adam and Eve's disobedience in the garden and the consequences God announced
Retell the account of Noah, the ark, and the flood, including God's rainbow promise
Describe how sin spread after the fall through the accounts of Cain and Abel and the tower of Babel
Summarize the main events in the lives of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph
Describe the work God gave humans in the garden and the purpose of the seventh day rest
Explain the two main sections of Genesis, the primeval history of chapters 1 to 11 and the patriarchal history of chapters 12 to 50
Explain the promises God made to Abraham of land, descendants, and blessing to all nations
Explain what Genesis 2 teaches about marriage as God's design for one man and one woman
Compare the condition of humanity at creation with its condition after the fall
Explain how Abraham was counted righteous by believing God's promise and how the New Testament uses this text
Explain how the beginnings recorded in Genesis lay the foundation for themes developed in the rest of the Bible
Interpret the testing of Abraham with Isaac in light of its New Testament interpretation
Analyze how the repeated toledot heading, these are the generations of, organizes the book of Genesis
Explain the significance of the Abrahamic covenant and its sign of circumcision as the Reformed tradition understands the covenant of grace
Trace the promise of the seed of the woman through the family lines of Genesis to the promised ruler from Judah
Compare the covenant God made with Noah to the covenant he made with Abraham
Explain the Reformed doctrine of election as illustrated in God's choice of Jacob over Esau
Explain the theological significance of the image of God in Genesis for human dignity
Analyze how Genesis portrays the patriarchs as flawed people through whom God keeps his promises
Contrast the theology of Genesis 1 to 11 with ancient Near Eastern creation and flood accounts
Evaluate arguments for and against Mosaic authorship of Genesis, including the Documentary Hypothesis
Explain how Genesis teaches the Reformed doctrine of original sin and its transmission from Adam to all humanity
Research the cultural background of patriarchal customs and explain how it illuminates passages in Genesis
Evaluate major interpretive views of the creation days in Genesis 1, including the literal six day view and the framework view, using principles of interpreting Scripture by Scripture
Synthesize the theme of God's providence in the Joseph narrative into a written argument drawing on the text and the confessions

BIB.9.4.4.t: Identify a command God gave and a promise God made in a Bible story from the books of Moses
Recall that God rescued Israel from Egypt before he gave them the Ten Commandments
State that no one except Jesus keeps all of God's commands perfectly
Name Jesus as the one who obeyed God's law perfectly in the place of his people
Retell God's first promise of a Savior after Adam and Eve disobeyed his command
Describe how God forgave and restored Israel after they broke his law with the golden calf
Explain how God's law works like a mirror that shows people their sin
Summarize the whole law in the two great commandments taken from Deuteronomy and Leviticus
Explain how the animal sacrifices pointed to God providing a substitute to bear the penalty for sin
Explain from the story of Abraham that God counted him righteous because he believed God's promise
Interpret the bronze serpent as a picture of salvation that comes by looking in faith to what God provides
Compare trying to earn God's favor by obedience with trusting God's promise, using God's words to Israel about why he chose them
Explain why the Reformed tradition teaches that the law guides the grateful life of the redeemed and is not a way to earn salvation
Distinguish the moral, ceremonial, and civil laws of the Pentateuch using examples of each
Analyze the three uses of the law as the Reformed tradition confesses them, showing how the law convicts, restrains, and guides
Interpret Paul's description of the law as a guardian that held God's people until Christ came
Trace how Deuteronomy anticipates Israel's failure to keep the law and promises a circumcised heart fulfilled in the New Covenant
Explain how Paul uses texts from Leviticus and Deuteronomy to show that the law demands perfect obedience and pronounces a curse that Christ bore
Explain how the Pentateuch administers the covenant of grace through promises, sacrifices, and types that foreshadow Christ
Explain the relationship between the covenant of works with Adam and the covenant of grace announced after the fall
Construct a law and gospel reading of a Pentateuch passage that distinguishes its commands from its promises and shows how each points to Christ
Compare the Reformed and Lutheran accounts of law and gospel, especially their treatment of the law's use in the believer's life
Evaluate the errors of legalism and antinomianism using the Pentateuch and Paul's teaching on the law
Defend the Reformed position that believers in both Testaments are saved by grace through faith in the one Mediator
Synthesize how the Torah as a whole bears witness to Christ through its commands, promises, and patterns

BIB.9.4.5.t: Identify Leviticus as the book where God teaches His people how to come near to Him because He is holy
Name Aaron and his sons as the priests God chose to serve Him at the tabernacle
Recall that God gave Israel rules about being clean so that they could live near Him
Explain from Leviticus that sin separates people from a holy God and that God provided sacrifices so sinners could be forgiven
Identify the five main offerings of Leviticus and state the basic purpose of each
Explain that holy means set apart for God and describe how Israel was to be set apart from the nations
Retell the ordination of the priests and the judgment on Nadab and Abihu and explain what it shows about approaching God His way
Outline the major sections of Leviticus from the offerings through the holiness laws
Compare clean and unclean animals and distinguish ritual uncleanness from moral sin
Explain the laws for skin disease and purification and connect them to Jesus cleansing a leper
Describe the Sabbath year and the Year of Jubilee and explain how they taught that the land belonged to God
Categorize the appointed feasts of Leviticus 23 by their timing and what each commemorated
Explain the neighbor-love commands of Leviticus 19 and show how Jesus uses them to summarize the law
Analyze the sequence of the Day of Atonement ceremony and the role of the high priest in it
Interpret the command to be holy as God is holy in Leviticus and in its New Testament use
Connect the food laws to Israel's separation from the nations and explain why the New Testament sets them aside
Explain how the two goats of the Day of Atonement together picture both payment for sin and its removal
Summarize the covenant blessings and curses of Leviticus 26 and explain God's promise to remember His covenant
Construct an explanation of substitutionary atonement from the laying on of hands and the shedding of blood in Leviticus
Evaluate how the laws of Leviticus apply to New Testament believers using the Reformed distinction of moral, ceremonial, and judicial law
Defend the Reformed teaching that atonement requires the shedding of blood
Synthesize the priesthood, sacrifices, and Day of Atonement of Leviticus with their fulfillment in Christ as taught in Hebrews

BIB.9.4.6.t: Identify Numbers as the book that tells how God led Israel through the wilderness from Mount Sinai toward the promised land
Recall that God led Israel through the wilderness with a cloud by day and fire by night
Recite the blessing God gave Aaron and his sons to speak over Israel
Retell how Joshua and Caleb trusted God's promise when the other spies were afraid
Describe how Israel complained about food in the wilderness and how God answered with manna and quail
Explain that the book of Numbers is named for the two times Israel's people were counted
Summarize the report of the twelve spies and Israel's refusal to enter the land at Kadesh
Retell the story of the bronze serpent and explain that the bitten people lived by looking to the remedy God provided
Explain why God sentenced Israel to forty years of wandering, one year for each day the land was spied out
Compare the faith of Joshua and Caleb with the unbelief of the ten spies and the people who followed them
Analyze the arrangement of the tribes and Levites around the tabernacle to explain what it showed about God dwelling in the midst of his people
Explain why Moses and Aaron were not permitted to enter the land after striking the rock at Meribah
Trace on a map Israel's route from Sinai to Kadesh and on to the plains of Moab
Describe the Nazirite vow and explain its purpose of setting a person apart to the Lord
Explain how Korah's rebellion and the budding of Aaron's staff show that God himself appointed the priesthood
Explain from Israel's grumbling in Numbers why the Reformed tradition teaches that discontent breaks the tenth commandment
Analyze the account of Balaam to explain how God turned an intended curse into a blessing on Israel
Explain how Numbers records the passing of the generation that left Egypt and the preparation of a new generation under Joshua to enter the land
Analyze the request of Zelophehad's daughters and the Lord's ruling to explain how each family's inheritance in the land was protected
Explain how the cities of refuge distinguished accidental killing from murder and protected the land from bloodguilt
Construct a timeline of the major events of Numbers from the census at Sinai to Israel's arrival on the plains of Moab
Analyze how the prophecy of a star from Jacob and a scepter from Israel points forward to a coming king
Evaluate how Jesus' use of the bronze serpent interprets Numbers 21 as a picture of salvation through faith in the lifted up Son of Man
Evaluate how the New Testament uses the wilderness generation of Numbers as a warning to the church against unbelief and idolatry
Create a written synthesis showing how the wilderness journey in Numbers serves as a type of the church's pilgrimage toward the rest God has promised

BIB.9.5.1.t: Identify from Ecclesiastes that God has made a time for everything, such as a time to laugh and a time to cry
Name everyday gifts that Ecclesiastes says come from the hand of God, such as food, drink, and work
Identify the Preacher as the speaker of Ecclesiastes, a son of David and king in Jerusalem
Describe examples from Ecclesiastes of things under the sun that do not last, such as wealth left to others and the passing of generations
Explain the Preacher's teaching that two are better than one using the pictures of the fallen friend and the threefold cord
Summarize the Preacher's search for satisfaction in wisdom, pleasure, and great works and what he concluded about each
Explain the meaning of the Hebrew word hebel, translated vanity or meaningless, as a vapor or breath that is fleeting and hard to grasp
Explain what Ecclesiastes means when it says God has made everything beautiful in its time and has put eternity into the human heart
Compare the Preacher's view of life under the sun with his descriptions of life received as a gift from God
Explain the book's conclusion to fear God and keep his commandments in light of God's coming judgment of every deed
Describe the Preacher's instructions for approaching God in worship, including guarding one's steps, listening, and keeping vows
Analyze how Ecclesiastes honestly portrays death and injustice, including oppression and the same end coming to the righteous and the wicked
Explain how Ecclesiastes teaches that God made humanity upright but that all have sinned, connecting it to the Reformed doctrine of the fall
Interpret the poem of aging as a figurative picture of old age and death that grounds the call to remember the Creator in youth
Analyze the Preacher's teaching that the love of money never satisfies and relate it to the Reformed teaching on contentment
Explain how Ecclesiastes presents God's sovereign providence and the limits of human wisdom to discover his work
Analyze the literary structure of Ecclesiastes, including the frame narrator, the recurring refrains, and its mix of reflection, poetry, and proverbs
Compare the Preacher's calls to enjoy life as God's gift with a self-centered pursuit of pleasure
Construct an apologetic argument from Ecclesiastes addressing the question of meaning in a world viewed without God
Analyze how the New Testament answers the futility of Ecclesiastes through creation's hope of redemption and labor that is not in vain in the Lord
Evaluate the arguments for Solomonic authorship and for a later sage writing in Solomon's voice
Evaluate competing interpretations of the Preacher as a skeptic or a faithful realist and defend the book's place in the canon
Compose an essay applying Ecclesiastes' teaching on work, joy, and mortality to a Christian understanding of vocation

BIB.9.5.2.t: Identify Job as a man who feared God and kept worshiping God after he lost his children and his belongings
Name God as the maker and ruler of all creatures, using examples from God's words to Job
Recite Job's words of worship that the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away and tell when Job spoke them
Summarize the opening story of Job, including Satan's accusation, Job's losses, and his sickness
Describe how Job's three friends first comforted him by coming to him and sitting with him in silence
Explain from the book of Job that suffering is not always punishment for a person's own sin
Explain how the New Testament uses Job as an example of steadfastness and of the Lord's compassion
Outline the structure of Job, distinguishing the prose prologue and epilogue from the poetic dialogues, Elihu's speeches, and God's speeches
Explain how the prologue shows that Satan can act only within the limits God sets
Interpret Job's confession that his Redeemer lives in its context and explain how the church has read it as hope of resurrection
Analyze the arguments of Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar to show how each assumes that suffering proves hidden sin
Explain the teaching of the wisdom poem in Job 28 that true wisdom is found with God and begins with the fear of the Lord
Interpret God's speeches from the whirlwind and Job's replies, explaining why God reveals his wisdom and power instead of giving Job the reason for his suffering
Explain why God says the friends did not speak rightly while Job did and how Job intercedes for them
Compare Job's honest lament and complaint to God with the cursing of God that Satan predicted and Job's wife urged
Explain the retribution principle and analyze how the book of Job and its epilogue challenge a mechanical reading of it
Evaluate the role of Elihu's speeches, weighing how they differ from the three friends and how they prepare for God's speeches
Explain how the Reformed doctrine of providence draws on Job to teach that God governs all things, including the afflictions of his people
Evaluate how the book of Job addresses the problem of evil and what questions it leaves unanswered
Synthesize how Job's longing for a mediator and his innocent suffering anticipate Christ as the righteous sufferer and intercessor

BIB.9.5.3.t: Identify Proverbs as a book in the Old Testament that gives wise sayings for everyday life
Recall that King Solomon asked God for wisdom and wrote many proverbs
Recall proverbs that teach children to listen to the instruction of their father and mother
Describe the difference between a wise person and a fool using examples from Proverbs
Explain what Proverbs means when it teaches that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom
Explain the difference between knowledge and wisdom as Proverbs presents them
Compare the sluggard with the ant to explain what Proverbs teaches about diligent work
Apply proverbs about speech and anger to everyday situations in class role plays or case studies
Classify two-line proverbs as synonymous, antithetic, or comparative parallelism
Outline the main collections of Proverbs using the headings that introduce each section
Analyze how chapters 1 to 9 alternate between a father's instruction to his son and the speeches of Woman Wisdom
Explain how Proverbs connects wisdom with the order God built into creation
Compare the invitations of Woman Wisdom with the warnings against the adulterous woman and Woman Folly
Analyze why proverbs are read as general observations of how life ordinarily works rather than unconditional promises
Explain how Proverbs teaches that the Lord governs human plans and their outcomes
Explain how New Testament writers quote and apply passages from Proverbs
Analyze how Proverbs ties wisdom to righteousness and to keeping God's law
Construct a topical study that traces a theme such as wealth, speech, or friendship across the collections of Proverbs
Compare the sayings of the wise in Proverbs with Ancient Near Eastern wisdom such as the Instruction of Amenemope
Evaluate interpretations of the personified Wisdom of Proverbs 8, including the church's reading in light of Christ as the wisdom of God
Analyze the acrostic poem of the excellent wife as a portrait of wisdom lived out that echoes Woman Wisdom
Evaluate how the teaching of Proverbs applies to contemporary moral questions when read alongside the rest of Scripture

BIB.9.5.4.t: Identify the Psalms as songs and prayers that God's people sang to the Lord
Recite Psalm 23:1 and tell one thing it says about God as a shepherd
Name David as the shepherd and king who wrote many of the psalms
Describe how the psalm writers prayed to God both in times of joy and in times of sorrow
Explain what Psalm 19 teaches about the heavens declaring the glory of God
Classify a psalm as praise, thanksgiving, or lament by pointing to words and features in the text
Explain the contrast between the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked in Psalm 1
Describe how a psalm title links the psalm to an event in David's life, such as Psalm 51 and David's sin with Bathsheba
Explain how Christians have used the Psalms as a pattern for their own prayers
Analyze a lament psalm by identifying its address to God, complaint, petition, statement of trust, and vow of praise
Compare Psalm 1 and Psalm 2 and explain how together they introduce the themes of the whole Psalter
Compose a written prayer in class that follows the structure of a praise, thanksgiving, or lament psalm
Explain what the images of God as rock, refuge, fortress, and shepherd teach about his character
Explain what Psalm 119 teaches about the word of God and describe its acrostic structure
Describe the five-book division of the Psalter, locate the doxology that closes each book, and explain the traditional comparison with the five books of Moses
Explain the setting of the Songs of Ascents as songs of pilgrimage to worship in Jerusalem
Analyze synonymous, antithetic, and synthetic parallelism in lines of Hebrew poetry
Summarize how the historical psalms retell Israel's story to teach the next generation God's faithfulness and Israel's failures
Explain what the penitential psalms teach about sin, confession, and God's forgiveness as the Reformed tradition confesses repentance
Interpret the Messianic psalms by tracing how the New Testament applies them to the suffering and reign of Christ
Explain the possible meanings of Selah and other musical terms in the superscriptions and why scholars remain uncertain about them
Compose an original psalm in a chosen genre that uses Hebrew parallelism and the genre's typical structure
Trace the movement of the Psalter from lament toward praise across its five books, ending in the closing Hallelujah psalms
Analyze how the Psalms bring the full range of human emotion before God and explain the Reformed teaching that they model honest prayer
Evaluate major interpretive approaches to the imprecatory psalms in light of God's justice and the New Testament teaching on vengeance
Defend the singing of psalms in corporate worship from Scripture and the confessions, and compare exclusive psalmody with the use of hymns within Reformed churches
Produce a study of the kingship of the Lord in the enthronement psalms and its fulfillment in the reign of Christ

BIB.9.5.5.t: Identify the Song of Solomon as a book of the Bible that is a song about the love between a husband and wife
Explain that God created marriage as a good gift for a husband and wife
Locate the Song of Solomon among the poetry and wisdom books of the Old Testament and name Solomon as the king in its title
Identify the main voices in the Song as the bride, the bridegroom, and the daughters of Jerusalem
Describe how the bride speaks of her husband as both her beloved and her friend
Describe how the Song uses pictures from nature such as gardens, vineyards, flowers, and animals to express love
Explain from Scripture the Reformed tradition's teaching that marriage is a covenant between one man and one woman
Explain the meaning of the repeated charge not to stir up or awaken love until it pleases
Describe the faithful mutual belonging expressed in the refrain my beloved is mine and I am his
Analyze the Song's figurative language, including similes, metaphors, and descriptive praise poems of the bride and groom
Trace the movement of the Song through its scenes of longing, searching, and reunion
Explain how the Song presents physical intimacy within marriage as a good part of God's creation
Interpret the climactic description of love as strong as death and unquenchable by many waters
Explain the identity and role of the Shulammite woman in the Song
Explain why the church received the Song as canonical Scripture even though it rarely or never names God directly
Compare literal, allegorical, and typological approaches to interpreting the Song in Jewish and Christian history
Analyze how the prophets use marriage imagery for God's covenant with Israel as background for reading the Song
Evaluate contemporary cultural views of sexuality in light of the Song's portrait of exclusive covenant love
Evaluate how the Song functions as wisdom literature that instructs God's people in love and marriage
Compose an essay that synthesizes the Song with New Testament teaching on the church as the bride of Christ

CFL.1.1.1.t: Recognize the three Greek accent marks by sight: the acute (´), the grave (`), and the circumflex (˜ or ῀).

greek: τίς (tis), 'who?' vs. τις (tis), 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Name which vowels in a written word carry an accent mark and read the word with stress on that syllable.

greek: τίς (tis), 'who?' vs. τις (tis), 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: State the rule that a Greek accent can stand only on one of the last three syllables (antepenult, penult, ultima).

greek: τίς (tis), 'who?' vs. τις (tis), 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Apply the rule that the acute may stand on any of the last three syllables, the circumflex only on the last two, and the grave only on the final syllable.

greek: τίς (tis), 'who?' vs. τις (tis), 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Explain how a final acute changes to a grave when another word follows without intervening punctuation.

greek: τίς (tis), 'who?' vs. τις (tis), 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Explain that Greek verb accent is recessive, moving as far back toward the antepenult as the length of the ultima allows, and predict a verb's accent placement.

greek: τίς (tis), 'who?' vs. τις (tis), 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.1.t: Distinguish word pairs and forms whose meaning or parsing is signaled only by accent (e.g., τίς 'who?' vs. τις 'someone'; enclitics and proclitics).

greek: τίς (tis), 'who?' vs. τις (tis), 'someone'; accent distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.2.t: Identify the smooth breathing (᾿) and the rough breathing (῾) marks placed over an initial vowel or diphthong.

greek: ἐν (en), 'in' vs. ἕν (hen), 'one'; breathing mark distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.2.t: Pronounce a word beginning with a rough breathing by adding an initial 'h' sound, and a word with a smooth breathing without it.

greek: ἐν (en), 'in' vs. ἕν (hen), 'one'; breathing mark distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.2.t: Read every word-initial upsilon (υ) and rho (ρ) with the rough breathing that always accompanies them.

greek: ἐν (en), 'in' vs. ἕν (hen), 'one'; breathing mark distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.2.t: Place the breathing mark correctly over the second vowel of an initial diphthong and before an initial capital vowel.

greek: ἐν (en), 'in' vs. ἕν (hen), 'one'; breathing mark distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.2.t: Contrast minimal pairs distinguished only by breathing (e.g., ἐν vs. the concept of aspiration) and explain how breathing affects both spelling and meaning.

greek: ἐν (en), 'in' vs. ἕν (hen), 'one'; breathing mark distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.2.t: Relate a rough breathing to its transliteration as 'h' and to derived English cognates (e.g., ὑπέρ → hyper-, ὁδός in exodus).

greek: ἐν (en), 'in' vs. ἕν (hen), 'one'; breathing mark distinguishes them

CFL.1.1.3.t: Recite the 24 letters of the Greek alphabet in order by name (alpha, beta, gamma …).
Match each lowercase Greek letter to its uppercase form.
Write each Greek letter, both lowercase and uppercase, in correct handwritten form.
Give the basic consonant and vowel sound of each letter and read simple Greek syllables aloud.
Write the final form of sigma (ς) at the end of a word and the medial/initial sigma (σ) elsewhere.
Transliterate a Greek word into Roman letters, including gamma-nasal (γγ, γκ) as 'ng'/'nk'.
Read an unfamiliar Greek word aloud smoothly, combining letters, breathings, and accents at sight.

CFL.1.1.4.t: Name the seven Greek vowels (α, ε, η, ι, ο, υ, ω) and identify which are always long (η, ω) and which are always short (ε, ο).
Pronounce each vowel with its standard classroom (Erasmian) sound.
Recognize and pronounce the proper diphthongs (αι, ει, οι, υι, αυ, ευ, ου, ηυ) as single vowel sounds.
Identify the iota subscript (ᾳ, ῃ, ῳ) and explain that it marks an original long-vowel diphthong that is no longer pronounced.
Distinguish a genuine diphthong from two vowels pronounced separately when marked by a diaeresis (¨).
Explain how vowel length and diphthongs affect syllable quantity and thus accent placement.

CFL.1.2.1.t: Explain that Greek verb tenses convey kind of action (aspect), not only time.
Define punctiliar (undefined/simple) aspect and linear (ongoing, progressive) aspect.
Contrast the aorist as portraying an action as a whole with the imperfect as portraying an action as ongoing or repeated in past time.
Identify the present tense as expressing continuous or habitual action in a given passage.
Analyze how the perfect aspect presents a completed action with continuing results.
Interpret a New Testament verse where the aspectual choice carries exegetical or theological weight (e.g., ongoing vs. once-for-all action).

CFL.1.2.2.t: Look up a Greek word by its Strong's number in a concordance or lexicon.
Find a word's dictionary (lemma) form and read its glosses in a beginning lexicon.
Distinguish a word's range of meaning (semantic range) and select the sense that fits its context.
Explain and avoid the root fallacy, recognizing that a word's meaning comes from usage, not from the sum of its parts or etymology.
Use an advanced lexicon such as BDAG (New Testament) or Liddell-Scott (classical) to trace a word's attested usage.
Conduct a word study that weighs usage across the New Testament and the Septuagint to establish a word's meaning in a passage.

CFL.1.2.3.t: Recognize common Koine prepositions (ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό, πρός, διά, μετά, κατά, ὑπό, σύν) and give a basic gloss for each.

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό: common prepositions

CFL.1.2.3.t: State which case each preposition governs and translate the prepositional phrase accordingly.

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό: common prepositions

CFL.1.2.3.t: Explain how a preposition that takes more than one case shifts meaning with the case it governs (e.g., διά + genitive 'through' vs. διά + accusative 'because of').

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό: common prepositions

CFL.1.2.3.t: Relate the spatial picture of a preposition to its case (e.g., genitive = motion from, dative = position in/at, accusative = motion toward).

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό: common prepositions

CFL.1.2.3.t: Analyze a preposition's contribution to the meaning of a New Testament clause, including prepositions prefixed to verbs.

greek: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ, ἀπό: common prepositions

CFL.1.3.1.t: Recognize the Greek definite article and decline it for the masculine, feminine, and neuter in the nominative singular and plural (ὁ, ἡ, τό, οἱ, αἱ, τά).
Match an article to its noun by agreement in gender, number, and case.
Distinguish the attributive position (article-adjective-noun or article-noun-article-adjective), in which the adjective modifies the noun.
Distinguish the predicate position (adjective without a repeated article), in which the adjective asserts something about the noun.
Identify anarthrous (article-less) constructions and describe how the absence of the article affects meaning.
Evaluate a disputed anarthrous construction (e.g., the predicate nominative in John 1:1) using word order and the Colwell/Granville Sharp considerations.

CFL.1.3.2.t: Name the five Greek noun cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, and vocative.
State the basic syntactic function of each case (subject, of/possession, to/for/in, direct object, direct address).
Decline a first-declension and a second-declension noun fully in the singular and plural.
Decline a third-declension noun, accounting for stem changes in the nominative and dative plural.
Identify the case, number, and gender of a noun in a New Testament sentence and translate it by its function.
Distinguish nuanced case functions in exegesis (e.g., subjective vs. objective genitive; dative of means, place, or reference).

CFL.1.3.3.t: Recognize a Greek participle as a verbal adjective and identify its participial ending.
Parse a participle for tense, voice, gender, number, and case.
Distinguish adjectival participles (attributive and substantival) from adverbial (circumstantial) participles.
Translate an adverbial participle with the appropriate relation to the main verb (temporal, causal, concessive, conditional, means, or manner).
Identify and translate the genitive absolute construction.
Identify supplementary (complementary) participles that complete the idea of verbs such as παύομαι and ἄρχομαι.
Analyze how a participle's tense conveys aspect and its time relative to the main verb in a New Testament passage.

CFL.1.3.4.t: Identify the six principal Greek indicative tenses: present, imperfect, future, aorist, perfect, and pluperfect.
Conjugate a regular (ω-) verb in the present active indicative across all persons and numbers.
Conjugate a verb in the imperfect and future active indicative, recognizing the augment and the tense formatives.
Recognize the augment as the marker of past-time (secondary) tenses in the indicative.
Conjugate first (sigmatic) and second aorist active indicative verbs and tell them apart.
Conjugate the perfect and pluperfect active indicative, recognizing reduplication.
Parse any indicative verb from the New Testament by tense, voice, mood, person, and number.

CFL.1.3.5.t: Name the three Greek voices: active, middle, and passive.
Explain that active voice presents the subject as doing the action and passive voice as receiving it.
Describe the middle voice as presenting the subject as acting with reference to or upon itself, and translate simple middle forms.
Recognize deponent verbs, which are middle or passive in form but active in meaning, and translate them actively.
Distinguish middle from passive forms where they share endings, using context to decide the voice.
Evaluate the theological significance of voice in a passage (e.g., the divine passive as a reverent way of referring to God's action).

CFL.1.4.1.t: Read aloud a short, familiar Greek verse (e.g., John 3:16 or 1 John 4:8) with correct pronunciation.

greek: ἐν ἀρχῇ (en archē): in the beginning

CFL.1.4.1.t: Translate simple, high-frequency clauses from the Gospel of John using known vocabulary.

greek: ἐν ἀρχῇ (en archē): in the beginning

CFL.1.4.1.t: Read a graded passage from Mark or John and identify subject, verb, and object.

greek: ἐν ἀρχῇ (en archē): in the beginning

CFL.1.4.1.t: Translate a short narrative passage from Mark, parsing its verbs and nouns.

greek: ἐν ἀρχῇ (en archē): in the beginning

CFL.1.4.1.t: Translate a paragraph from a Pauline epistle, working through its clauses and connectives.

greek: ἐν ἀρχῇ (en archē): in the beginning

CFL.1.4.1.t: Read a previously unseen New Testament passage at sight, using known vocabulary and a lexicon for rarer words.

greek: ἐν ἀρχῇ (en archē): in the beginning

CFL.1.4.2.t: Use an interlinear Greek-English New Testament to locate the Greek word beneath its English gloss.
Look up an unfamiliar form in a parsing guide or analytical lexicon to find its dictionary form.
Consult a reference grammar to check a specific syntactic question rather than reading a whole translation from it.
Translate a clause first from the Greek text, then use an interlinear only to check the result, noting where over-dependence would have masked the grammar.
Evaluate the strengths and limits of interlinears, recognizing that their word-for-word English order distorts Greek syntax.
Demonstrate growing independence by reading and parsing a passage directly, reserving tools for confirmation.

CFL.1.4.3.t: Explain that the New Testament survives in many handwritten manuscripts that differ in small ways, producing textual variants.
Locate the critical apparatus at the foot of the page in a Greek New Testament (e.g., NA28 or UBS).
Read the basic sigla and abbreviations of the apparatus to identify a variant reading and the witnesses cited for it.
Compare two variant readings of a verse and state how each would affect translation or meaning.
Apply introductory canons of textual criticism, weighing external evidence (age and distribution of witnesses) and internal evidence (the reading that best explains the others).

CFL.2.1.1.t: Recognize that small marks appear above and below Hebrew words in a printed Hebrew Bible and that they help guide reading aloud
Identify cantillation (te'amim) marks as a system separate from the consonants and vowel points
Explain that cantillation marks serve three roles: musical chant, word stress (accent), and punctuation that groups words into phrases
Distinguish disjunctive from conjunctive accents and locate the major dividers such as silluq, atnach, and zaqef
Use the atnach to identify the main clausal division of a verse and discuss how that division can affect interpretation
Analyze a verse where the Masoretic accentuation supports or challenges a particular translation or theological reading

CFL.2.1.2.t: Recite the names of the 22 Hebrew consonants in order
Recognize and name each of the 22 consonantal letters by sight
Write each Hebrew consonant by hand in the square (Aramaic) script
Produce the standard consonantal sound value of each letter, including the gutturals aleph, he, chet, and ayin
Transliterate Hebrew consonants into Roman letters using a consistent academic scheme
Distinguish easily confused letter pairs such as bet/kaf, dalet/resh, he/chet, and vav/zayin in unpointed text
Compare academic and general-purpose transliteration systems and apply one consistently to a printed verse

CFL.2.1.3.t: Notice that a dot inside a Hebrew letter changes how some letters look
Distinguish the dagesh lene in the begadkefat letters (bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, pe, tav) and pronounce the hard and soft forms
Identify the dagesh forte as a doubling of a consonant and read a word with a doubled letter
Read and classify the shewa as either vocal (a reduced vowel) or silent (a syllable closer)
Recognize the mappiq in final he and the meteg, and explain the pronunciation effect of each
Explain how a dagesh forte in doubling can signal grammatical information such as the Piel binyan or an assimilated nun

CFL.2.1.4.t: Recognize that some Hebrew letters take a different shape at the end of a word
Name the five letters that have a final (sofit) form: kaf, mem, nun, pe, and tsade
Match each final form to its ordinary medial form
Write the five final forms by hand and place them correctly at the end of a word
Read words containing final forms without mistaking a sofit letter for a different consonant

CFL.2.1.5.t: Recognize that small dots and dashes below and beside the consonants stand for vowels
Name the basic full vowels (qamets, patach, tsere, segol, chireq, cholem, qibbuts, shureq) and their sounds
Read a fully pointed Hebrew word by combining each consonant with its vowel
Distinguish long, short, and reduced (chateph) vowels and identify the chateph vowels under gutturals
Explain the difference between qamets gadol and qamets chatuph and read each correctly
Divide a pointed word into syllables and mark whether each syllable is open or closed

CFL.2.2.1.t: Recognize the letter vav prefixed to a word as the common word meaning 'and'
Translate the conjunction vav as 'and,' 'but,' 'or,' or 'now' according to context
Identify the vav-consecutive (vav plus a prefixed verb) as the signal of Hebrew narrative sequence
Distinguish the vav-consecutive (wayyiqtol) chain that carries a story forward from a simple conjunctive vav
Translate a wayyiqtol narrative chain into smooth English past-tense sequence
Analyze how a break in the wayyiqtol chain marks a scene shift, background information, or theological emphasis in a narrative

CFL.2.2.2.t: Recognize that Hebrew has verb forms that act like nouns or adjectives

CFL.2.2.2.t: Identify the participle and explain that it describes ongoing or characteristic action

CFL.2.2.4.t: Recognize that a Hebrew verb can change its ending or its prefix to show a different form
Identify the perfect (qatal) conjugation by its suffixed person endings
Identify the imperfect (yiqtol) conjugation by its prefixed person markers
Explain the perfect as viewing action as complete and the imperfect as viewing action as incomplete
Translate perfect and imperfect verbs into appropriate English tenses using context rather than a fixed rule
Analyze how Hebrew verbal aspect, not tense, shapes the meaning of a chosen prophetic or poetic verse

CFL.2.2.5.t: Recognize that some short Hebrew words are attached to the front of another word
Identify the inseparable prepositions bet ('in/with'), kaf ('like/as'), and lamed ('to/for') as prefixed letters
Translate a word carrying a prefixed preposition, restoring the base word
Explain how a prefixed preposition merges with the definite article and changes its vowel
Parse a word that combines a prefixed preposition, an article, and a pronominal suffix

CFL.2.2.6.t: Recognize the common independent pronouns such as ani ('I'), atah ('you'), and hu ('he')
Identify the definite article ha- prefixed to a noun and explain that Hebrew has no indefinite article
Match independent personal pronouns to their person, gender, and number
Identify a pronominal suffix on a noun and translate it as a possessive (e.g., 'his,' 'their')
Identify a pronominal suffix on a verb or preposition and translate it as an object
Parse the doubling of the article's following consonant and the article's vowel changes before gutturals

CFL.2.2.8.t: Recognize that a Hebrew root can appear in several verb patterns with related meanings
Name the seven major binyanim (Qal, Niphal, Piel, Pual, Hiphil, Hophal, Hithpael)
Identify the Qal as the simple active stem and the Niphal as its common passive or reflexive
Explain the intensive Piel/Pual pair and the causative Hiphil/Hophal pair by voice and function
Recognize the reflexive Hithpael by its characteristic infixed tav
Parse a finite verb fully by stating its binyan, conjugation, person, gender, and number
Analyze how a change of binyan shifts the meaning of a root in a chosen verse

CFL.2.3.1.t: Look up the meaning of a Hebrew word using a glossary or interlinear tool
Conduct a basic word study by tracing how one Hebrew term is used across several passages
Explain the grammatical-historical method as reading a text according to its grammar, its author, and its original setting
Interpret a verse by combining word study, grammatical parsing, and its literary context
Synthesize the exegetical findings of several passages into a careful summary of a biblical theme
Distinguish sound exegesis (drawing meaning out of the text) from eisegesis (reading meaning into it) in a worked example

CFL.2.3.2.t: Recognize that a Hebrew lexicon lists words with their meanings and references
Locate a Hebrew word in a lexicon by its root or dictionary form
Read a lexicon entry and identify its glosses, grammatical notes, and cited passages
Explain that a word carries a semantic range and select the gloss that fits a given context
Compare the arrangement and information of BDB and HALOT and use each to research a word

CFL.2.3.3.t: Locate a verb form on a paradigm (morphology) chart
Use a paradigm chart to match a suffix or prefix to its person, gender, and number
Parse regular (strong) verbs by comparing them to the Qal paradigm chart
Parse nouns and pronouns using reference charts for endings and suffixes
Parse weak verbs (I-nun, I-guttural, III-he, hollow) with the aid of morphology charts

CFL.2.3.4.t: Recognize that Hebrew continued to be used and studied in the centuries between the Old and New Testaments
Identify the Second Temple period and name key bodies of literature such as the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint
Explain how the Masoretes preserved and pointed the Hebrew text long after the biblical period
Describe the rise of rabbinic literature (Mishnah and Talmud) and its relationship to Mishnaic Hebrew
Discuss how Second Temple and rabbinic sources illuminate the language and background of the Old Testament

יהוה (YHWH): the LORD, the divine name

CFL.2.3.6.t: Recognize that much of the Old Testament is poetry set apart from prose
Identify a psalm or proverb as poetry by its paired, balanced lines
Explain that Hebrew poetry works by parallel lines rather than by rhyme or meter
Identify poetic features such as imagery, repetition, and figurative language in a psalm
Analyze the poetic devices of a wisdom or prophetic passage and describe their effect on meaning

CFL.2.4.2.t: Recognize that a Hebrew sentence often begins with its verb
Identify the default verb-subject-object order in a Hebrew clause
Explain that placing a word before the verb (fronting) usually signals emphasis or contrast
Distinguish a verbal clause from a verbless (nominal) clause and translate each
Analyze how word order, fronting, and dislocation create emphasis or mark a topic in a chosen verse

CFL.2.4.3.t: Recognize that some Hebrew expressions cannot be translated word for word

CFL.2.4.3.t: Identify common Hebrew idioms such as 'to find favor in the eyes of' or 'to lift up the face'

greek: כָּרַת בְּרִית (karat berit): 'to cut a covenant'

CFL.2.4.3.t: Explain a Hebrew anthropomorphism (e.g., God's 'outstretched arm') as figurative language

greek: כָּרַת בְּרִית (karat berit): 'to cut a covenant'

CFL.2.4.3.t: Translate an idiomatic expression into natural English while noting its literal wording

greek: כָּרַת בְּרִית (karat berit): 'to cut a covenant'

CFL.2.4.3.t: Analyze how a Hebrew figure of speech reflects an underlying pattern of Hebrew thought in a chosen passage

greek: כָּרַת בְּרִית (karat berit): 'to cut a covenant'

CFL.2.4.4.t: Recognize that Hebrew poems are built from pairs of matching lines
Identify synonymous parallelism, where the second line restates the first
Identify antithetic parallelism, where the second line contrasts with the first
Distinguish synthetic parallelism, where the second line advances or completes the first
Identify climactic (stairstep) parallelism that repeats and builds across lines
Analyze the parallelism of a psalm and explain how the paired lines shape its meaning

CFL.2.4.5.t: Recognize that the same Hebrew verse can be rendered in more than one English wording
Distinguish a formal (literal, word-for-word) translation from a dynamic (thought-for-thought) translation
Compare two English versions of a verse and account for their differences from the Hebrew
Produce a literal working translation of a verse, then a smoother idiomatic rendering
Explain the special challenges of translating Hebrew poetry, including imagery and parallelism
Defend translation choices for a passage by appealing to grammar, semantic range, and context

CFL.2.4.6.t: Recognize the vav-consecutive verb form as the marker that keeps a Hebrew story moving
Identify the wayyiqtol chain that forms the backbone of Old Testament narrative
Explain how the narrative chain distinguishes the main storyline from background comments
Trace the sequence of events in a narrative by following its wayyiqtol verbs
Analyze how a shift in the narrative chain (a disruption or aside) carries theological weight in a chosen story

CFL.3.1.1.t: Identify who or what a sentence is about (the subject) and who or what receives the action (the object).
Point out small words that show relationship or position, such as 'to,' 'from,' 'with,' and 'in.'
Explain how English uses word order and prepositions to show a noun's job in a sentence.
Compare how a language with cases (such as Latin) changes a noun's ending to show its function, while English uses word order or a preposition instead.
Match common Latin or Greek cases (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative) to the English prepositions or roles that express the same idea.
Analyze how a single case can carry several functions and why translators must choose the right English preposition from context.
Evaluate the trade-offs between case-marking and prepositional systems, explaining what each gains in precision or flexibility.

CFL.3.1.2.t: Recognize that people around the world speak many different languages.
Identify that some languages look and sound similar because they are related, like members of a family.
Name major language families, such as Indo-European and Semitic, and give an example language in each.
Explain how linguists group languages into families using shared vocabulary, sound patterns, and grammar.
Trace how Latin, Greek, and the Germanic languages (including English) descend from a common Indo-European ancestor.
Compare features of the Semitic family (such as Hebrew's triconsonantal roots) with those of Indo-European languages.
Analyze cognate sets across related languages to infer their shared origin and reconstruct likely ancestral forms.

CFL.3.1.3.t: Learn that many English words come from older languages, especially Latin and Greek.
Identify a common root within a word, such as 'port' in 'transport' and 'import.'
Define frequent Latin and Greek roots (such as 'aqua,' 'bio,' 'graph,' 'spect') and use them to explain word meanings.
Break unfamiliar words into root, prefix, and suffix to predict their meaning.
Trace the etymology of an English word back through Latin or Greek and explain how its meaning shifted over time.
Use knowledge of Latin and Greek roots to decode specialized academic, scientific, and theological vocabulary.

CFL.3.1.4.t: Arrange words in the right order so that a sentence makes sense.
Explain why changing word order can change or destroy a sentence's meaning.
Identify the parts a complete sentence needs, such as a subject and a verb.
Explain how grammatical rules follow a logic that lets a listener recover the intended meaning.
Analyze how ambiguous sentences arise and how syntax resolves or preserves the ambiguity.
Evaluate why certain grammatical structures are necessary for clear reasoning and valid argument, connecting syntax to logic.

CFL.3.1.5.t: Notice that verbs can tell whether something happens now, happened before, or will happen later.
Identify the tense of an English verb as past, present, or future.
Distinguish when an action is ongoing versus completed (for example, 'was building' versus 'built').
Define grammatical aspect and explain how it differs from tense (time of action versus the way the action unfolds).
Compare how Koine Greek verbs foreground aspect (aorist, present, perfect) while English verbs foreground time.
Analyze a Koine Greek verb's aspect in a passage and explain what nuance it adds beyond an English tense translation.

CFL.3.2.1.t: Break a compound or affixed word into smaller meaningful parts.
Identify a root word and the prefix or suffix added to it.
Explain how adding an affix changes a word's meaning or its part of speech.
Distinguish inflection (changing a word's form for grammar, like plural or past tense) from derivation (making a new word).
Analyze how an inflected language builds many word forms from one root through systematic endings.
Compare morphological strategies across languages, contrasting isolating, agglutinative, and fusional patterns.

CFL.3.2.2.t: Match letters and letter combinations to the sounds they make.
Identify the separate sounds (phonemes) that make up a spoken word.
Distinguish vowels from consonants and describe how each is produced.
Explain how a language's sound system allows only certain sounds and combinations.
Use phonetic symbols to describe how a sound is articulated (place and manner).
Analyze how sounds change in connected speech and across related languages (sound shifts).
Compare the phonological inventories of two languages and explain why some sounds are hard for a foreign speaker to hear or produce.

CFL.3.2.3.t: Notice that the same words can mean different things depending on the situation.
Explain how tone of voice or setting changes what a sentence means.
Identify when a speaker means something other than the literal words (for example, sarcasm or a hint).
Explain how context and shared assumptions let a listener infer a speaker's intended meaning.
Analyze how implication, presupposition, and politeness shape meaning beyond the literal sentence.
Evaluate how cultural and historical context governs the meaning of an utterance, including biblical texts.

CFL.3.2.4.t: Give the meaning of a familiar word.
Identify words that mean the same (synonyms) and words that mean the opposite (antonyms).
Explain how one word can have several related meanings.
Distinguish a word's denotation (dictionary meaning) from its connotation (feeling or association).
Analyze sense relations among words, such as hyponymy, and map how a word's semantic range overlaps with others.
Evaluate how the semantic range of a Hebrew or Greek term shapes translation and interpretation choices.

CFL.3.2.5.t: Notice that people in different places or groups may say the same thing in different ways.
Identify formal versus casual ways of speaking for different situations.
Explain what a dialect is and give examples of regional word or pronunciation differences.
Distinguish register, jargon, and slang, and explain when each is appropriate.
Analyze how social factors such as region, group, and setting shape the way people use language.
Evaluate how a speaker adjusts register and dialect for audience and purpose, and what that signals socially.

CFL.3.2.6.t: Put words in order to build a complete sentence.
Identify the subject and the predicate of a sentence.
Label the main parts of a sentence, including phrases and clauses.
Diagram a sentence to show how its parts relate to one another.
Compare word-order patterns across languages (such as subject-verb-object versus subject-object-verb).
Analyze how a surface sentence can express a deeper underlying structure, and how one meaning yields different arrangements.

CFL.3.3.1.t: Use kind and honest words when speaking to others.
Explain why telling the truth honors God and respects other people.
Identify speech that builds others up versus speech that tears them down.
Choose words that edify and avoid coarse, profane, or deceitful language.
Explain how Scripture calls believers to speak truth in love and to let their speech give grace to hearers.
Evaluate how a Christian's language should reflect truthfulness, charity, and reverence in different settings.

CFL.3.3.2.t: Read simple, familiar texts smoothly and with understanding.
Read comfortable books often to build fluency and enjoyment.
Explain how reading material slightly above one's current level helps language grow.
Apply extensive reading by choosing texts with mostly known words to build fluency in a new language.
Explain the idea of comprehensible input and how it supports acquiring a language.
Design a reading plan that gradually increases difficulty to build fluency in a target language such as Latin or Greek.

CFL.3.3.3.t: Practice new words using picture cards or simple flashcards.
Use flashcards to review vocabulary and check what has been learned.
Practice speaking or writing new words, not just recognizing them.
Explain the difference between input (reading and listening) and output (speaking and writing) in language learning.
Combine flashcards, immersion, and output practice into a balanced study routine.
Evaluate the strengths and limits of each strategy and adjust the balance for a specific learning goal.

CFL.3.3.4.t: Use a simple rhyme or picture to help remember something.
Create a mnemonic, such as a phrase or acronym, to recall a list or rule.
Review material over several days rather than all at once.
Explain how spaced repetition strengthens memory by reviewing at increasing intervals.
Apply spaced repetition and mnemonic techniques to memorize vocabulary or grammar forms.
Explain encoding specificity and design study conditions that match the way information will later be recalled.

CFL.3.3.5.t: Look up a word in a dictionary to find its meaning.
Use alphabetical order and guide words to find an entry quickly.
Read a dictionary entry to find a word's part of speech, meanings, and example uses.
Explain the difference between a bilingual dictionary and a monolingual (same-language) one, and when to use each.
Use a lexicon to look up a Hebrew or Greek word by its root or lemma and read its glosses.
Analyze a lexicon entry to weigh a word's semantic range, cited references, and usage before choosing a meaning in context.

CFL.4.1.1.t: Recognize familiar Latin phrases from Christian worship and Scripture, such as Gloria in excelsis Deo, Pater noster, and Amen
Read aloud short memorized Vulgate verses, such as the Lord's Prayer or Psalm openings, with ecclesiastical pronunciation
Translate simple Vulgate passages using known vocabulary, comparing the Latin wording to a familiar English version
Identify distinctive features of Late and Ecclesiastical Latin, such as simplified word order and Greek loanwords, in Vulgate and patristic texts
Translate and analyze selected passages from the church fathers, such as Augustine's Confessiones or Ambrose's hymns, noting grammar and vocabulary
Read an extended Latin passage from Augustine or Ambrose and discuss how its Latin style conveys theological meaning

CFL.4.1.2.t: Retell key stories of early Rome, such as Romulus and Remus and the founding of the city, and locate Rome on a map
Distinguish the Roman Republic from the Roman Empire and describe how each was governed
Identify major Roman officials and institutions, such as consuls, the Senate, and tribunes, and explain their roles
Describe the careers and significance of key figures such as Julius Caesar, Cicero, and Augustus
Explain foundational concepts of Roman law, such as the Twelve Tables, citizenship, and the ius civile, and their influence on Western legal traditions
Read adapted or original Latin historical prose, such as passages from Caesar or Livy, and analyze how Romans described their own government

CFL.4.1.3.t: Name the major Roman gods and goddesses and describe their chief attributes and domains
Match Roman deities to their Greek counterparts, such as Jupiter/Zeus and Venus/Aphrodite, and note key differences
Retell the deeds of major Roman heroes and legendary figures, such as Aeneas, Hercules, and Romulus
Explain how Roman myths reflected and reinforced Roman values such as pietas, virtus, and civic duty
Summarize the plot and major themes of Virgil's Aeneid and describe its role in Roman national identity
Translate and scan selected passages from Virgil's Aeneid, analyzing imagery, allusion, and poetic technique

CFL.4.2.1.t: Recognize that Latin is read with two main pronunciation systems, Classical and Ecclesiastical
Contrast how key letters and combinations are pronounced in each system, such as c, g, v, ae, and ti
Read the same passage aloud in both Classical and Ecclesiastical pronunciation
Explain the historical and cultural contexts in which each pronunciation system is used and choose the appropriate one for a given text

CFL.4.2.2.t: Recite the Latin alphabet and name the letters that differ in use from English, such as the absence of j and w
Pronounce the Latin vowels with their long and short sounds
Pronounce the Latin diphthongs, such as ae, oe, au, and ei
Pronounce Latin consonants and consonant combinations correctly, noting differences from English
Read aloud unfamiliar Latin words accurately by applying the sounds of vowels, diphthongs, and consonants

CFL.4.2.3.t: Divide Latin words into syllables using vowel and consonant patterns
Determine whether a syllable is long or short by nature or by position
Apply the penultimate rule to place the stress accent correctly in two- and three-syllable words
Explain the difference between the classical quantitative rhythm of Latin and the stress-based accent used in reading, and mark accents in longer words

CFL.4.2.4.t: Learn and use a core set of high-frequency Latin words for everyday nouns, verbs, and adjectives
Identify English words derived from Latin roots and explain their shared meaning
Analyze how common Latin prefixes, such as ad-, con-, in-, and trans-, change the meaning of a base word
Analyze how common Latin suffixes form English derivatives and use them to infer word meanings
Determine the meaning of unfamiliar English and Latin words by breaking them into roots, prefixes, and suffixes

CFL.4.3.1.t: Recognize that a Latin adjective must agree with its noun in gender, number, and case
Decline first- and second-declension adjectives and match them to nouns of each gender
Decline third-declension adjectives and use them with nouns of any declension
Form the comparative and superlative degrees of regular adjectives
Form and translate irregular comparisons, such as bonus, melior, optimus, and use comparison in sentences

CFL.4.3.2.t: Name the six Latin cases and state the basic question each answers
Use the nominative for the subject and the accusative for the direct object in simple sentences
Use the genitive to show possession and the dative to show the indirect object
Identify common uses of the ablative, such as means, manner, and accompaniment
Use the vocative for direct address and recognize special vocative forms
Identify the case and syntactic function of any noun in a Latin sentence and translate it accordingly

CFL.4.3.3.t: Recognize that Latin nouns belong to declensions and that endings signal case and number
Decline first- and second-declension nouns fully in the singular and plural
Decline third-declension nouns, including i-stems, and identify their gender patterns
Decline fourth- and fifth-declension nouns and note their characteristic endings
Determine a noun's declension and gender from its nominative and genitive forms and give the correct stem
Identify and correctly form exceptional and irregular nouns, such as vis, deus, and Greek-declension nouns

CFL.4.3.4.t: Recognize common Latin prepositions and their basic meanings
Use prepositions that take the accusative case, such as ad, per, and trans, in phrases of motion and direction
Use prepositions that take the ablative case, such as in, cum, ab, and de, in phrases of place and separation
Distinguish the difference in meaning when a preposition such as in governs the accusative versus the ablative

CFL.4.3.5.t: Recognize that Latin verbs change endings to show person and number and identify the personal endings
Conjugate first- and second-conjugation verbs in the present tense, active voice
Conjugate third-, third-io, and fourth-conjugation verbs in the present tense
State the four principal parts of a verb and explain what each provides
Conjugate verbs in the imperfect and future tenses across all conjugations
Form the perfect, pluperfect, and future perfect tenses from the perfect stem
Produce and translate complete verb paradigms across all tenses, persons, and numbers

CFL.4.3.6.t: Distinguish between an active verb, whose subject acts, and a passive verb, whose subject is acted upon
Conjugate verbs in the present, imperfect, and future passive using the passive personal endings
Form the perfect passive tenses using the perfect passive participle with forms of sum
Convert sentences between active and passive voice and translate each accurately

CFL.4.4.1.t: Identify subordinate clauses in a Latin sentence and the conjunctions that introduce them

LIF.5.1.1.t: Name the main documents a car needs to be driven legally: a title, a registration, and insurance.
Explain what a car title is and why it proves who owns the vehicle.
Describe the steps to register a car and keep the registration and license plates current.
Compare basic types of auto insurance coverage (liability, collision, comprehensive) and explain why insurance is required.
Inspect a used car and its title history for warning signs before buying, and know when to ask a trusted mechanic to check it.
Complete a private-party car sale or purchase safely: agree on price, transfer the title correctly, sign a bill of sale, and update registration and insurance.

LIF.5.1.2.t: Explain that cars need regular maintenance to stay safe and last longer.
Find the recommended maintenance schedule in the owner's manual and identify when the next service is due.
Describe why engine oil, filters, and other fluids must be changed on schedule.
Explain the purpose of tire rotation and how it helps tires wear evenly.
Identify wear items such as belts, hoses, brake pads, and the timing or serpentine belt, and describe signs they need replacing.
Keep a maintenance log and plan a yearly service schedule for a specific vehicle based on mileage and manufacturer intervals.

LIF.5.1.3.t: Explain why you must pull completely off the road to a safe, flat spot and turn on hazard lights before changing a tire.
Identify the tools needed to change a tire: spare, jack, lug wrench, and wheel chocks.
Locate the correct jack points on a vehicle using the owner's manual so the jack lifts safely.
Loosen the lug nuts before jacking, then raise the car, remove the flat, and mount the spare in the correct order.
Tighten lug nuts in a star pattern to the proper torque, lower the car safely, and stow the flat and tools.
Demonstrate a complete, safe roadside tire change and explain the speed and distance limits of a temporary spare.

LIF.5.1.4.t: Explain that a car uses several fluids and that low fluids can be unsafe.
Show that the engine must be off and cool before opening the hood to check fluids.
Check the engine oil level with the dipstick and read whether it is between the low and full marks.
Check the coolant level at the reservoir (only when cool) and top off windshield washer fluid.
Inspect brake fluid and power steering fluid levels and recognize when a fluid looks dirty or low.
Identify each fluid's correct type from the owner's manual and top off or report low levels safely.

LIF.5.1.5.t: Explain that an engine burns fuel to make the power that moves a car.
Name basic engine parts such as cylinders, pistons, spark plugs, and the crankshaft.
Describe the four strokes of a gasoline engine: intake, compression, combustion, and exhaust.
Explain how air, fuel, and spark combine to create combustion inside a cylinder.
Describe how the engine's power reaches the wheels and how cooling, lubrication, and exhaust systems support it.

LIF.5.1.6.t: Explain that a car battery can lose charge and that a dead battery keeps the car from starting.
Identify the positive and negative battery terminals and the safety gear (glasses, gloves) used when working near a battery.
State the correct order for connecting and removing jumper cables between two vehicles.
Demonstrate safely jump-starting a car, avoiding sparks near the battery and never letting the clamps touch.
Inspect a battery for corrosion, clean the terminals safely, and describe how to extend battery life and when to replace it.

LIF.5.1.7.t: Point out the dashboard warning lights in a car and explain that they signal a problem.
Match common warning lights (check engine, oil pressure, temperature, battery, brake) to what they mean.
Explain which warning lights mean 'stop the car safely now' versus 'have it checked soon.'
Recognize warning signs beyond the dashboard, such as unusual noises, smells, smoke, or vibration.
Describe an appropriate response to each major warning indicator and when to seek professional help.

LIF.5.2.1.t: Locate the main water shutoff and the shutoff valves under sinks and toilets so water can be turned off in an emergency.
Explain the job of a P-trap under a sink and why it holds water.
Turn off the water supply, then tighten or replace a worn washer or gasket to fix a dripping fixture.
Clear and reseat a P-trap, using a bucket and rag to catch water, and check for leaks afterward.
Replace a sink faucet: shut off water, disconnect supply lines, remove the old faucet, and install and seal the new one.
Test completed repairs for leaks under pressure and know when a plumbing job requires a licensed plumber.

LIF.5.2.2.t: Identify common household problems such as leaks, clogged drains, loose handles, and squeaky doors.
Oil a squeaky door hinge and tighten a loose screw on a handle or fixture.
Clear a slow or clogged drain safely using a plunger or drain snake instead of harsh chemicals.
Find the source of a small leak, shut off the supply if needed, and make a simple repair.
Diagnose a recurring problem, choose the right fix and materials, and decide when to call a professional.

LIF.5.2.3.t: Explain that saving energy at home lowers costs and helps the environment.
Identify simple ways to save energy, such as turning off lights and switching to LED bulbs.
Find drafts around doors and windows and apply weather stripping or draft stoppers.
Explain how insulation keeps a home warm or cool and where it is commonly added.
Perform a simple home energy audit, listing the biggest energy wasters and low-cost fixes.
Recommend and estimate the payback of energy-efficiency upgrades for a specific home.

LIF.5.2.4.t: Explain that electricity is powerful and dangerous, and that you never put objects into outlets.
Describe what switches and outlets do and why cords and outlets should not be overloaded.
Explain in simple terms what an electrical circuit is and how a switch opens or closes it.
Locate the breaker box and safely reset a tripped breaker, and identify GFCI outlets and their test/reset buttons.
Describe basic electrical safety rules: shut off power at the breaker before work, and know when a job requires a licensed electrician.
Read the panel labeling to map which breaker controls which circuit and explain the role of grounding.

LIF.5.2.5.t: Help prepare a room for painting by moving items and laying down a drop cloth.
Prepare a wall surface: clean it, and apply painter's tape to edges and trim.
Patch small holes and cracks with spackle or filler, then sand the patch smooth once dry.
Choose the right paint, primer, brushes, and rollers for a given surface and explain when primer is needed.
Apply paint evenly with proper brush and roller technique, keeping a wet edge and working in good ventilation.
Complete a full paint job from prep to cleanup, including a second coat and safe disposal of materials.

LIF.5.2.6.t: Explain that homes need different care in different seasons.
Locate and replace an HVAC air filter and explain why a clean filter matters.
Clean gutters and downspouts safely, using stable footing and never overreaching on a ladder.
Winterize outdoor faucets and hoses to prevent frozen, burst pipes.
Create a seasonal home-maintenance checklist and schedule tasks for spring, summer, fall, and winter.

LIF.5.2.7.t: Name common hand tools (hammer, screwdriver, tape measure, level) and tell what each is used for.
Measure a length accurately with a tape measure and check that something is straight with a level.
Use a hammer and screwdriver safely, keeping fingers clear and choosing the right size.
Put on safety glasses and hearing protection and explain why personal protective equipment matters when using tools.
Operate a power drill safely: secure the workpiece, choose the right bit, and keep hands away from the moving parts.
Demonstrate safe setup, use, and storage of common power tools, including checking guards and unplugging before changing bits or blades.

LIF.5.3.1.t: Name the parts of a simple circuit (power source, wire, and a device like a bulb) and explain that they must form a loop.
Explain that a soldering iron is very hot and describe the safety gear and ventilation needed before using one.
Set up a safe soldering station: heat-proof surface, stand for the hot iron, eye protection, and good airflow.
Make a clean solder joint on a practice board, heating the joint and applying solder correctly.
Diagnose and repair a simple broken connection, such as re-soldering a loose wire, and inspect the joint for quality.

LIF.5.3.2.t: Explain that an engine needs fuel, spark, and air to run.
Check the simple things first when equipment won't start: fuel level, on/off switch, and safety controls.
Inspect and test for spark and airflow, including checking or replacing a dirty air filter or fouled spark plug.
Follow a step-by-step troubleshooting process to find whether a no-start is a fuel, spark, or air problem.
Use a systematic diagnostic approach to isolate and fix a small-engine fault, and know when a repair is beyond your skill.

LIF.5.3.3.t: Clean dirt and grass off tools and equipment after using them.
Store tools and equipment properly in a dry place so they don't rust or get damaged.
Explain why fuel and moisture cause problems if equipment sits unused over winter.
Winterize a small engine: stabilize or drain the fuel, and follow the manual's storage steps.
Prepare a full range of tools and powered equipment for long-term or seasonal storage, including battery and oil care.

LIF.5.3.4.t: Explain that lawn equipment must be turned off and cool before you clean or work on it.
Clean a mower deck and trimmer safely with the spark plug wire disconnected so it cannot start.
Check and change the oil in a small engine following the owner's manual.
Inspect, clean or replace a spark plug and air filter on a mower or trimmer.
Perform seasonal tune-up maintenance on lawn equipment and keep a service record.

LIF.5.3.5.t: Explain that a sharp blade is often safer than a dull one because it needs less force, and that blades must be handled carefully.
Sharpen a kitchen knife safely using a whetstone or guided sharpener, keeping fingers behind the edge.
Sharpen a lawn-tool blade such as a mower blade or shears, wearing gloves and securing the blade.
Choose the right sharpening tool and angle for a given blade and test the edge safely.

LIF.5.4.1.t: Sort and count the parts and hardware in a furniture kit and match them to the instruction sheet.
Read assembly instructions step by step and identify the tools each step requires.
Assemble a simple piece of furniture in the correct order, using the right hardware in each spot.
Check that a finished assembly is square, tight, and stable, and fix any loose or missing fasteners.
Plan and complete a multi-step furniture build, troubleshooting mismatched parts and confirming safety before use.

LIF.5.4.2.t: Explain that joinery is how two pieces of wood are connected.
Make a simple butt joint by gluing and fastening two boards together.
Cut and assemble a lap joint so two pieces fit flush.
Drill and use dowels to align and strengthen a joint.
Perform a clean glue-up: apply glue evenly, clamp the pieces square, and wipe away squeeze-out.
Choose the right joint for a project based on strength and appearance, and build it accurately.

LIF.5.4.3.t: Help build a very simple wood project, such as gluing and nailing a small box, with adult supervision.
Follow a simple plan to build a birdhouse, measuring and fastening the pieces.
Build a small shelf or toolbox, cutting parts to size and joining them squarely.
Read or sketch a project plan, create a cut list, and gather the needed materials and tools.
Design and build a small woodworking project from plan to finish, applying safe tool use throughout.

LIF.5.4.4.t: Measure and mark a length on a board with a tape measure and pencil.
Use a square to mark a straight, accurate cut line across a board.
Cut wood along a marked line using a handsaw and a miter box, keeping hands clear of the blade.
Apply the 'measure twice, cut once' habit and account for the saw blade's width (kerf) when marking.
Cut accurate straight and angled (miter) cuts and check the finished pieces for fit and square.

LIF.5.4.5.t: Sand a piece of wood smooth by hand, following the direction of the grain.
Explain why finishing protects wood and choose sandpaper from coarse to fine grits in order.
Wear a dust mask and work in good ventilation when sanding, staining, or finishing.
Apply wood stain evenly and wipe off the excess, following the product directions.
Apply a protective finish such as polyurethane in thin coats, sanding lightly between coats.
Complete a full finishing process from surface prep to final coat, and dispose of oily rags safely to prevent fire.

LIF.5.4.6.t: Explain that wood comes from trees and that different woods look and feel different.
Describe the difference between hardwood and softwood.
Identify common woods (such as pine, oak, and plywood) and a typical use for each.
Match a type of wood to a project based on strength, cost, and appearance.
Explain how grain, moisture, and wood type affect how wood is cut, joined, and finished.

LIF.5.4.7.t: Help keep a work area clean by picking up scraps and putting tools away.
Explain why a clean, uncluttered workshop is safer, and keep floors and benches clear.
Wear the right safety gear (eye and hearing protection, no loose clothing) and know where the first-aid kit is.
Keep tools clean, oiled, and properly stored so they work safely and last.
Sharpen and maintain cutting tools, and inspect power tools and guards before use.
Set up and follow a complete workshop safety routine, including dust control, tool checks, and safe storage of materials.

PER.1.2.3.t: Name that Jesus makes us right with God as a gift, not something we earn.
Explain the difference between a gift you receive and a prize you earn.
Describe what it means to be justified, or declared right with God, by faith in Christ.
Compare receiving your worth from God with trying to build your worth by achievement.
Explain why an identity received from God is more secure than one built on performance.
Evaluate how resting in justification frees you from the pressure to prove yourself.

PER.1.2.4.t: Name that a Christian belongs to Jesus and is never alone.
Identify that believers are 'in Christ' and joined to him.
Explain what it means to be united to Christ so that his life becomes ours.
Describe how union with Christ is the deepest truth about who a believer is.
Reflect on how finding your core identity in Christ reshapes how you handle success and failure.

PER.1.3.1.t: Name that God made you and everything that exists.
Explain that we are created by God and do not make ourselves.
Describe from Genesis 1-2 how God formed human beings on purpose.
Compare the biblical view that we are created with the modern idea that we invent ourselves.
Evaluate why receiving your identity as a creature of God gives more freedom than self-creation.

PER.1.3.2.t: Name that every person is made by God and is valuable.
Identify that all people are made in the image of God.
Explain why every human life, whether young, old, weak, or strong, has equal dignity.
Describe how the image of God calls us to respect people who are different from us.
Explain how belief in human dignity shapes the way we treat the vulnerable.
Evaluate cultural attitudes about human worth in light of the image of God.

PER.1.3.3.t: Name that God made people male and female.
Identify from Genesis that God created humanity as male and female and called it good.
Explain that being made male or female is a good gift from God.
Describe how male and female together reflect God's image and design.
Evaluate God's design for male and female as good in a culture that questions it.

PER.1.3.4.t: Name that sin entered the world when people disobeyed God.
Explain what happened at the Fall and how it brought brokenness into the world.
Describe how the Fall affects our hearts, our relationships, and the world around us.
Explain why understanding the Fall helps us have compassion for our own and others' brokenness.
Evaluate how the reality of the Fall, alongside hope in Christ, shapes how we view sin in ourselves and others.

PER.1.3.5.t: Name that God made both your body and your soul, and that both are good.
Explain that a human being is one whole person, body and soul together.
Describe why the body is good and not something to despise.
Compare the biblical view of the whole person with the idea that only the soul matters.
Evaluate how the unity of body and soul shapes how we care for our bodies and honor God with them.

PER.2.1.2.t: Describe what it means to be an image-bearer whose worth comes from God, not from being unique.
Explain the popular message 'be true to yourself' in your own words and where you hear it.
Describe expressive individualism as the belief that the truest self is found by looking inward and expressing it.
Compare finding identity by looking inward with finding identity by looking to God who made and defines us.
Analyze how advertising, music, and social media promote expressive individualism to young people.
Explain how the gospel calls us to deny ourselves and follow Christ rather than to express an autonomous self (Luke 9:23).

PER.2.1.3.t: Describe ways people group themselves and others (by team, age, or background) and how that can help or divide.

Evaluate what identity politics rightly names about injustice and where it conflicts with a biblical view of the person and reconciliation.

PER.2.1.4.t: Describe yourself as more than your body and feelings, a person God made with a soul.
Explain the difference between how you feel and what is true about who God says you are.
Describe 'psychological man' as someone whose main goal is to feel good and be inwardly at peace with self.
Compare psychological man, who seeks self-fulfillment, with spiritual man, who seeks to please and know God (1 Corinthians 2:14-15).

Evaluate the psychological self against the biblical self, affirming real emotional care while grounding wholeness in Christ rather than self-actualization.
